name: Mississippi Today
title: Don’t let scammers crash back-to-school season
description: Today’s students and young adults are true digital natives, having grown up online, learning to navigate digital spaces as a normal part of daily life. As they transition to college, they turn to digital platforms and social media for everything  from apartment hunting and job searches to shopping, banking and talking with friends. That familiarity, […]
text:
Today’s students and young adults are true digital natives, having grown up online, learning to navigate digital spaces as a normal part of daily life. As they transition to college, they turn to digital platforms and social media for everything  from apartment hunting and job searches to shopping, banking and talking with friends.
That familiarity, however, can create a false sense of security, making younger adults just as much of a target for fraud and scams as older individuals. According to the FBI’s Internet Crime Report, Americans ages 20–29 reported more than $500 million to internet-crime losses in 2025.
As scammers become more sophisticated, including using AI, students need to be more vigilant than ever about fraud and scams. Understanding the most common ones can help you and your children avoid becoming victims.
Common scams targeting students (and the families supporting them)
Online shopping and marketplace scams
Whether your student is furnishing a dorm, moving into an apartment or buying textbooks–or you’re helping them pay for essentials—online deals and secondhand marketplaces can help you save money while also creating more opportunities for scammers.
Buy from official and trusted retailers whenever possible, double check website URLs for misspellings or other red flags, and make sure the site uses https://. Be wary of deals that seem too good to be true as well. Avoid clicking links in unsolicited emails or text messages, including fake “missed delivery” notifications that often lead to fraudulent websites or malware.
Before making a purchase, read seller reviews and ratings. If you’re buying locally, meet in a safe public place and inspect the item before paying.
Job scams
As students return to school this fall, some may be looking for part-time jobs or internships. Scammers target students with fake jobs offering high salaries, flexible schedules or jobs you can do from a residence hall, apartment or home.
If your child receives a job offer by text, email, or direct message – be cautious, especially if they never applied to work at that company. Encourage them to use well-known job boards and then apply directly through the company’s official website. 
Also, if an employer asks them to pay upfront for training, equipment, background checks or application fees, it may be a sign of a scam. Legitimate companies will never charge you to get a job. They also won’t send you money and then ask you to return a portion of it.
Rental and housing scams
Scammers know student housing is in high demand. They’ll often post fake apartment listings or copy legitimate ones to trick potential renters (or their families) into sending money for a deposit.
Rental prices that seem unusually low should raise a red flag. Use a reverse image search to see if photos of the property appear on a different website or in a different location. Research unfamiliar property managers or housing websites before sending money, and avoid paying deposits through wire transfers, gift cards or peer-to-peer payment apps.
Double check the address, read online reviews of the property management company and schedule a tour of the house or apartment before signing a lease or sending a deposit. That way, you’ll know the listing and location is real. 
The influence of AI
Thanks to artificial intelligence, scammers can now create cloned voices and deepfake videos, along with fraudulent emails, text messages and even websites and apps that look real. These AI tools let scammers impersonate family members, employers, banks, law enforcement, delivery companies and trusted brands to get you to send money or share personal information. They may even target parents directly—claiming your child is in trouble and needs money immediately.
How to protect yourself (and your children)
No matter what type of scam you encounter, a few simple habits can go a long way toward reducing your risk:

Limit the personal information you and your children share online and make social media profiles  private whenever possible. This can help reduce the information scammers can use to target you, guess your security questions or attempt to access your financial accounts.


When you’re making a payment, use more protected methods, such as credit and debit cards, which generally offer stronger consumer protections than wire transfers, gift cards or peer-to-peer payment apps. Treat peer-to-peer payments, such as Zelle, like cash — once the money is sent, it’s often difficult to recover.


Scammers can spoof phone numbers to make calls look like they’re coming from your bank, law enforcement or another trusted organization. Don’t automatically trust your caller ID – if you get a call demanding immediate action or claiming there’s a problem with your account, hang up and call back directly using a verified phone number. Banks will never call and ask you for account information, tell you to transfer money to ‘protect’ it or pressure you to act immediately.


Don’t click links or download attachments from unexpected emails or text messages and avoid accessing your financial accounts or making online purchases on public Wi-Fi, where savvy cybercriminals can gain access to your login credentials. 


Perhaps most importantly, slow down. Back-to-school season brings a flurry of financial decisions and scammers know students and families are looking for deals. They often create a false sense of urgency to try to pressure people into making quick decisions. Taking a few extra minutes to verify information can make the difference.

The bottom line
Whether your student is shopping for school supplies, searching for a job or signing a first lease, their status as a student can make them a prime target for scammers—and families can be targeted too.
Stay skeptical of unsolicited offers, verify before you pay or share personal information, and slow down when something feels rushed. Those simple habits can help protect your money, your identity and your family’s peace of mind throughout the school year from scams and fraud.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: More out-of-state students opt for University of Alaska Southeast, with new in-state tuition rate
description: Under a driving Juneau rain, dozens of new students at the University of Alaska Southeast gathered Friday for orientation and to kick off the fall semester. This year, the public university saw a boost in enrollment of out-of-state students, which officials and students say is largely due to a new policy eliminating the non-resident tuition […]
text:
New students at the University of Alaska Southeast attend orientation at the Egan Library on the Juneau campus on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Under a driving Juneau rain, dozens of new students at the University of Alaska Southeast gathered Friday for orientation and to kick off the fall semester. This year, the public university saw a boost in enrollment of out-of-state students, which officials and students say is largely due to a new policy eliminating the non-resident tuition rate. 
UAS piloted the new tuition policy this year, called Alaska Unlocked, which offers the standard in-state tuition rate for all undergraduate courses, regardless of the student’s residency.
That’s resulted in an estimated 36% increase this year in out-of-state students enrolling at UAS compared to last year, according to university officials.     

New students at the University of Alaska Southeast attend orientation at the Egan Library on campus in Juneau on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

“We are so thrilled with that much of an increase,” said UAS Chancellor Aparna Palmer, in an interview after her welcoming remarks to students at the Egan Library. “We know that a high percentage of our graduates stay in Alaska and work in Alaska within one year of graduation. And so most of these students are our future Alaskans.” 
New students have arrived from 28 states, according to university data, with the top home states including Washington, California, Colorado, Idaho, Minnesota and Wisconsin. 
The in-state tuition rate was a draw for 22-year-old Nicole Wilson of Phoenix, Arizona. After classes at community college, she enrolled at UAS to pursue a bachelor’s degree in marine biology with a focus on mammals. “I decided to come here both based on the in-state tuition and also because it was such, like, an ‘open to marine biology’ type school. My original plan was to go out to Hawaii, but it’s extremely expensive from out of state,” she said. 
Wilson said housing was also a factor. “I did the math. If I were to take a dorm, which I would have had to, at any of the major universities in Arizona, it was actually more expensive than coming out to Alaska,” she said. 
Cost of housing was the main consideration for 20-year-old Owen Kellon of Portland, Oregon, who is pursuing a bachelor’s degree in environmental sciences. “It was the bigger concern when it came to the cost of schooling, just because tuition was like a couple hundred bucks per class, which is perfectly reasonable. It’s about how much I was paying back at my community college in Portland, but the housing cost was the biggest factor.”     

The John Pugh Hall student dorms houses 120 beds for students on-campus in Juneau, seen on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

The standard in-state tuition rate is expected to be available across the University of Alaska system next year. Earlier this month, the UA Board of Regents moved to eliminate out-of-state tuition rates for all locations and degree types, aiming to draw more students to Alaska. 
Currently, out-of-state tuition is double to quadruple the amount of resident tuition, depending on degree type. The Board of Regents is expected to take up a final vote on the policy change in November. 
UAS has the smallest student population of Alaska’s public universities, with roughly 1,800 students last year across campuses in Juneau, Ketchikan and Sitka.
This year’s preliminary enrollment data shows roughly the same number of students as last year, signalling Alaskan student enrollment may have declined. But Palmer emphasized that it’s too soon to tell, as enrollment numbers are subject to change in the next few weeks with more Alaska students possibly signing up for dual enrollment programs or classes beginning later in the fall.     

University of Alaska Southeast Chancellor Aparna Palmer welcomes new students at orientation in Juneau on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

This year, UAS saw a 21% increase in applications from out-of-state students, and a 36% increase in newly enrolled out-of-state students. More than 80 new out-of-state students have enrolled this year, compared to 60 students last year, according to university officials.
UAS is an open access enrollment institution, Palmer noted. “What that means is, no matter where you are in life, whether you just graduated from high school, in high school, or whether you’re, you know, in your sixties or seventies, there is a way in which you can access UAS,” she said.
Most students are working adults or part-time students, Palmer said, and can enroll in classes in-person or online. “So, we do have a really diverse group of students,” she said.
In Juneau, new students had a jam-packed schedule for orientation week. On Friday, students were welcomed by UAS administrators, a Tlingit elder and student leaders, followed by a campus tour and briefings on campus resources, student clubs, tutoring, career counseling, and anti-discrimination and Title IX rights and reporting. 
Students expressed excitement for the new school year and to be in Alaska, including Owen Kellon of Oregon.
“I love the rain,” he said. “ I am excited to see how the winter months will look like with only like six hours of sunlight. I’m scared, but I’m also excited.”
New students at the University of Alaska Southeast pose for a photo by Auke Lake during a campus tour as part of orientation in Juneau on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Is a U.S. Department of Justice investigation about to disrupt Alaska’s U.S. Senate race?
description: On Alaska’s primary election day, NBC News — citing unidentified sources — reported that the U.S. Department of Justice has issued grand jury subpoenas as it investigates whether Petersburg candidate Dan J. Sullivan may have somehow violated federal law.  If that’s true, subpoenas haven’t reached Sullivan, currently running third in this week’s election and[...]
text:
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, talks to staffers on the morning of Aug. 18, 2026, at the intersection of the Seward Highway and Northern Lights Boulevard. The Midtown Anchorage intersection is a favored spot for candidate sign-waving, and Sullivan, who is running for re-election, was there with U.S. Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, also running for re-election. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)On Alaska’s primary election day, NBC News — citing unidentified sources — reported that the U.S. Department of Justice has issued grand jury subpoenas as it investigates whether Petersburg candidate Dan J. Sullivan may have somehow violated federal law. 
If that’s true, subpoenas haven’t reached Sullivan, currently running third in this week’s election and the person that incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan has accused of running a sham campaign.
Subpoenas also haven’t reached anyone in the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola as of Friday, according to the campaign. That includes Anton McParland, Peltola’s former campaign manager, who is still with the campaign. 
Jalen Lee, a spokesman for the Alaska Democratic Party, said on Thursday that no one at the party has gotten a subpoena. 
Amber Lee, a consultant who helped Dan J. Sullivan start his campaign, said on Thursday that she has not been subpoenaed. Lee is no longer working with Sullivan’s campaign.
A spokesperson for the Alaska Division of Elections said no one with the division has received a subpoena about Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign. 
Dan J. Sullivan said by email on Thursday that he has not received a subpoena. He said he’s refraining from saying more about the issue until he understands more about what’s happening.
In July, NBC News reported that the U.S. Attorney’s office and acting Alaska Attorney General Cori Mills were looking for evidence of wire fraud or a conspiracy to deprive Alaska voters of a free and fair elections process, which could be a civil rights violation.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Reagan Zimmerman-Hartzheim, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney’s office in Alaska, said that under DOJ policy, she could neither confirm nor deny the existence of an investigation.
Throughout his campaign, Dan S. Sullivan has called Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign fake, and a trick to deceive Alaska voters. Dan J. Sullivan, also a registered Republican, has denied that claim.
“My intention is not to trick people,” Dan J. Sullivan told the New York Times in an interview this month. “I would hope people are informed enough to know the difference between an incumbent senator and a teacher.”
Dan J. Sullivan, a Republican, remains on track to advance to November’s general election, alongside Dan S. Sullivan, Peltola and a fourth person. Progressive Democrat David Leslie led the race for that spot on Friday. 
A spokesperson for Dan S. Sullivan’s re-election campaign did not return emails about the possible Department of Justice investigation.
Ahead of this week’s statewide primary election, President Donald Trump took to social media with a statement that closely resembled Dan S. Sullivan’s remarks. 
In the statement, the president claimed Dan J.’s candidacy is the result of “trickery” by “Crooked, Radical Left Dumocrats” who put up another Dan Sullivan “to take Votes away from our Great Senator of the same name.”
The Alaska Democratic Party was not involved in Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy, both Sullivan and the party have said repeatedly.
“I have not spoken to Mary (Peltola). I wouldn’t even know who to speak to,” Dan. J. Sullivan told his hometown newspaper, Petersburg Pilot, in June. 
In the Times interview, Dan J. Sullivan suggested he was worried about the possibility that he could face federal investigation.
“I’m just a guy, and they’re scary,” he said. “Whether you’ve done something right or wrong, it doesn’t seem to matter anymore.”
Across the country, federal judges are tracking an increasing number of ungrounded, politically motivated prosecutions by the Department of Justice. 
These include high-profile failed prosecutions against anti-ICE protesters in Chicago, a man who threw a sandwich at a federal official in Washington, D.C., and a man the president accused of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C.
Last weekend, new U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said he would take the president’s views into consideration when making decisions on prosecutions. 
Traditionally, the Department of Justice has acted independently from presidents and has sought to preserve that independence. 
In 1973, Attorney General Elliot Richardson and his deputy both resigned rather than follow President Richard Nixon’s orders to fire a special prosecutor examining the Watergate scandal. Those resignations spurred impeachment proceedings against Nixon.
Last month, the U.S. Senate confirmed Blanche in office by a 50-49 vote. Dan S. Sullivan, who voted “yes,” was a decisive vote in favor of Blanche’s confirmation. 
Aubrey Wieber is the director of the 907 Initiative, an organization opposing Dan S. Sullivan’s re-election. 
Wieber said he doesn’t know if Dan S. Sullivan is working with the Trump administration to manufacture false claims, but he does see the accusations as part of a broader national pattern, with Trump attempting to sow doubt about elections in general.
“I do think this is bogus,” he said of the accusations against Dan J. Sullivan. “Look how many investigations and how many people have looked into this, and no one has found any indication that Dan J. Sullivan is a sham candidate.”
In the just-completed primary election, third-party groups spent millions of dollars to advertise fringe candidates in hopes that they would finish in the top four and advance to the November general election. Dan J. Sullivan wasn’t generally targeted by those ads.
“If this is the ace in the hole,” Wieber asked, “Don’t you think you would spend to make sure that he makes it into the top four?”

name: Nevada Current
title: Feds announce water cuts under new Colorado River plan
description: The Bureau of Reclamation released its two-year operating plan on Friday detailing how the agency will manage the Colorado River, and the nation’s two largest reservoirs Lake Powell and Lake Mead, amid ongoing drought and record low water storage. Under the new federal framework, Nevada, California, and Arizona will be required to reduce their water […]
text:
The Colorado River is pictured where if flows near Hite, just beyond the upper reaches of Lake Powell, on Friday, Sept. 19, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The Bureau of Reclamation released its two-year operating plan on Friday detailing how the agency will manage the Colorado River, and the nation’s two largest reservoirs Lake Powell and Lake Mead, amid ongoing drought and record low water storage.
Under the new federal framework, Nevada, California, and Arizona will be required to reduce their water use by 1.25 million acre-feet over the next two years, with Nevada facing a reduction of 50,000 acre-feet. Arizona will have to reduce its water use by 760,00 acre-feet, while California will have to cut about 440,000 acre-feet.
The three states will also provide an additional 700,000 acre-feet of water conservation over the next two years under the plan.
If conditions worsen, the Lower Basin states could be required to cut up to 3 million acre-feet of water– roughly about 40% of their supply per year. The plan doesn’t outline how those cuts would be divided among the three states.
“These decisions provide a water management strategy for Basin stakeholders to respond to the prolonged drought by incorporating flexible tools and voluntary actions while leaving room for consensus agreements,” said Andrea Travnicek, the Interior Department’s assistant secretary of water and science.
The federal government also released its record of decision finalizing a 10-year framework that emphasizes voluntary reductions and flexibility for future adjustments as Colorado River basin states continue to work towards a consensus agreement. 
For the last three years, the Upper Basin states and the Lower Basin states have blown through deadline after deadline in attempts to come to a seven-state consensus.
JB Hamby, chairman of the Colorado River Board of California and California’s chief negotiator, said the framework established “a workable path for the next two years” but warned it was “a bridge, not a permanent solution.”     
Hamby called on Upper Basin states – Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, and New Mexico – to cut water use and “maintain sustainable deliveries to the Lower Basin.”  
Reclamation set a target for voluntary water cuts in Upper Basin states of up to 200,000 acre-feet, but the framework does not include mandatory water cuts for Upper Basin states. 
Tom Buschatzke, the director of the Arizona Department of Water Resources and the state’s top water negotiator, said he welcomed the short-term agreement which he said would allow Lower Basin states to focus on a “longer-term, equitable, basin-wide outcome that includes shared sacrifices along with our Upper Basin partners in an effort to avoid protracted litigation.”
The new guidelines will be issued every two years, based on the framework, and implemented through annual plans.
The new framework is a departure from the 1922 Colorado River Compact, which allocated 7.5 million acre-feet for each basin. That measure was based on a faulty model that assumed the river system could supply 15 million acre-feet annually.
Officials acknowledge only 12.4 million acre-feet flows from the river each year, meaning more than 3 million acre-feet of cuts are needed to bring the Colorado River back into balance. Since the turn of the century, Lake Mead has lost more than 65% of its storage.
Lake Powell and Lead Mead both hit record lows this month. Water levels at Powell sat at 3,519 feet above sea level on August 20 — just 9 feet above the level Reclamation says is critical for continued hydropower at Hoover Dam. Combined the two reservoirs have not been this low since Lake Powell began filling in 1963, according to Reclamation.
Nevada officials didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment Friday afternoon.

name: Washington State Standard
title: The future of the Northwest’s power grid is at risk. Where is the leadership?
description: The Pacific Northwest is drifting toward an energy crisis of its own making. The newly appointed leader of the Bonneville Power Administration, Travis Kavulla, with support from Secretary of Energy Chris Wright, has the background and ability to stop the drift and return BPA to the leadership role it has traditionally played.  Congressional lawmakers need […[...]
text:
Powerlines above the Columbia River move electricity from the Bonneville Dam to customers across the region in Hood River County, Oregon, on Thursday, July 25, 2024. (Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle)The Pacific Northwest is drifting toward an energy crisis of its own making. The newly appointed leader of the Bonneville Power Administration, Travis Kavulla, with support from Secretary of Energy Chris Wright, has the background and ability to stop the drift and return BPA to the leadership role it has traditionally played. 
Congressional lawmakers need to step up. Most of BPA’s customers are in Washington state. Yet both of our senators, Patty Murray and Maria Cantwell, seem silent about the slow-cooking crisis afflicting the grid. Cantwell’s silence is particularly perplexing, as her tenure as chair of the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources provided her with a close-up view of the region’s energy developments.
We have known this reality for some time but have done too little to address it. Electricity demand is rising rapidly, yet our region is not adding generation and transmission line capacity fast enough to keep pace. Rather than confronting this reality, much of the public debate has focused on scapegoats — data centers and other large electricity users. 
The real issue is not who just consumes power, but whether we have the foresight and resolve to build the infrastructure needed for reliable and affordable service.
The Northwest has scores of small and large electric utilities — private, public, rural and urban — as well as many interest groups with skin in the game.
Large industrial customers, technology companies, independent power providers, environmental advocates, labor unions, farmers, and other interest groups all have their own agendas. They often pursue separate solutions for their own specific challenges and prioritize their parochial concerns over those of the region as a whole. 
The inevitable result is fragmentation, delay, and higher costs.
Congress anticipated this very problem when it enacted the Northwest Power Act of 1980, providing the framework and the tools for a coordinated response.
Forty-six years later, the effective use of that law, together with the original Bonneville authorizing statute and the Transmission System Act, is falling short.
Inexplicably, Bonneville has walked away from its legal authorities and mandates, retreating under the pretext of listening to its customers. 
Congress gave BPA $10 billion of borrowing authority in the 2021 infrastructure law, yet BPA is not using these funds. Instead, it plays conservatively out of an abundance of caution regarding its obligation to repay the Treasury annually. 
Paying debt versus using this borrowing authority to serve the region is a false choice for BPA. Bonneville has never missed a Treasury payment. And to forgo needed upgrades to its existing infrastructure and its failure to build new east-west transmission for renewable solar and wind at this critical time is indefensible.
Here is but one example. BPA was originally an in-part owner of the critical Boardman-Hemingway 500 kilovolt line, but gave up ownership to Idaho Power and PacifiCorp. Ownership would have protected its public utility customers from rate increases and provided accessibility to this infrastructure. No ownership, no protection.
For its public utility customers, BPA also failed to secure additional electricity resources despite, according to the Northwest Power and Conservation Council, the region needing to increase supply from today’s average 22,000 megawatts to 40,000 by 2046. Instead, BPA has chosen to divide up its current supplies and tell customers to fend for themselves for the rest of what they need. 
Kavulla is a former Montana utility commissioner. He knows these issues and, with a reengaged congressional delegation and BPA stakeholders, can work to solve these challenges.
For decades, the Northwest prospered under a coordinated “one utility system” that delivered reliable, low-cost electricity and broad economic benefits. We have solved challenges like this before by working together. The choice is clear: restore regional cooperation and leadership now or wait for the lights to go out and explain why we failed to act while there was still time.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: DNR investigating fish kill in Hecker Creek, potentially related to fire in Postville
description: Iowa Department of Natural Resources field staff in Manchester confirmed Friday the office was investigating a fish kill that occurred during the time period of a massive fire at a meat processing plant in Postville.  Brett Meyers, an environmental specialist with the field office in Manchester. said the office has not received test results of […]
text:
Iowa Department of Natural Resources is investigating a fish kill in Hecker Creek. (Photo via Google Earth)Iowa Department of Natural Resources field staff in Manchester confirmed Friday the office was investigating a fish kill that occurred during the time period of a massive fire at a meat processing plant in Postville. 
Brett Meyers, an environmental specialist with the field office in Manchester. said the office has not received test results of water in Hecker Creek, where the fish kill was observed, to be able to determine the cause of the kill. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A fire July 28 in Postville at the city’s largest employer, Agri Star Meat and Poultry, burned three quarters of the kosher meat plant and smoldered for several days, according to news reports. 
Meyers said DNR staff were investigating a fish kill in Hecker Creek “during that time period.”
While DNR typically sends out public releases about spills or fish kill investigations, Tammie Krausman, the communications director for DNR, said public information related to the incident would be pushed out by the “incident command” because the fire triggered a county emergency response. 
According to the Iowa Department of Homeland Security, in the event of an emergency or disaster, responders operate in an incident command system, which allows the incident commander to determine priorities, coordinate the response and authorize any information released to the media. 
The Postville Volunteer Fire Department noted that more than 20 area fire departments and several additional emergency response teams responded to the fire.
Krausman said the incident command with Allamakee County was given information from DNR about Hecker Creek and the fish kill.
Allamakee County officials did not respond to a request for additional information Friday. 
Krausman said staff investigating the fish kill reported that no livestock were using the creek for watering at the time. 
DNR lists Hecker Creek as an impaired waterway due to E. coli bacteria and high levels of chloride. The creek, along with the nearby Yellow River, have also been the subject of various lawsuits that allege Agri Star polluted the streams.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Western South Dakota lawmaker takes plea deal to drop road-damage charge from felony to misdemeanor
description: A South Dakota Republican state lawmaker pleaded no contest Friday to a misdemeanor for damaging a road in Butte County in a case that began with a felony charge. Rep. Travis Ismay, 49, of Newell, was charged in early June for felony intentional damage to a highway or bridge, a crime punishable by up to […]
text:
Rep. Travis Ismay, R-Newell, listens to the governor's budget address on Dec. 3, 2024, at the South Dakota Capitol in Pierre. At left is Rep. Tony Randolph, R-Rapid City. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)A South Dakota Republican state lawmaker pleaded no contest Friday to a misdemeanor for damaging a road in Butte County in a case that began with a felony charge.
Rep. Travis Ismay, 49, of Newell, was charged in early June for felony intentional damage to a highway or bridge, a crime punishable by up to two years in prison and a $4,000 fine.
On Friday, Ismay was sentenced to pay $1,750 in restitution and $78 in court costs after entering a plea of “nolo contendere” to a misdemeanor charge of destruction of a highway. Such a plea allows defendants to admit that the state has enough evidence to prove they’ve committed a crime without formally admitting guilt. 
The lesser charge was filed earlier this month by Butte County State’s Attorney Brian Knox “pursuant to the plea agreement of the parties.” 
South Dakota lawmaker charged with felony for allegedly damaging public road on purpose

Knox was appointed this summer to replace Timothy Barnaud, who’d filed the felony charge against Ismay before being appointed to a magistrate judge position. Barnaud did not preside over Ismay’s case.            
The felony indictment did not include details on the alleged damage, nor on the location of the highway in question. The same is true of the misdemeanor complaint.
Like Barnaud, Knox has declined to offer details on what Ismay might have done to spur a criminal investigation into roadway damage. 
Ismay’s plea, like any plea of guilt or nolo contendere entered in an adult criminal case, involves the entry of a verbal statement of facts in open court. The statements are entered into the court record, but typically are not filed with the clerk of courts. Knox told South Dakota Searchlight he was “working with Mr. Ismay’s attorney on a joint press release” when asked to share the factual basis statement, and Knox declined to offer comments on the decision to offer a plea deal. 
Ismay’s plea, sentence and fine were logged electronically after the hearing, but Knox had yet to file any judgment paperwork with the Butte County Clerk of Courts as of Friday afternoon. As of 4:45 p.m. Mountain time, Knox hadn’t sent a press release. 
Ismay told South Dakota Searchlight he’d graded a section of Wilson Cemetery Road, the gravel road off his driveway. He said he’d asked the county to regrade it, but that the county hadn’t done so. The plea deal, he said, essentially has him paying to have the work redone.
“Basically, I graded the road because it was rough, and they said I damaged it and tried to hit me with a felony,” Ismay said. “And then the new state’s attorney came in, and I was really impressed with his common sense way of doing things.”
The incident allegedly occurred three days after Ismay won his primary contest in the June 2 election. He is unopposed for the Nov. 3 general election. 
Rep. Scott Odenbach, the majority leader for the state House of Representatives, said Friday that a plea to a class 2 misdemeanor has “no repercussions that I know of” for a member of the chamber.
Election case unresolved for state senator
Felony charges are still pending in Minnehaha County, meanwhile, for another Republican state lawmaker, Sen. Tom Pischke of Dell Rapids.
Pischke faces two felony counts for allegedly filing false or forged election-related documents. Prosecutors in Sioux Falls allege he signed and mailed 16 applications for precinct committeeman and committeewoman to the Minnehaha County Auditor’s Office, aiming to get those candidates listed on the June 2 primary ballot without their knowledge.
South Dakota state senator facing election-related criminal charges ends his reelection campaign

Under state law, applications for those positions needn’t be notarized, and no signatures from supporters are needed to qualify for the ballot.
At least 20% of precinct committee members must be present at Minnehaha County Republican Party meetings to conduct official business. The number of committee members fluctuates, and could have swollen in Minnehaha County if the unaware candidates noted in Pischke’s case had been elected during the primary.
When charges against Pischke were filed, the Minnehaha County party chairman told South Dakota Searchlight the lawmaker’s alleged behavior was likely meant to undermine the chairman’s ability to lead the party by making it more difficult to have a quorum at party meetings. 
Pischke has pleaded not guilty. He waived his right to a preliminary hearing on Aug. 17, and is scheduled be arraigned on the charges Sept. 15
County chooses third-place primary finisher to replace Pischke
On July 28, Pischke abandoned his reelection campaign. He said in a written statement that he’s always prided himself on “complete transparency,” but that he “would not have been able to maintain that standard during the upcoming November election.”
Recently, the Republican Party chose Bart Sample, of Flandreau, to replace Pischke on the ballot for his district, which includes northern Minnehaha County and all of Moody County. Sample finished third in a three-way primary race on June 2 for two Republican nominations for the district state’s representative seats. 
Sample will face Brian Breitling, an independent candidate and former Republican lawmaker, in the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Illegal drugs found at Whitfield mental hospital, sparking K-9 sweeps, roadblocks
description: Contraband found at the Mississippi State Hospital in Whitfield.
text:
Multiple bags of illegal drugs and contraband were found last week at the Mississippi State Hospital in Whitfield.
The discovery prompted K-9 units to descend on the hospital and law enforcement agents have conducted roadblocks and vehicle inspections upon entry and exit of the campus. It has also sparked an ongoing investigation by the facility’s police force and investigators with the Mississippi Department of Corrections. 
Mississippi Today was provided photos of bags of pills and powdered substances, what appeared to be a large bag of marijuana, lighters, wrapping papers and electronic devices.
Contraband found at the Mississippi State Hospital in Whitfield.  Credit: Submitted phto
While the smuggling of drugs and contraband has been a long-running problem inside Mississippi prisons, the discovery of these substances at Mississippi’s largest public psychiatric facility is more uncommon. 
In a statement to Mississippi Today, Adam Moore, a spokesperson for the Mississippi Department of Mental Health, said the contraband was not located near any patients or patient areas of the campus. He also said the agency did not believe any drugs were used by or distributed to patients at the hospital, but how the contraband entered the facility or who may be responsible remains under investigation.
“MSH and other DMH programs treat people with the most intense and severe needs. Our highest concern is the safety of the people we serve and supporting their recovery and resiliency. If it is discovered that any hospital staff was involved in this event, we will take appropriate action immediately,” Moore said. “We will continue to implement any necessary measures to maintain patient and staff safety.” 
While the investigation is ongoing, Moore suggested the source of the drugs could be linked to participants in a re-entry program that allows people to leave facilities and work with the grounds and maintenance crews at Whitfield.
Contraband found at the Mississippi State Hospital in Whitfield.  Credit: Submitted photo
The drugs were discovered last week after hospital staff found a suspicious package believed to be contraband in an area of the Mississippi State Hospital campus that is designated for Mississippi Department of Corrections inmate work programs only, Moore said. 
The Central Mississippi Correctional Facility in Rankin County is just over a mile away from Whitfield, and allows some prisoners to participate in the program. The prison has also been investigated for alleged overdose deaths of prisoners. The possibility that the drugs came from a participant in the re-entry program has not been confirmed. In a statement, Mississippi Department of Corrections Commissioner Burl Cain did not offer additional details, but said the agency would make a statement following an investigation.
“The MDOC is aware of the contraband seizure, and once the investigation is completed, the MDOC will make a statement,” Cain said. 
Contraband found at the Mississippi State Hospital in Whitfield.  Credit: Special to Mississippi Today
When the package was found at the Whitfield hospital, the only identifiable contraband was two cellphones, Moore said. Hospital police then secured the room and contacted the Department of Corrections because the agency “has jurisdiction over areas where inmates work,” Moore said.
The Corrections Department sent K-9 units to the hospital and took custody of the suspected contraband. Hospital staff did not open the package or photograph its contents, Moore said. Corrections officials later reported to hospital staff that the package contained various illegal substances.
The photos show a bag of what appears to be marijuana on a scale that displays a weight of 460 grams, or just over 1 pound. That quantity of marijuana could be worth thousands of dollars. The photos also show bags of unidentified pills, powdered substances and “SIM devices,” which could be linked to illegal phones.
After the drugs were discovered, the prisoners were taken off hospital grounds. The work program partnership with the Corrections Department “has been suspended until further notice to ensure the safety of our patients and staff,” Moore said. 
“We have a zero tolerance policy for illegal contraband on MSH campus,” Moore added.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: State approves permit for controversial Cherry County hog operation
authors: Jackie Ourada, Nebraska Public Media News
description: The State of Nebraska on Aug. 13 approved a permit for TK Angus to construct a hog operation in Cherry County. The approval follows a campaign of letters to the Nebraska Department of Water, Energy and Environment (DWEE) that mostly opposed the plans. TK Angus Co. is a family cattle operation that aims to add […]
text:
A bill takes another step forward in the Nebraska Legislature that would merge two Nebraska agencies with a goal to improve management of and focus on water resources. Shown here is Smith Falls State Park, Niobrara River in 2019. (Courtesy of Aaron Sanderford)The State of Nebraska on Aug. 13 approved a permit for TK Angus to construct a hog operation in Cherry County. The approval follows a campaign of letters to the Nebraska Department of Water, Energy and Environment (DWEE) that mostly opposed the plans.
TK Angus Co. is a family cattle operation that aims to add two hog finishing barns that would house up to 4,999 pigs, alongside 600 feeder cattle on land about three miles from the Niobrara River. About 40 letters sent to DWEE showed that Cherry County residents were concerned the operation would have significant environmental implications
In its approval letter, the department directed TK Angus to verbally notify DWEE after the company completed building its concrete construction work on the underfloor pits “in an effort to alleviate safety concerns and streamline final project approval.”
DWEE said the animal operation wasn’t required to obtain coverage under a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Permit for Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations based on its current operation. But it could be required in the future if the operation discharges into state rivers.
Sunny Elliott, a Cherry County resident and science teacher, built a website that kept her neighbors informed about the project. As interest for information on the project grew, Elliott created a petition that gathered around 300 signatures within several days.
She said the petition wasn’t meant to decide the permit’s fate, but she wanted to show the state how many people either opposed the hog operation or wanted a public hearing to be held before the permit could be issued.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“My primary concern is whether the permit application and nutrient-management plan adequately account for the conditions at this particular location,” Elliott said, pointing to the county’s permeable soil and groundwater as vulnerabilities to the hog operation.
The Nebraska Examiner reported that Cherry County commissioners initially denied TK Angus a conditional use permit in 2023, despite approval from the county’s planning commission. A county district judge later overruled the county board and ordered it to provide a conditional use permit.
Tim Marlatt, whose name is on the DWEE filing and has owned the operation for years, told the Nebraska Examiner that the initial concerns about odor and leaks that were raised during that effort were unfounded, and that the facility’s design would prevent both.
Theodore Ball contributed to this report.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Federal judge permanently blocks Arkansas laws restricting direct democracy process
description: A federal judge on Friday declared laws restricting Arkansas’ initiative and referendum process unconstitutional and permanently blocked their enforcement.  U.S. District Judge Timothy Brooks wrote Friday that laws requiring all canvassers to be Arkansas residents and paid canvassers working on a statewide initiative petition or referendum to be residents li[...]
text:
The John Paul Hammerschmidt Federal Building in Fayetteville on July 18, 2025. (Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)A federal judge on Friday declared laws restricting Arkansas’ initiative and referendum process unconstitutional and permanently blocked their enforcement. 
U.S. District Judge Timothy Brooks wrote Friday that laws requiring all canvassers to be Arkansas residents and paid canvassers working on a statewide initiative petition or referendum to be residents living in the state violate the First Amendment of the Constitution. 
He also declared unconstitutional a prohibition on paying canvassers based on the number of signatures obtained.
The decision resulted from a lawsuit filed against Secretary of State Cole Jester in 2025 by the League of Women Voters of Arkansas. Two ballot question committees, Protect AR Rights and For AR Kids, were later allowed to intervene in the case.
Judge hears testimony in case over Arkansas’ initiative process restrictions 

Jeff LeMaster, a spokesperson for Attorney General Tim Griffin, said the state intends to appeal the ruling.
“This is a good day for the voters of Arkansas,” said Kristin Foster, Executive Director of the League of Women Voters of Arkansas. “The power to make our voices heard belongs to the people. The ballot initiative process gives Arkansans a direct say in their government, and we’re proud to stand with voters and defend that right.”
The three ballot measure groups involved in the case have argued the statutes challenged in the lawsuit make it nearly impossible for Arkansans to propose their own constitutional amendments and laws and place them before voters. Supporters of the laws have said they’re needed to protect the process. 
The League of Women Voters and For AR Kids did not collect sufficient signatures for the November ballot, while Protect AR Rights had their signatures tossed because the incorrect ballot measure name was printed on petitions, according to Jester. The Arkansas Supreme Court on Wednesday denied the group’s request to reverse Jester’s decision. 
Brooks, who was nominated to the bench by former President Barack Obama, issued a preliminary injunction in November that temporarily blocked the state from enforcing some of the challenged laws against parties involved in the lawsuit. The challenged laws include two that require canvassers to request a photo ID from potential signers and inform them that petition fraud is a criminal offense.
Friday’s ruling focused on arguments made during a July trial and in briefs submitted after the hearing. 
Samantha Boyd, a spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office, said that while the trial concluded with Friday’s order, the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals will hear the state’s appeal of the preliminary injunction this fall. Ten of the 11 active judges on the 8th Circuit were nominated by Republican presidents.
“These petition laws are basic safeguards to prevent fraud,” Boyd said. “Without them, it makes our electoral system vulnerable to bad actors.”
Protect AR Rights called Friday’s ruling “a major win for Arkansas voters and the First Amendment.” Both the preliminary and permanent injunctions issued by Brooks “preserve a vital path forward for Arkansas voters to make important decisions and hold politicians accountable through the citizen ballot initiative process,” the group said in a statement.


Let us know what you think...




While the state asserted the Arkansas resident requirement for all canvassers doesn’t implicate the First Amendment because it doesn’t affect the communication of ideas, Brooks argued in his 45-page opinion and order that Americans have the right to speak about and advocate for political change in all states, not just the one where they live. 
“The residency requirement implicates the First Amendment by making 99% of Americans effectively unavailable as messengers for Plaintiffs’ and Intervenor-Plaintiffs’ ideas, thereby limiting their ability to select what they believe to be the most effective means for advocating for their petitions,” Brooks said.
The domicile requirement implicates the First Amendment for the same reasons as the residency requirement, he said. Though the domicile requirement only applies to paid canvassers on statewide initiative and referendum petitions, the burdens imposed “remain severe.”
Arkansas Supreme Court dismisses lawsuit challenging rejection of direct democracy ballot measure

Because most professional canvassers aren’t Arkansas domiciliaries, ballot measure sponsors are unable “to hire the best, most experienced, or most reputable canvassers from around the nation,” Brooks said. Instead, they must choose from a smaller pool of candidates who are likely less experienced.
“Less skilled, less experienced canvassers are less effective and less efficient than more skilled, more experienced canvassers, which increases the cost and decreases the efficacy of the sponsor’s campaigns,” he said. “Those less experienced canvassers also receive worse training because they cannot watch experienced professional canvassers at work.”
The pay-per-signature ban also implicates the First Amendment because it restricts how ballot measure sponsors pay for political speech, Brooks said. 
Like the residency and domicile requirements, Brooks wrote, “the pay-per-signature ban is limited to initiative and referendum petitions and therefore imposes a content-based restriction on speech because it defines the category of regulated speech by its content.” 
Even though Brooks said there was not enough evidence that the pay-per-signature ban imposed a severe burden, the judge said the state “provided no evidence connecting payment on a per-signature basis to even a single instance of fraud.”  
“While the weakness of the evidence on both sides makes this a close case, the Court must err on the side of protecting political speech,” Brooks wrote.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Fish and Wildlife Commission takes middle ground on wolf hunting quotas
description: The Montana Fish and Wildlife Commission this week adopted new wolf hunting and trapping regulations, with a 300-wolf limit for the upcoming season, reflecting the state’s lower population estimate for the species.  The decision on Wednesday took a middle-of-the-road stance between a Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks department recommendation of 250, and last[...]
text:
A Yellowstone wolf (Courtesy NPS/Jacob W. Frank)The Montana Fish and Wildlife Commission this week adopted new wolf hunting and trapping regulations, with a 300-wolf limit for the upcoming season, reflecting the state’s lower population estimate for the species. 
The decision on Wednesday took a middle-of-the-road stance between a Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks department recommendation of 250, and last year’s quota of 452 wolves.
“Why not split the difference?” said Commissioner Ian Wargo. “We’re bound by the law on one side, we’re bound by relisting on the other. I don’t know why we’re not trying to thread that needle a little bit more.” 
The Fish and Wildlife Commission, which sets department regulations, established a 452-wolf quota for last year following legislative directives to bring down the population, despite wolf advocates saying it was too risky to kill that many animals. 
Earlier this year, Montana FWP released a new version of its integrated Patch Occupancy Model, or iPOM, for estimating the statewide wolf population that showed a drastically smaller wolf population than previously thought — 725 instead of 1,094. 
Molly Parks, carnivore coordinator for FWP, gave the commission a presentation on how the new model incorporated different amounts of data about wolf observations, pack sizes and pack ranges, which includes a lot of modeling as wolves are a hard species to accurately count individually. 
The new estimate by the department doesn’t mean the population has suddenly experienced a decline during the last year, but rather that wolf populations have likely been overestimated for years. 
Estimated number of packs and wolves in Montana, 2007 – 2025 under iPOM 1.0 and iPOM 2.0. Ribbons indicate 95% uncertainty interval. (Courtesy FWP)
Gray wolves were removed from the endangered species list in 2009 with the states of Montana, Idaho and Wyoming taking over wolf management in each state. 
Montana FWP has set a 450-wolf management baseline to ensure the population remains high enough to avoid a federal government takeover. 
In response to the new data showing a lower population in the state, FWP recommended dropping the hunting and trapping quota from 452 to 250.
During the 2025-26 wolf season, which ended on March 15, harvest totaled 247 wolves, including 145 by hunters and 102 by trappers. The number was the lowest since 2016. The new season with new quota starts Sept. 15.
Wargo asked for an amendment to bring it up to a 300-wolf quota statewide, with regional sub-quotas, pointing out that the department’s forecasting models show killing 300 wolves won’t reduce the population to risky levels. 
“iPOM 2.0 is overly conservative,” Wargo said of the new model. “We have layers upon layers, safety factors on safety factors.”
 The great wolf debate

Dozens of members of the public showed up in person and online to comment on the new hunting and trapping regulations, many criticizing the department’s population models — either for vindicating wolf advocates who have long argued the state’s method overestimates wolves, or from detractors who say the new model is overly cautious and hasn’t been thoroughly vetted. 
Mark Cooke, with Wolves of the Rockies, said while the new population model is being scrutinized, the department should manage wolves with a higher level of caution. 
“We aren’t asking Montana to not manage wolves. We’re asking Montana to manage them carefully, transparently, and with the best available science,” he said. “And I’ll close with one comment: Uncertainty should lead to caution, not greater killing.”
Montana Rep. Jedidiah Hinkle, a Belgrade Republican who leads the House Fish and Game Committee and has pushed for drastically reducing wolf populations, called the whole plan “a mess.” 
During the Legislature when lawmakers debated several bills authorizing killing a much higher number of wolves, Hinkle said the department “vigorously defended” its original iPOM model. 
“By just changing the pack size and the distribution of the territory, we’re able to knock off 400 wolves,” he said. “The only thing that happened between that time is a lawsuit over the management of wolves. Looks pretty fishy to me.”
Several commenters pointed out that wolves are an economic driver in the areas near  Yellowstone National Park, and reducing the population in Montana could affect that area. 
But ranchers from around the state offered a different view: The economy they participate in takes a bigger hit from having more wolves around. 
“No one’s coming to Ovando, Montana, to watch wolves,” said rancher Bob Rowland. “They’re all going to the park, and so our economy is based on livestock, hunting, big game.”
According to Montana FWP’s annual wolf report, the state Livestock Loss Board paid out more than $90,000 to reimburse livestock producers for wolf kills in 2025 — half the amount paid out for grizzly bear kills. 
Lance Fourstar, a member of the Fort Peck Assiniboine Tribe, asked for the commission to consider a 200-wolf quota, drawing on his perspective as an Indigenous person “whose ancestors shared this land with the wolf for thousands of generations.”
“To our people, the wolf is not a trophy, a pest, or a number on a spreadsheet to be manipulated for political motives,” Fourstar said. “The wolf is a sacred relative, a teacher of family unity, and a crucial balance keeper of the natural world.”
Diane Boyd, a retired wolf and carnivore specialist with FWP, said the department’s revised modeling was a good start, but killing more than 200 wolves next year would likely lead to a declining population. 
“If Montana continues along the ‘kill more wolves’ paradigm instead of science, Montana’s wolf population will continue to decline and will likely fail to maintain its stated population goal of 450. Montana will then lose control of wolf management as the federal government takes over,” Boyd said. “You can change its trajectory with significantly lowering quotas and more conservative management objectives.”
Unlike most species, the wolf hunting and trapping regulations are reviewed annually. 
At the end of the meeting, the commission unanimously approved a 300-wolf limit for the upcoming season, along with sub-quotas that include just one wolf in each of the two management areas outside Yellowstone National Park.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: AG candidate Nate Willems says he’ll focus on Iowans, not out-of-state lawsuits
description: Democratic candidate for Iowa attorney general Nate Willems laid out his history of winning legal battles for Iowans’ benefit Friday and said his office’s priority would be helping Iowans, rather than focusing on out-of-state litigation. Willems spoke on the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox stage at the Iowa State Fair about his bid for the […]
text:
Iowa Attorney General candidate Nate Willems speaks at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic candidate for Iowa attorney general Nate Willems laid out his history of winning legal battles for Iowans’ benefit Friday and said his office’s priority would be helping Iowans, rather than focusing on out-of-state litigation.
Willems spoke on the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox stage at the Iowa State Fair about his bid for the state attorney general position, for which Republican Attorney General Brenna Bird is seeking reelection.
“Over the last 18 years, I’ve represented tens of thousands of Iowans and recovered tens of millions of dollars,” Willems said. “But the truth is, a lot of the work that I’ve been doing is work that the attorney general’s office could be doing but does not.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Willems said $900 million “is stolen from Iowa workers’ paychecks” every year, through off-the-clock work, no paid overtime, stolen tips, illegal pay stub deductions and misclassification of employees as independent contractors.
In order to combat wage theft in Iowa, Willems told reporters he’s planning to form a “small unit” within state government that will work with private attorneys, nonprofits, “the labor movement” and law enforcement in cases with a “criminal element.” He also told fairgoers he would ensure that every county attorney in Iowa has the ability and resources to “prosecute the most violent felonies.”
On environmental enforcement, where Willems said Bird has given minimal fines to companies found to be polluting Iowa air and water as a “slap on the wrist,” he would “seek meaningful penalties” against these corporations.
“Corporations are reasonable, logical entities, and they see that if it costs more money to break the law rather than to follow the law, that will lead them to follow the law,” he said.
Bird campaign spokesperson Rachel Ostergren called Willems a “far-left liberal with a dangerous and radical record” in an emailed statement.
“Iowans deserve an attorney general who stands with law enforcement, upholds the law, and serves every Iowan. As Attorney General, Brenna has held companies accountable to the law, not politics,” Ostergren said in her statement. “Nate has proven he would be an extreme liberal, who would pursue an agenda Iowans cannot afford.”
During her own time at the political soapbox, Bird responded to questions about wage theft by saying they are mostly federal violations that must be dealt with by federal enforcement of wage laws.
While some cases do fall under federal law, Willems said, Iowa code has its own rules that he’s used when representing Iowa City hospital workers who were being paid “systematically, illegally late,” and emphasized state government’s role in taking on this issue.
Bird also said during her soapbox speech that she and Willems don’t see “eye to eye” on voter ID laws, which she supports, as well as other topics. Willems told reporters he will enforce the voter ID laws currently enacted, as that is the job of the attorney general,
Increasing the Attorney General Office’s focus on Iowa and its residents is one of Willems’s main goals should he be elected to the position, he said, another departure from Bird’s focus on challenging or defending various federal policies.
He added that based on Bird’s previous promise to sue the Biden administration, “it’s very foreseeable” that if she wins the attorney general spot and Rob Sand wins the gubernatorial race, “she’ll file a suit against Rob Sand at every opportunity.”
“I certainly recognize that there are times when there is a real threat to Iowans or a real harm which … Iowans have suffered, that it’s appropriate to take legal action,” Willems said. “But I really do want the office a bit more focused on Iowa, on Iowa law, on helping regular Iowans, than you know getting into political lawsuits like that.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: UM President Shinn gives first state-of-the-university address
description: In his first state-of-the-university address as president of the University of Montana, Jeremiah Shinn announced a major fundraising initiative to support students. “Our goal is simple: If a talented Montana student wants to earn a degree from this university, they will have the resources,” Shinn said. Shinn in his address Friday pointed to specific achievem[...]
text:
The M on Mt. Sentinel stands above Main Hall on the University of Montana campus. (Provided by the University of Montana)In his first state-of-the-university address as president of the University of Montana, Jeremiah Shinn announced a major fundraising initiative to support students.
“Our goal is simple: If a talented Montana student wants to earn a degree from this university, they will have the resources,” Shinn said.
Shinn in his address Friday pointed to specific achievements from students and accomplishments for the Treasure State.
He spoke to an estimated 800 people, 400 at UM and another 400 online, acknowledging the challenges higher education faces, and asking Montanans to see the Missoula flagship as bigger than any one program or interest.
In underscoring the students UM attracts and supports, Shinn pointed to James Straw.
He said Straw’s career with the U.S. Marine Corps was cut short by an autoimmune disease, but he earned an associate’s degree, transferred to UM, and became a Marshall Scholar and future physician.
The Marshall Scholarship supports intellectually distinguished students to contribute to the advancement of science, the humanities and creative arts.
“His story reminds us that there is no single front door to the University of Montana,” Shinn said.
University of Montana President Jeremiah Shinn stands for a portrait on June 29, 2026, in Missoula. (Provided by UM)
In highlighting service to the state, Shinn said UM marks an historic moment this week welcoming an inaugural cohort of physician assistants, 24 students, including 20 from Montana, in a state needing 67 new physician assistants every year.
“Many of those students will complete clinical rotations in rural Montana, and many will choose to stay,” Shinn said. “And because they stay, families across the state will have better access to health care.”
He said UM has made similar contributions to increase the number of teachers who stay in Montana and said the institution is working to close the shortage of cybersecurity professionals in the state’s school districts, hospitals and businesses.
Shinn, who took the helm at UM on July 1 after President Seth Bodnar stepped down to run for the U.S. Senate, also asked people to do their part to welcome those students and help them feel like they belong — “every interaction matters.”
He said those interactions happen across campus and in many ways, as students stand in line for one of the 4,000 hamburgers it serves in a week, at Campus Recreation, or even at the Curry Health Center.
Susan Connelly, of the Blackfeet Nation, found community at Curry Health Center Wellbeing, an office focused on the physical, mental and emotional health of students, and Shinn said Connelly found her purpose there.
He said people like to ask about enrollment, but he said another important measure is how many people remain enrolled. In the past decade, he said, UM has increased the rate of people who stay at UM from their first to second year by nine percentage points.
He pointed to Connelly.
“Because she stayed, she flourished. Last spring, Susan, along with her friend Elannah Flat Lip, became the university’s first Indigenous Udall Scholars in two decades,” Shinn said.
The Udall Scholarship Program identifies future leaders in environmental, tribal public policy and health care fields, and it describes itself as highly competitive. In May, UM said it is No. 1 in the nation for Udall recipients at 51.
Shinn, previously interim president of Boise State University, also said UM must be “much louder and prouder” about its identity as a science university.
“The University of Montana is a great science university, and I don’t mean that as an aspiration. I mean that as a fact,” Shinn said.
For instance, he said, across the country, just 40% of students who apply to medical school are accepted, but UM students are accepted at nearly twice that rate, 74%.
“That’s not an accident. It’s evidence that our students are receiving an exceptional scientific education and world-class advising and support,” Shinn said.
Although he lauded UM’s accomplishments for students and the state, Shinn also said public confidence in education has declined. He said families and legislators have questions about the value of higher education, and “frankly, we ought to be asking those same questions.”
He said just 35% of Montana’s high school students enroll in the Montana University System, and while the university isn’t for everyone, for some, cost is a barrier, and the new fundraising initiative at UM aims to remove it.
After the address, UM spokesperson Dave Kuntz said the university still needs to collect more data to calculate a fundraising target, but he provided more details about Shinn’s vision.
Kuntz said many scholarships are narrowly tailored to specific programs or student demographics, but Shinn’s goal is that deans will have access to a renewable scholarship fund that closes the gap for any resident student who wants to attend UM and can’t afford it.
In his speech, Shinn repeatedly asked to put students first, to “choose patience over frustration, curiosity over assumption, kindness over our own convenience.”
“We exist to serve students. We exist to serve Montana,” Shinn said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: NM residents protest pending Project Jupiter air quality permit outside Environment Department
description: Residents from across New Mexico gathered outside the state Environment Department office in Santa Fe Friday afternoon and called on its officials to deny an air quality permit for the controversial Project Jupiter data center under construction in Doña Ana County.
text:
New Mexico residents protested a pending air quality permit application for the Oracle and OpenAI data center, Project Jupiter, outside the New Mexico Environment Department in Santa Fe on Aug. 21, 2026. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)Residents from across New Mexico gathered outside the state Environment Department office in Santa Fe Friday afternoon and called on its officials to deny an air quality permit for the controversial Project Jupiter data center under construction in Doña Ana County.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The New Mexico Environment Department is currently scheduled to begin a hearing on whether to issue an air quality permit for the project on Sept. 14. If approved, the permit would allow Project Jupiter’s power supply to emit as many greenhouse gases as New Mexico’s largest cities combined.
Protesters arrived at NMED’s office carrying signs with messages such as, “Project Jupiter makes NM stupider” and “Support these data centers: Schools, libraries, bookstores.” Those in attendance frequently criticized elected officials in Doña Ana County for approving the controversial Oracle and OpenAI development.
Lifelong Sunland Park resident Irene Rodriguez addressed the crowd from a podium set up outside NMED’s front door.
“We’ve been to the City Hall and the county commission and nobody has listened to us,” she said, to cries of “shame” in the audience.
Critics of the project have filed multiple lawsuits over the local county commission’s 2025 vote to approve the project, alleging that commissioners violated the state Open Meetings Act and that they approved draft forms of development agreements rather than finalized ones.
Lifelong Sunland Park Irene Rodriguez drove to Santa Fe on Aug. 21, 2026, to call on environment officials to deny an air quality permit for the Project Jupiter data center under construction in her community. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)
Rodriguez told Source NM she is most concerned for water resources. Although developers have promised a “closed-loop” cooling system that will use less water than the evaporative cooling in many data centers, much of the surrounding area relies on water infrastructure that is already in disrepair.
Environmental group asks NM Supreme Court to pause Project Jupiter’s air quality permit hearing

Albuquerque resident Patrick Jaramillo, co-director of the American Friends Service Committee’s New Mexico Program, voiced the same concern.
“We believe that water is a gift from God. And the creator gave us that gift for us to nourish our life and our communities,” he said into a microphone. “And these vendidos want to take God’s gift to us to power AI slop and hate and artificial intelligence when they won’t invest in human intelligence?”
Several protesters wore cardboard face masks of New Mexico officials and staged an exaggerated re-enactment of how they believed state officials paved the way for the controversial data center project, sacrificing the environment for purported economic gains.
Two new legal challenges this week also took aim at elected officials’ roles in paving the way for the project.
The Center for Biological Diversity, a national conservation group, filed a petition with the New Mexico Supreme Court alleging that State Engineer Elizabeth Anderson approved the drilling of emergency wells, which supplied millions of gallons of water to the development, in violation of a state law that requires a public notice and hearing in such instances.
“These are critical due process protections that have been cast aside for Project Jupiter,” Colin Cox, a New Mexico-based Center for Biological Diversity attorney, wrote in a statement.
Protesters outside the New Mexico Environment Department in Santa Fe on Aug. 21, 2026, dressed up as state officials whom they accused of fast-tracking the Project Jupiter data center under construction in Doña Ana County. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)
The Office of the State Engineer did not respond to a request for comment.
Cox’s group also filed a joint motion with the New Mexico Environmental Law Center seeking to remove Max Shepherd, the hearing officer presiding over NMED’s air quality permit process for Project Jupiter, after he abruptly rescheduled the hearing from October to September. Cox’s filing argues that Shepherd’s decisions have deprived involved parties of their due process rights — which the Santa Fe-based clean energy organization New Energy Economy also argued in a separate state Supreme Court filing this week.
The joint filing includes a screenshot of Lujan Grisham’s calendar, which shows that she met with Oracle representatives two days before Shepherd filed an order rescheduling the hearing to September.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Lujan Grisham said the governor “takes seriously the concerns Doña Ana County residents have raised about Project Jupiter — including on air quality and groundwater use — and expects any data center operating in New Mexico to meet the state’s rigorous environmental standards and use water responsibly.”
Lujan Grisham “routinely” meets with companies like Oracle, the statement said, adding that July’s meeting was a “general update.”
“The governor does not interfere in state agencies’ regulatory decisions and has made no effort to influence the outcome of Project Jupiter’s air permit application,” the statement said. “Instead, it is her responsibility to ensure that state agencies meet their statutory obligations for a fair, transparent and independent process.”
Environment Department spokesperson Drew Goretzka in a statement to Source NM said that department staffers are adhering to the current schedule but will meet the requirements of any revised schedule.
“As for the motion to remove the hearing officer, that decision ultimately lies with the department’s decision-maker — the deputy cabinet secretary in this case — with whom NMED staff are not permitted to discuss Project Jupiter matters with,” Goretzka wrote.
Residents from across New Mexico protested a pending air quality permit application for the Project Jupiter data center outside the New Mexico Environment Department in Santa Fe on Aug. 21, 2026. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)
