name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC legislators to return to vote on $350M agreement on local spending
description: A week after negotiations publicly blew up, the Legislature's chief budget writers have reached a deal on spending $350 million on local projects.
text:
The South Carolina Statehouse dome is seen on Tuesday, May 5, 2026, in Columbia, framed by palm tree fronds. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA)COLUMBIA — A week after negotiations publicly blew up, the Legislature’s chief budget writers have reached a deal on spending $350 million on local projects.
An agreement that shaves $100 million from the House’s list of legislator-sponsored projects and changes the process for future budgets means most of this year’s proposed earmarks — or community investments, as legislators call them — will be at least partially funded, according to the chambers’ budget chairmen.
The House and Senate will return Tuesday to vote on whether to send the pared-down list to Gov. Henry McMaster’s desk.
“I think what we’ve done and investments we’ve made are good things for our constituents,” House Ways and Means Chairman Bruce Bannister told the SC Daily Gazette on Friday. “Resolving it this way is helping the people of South Carolina.”
Last week, he announced that the House wasn’t coming back. After a compromise to separately review local requests fell apart, Bannister said the budget sent to McMaster would be the final word on spending for the year. And he meant it — at the time, anyway.
$15B state spending plan approved with no legislator-requested projects

“I believed we were finished,” said the Greenville Republican.
But negotiations between legislative leaders continued.
Under the agreement, the Senate keeps its $131 million worth of spending on projects that include public parks, water and sewer upgrades, and improvements to police and fire departments. The House has whittled its total to $220 million.
None of the earmarks for first responders, including local fire and police departments, got trimmed. And all projects receiving less than $300,000 stayed. But the rest of the House’s list got reduced by 39%. Those cuts weren’t across the board. Legislative delegations prioritized what to eliminate and fully fund within their counties, Bannister said.
As an example, he said, “If there’s a sidewalk project that is for kids’ safety, and they want to do it right now, and there’s a park renovation that can wait, they may have cut their park out completely in favor of the sidewalk safety project.”
The governor’s office was also part of negotiations. The items he planned to veto have already come off the list, Bannister said.
The agreement leaves roughly $30 million of the money set aside for local projects unspent.
SC Senate budget includes $130M for local projects, but zero earmarks for nonprofits

When the Legislature met last week to send the $15 billion budget package to McMaster, six weeks after the start of the fiscal year, both chambers blamed the other for negotiations dragging out and the compromise on local spending falling apart.
Senators’ protests over the process included that the House waited until after the Senate passed its budget proposal to add its long list of earmarks and that the House’s total for local spending was nearly 2½ times the Senate’s tally. House members countered that’s because there are more representatives than senators: 124 to 46. But senators argued they represent more people in larger districts.
The agreement worked out between the two leaders who control the budget process makes several changes starting next year: The House will include local projects in its initial budget proposal sent to the Senate. The chambers will spend roughly the same amount on earmarks. And there will be no direct funding to nonprofits. That doesn’t mean a ban. But any earmarks for nonprofits must be sponsored by a local government, the leaders said.
Those changes won’t be put into chamber rules or law. Rather, it’s a “gentlemen’s agreement,” Bannister said.
The fight over local spending comes one year after legislators took a one-year hiatus from earmarks, at Peeler’s insistence. After spending that had been in the tens of millions of dollars climbed to hundreds of millions, reaching a high of $713 million in 2023, the Gaffney Republican said a break was needed to rein it in.
On Friday, he called the agreement a great first step.
“If handled properly,” earmarks benefit taxpayers, he said.
“It’s a very good budget,” he said, adding that Bannister is a “good negotiator.” “It was worth fighting for.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Troy Jackson secured third-most donations of Senate candidates through ActBlue in July
description: Troy Jackson raised the third most out of U.S. Senate candidates through his party’s national fundraising platform in July.  Jackson, who replaced former Democratic nominee Graham Platner during the final week that month, raised just over $5.3 million through ActBlue, according to the latest filing Thursday night.  Much of that total, more than $1.2 million,[...]
text:
Troy Jackson speaks to delegates at the Democratic U.S. Senate nominating convention in Bangor on July 25, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Troy Jackson raised the third most out of U.S. Senate candidates through his party’s national fundraising platform in July. 
Jackson, who replaced former Democratic nominee Graham Platner during the final week that month, raised just over $5.3 million through ActBlue, according to the latest filing Thursday night. 
Much of that total, more than $1.2 million, came in on July 25, the day he was officially selected. That was the most on a single day for any committee on ActBlue in July. 
Jackson’s fundraising through the platform tapered off through the rest of the month. August figures won’t be available until next month. ActBlue data is not comprehensive of his campaign’s entire stockpile, which he isn’t required to report to the Federal Elections Commission until October. 
That $5 million is still below the $11 million cash on hand incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins reported during the last filing deadline through June 30. The five-term senator also maintains a financial edge via the backing of outside groups. 
Jackson is navigating a compressed campaign after Platner dropped out of Maine’s Senate race on July 8 following an accusation of sexual assault. Coming off of a recent loss in the Democratic gubernatorial primary, Jackson quickly consolidated support for his Senate bid, becoming the presumptive replacement before official votes were cast at a nominating convention organized by the state party in a matter of weeks. 
As for other Democratic Senate candidates, incumbent Jon Ossoff of Georgia raised the most via ActBlue in July, about $8.7 million, and James Talarico of Texas raised the second-most, roughly $7.6 million.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: In 1876, Colorado’s first-ever Republican ticket united ‘the old and the new’
description: The last of the delegates elected to Colorado’s first-ever state party convention arrived in Pueblo on a special train from Denver on Aug. 23, 1876. The newly proclaimed Centennial State’s Republican establishment opened proceedings at the county courthouse just after 8 p.m. “The prospects at present are exceedingly good for a tolerably lively contest for […[...]
text:
Left: John Long Routt, first governor of the state of Colorado. Right: Lafayette Head, the state's first lieutenant governor and an early settler of the San Luis Valley. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, Z-1971)The last of the delegates elected to Colorado’s first-ever state party convention arrived in Pueblo on a special train from Denver on Aug. 23, 1876. The newly proclaimed Centennial State’s Republican establishment opened proceedings at the county courthouse just after 8 p.m.



← Aug. 13–19
Aug. 20–26 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

“The prospects at present are exceedingly good for a tolerably lively contest for the nominations for the various offices to be selected by the convention,” reported the Pueblo Chieftain.
The state of Colorado’s inaugural elections were to be held on the first Tuesday in October. In a tense presidential election year, Republicans and Democrats would battle for control of the 75-seat state Legislature, the three-member state Supreme Court, the office of governor and a half-dozen other executive-branch positions, and the state’s at-large representative to Congress.
After the appointment of a credentials committee and a song by the GOP’s glee club, Rev. Benjamin F. Watson, a Black delegate from Denver, led the convention in prayer, making “an eloquent appeal to the Throne of Grace, in behalf of the convention and its objects,” said the Chieftain.
Watson, who’d arrived in Colorado earlier that year, had been born a slave in Missouri, escaped to Illinois via the Underground Railroad at 14 years old and later served in the Union Army during the Civil War. Later in 1876, he would be appointed the first chaplain of the Colorado Senate.
With some introductory business out of the way, the Republican faithful marched through the streets of Pueblo in a torchlight parade.
“Great enthusiasm prevails, and a general desire for a strong ticket, and one that will harmonize the party and all sections of the state,” said the Rocky Mountain News, whose editor and publisher, William N. Byers, was another of Denver’s convention delegates.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Harmony in the Colorado GOP was easier said than done. It was a fraught and anxious time for the Republican Party nationally, with President Ulysses S. Grant’s administration plagued by scandal and Democrats confident their party was poised to sweep back to full control of the federal government for the first time since the Civil War.
In Colorado, long-simmering tensions between Denver’s business and political establishment and other parts of the new state — southern Colorado, with its large Catholic Hispano population, and the frontier mining settlements in the mountains — threatened to complicate any consensus the convention hoped to reach.
“Most of the southern delegates got in on Tuesday evening, and spent the time yesterday in caucusing and laying plans to head off the common enemy — the Denver ring,” reported the Chieftain.
To counter Denver’s influence, southern delegates united behind San Luis Valley rancher Lafayette Head for governor.
In a state where being a “59er” carried no small amount of prestige, Head had made his home in Colorado even before the 1859 gold rush. After settling in the conquered territory of New Mexico in the wake of the Mexican-American War, he moved north and in 1854 helped found the town of Guadalupe in what would become Colorado’s Conejos County. A Catholic convert and fluent Spanish speaker, he went on to serve as an Indian agent for both the Apache and Ute tribes, a territorial legislator and delegate to Colorado’s constitutional convention.
Northern delegates had the votes to prevent Head’s nomination, but needed to pick which horse to back. Both Gov. John Routt, a newcomer to Colorado appointed by Grant in 1875 as its final territorial governor, and Samuel Hitt Elbert, a former territorial governor himself and a prominent Republican attorney in Denver, were touted as candidates for governor, but both men appeared to send mixed signals as to whether they’d accept the nomination.
After several informal ballots among the 140 or so GOP delegates on Aug. 24, no clear winner emerged. It took a compromise reached behind closed doors to break the deadlock.
“After the adjournment of the convention in the afternoon caucusing was carried on industriously, and about five o’clock it became noised abroad that a compromise had been effected,” the Chieftain reported. “Gov. Routt would be nominated for governor, and Lafayette Head for lieutenant governor.”
The full convention nominated both men by acclamation that evening. Elbert received the consolation of a nomination to the Colorado Supreme Court, where he would serve until 1888.
“Gov. Routt then stood up beside Maj. Head and said: ‘Now, gentlemen you have the old and the new,’” said the Chieftain’s account. “The glee club then sang a song the chorus of which was ‘Hurrah for Routt and Head.’”

title: Florida employers could see a 7.4% average reduction in workers’ comp costs
description: Florida employers could see another round of decreases in the costs of their workers’ compensation insurance. The National Council on Compensation Insurance (NCCI) is recommending that workers’ compensation rates be reduced by an average 7.4% beginning Jan 1, 2027. NCCI is the licensed rating organization in Florida, authorized to suggest workers’ compensati[...]
text:
Florida employers could see another reduction in their workers compensation rates. (Photo by Tim Henderson/Stateline)Florida employers could see another round of decreases in the costs of their workers’ compensation insurance.
The National Council on Compensation Insurance (NCCI) is recommending that workers’ compensation rates be reduced by an average 7.4% beginning Jan 1, 2027.
NCCI is the licensed rating organization in Florida, authorized to suggest workers’ compensation rates. NCCI’s filing is a recommendation only. Florida’s insurance commissioner is charged with setting the rates. Often, the commissioner’s office holds a public meeting on proposed rates.
The reduction is largely driven by a reduction in the frequency of “lost-time claims,” when employees miss work because of injuries.
Workers’ compensation is a no-fault system that aims to protect employers from getting sued by injured employees and, in exchange, employers provide employees injured on the job the care they need to return to work. Employers are required to provide compensation for lost wages if an employee misses more than eight days of work due to an on-the-job injury.
Most employers in Florida are required to carry workers’ compensation insurance but there are exceptions for businesses with four or fewer employees and for construction companies with four or fewer officers. While those firms aren’t mandated to carry the coverage, they are required to file for exemptions with the state.
NCCI reviewed the premium and loss experience for Florida employers in policy years 2023 and 2024 in making the recommendation.
While the NCCI is recommending an overall reduction, its proposed rate filing does take into consideration minor increases to the maximum allowable rates for physician and other non-hospital providers that treat injured workers. And despite the small bump (0.06%), NCCI’s recommendation reflects a lower-than-anticipated medical loss-ratio trend.
According to a summary, the lower medical loss ratio is tied to strong wage growth. Nationwide, payroll increased 4.8% from 2024 to 2025, while employment growth (largely driven by the healthcare sector) rose just 0.5% during that same time.
If the proposed reduction (or a modified reduction) is approved, it would be the 10th consecutive year in which workers’ compensation rates have fallen for Florida employers. Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky last year ordered an average  6.9% reduction in workers’ compensation rates effective Jan. 1.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Low Alaska wildfire season punctuated by serious Interior blaze
description: A quiet year for Alaska wildfires is closing out in dramatic fashion with a late-season blaze that has burned homes and prompted evacuations in an Interior Alaska community. As of Thursday, only about 83,400 acres had burned in Alaska wildfires this year, far short of the approximately 1 million acres that has become typical for […]
text:
A smoke column from the Mukluk Fire is visible north of the Tok School. The fire, ignited by a downed power line, was first reported on Aug. 17, well after the normal peak of the annual Alaska fire season. (Photo by E. Hjortstorp/Alaska Division of Forestry and Fire Protection)A quiet year for Alaska wildfires is closing out in dramatic fashion with a late-season blaze that has burned homes and prompted evacuations in an Interior Alaska community.
As of Thursday, only about 83,400 acres had burned in Alaska wildfires this year, far short of the approximately 1 million acres that has become typical for recent years.
But the Mukluk Fire, first reported on Aug. 17 and ignited by a downed power line and estimated at about 5,000 acres as of Thursday, has caused particular problems.
It broke out in the Alaska Highway community of Tok, home to about 1,600 people. At least 20 structures have been lost, said Jessi Morse, an Alaska Division of Forestry public information officer.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Several residents have had to evacuate, and the American Red Cross of Alaska set up a shelter this week at the local school.
Alaska’s fire season usually peaks in June or early July, paralleling the time of maximum lightning strikes and summer daylight.
That makes it “very unusual” for a new fire to break out in mid-August, Morse said.
The Mukluk Fire’s acreage estimate is likely to change as fire managers gather more accurate information, she added.
Over the past half century, wildfire frequency, acreage and intensity have increased in Alaska, though there are wide variations year to year.
This year’s low acreage total was the product of several factors, said Rick Thoman, a scientist with the Alaska Center for Climate Assessment and Preparedness at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.
An abnormally cold spring limited the spread of fires, even as summer lightning strikes were about normal in number, he said. Reports from smokejumpers assigned to new blazes indicated that in Interior and Western Alaska, at least, the vegetation on the ground had limited burn potential, even in midsummer.
“They’d be working to put them out and they’re encountering frozen ground, you know, six inches below the ground. And this is in June,” Thoman said. “We had lightning, but the ground wasn’t really ready to burn yet.”
Another factor was the lack of sustained hot weather this summer, he said. There were hot days, but not several of them in a row, he said.
Another contributor was likely “happenstance,” part of the wide variation from year to year, he said.
The most recent ultra-low year for Alaska wildfires was 2008, when only 105,600 acres burned, according to state records. Before that, the lowest year in recent decades was 1995, with only 43,900 acres, according to the records. In prior decades, there were several years with similarly low fire acreage, or even much lower, though past records may lack the accuracy provided by satellite observations.
Despite the low total this year, the late emergence of the Mukluk Fire fits a long-term pattern of expanding fire seasons, Thoman said.
The Tok area, in eastern Interior Alaska about 90 miles from the Canadian border, might be particularly vulnerable to late-season fires.
“Tok tends to be drier. So when the rest of the state is getting wet and rainy, sometimes Tok is left out of that,” Morse said.
Last year, a different fire near Tok continued to burn late in the season, she noted. Last year’s 7 Mile Lookout Fire, which burned about 4,000 acres in a spot southwest of the town, was ignited by lightning in June and prompted a response through early August.
Alaska wildfire acreage from 1950 to mid-Aug. 18, 2026, is shown in a graph. There are wide variations from year to year, but seasons with more than 1 million acres have become more common over the past three decades. (Graph provided by Rick Thoman/Alaska Center for Climate Assessment and Preparedness/University of Alaska Fairbanks International Arctic Research Center)

name: VTDigger
title: ‘USPS isn’t delivering for Vermont’: Congressional delegation complains to postmaster general about mail issues
description:
Vermont lawmakers posed a series of questions to the Postal Service about what it’s doing to retain staff and prevent delays. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘USPS isn’t delivering for Vermont’: Congressional delegation complains to postmaster general about mail issues.
text:
Drive-by mailboxes bearing the logo of the United States Postal Service on Elmwood Avenue in Burlington. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Vermont’s congressional delegation has received more than 2,000 complaints from constituents about mail service so far this year, the lawmakers wrote in a letter to Postmaster General David Steiner on Friday. 
“As you know, the Postal Service’s Delivering for America ten-year plan was launched in 2021, supposedly to modernize and support the financial self-sustainability of the postal network,” the letter begins. “Five years into this plan, mail delivery service in Vermont is at an all-time low, staffing shortages in the state are pervasive, and USPS has not improved its financial outlook.”
The Postal Service did not respond to a request for comment by publication time. 
Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., sent the letter to Steiner to share Vermonters’ complaints about the U.S. Postal Service and posed a series of questions to his office that they hope to have answered by Sept. 1. 
“It’s clear the national leadership of USPS isn’t delivering for Vermont,” Welch said via email to VTDigger. “The postal service is a critical public service, and we want answers about what steps USPS is taking to improve delivery for Vermonters.”
The letter cited local news coverage about Vermonters receiving only one or two days of mail delivery per week, leading to paperwork mishaps, missed birthdays and gaps in prescription medications. 
The issue has also affected state government operations: According to the letter, the Vermont Agency of Administration has reported two separate batches of vehicle titles have been lost in the mail. 
“These incidents not only create unnecessary administrative burdens for the state, they also present real security threats to customers’ most sensitive personal information,” the letter said. 
Steve Hutkins is a mail quality advocate who tracks Postal Service news on his blog Save the Post Office. He said he wasn’t surprised to hear that Vermonters have been experiencing poor service — because he’s been hearing about it, nationwide, for years. 
Data from the Postal Service shows that about 84% of first-class letters in the Maine-New Hampshire-Vermont region get to their destination on time, roughly in line with the national average but far below the Postal Service’s target of 90% to 95%. 
But even that “on time” designation is suspect, since the Postal Service has changed its definition, so what was supposed to take two days is now supposed to take three, Hutkins said. 
“They slow down the literal standard of what it’s supposed to be, and then they can’t even make the new, more relaxed standards,” he said. 
The letter alleges that some Vermont postal workers are being told to prioritize Amazon and United Parcel Service deliveries over traditional USPS mail service, delaying the mail further. That, too, is a national issue, Hutkins said. 
Postal workers are “being told at the office, ‘Get those Amazon packages out, because we have to have a high rating with Amazon,’” he said. 
Among the congressional members’ questions are several asking about what the Postal Service is doing to address an alleged staff shortage. 
“In January 2026, USPS’ NNE District Office confirmed to the Vermont Congressional Delegation that Vermont lags behind its regional neighbors in new employee recruitment numbers,” the letter reads. “What resources or strategies have you committed directly to the NNE District to boost statewide hiring efforts?” 
Hutkins said federal reports have shown the Postal Service particularly struggles to retain “pre-career” employees, temporary workers who do not have the same benefits as career employees and are not guaranteed a regular schedule. 
“The usual problem is, the job is too hard,” he said. “They don’t like the forced overtime. Then people get burned out really quickly.”
He said rural mail carriers might struggle even further because their routes take them down mountainous dirt roads. 
The three congressional members also expressed concern about the possibility of mail-in ballots not arriving in time to be counted for the election, since mail-in ballots must be received by local election officials by the close of polls on Election Day, according to the Vermont secretary of state. 
According to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission, Vermont has a relatively low rate of mail-in ballots getting rejected, including for late delivery — only 0.2% of returned ballots in 2024. 
Hutkins said the Postal Service takes “extraordinary measures” to ensure that mail-in ballots are delivered promptly for November elections. But the rhetoric from the federal government against mail-in ballots has some advocates worried. 
President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March that would require states to share voter information with the U.S. Postal Service in order to utilize mail-in ballots. A group of Democratic states challenged the order, taking the case all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court, where it is pending. 
“This is a huge deal, and the Postal Service is right in the middle of it, and that’s why it’s provoking questions like that from Vermont elected officials,” Hutkins said. 
This story will be updated. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘USPS isn’t delivering for Vermont’: Congressional delegation complains to postmaster general about mail issues.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Ending the ‘Roadless Rule’ could end Montana’s wilderness
description: Our public lands are the backbone of Montana. Our sporting heritage, wildlife habitat, clean water and local economies depend on healthy national forests. Hunters and anglers understand this as well as anyone, which is why sportsmen and women from across Montana are standing up to champion the Roadless Area Conservation Rule from the U.S. Department […]
text:
A view of the Ten Lakes Wilderness Study Area in northwest Montana. (Micah Drew/ Daily Montanan)Our public lands are the backbone of Montana. Our sporting heritage, wildlife habitat, clean water and local economies depend on healthy national forests. Hunters and anglers understand this as well as anyone, which is why sportsmen and women from across Montana are standing up to champion the Roadless Area Conservation Rule from the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s misguided plan to do away with it.
This week, the USDA released its Draft Environmental Impact Statement on rescinding the rule and opening our roadless backcountry to new road building and development. This opens a public comment period that the USDA has limited to just 33 days. For those 2,000 miles away in Washington, D.C., the lack of vision may be understandable. But for those of us who cherish these places that we consider our backyard, their value and what’s at risk is as plain as day.
Montana’s roadless backcountry lands are the places we hunt. Elk seek out areas that are away from roads, and so do the hunters who pursue them. If you hunt Montana’s public lands, chances are you’ve put in many miles hiking though the U.S. Forest Service Inventoried Roadless Areas to fill your tag.
Not unlike elk and other big game, our wild trout populations also depend on the clean water and healthy streams found in roadless areas. These are not only the blue line fisheries we fish in solitude; they are the nurseries that support our most famous rivers. Quite simply, our Roadless Areas help ensure that we continue to have both thriving trout and wildlife populations for future generations of Montanans.
But Inventoried Roadless Areas still fly a bit under the radar. Unlike national parks or wilderness areas, they don’t have big signs announcing that you are crossing a line on the map. Chances are you’ve hunted, fished or otherwise recreated in these places without even knowing it. They offer us wild places without the big “W” wilderness, and provide easy access without the spiderweb of roads, giving us places that feel far from civilization while being accessible from where we live.
In early March, nearly a thousand Montanans turned out for one of seven public meetings held in Kalispell, Libby, Missoula, Hamilton, Butte, Bozeman and Helena. People who have walked these ridgelines, fought fires, studied wildlife populations and rely on the clean water from these headwaters shared what these places mean to them and why the Roadless Area Conservation Rule should remain in place.
Notably, those hearings were organized and hosted by community organizations, including Backcountry Hunters & Anglers, and not the USDA. Unlike in 2000, when the USDA first proposed the rule and held more than 600 public meetings nationwide to solicit public input, including 34 here in Montana, this time the USDA held zero hearings and is doing its best to ignore rather than seek public comment.
But we won’t be quiet.
Despite a rushed comment period last fall, 625,000 Americans still weighed in, with 99% of comments opposing rescission. And what does the USDA offer after hearing strong opposition from Americans? A draft environmental impact statement that ignores the science, the history, and the lived experience of the hunters, anglers, foresters and rural communities who steward these places.
But this fight is not over, and we must still make our voices heard.
We hold our roadless backcountry dear, our way of life depends on these places, and that the public’s opinion matters.
BHA is collecting comments to submit to the USDA at backcountryhunters.org/roadless.
The comment period ends Sept. 21.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Trump appeals loss in case against NJ sanctuary cities
description: A federal in judge dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit targeting local sanctuary policies for immigrants. The administration is appealing.
text:
A federal in judge dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit targeting local sanctuary policies for immigrants. The administration is appealing. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The Trump administration has appealed a federal judge’s dismissal of its challenge to policies in four New Jersey cities that limit how local law enforcement can cooperate with federal civil immigration enforcement.
In June, U.S. District Court Judge Evelyn Padin tossed the feds’ lawsuit that sought to overturn sanctuary policies for immigrants in Hoboken, Jersey City, Newark, and Paterson, saying an existing state directive already barred local authorities from supporting federal immigration enforcement and the local policies merely underscored that state prohibition.
In a one-page notice filed Friday, U.S. Department of Justice attorneys asked the U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals to reconsider Padin’s dismissal. The feds have argued that the cities’ policies seek to regulate the actions of federal officials and so should be struck down.
The local policies and the state directive, though, only apply to the actions of local law enforcement, Padin noted.
The cities’ policies largely repeat the state directive, which forbids state and local authorities from initiating stops based on someone’s suspected immigration status or for violations of civil immigration law and bars officers from asking about a person’s immigration status unless it pertains to an ongoing felony investigation.
The feds did not challenge the state directive in their lawsuit, and multiple courts have upheld the directive as constitutional. Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, signed a version of it into law in March.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘The Rock’ at USM gets a new and more proper name: Renasant Stadium
description: Renasant Bank will pay $13.7 million over 10 years for the naming rights to the football stadium at Southern Miss.
text:
The former M.M. Roberts Stadium at Southern Miss is now Renasant Stadium, named for Renasant Bank. This is welcome news for far more than the 13.7 million obvious reasons.
No: 1, Tupelo-based Renasant, which purchased The First Bank of Hattiesburg in 2025, will pay Southern Miss athletics a badly needed $13.7 million over 10 years for the naming rights to the stadium.
Rick Cleveland
No. 2, and more importantly in my mind, the stadium is no longer named for Malcolm Mettle (M.M.) Roberts, the self-avowed racist and Hattiesburg lawyer, who chaired the state’s Institutions of Higher Learning when the expansion of the stadium was funded in the 1970s. For nearly half a century, Black athletes such as Reggie Collier, Sammy Winder, Jerald Baylis, Hanford Dixon, Damien Fletcher and Frank Gore, Jr.  and hundreds more have spearheaded Southern Miss football to victories in a stadium named for a man who would have preferred they never be allowed to attend college there. Roberts died in 1982.
That was blatantly wrong. Anybody who has read this column over the years might have noticed I nearly always referred to the stadium by its nickname, “The Rock,” rather than by its official name. Perhaps it was my own little protest, but I’m glad I don’t have to do it any longer.
M.M. Roberts was appointed chairman of the state College Board in 1959 by Gov. Ross Barnett. Roberts presided over the board when James Meredith at first was denied admission to Ole Miss. Indeed, Roberts later voted to withhold Meredith’s hard-earned degree from Ole Miss.
In a speech to professors at USM, Roberts once said these words: “But as I’ve gone along through the years and looked back, I’ve said to myself really that I am a racist. Every time I read a definition I say, ‘Well, that’s me.’ I have no apologies for it, though. It’s me.”
File this name change in the folder called: Goodbye, good riddance.
Enough of that. Let’s examine what this means for Southern Miss athletics and Mississippi sports in general. In short, expect more of the same to follow.
The deal between Southern Miss and Renasant breaks the ice in Mississippi as far as corporate sponsorships and naming rights. Such deals have become common around the country, from Kroger Field at Kentucky, to the Carrier Dome at Syracuse, to Hancock Whitney Stadium at South Alabama, to Hard Rock Stadium at Miami and Heinz Field at Pittsburgh.
As Ole Miss athletic director Keith Carter has put it, “It’s all about revenue generation these days.”
The cost of funding college athletics programs continues to skyrocket higher and higher in this age of Name, Image and Likeness, known as the NIL, and the transfer portal. Starting quarterbacks at Power Four schools can make $5 million and more. Friday night starters in the SEC can make half a million a year. An All-American point guard can command millions.
The fundraising issue is magnified at mid-major schools like Southern Miss, which doesn’t receive the more than $70 million annual distribution the Southeastern Conference doles out. The $13.7 million is a huge chunk for USM. While it doesn’t solve funding issues, it certainly helps. The 10-year deal begins with a $500,000 payment this year, escalating to a $1.64 million payment in 2036.
You can expect more deals like this at Southern Miss and other Mississippi schools. There will be corporate patches on jerseys and headgear – think PGA Tour. 
And there will be more, such as corporate names for entertainment districts that surround stadiums. In Mississippi, this begins with Renasant Stadium at Southern Miss. Again, much, much more will follow — and soon.

title: Special election called to fill vacancy created by Arkansas lawmaker’s resignation
description: EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussions of domestic violence. If you or someone you know needs help, please call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233. A special election to fill the House District 8 vacancy resulting from Austin McCollum’s resignation following domestic violence charges will coincide with the Nov. 3 general electio[...]
text:
A sign directs voters inside a west Bentonville polling site to cast ballots on March 31, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussions of domestic violence. If you or someone you know needs help, please call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.
A special election to fill the House District 8 vacancy resulting from Austin McCollum’s resignation following domestic violence charges will coincide with the Nov. 3 general election, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders announced Friday. 
The Bentonville Republican stepped down earlier this month, just days after being arrested on charges of aggravated assault against his wife. Sanders and other top Republicans urged him to resign after the arrest.
Arkansas state Rep. Austin McCollum resigns after domestic violence arrest

McCollum, who served in the House since 2017, was not running for reelection and won the Republican nomination for Benton County judge in March. 
Parties shall issue certificates of nomination by noon Aug. 28 and candidates must file by 5 p.m. that same day, according to a press release from the governor’s office. Independent candidates must submit petitions to the secretary of state’s office by noon Aug. 28. Petitions can be circulated from Monday through noon Wednesday. 
The winner of the special election will serve the remainder of McCollum’s term, which ends in January. McCollum’s resignation leaves Republicans with a 79-20 majority in the House.
Republican Brian Armas, who serves on the Benton County Quorum Court, is running unopposed in November’s general election for a new two-year term to represent House District 8, which includes a portion of northeastern Benton County. 
McCollum’s vacancy is the fifth that will be filled in 2026. Republican Sen. Brad Simon and Democratic Rep. Alex Holladay won special elections in March to represent Senate District 26 and House District 70, respectively. 
Republican Bill Teeter won the House District 44 special election earlier this month to replace the late Republican Rep. Stan Berry.  
Harrell Wilson won the Republican nomination for the Senate District 1 seat Tuesday. He’ll face Eudora Mayor Tomeka Butler, the only Democrat who filed to run for the seat, in November’s special general election. 
The candidates are vying to replace former Republican Sen. Ben Gilmore who resigned in June to work for Attorney General Tim Griffin. The winner of November’s general election will serve until the end of Gilmore’s term in 2029, and represent a district that includes Ashley, Bradley, Chicot and Cleveland counties, and parts of Drew, Grant, Jefferson and Lincoln counties.
Republicans hold a 28-6 majority in the Senate with the vacancy.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana marks America’s 250th year with commemorative highway signs
description: Indiana motorists will soon see new reminders of America’s 250th birthday along two of the state’s busiest highways. Gov. Mike Braun unveiled one of the commemorative Freedom 250 signs Friday at an Interstate 70 rest area near Plainfield. The Indiana Department of Transportation plans to install 20 signs along I-70 and U.S. 30 over the […]
text:
Gov. Mike Braun and Indiana transportation officials mark the rollout of Freedom 250 signs Friday near Plainfield. The signs will remain along I-70 and U.S. 30 through the end of 2027. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana motorists will soon see new reminders of America’s 250th birthday along two of the state’s busiest highways.
Gov. Mike Braun unveiled one of the commemorative Freedom 250 signs Friday at an Interstate 70 rest area near Plainfield. The Indiana Department of Transportation plans to install 20 signs along I-70 and U.S. 30 over the next week.
The signs were created in partnership with the U.S. Department of Transportation and the White House Freedom 250 initiative. They will remain in place through the end of 2027, according to the governor’s office.
“For generations, Indiana’s highways have served as a central hub connecting Americans to family, communities, businesses and opportunities across our nation,” Braun said in a statement. “As we celebrate 250 years of American freedom, these signs are a fitting tribute to Indiana’s proud legacy as the Crossroads of America.”
Indiana going all out to celebrate America’s 250th birthday

The markers also recognize the 70th anniversary of the Eisenhower Interstate System and 100 years of the Lincoln Highway. U.S. 30 follows the route of the Lincoln Highway, the country’s first transcontinental road.
Similar signs and flags are appearing in other states through the federal “Freedom Moves You” campaign, part of the White House’s broader celebration of 250 years since adoption of the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776.
Indiana Secretary of Transportation and Infrastructure Matt Ubelhor called the project a “unique opportunity” for the state.
“I-70 and U.S. 30 are main thoroughfares traveled by thousands of Indiana residents and visitors each day,” Ubelhor said at Friday’s unveiling. “Both are significant in the history of transportation.”
Braun said Indiana’s location makes the state a fitting participant in the national campaign.
“You can reach more commerce in two days of ground transportation from our great state than any other place in the country,” he said. “We are the center of the world’s economy.”
Hundreds of other events and programs have been organized across Indiana for the semiquincentennial. A bipartisan state commission has coordinated the celebrations intended to highlight Indiana’s role in U.S. history.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lt. Gov. Hosemann ousts top Senate Democrat from redistricting committee
description: Republican Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann presides over the Senate in a special legislative session at the Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, July 15, 2026.
text:
Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann has removed Senate Democratic Leader Derrick Simmons of Greenville from a select committee on redistricting that is tasked with advising the full chamber on redrawing electoral maps after the U.S. Supreme Court’s Callais decision. 
Republican Hosemann did not respond to a question on why he removed Simmons from the committee. But he did replace Simmons with another Democrat, Sen. Albert Butler of Port Gibson. 
The lieutenant governor’s removal of Simmons from the committee comes after Simmons, House Minority Leader Robert Johnson and Legislative Black Caucus Chairman Kabir Karriem wrote a letter to Hosemann and House Speaker Jason White saying they did not believe lawmakers should redraw political districts now. 
“The Legislature cannot and should not revert to lines or schemes that have already been determined to dilute Black voting strength, which would constitute intentional discrimination,” the letter reads. “Indeed, it does not need to draw new lines at all.” 
Sen. Derrick Simmons, D-Greenville, asks a question about a bill in the Senate chamber at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, April 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Simmons, in a statement, said he respects the lieutenant governor’s authority to appoint senators to committees, but he still believes the Legislature should not redraw political lines right now. 
“My position on mid-decade redistricting remains unchanged,” Simmons said. “I continue to believe that any consideration of redistricting should be legally justified, transparent, and accompanied by meaningful public input.” 
The Legislature typically redraws congressional and state legislative districts once every 10 years after U.S. Census data is released. But the U.S. Supreme Court’s recent Louisiana v. Callais decision gave state legislatures more freedom to redraw districts for partisan reasons. 
A joint House and Senate redistricting committee is currently holding hearings across the state to gather voter input on how legislative and congressional districts should be redrawn. Republican Gov. Tate Reeves is expected to call lawmakers into special session on redistricting before year’s end.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Governor seeks expedited federal disaster aid for 54 Indiana counties
description: Indiana has asked the federal government to expedite a major disaster declaration that could unlock additional aid for Hoosier residents and communities across 54 storm-damaged counties. Gov. Mike Braun signed and submitted the request to President Donald Trump on Thursday night, earlier than state officials had expected to complete their damage assessments.[...]
text:
Gov. Mike Braun, left, surveys flood damage in Noblesville on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the governor’s office)Indiana has asked the federal government to expedite a major disaster declaration that could unlock additional aid for Hoosier residents and communities across 54 storm-damaged counties.
Gov. Mike Braun signed and submitted the request to President Donald Trump on Thursday night, earlier than state officials had expected to complete their damage assessments.
Braun said Friday that a federal decision would typically take at least a week, but his administration is seeking a faster review by the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
“I would hope that it doesn’t take seven to 10 days,” Braun told reporters. “That is typical, and the other issue will be: does it reach the threshold of what other recent similar disasters have had to reach in terms of whether we get it or not? I’m optimistic.”
Indiana seeking federal storm assistance at time when Trump wants to scale it back

The request seeks both individual and public assistance. Individual assistance can help residents with uninsured or underinsured losses, while public assistance can help governments and certain nonprofit organizations pay for debris removal, emergency work and repairs to damaged infrastructure.
It follows a federal emergency declaration Trump previously approved for 53 counties. That declaration supports immediate response efforts but is capped at $5 million. The major disaster declaration would make substantially more federal help available.
Recent storms and flooding displaced more than 1,000 families and contributed to at least seven deaths around Indiana, according to officials.
Central Indiana experienced widespread flooding, while powerful winds caused heavy damage and prolonged power outages in the northwestern part of the state.
“This is a more granular approach that’ll help entities, families that were displaced, losing their home, underinsured, no insurance, that type of stuff,” Braun said of the latest request.
The governor’s office said Braun has also pressed utilities to restore power in northwest Indiana, directed additional relief money to affected families and secured more time for eligible residents of Lake and Porter counties to seek replacement Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits for food lost during outages.
State emergency grants of up to $5,000 are available for displaced families to cover immediate needs such as food and clothing. Braun said earlier this week that Indiana had restored its State Disaster Relief Fund to $5 million using state reserves.
“If granted, this declaration will mean significantly more resources to accelerate Indiana’s recovery from the recent severe weather. I will do everything in my power to ensure Hoosiers have the resources needed to recover,” Braun said in an additional statement on X. “My commitment to every impacted Hoosier is that the state will continue working alongside them in the weeks and months ahead, deploying the resources they need to recover and rebuild.”

Montana Jewish Project honors outgoing director Rebecca Stanfel, passing the baton in August 2026 to Rabbi Jeanne Snodgrass. (Provided by the Montana Jewish Project and Facebook)Montana Jewish Project announced this week the appointment of Rabbi Jeanne Snodgrass as its new executive director.
Snodgrass, who takes the post Monday, succeeds Rebecca Stanfel, who stepped down June 1 following years of “transformative leadership,” the organization said in a news release.
Snodgrass said she is honored to join the Montana Jewish Project.
“This community has built something remarkable, and I look forward to listening, learning and helping carry that work forward across Montana,” Snodgrass said in a statement.
Rabbi Jeanne Snodgrass, executive director for the Montana Jewish Project. (Provided photo)
According to the news release, Snodgrass brings more than 15 years of experience as a Jewish communal professional, most recently as executive director of Hillel at the University of Missouri, Columbia.
It said she has a record of strengthening local economies and supporting small businesses.
Snodgrass also is an interfaith organizer and former public school board director who has worked in communities of different sizes, geography and demographics, according to the news release.
She has developed financially sustainable organizations, mentored staff and student leaders, and built partnerships with elected officials and other community members.
Montana Jewish Project Board Chairperson Julie Bir said the search for a new leader resulted in “remarkable candidates.”
“Rabbi Jeanne stood out for her warmth, her experience building sustainable Jewish community, and her excitement for Montana,” Bir said in a statement.

title: Another new CEO hired to lead Oklahoma regional university system
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — The board that governs six of Oklahoma’s regional universities has hired its third new chief executive officer in two years.  Kent Lashley will assume the role of CEO for the Regional University System of Oklahoma beginning Sept. 1. Lashley will be paid $220,000, plus benefits, to head the university system, which serves […]
text:
East Central University's Memorial Student Union in Ada is pictured on Dec. 4, 2024. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — The board that governs six of Oklahoma’s regional universities has hired its third new chief executive officer in two years. 
Kent Lashley will assume the role of CEO for the Regional University System of Oklahoma beginning Sept. 1. Lashley will be paid $220,000, plus benefits, to head the university system, which serves over 40,000 students, according to RUSO’s offer letter. 
Kent Lashley, the new CEO of the Regional University System of Oklahoma, is pictured. (Photo provided by RUSO)
He currently serves as executive vice president and chief financial officer at Rose State College and has held various senior leadership positions at the school for about 17 years.
“I am grateful for the opportunity to serve RUSO and work alongside the board, our presidents, staff and partners,” he said in a statement. “Higher education has been the focus of my career because of the difference it makes for students, families and communities. … I look forward to strengthening the pathways that connect RUSO students with Oklahoma’s workforce and its future.”
Lashley, who will serve as a liaison between RUSO’s governing board and its universities, will be the university system’s third CEO appointed since June 2024.
He replaces Ellen Buettner, who was appointed to the role in October. Brandon Tatum, who had served as Gov. Kevin Stitt’s chief of staff, announced his resignation in August 2025 after a little more than a year in the position. Debra Lyon, RUSO’s general counsel, has been serving as interim CEO since June.
The system governs East Central University, Northeastern State University, Northwestern Oklahoma State University, Southeastern Oklahoma State University, Southwestern Oklahoma State University and the University of Central Oklahoma 
Lashley previously practiced corporate law with The ServiceMaster Company and taught as an adjunct professor at Rose State and UCO. 
He earned a Juris Doctor from the University of Memphis School of Law as well as a masters in education and a bachelor’s degree in social science from Harding University. 
“Kent brings a depth of higher education experience, sound judgment and a clear commitment to public service,” RUSO Board Chair Lake Carpenter said in a statement. “He understands the opportunities and challenges facing our regional universities, and he is committed to furthering RUSO’s mission.”

name: Delaware
title: School Boards Face Bigger Literacy Decisions Under Delaware’s New Funding Model
description: Greater local flexibility will require boards to balance student needs, community priorities and evidence about what improves reading Editor’s note: This is the final installment of a three-part Delaware LIVE series examining Delaware’s literacy challenge, the state’s 2028 goal and the changing responsibilities of local school boards. By George D. Rotsch, Ed[...]
text:
Caption: A major shift in school funding and School Board decision making come as Delaware attempts to raise third-grade reading proficiency from 40% to 53% by 2028.

Greater local flexibility will require boards to balance student needs, community priorities and evidence about what improves reading
Editor’s note: This is the final installment of a three-part Delaware LIVE series examining Delaware’s literacy challenge, the state’s 2028 goal and the changing responsibilities of local school boards.
By George D. Rotsch, Editor of Delaware LIVE
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s new school funding model will give local school boards greater influence over how education resources are used, placing more responsibility for literacy decisions closer to students, parents and communities.
That shift comes as Delaware attempts to raise third-grade reading proficiency from 40% to 53% by 2028 and as school boards have more information available to understand where students are performing, whether they are making progress and where additional support may be needed.
For school boards, those two changes are connected.  Assessment results provide a lagging measure of where students ended the year. Leading indicators collected throughout the year can show whether students are on track and whether the district’s strategy is working. Together, that information can help boards evaluate whether district spending is aligned with the needs of students and the outcomes the district is trying to achieve.
“The opportunity is to make a much clearer connection between what we know about student performance and where we invest our resources,” said Julia Keleher, executive director of First State Educate. “What are the results telling us? What does the district believe is driving them? What is the strategy for improving them? And does our budget put resources behind that strategy?”
From approving budgets to aligning investments with outcomes 
School boards have always approved district budgets. Greater funding flexibility makes it even more important for boards to understand what need an investment is intended to address and what result it is expected to produce.
In literacy, for example, annual assessment results may show where proficiency remains low, while screening, student progress, attendance, intervention participation and other leading indicators can provide more current information about where students are struggling and whether existing strategies are working.
The superintendent and district team use that information to diagnose needs and recommend how resources should be used. The board’s role is to determine whether the proposed investments are aligned with the district’s student outcome goals, whether there is evidence supporting the strategy, and what information the board will receive to know whether the investment is producing the intended result.
Those decisions could include investments in classroom instruction, intervention for struggling students, professional learning, staffing, student supports or other strategies identified by the district.
“The budget should tell the same story as the district’s student outcome goals,” Keleher said. “If third-grade reading is a priority, the board should be able to see how resources are supporting the district’s strategy for improving it. Then, throughout the year, the board should be looking at the indicators the district has identified to understand whether that investment is helping move students toward the goal.”
Local flexibility creates different choices
Not every Delaware district faces the same literacy challenge.
One district may need to strengthen reading instruction across all elementary schools. Another may find that its greatest needs are concentrated in a small number of schools. Some districts may need to focus on students entering school without foundational skills, while others may need stronger intervention for children who have fallen behind.
The new funding model gives boards an opportunity to respond to those differences rather than applying the same solution everywhere.
But local flexibility also carries risk. Boards could spread resources across too many priorities, continue programs without sufficient evidence or focus on activities that are visible to the community but have little effect on reading.
The central question is not whether a district spends more. It is whether the board can connect its spending choices to a clearly identified student need and a measurable academic objective.
Parents can help define the problem
Greater local control also creates an opportunity for parents and community members to become more involved in setting education priorities.
Assessment data can show where students are struggling, but it may not explain why. Parents can help boards understand whether families receive clear information about reading performance, whether students can access additional support, and whether attendance, transportation, language, scheduling, or other barriers limit participation. That information can help a board evaluate whether the district’s proposed spending responds to the needs behind the data.
“Community engagement should help shape the decision, not simply react to it,” Keleher said. “Parents can help boards understand barriers and student needs that may not be visible in a spreadsheet. When resources are limited, that perspective matters in deciding where an investment is most needed and what problem it should solve. “Meaningful engagement would occur before the district commits to a strategy, not only after administrators have presented a finished proposal.
Complex decisions require the right expertise 
Greater flexibility does not mean boards or districts are expected to have every type of expertise internally. Decisions about how to improve literacy and where to invest limited resources can involve student performance data, instructional research, implementation evidence, financial analysis, community input and governance considerations.
Districts can draw on the expertise needed to strengthen those decisions, whether from state education officials, educators and literacy specialists, researchers, financial experts, community organizations or others with relevant knowledge and experience. The question is not whether outside perspectives should influence the decision, but whether the district has assembled the information and expertise necessary to make a well-supported investment.
For boards, that expertise should strengthen, not replace, their governance role. The board still must understand what student need the investment addresses, why the proposed approach is expected to help, what it will cost, what results are expected and how progress will be monitored.
Measuring whether the decision worked
The new funding model also will require boards to think more carefully about results.
Annual state testing remains an important measure, but boards cannot wait until the end of the school year to determine whether students are progressing.
They will need regular, understandable information showing whether the district’s strategy is reaching the intended students and whether reading performance is moving in the right direction.
That does not require board members to manage daily instruction. It requires them to agree with district leadership in advance about what progress should look like, when it should be visible and how the administration will respond if improvement does not occur.
A literacy investment should begin with several broad questions:

What student need is the district trying to address?
Why is the proposed approach appropriate?
How did parents and educators help shape the decision?
What result should the board expect?
When will the board know whether the strategy is working?
What will change if progress falls short?

Those questions preserve the distinction between governance and management while creating meaningful accountability.
A test of local governance
Delaware’s new funding model is based partly on the idea that local leaders can make better decisions when resources and authority are placed closer to students.
Literacy will provide an early test of that premise.
Experts such as First State Educate can help boards understand data and strengthen their decision-making processes. Administrators can recommend strategies. Educators can explain classroom needs. Parents can identify barriers and community priorities. School boards must bring those perspectives together and make choices that reflect both local needs and the state’s larger academic expectations.
By 2028, the public will be able to judge the new funding model by more than the amount of money distributed or the percentage placed under local control. Its most important measure will be whether substantially more Delaware children can read at grade level.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Strafford County food pantries raise alarm about increasing hunger and food insecurity
description: New Hampshire families are struggling to put food on the table and the problem is only getting worse, according to a new report from Feeding America and a group of local charity leaders who gathered to discuss the issue in Rochester this week. Feeding America, a national nonprofit, reported that food insecurity in New Hampshire […]
text:
New Hampshire Food Bank Executive Director Elsy Cipriani (center) speaks about her concerns that recent state policy changes will harm the state’s already low SNAP enrollment rates. On her left and right, respectively, are Annie Hayes, executive director at the Portsmouth food pantry Gather NH, and Marion Harris, also with the New Hampshire Food Bank. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)New Hampshire families are struggling to put food on the table and the problem is only getting worse, according to a new report from Feeding America and a group of local charity leaders who gathered to discuss the issue in Rochester this week.
Feeding America, a national nonprofit, reported that food insecurity in New Hampshire rose from 10.7% of residents in 2023 to 11.7% in 2024 in its recently released annual report. Among children, the problem is even more severe. Child food insecurity rose in the state 6% during that time period, from 14.4% to 15.5% of New Hampshire children.
Data for 2025 and 2026 isn’t available because of delays in federal data reporting. However, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which had been providing this data for around 30 years, canceled its annual Food Security Survey last year. Hunger nonprofits and others are concerned that without the survey they’ll lack an accurate picture of the state and national landscape.
Food insecurity rose from 2023 to 2024, according to the most recent data available from Feeding America. This Bulletin graphic shows the breakdown of that data by county. (Canva graphic by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“These redundant, costly, politicized, and extraneous studies do nothing more than fear monger,” the Trump administration wrote in a press release announcing the cancellation. “For 30 years, this study — initially created by the Clinton administration as a means to support the increase of SNAP eligibility and benefit allotments — failed to present anything more than subjective, liberal fodder.”
Elsy Cipriani, executive director of the New Hampshire Food Bank, told the Bulletin she’s confident food insecurity has only worsened since 2024.
During a roundtable on Tuesday, food pantry and food bank officials described an increasing number of sign-ups from people concerned about the economy, as well as a rise in homelessness among those they help. Others have been asking if they can visit the pantry after hours because they’re working jobs during operating hours, which don’t pay enough to cover expenses, they said.
Officials also lamented the rising cost of food, fuel (which adds to delivery costs), and other necessary resources, which is inhibiting their ability to meet the growing demand. They said inflation is also hitting their benefactors’ wallets and decreasing donations.
Cipriani said last year it cost the food bank 90 cents per meal to provide food to its partner organizations, such as local food pantries, but this year that’s risen 8 cents per meal.
“Which a lot of people think, ‘Now, doesn’t sound like a lot. That’s only eight cents,’” she said. “But you multiply that for 20 million pounds of food.”
U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who organized the roundtable, took aim at federal cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program implemented by Republicans in their One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
That new law, among other things, capped future SNAP funding increases at the rate of inflation; restricted the factors that can be taken into account when deciding a family’s benefit amount; banned many legal migrants (specifically refugees and asylees) from benefitting from the program (people in the country without legal status were already ineligible); and implemented stricter work requirements. Those measures have been going into effect in a piecemeal schedule since the bill was signed into law in July 2025.
“This was done as a deliberative design to try and reduce the number of people who are getting assistance,” Shaheen said. “And that’s part of the problem because people are dealing with the increased cost of everything from energy to groceries to rent, and we should be doing everything possible to ensure that people have enough to eat.”
The nonprofit leaders also discussed how other issues, such as homelessness, are compounding the problem. Rochester Mayor Chuck Grassie said the city is struggling to build shelters because neighbors oppose them.
“Everybody says, ‘Oh yeah, we need more of that, but no, we don’t want it in my neighborhood or not here. Do it there,’” Grassie said. “Hopefully, working with the county, we’ll be able to get some more of that stuff, because I think they’re in a good place to try to promote that.”
All the nonprofit leaders were most concerned about the youth going hungry in the state.
“I just learned that we’re serving 46 homeless high school students,” Annie Hayes, executive director of Gather, a food pantry in Portsmouth, said.
U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (left) and Rochester Mayor Chuck Grassie (right) listen to food bank and food pantry officials during a roundtable discussion in Rochester on food insecurity, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: 150 people evacuated as crews battle wildfire in south Arkansas
description: About 150 people in Union County have been evacuated as crews worked to contain a wildfire that’s grown to 2,000 acres, Arkansas authorities said Friday morning. The Arkansas Department of Agriculture said in a post on X that the fire at Pine Tree Road has been burning since Thursday night. “Ten bulldozers are currently working […]
text:
(Getty Images)About 150 people in Union County have been evacuated as crews worked to contain a wildfire that’s grown to 2,000 acres, Arkansas authorities said Friday morning.
The Arkansas Department of Agriculture said in a post on X that the fire at Pine Tree Road has been burning since Thursday night.
“Ten bulldozers are currently working the fire, and we are preparing replacement crews from other parts of the state,” the department’s post said. “A detection flight over southeast Arkansas is planned this morning. Air tankers are scheduled to begin aerial operations immediately.”
Shelters have been opened in El Dorado at the Municipal Auditorium and Immanuel Baptist Church, according to the Union County Sheriff’s Office.
Union County Judge Mike Loftin said by mid-morning Friday aircraft had dropped water on the fire about five or six times. Loftin said there were no reports of any injuries or homes lost from the fire.
“The wind was changing direction on us,” Loftin said. “Today the wind has died down.”
Arkansas launches online wildfire tracker as drought continues

A months-long drought has left a third of Arkansas at high risk of wildfires and all but a handful of counties are under burn bans. 
As of Friday, there have been 1,120 wildfires in Arkansas so far this year affecting more than 29,000 acres, according to an online tracker launched by the state earlier this week. 
The agriculture department has warned that fire risk is expected to go up across the state in the coming weeks. 
“It’s probably been a month since we had a measurable rain in this area,” El Dorado Mayor Paul Choate said. “The woods were primed for a fire.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: $10M in grant funding will expand in-district special education in CT
description: Funds from CT's High-Quality Special Education Incentives Grant Program will largely go toward hiring more specialists in several districts.
text:
A series of grants first set in motion in 2025 is making its way to schools across the state.
The High-Quality Special Education Incentives Grant Program originated in the biennial budget proposal Gov. Ned Lamont released at the start of the 2025 legislative session. State legislators kept the idea and wrote it into law (along with some bigger special education funding boosts the governor wasn’t quite as enthusiastic about). 
Now that fiscal year 2027 has officially begun, the first round of grant money is ready to go out.
In total, the state is sending $10.6 million to 41 school districts. The grant was competitive, with over 100 districts submitting proposals, and the money was awarded based on the strength and specificity of the application. Individual districts could qualify for a maximum of $350,000, while collaborative projects could qualify for $500,000.
The general aim of the grant is to get schools to build more in-district special education programming. 
It’s common for schools to send students with disabilities to outplacement facilities, which can be extremely expensive. Until recently, however, those were also the only costs the state would (partially) reimburse. The idea behind the new grants was that by boosting in-district services, costs for both schools and the state should go down.
Plus, students receiving in-district services can spend more time with their general education peers. That’s a major goal of special education advocates in the state and throughout the country. 
Lamont acknowledged as much in a statement announcing the release of the grant funds.
“It is important that school districts have the resources to support special education programming that allows more students to learn alongside their peers in their own communities,” Lamont said.
What exactly schools will do with the money will vary, though it generally involves hiring staff. For example:

Hartford is using its $350,000 to hire two special education teachers and a social worker; those staffers will expand the district’s RISE Academy into Bulkeley High School, where they will serve an estimated 30 students. 
Putnam is receiving $315,000 to hire a specialized program coordinator and a special education coach; the former will provide much-needed administrative support, while the latter will train teachers on implementing IEPs and providing quality services.
West Hartford is using $350,000 to hire two special educators and a board certified behavior analyst as part of its “push-in” model — sending extra hands into classrooms to support students with high needs rather than pulling them out into isolated settings.
Simsbury already opened a new building earlier this year for its New Path program, which supports students grades 9 to 12 with high behavioral needs. It’s using $350,000 to expand that to grades 7 and 8 by hiring a new teacher and paraeducator. The money will also support the purchase of a van to transport students back to the main school, giving them more time to spend with general education peers.
New Haven will spend part of its $350,000 to create one new specialized classroom program for children in kindergarten through 5th grade with autism. The district came under fire earlier this year after a state complaint alleged it had failed to staff such a classroom with a special education teacher. The rest of the money will go toward professional development.

Some proposals also involve opening or expanding new facilities. That includes Bethel and Brookfield, one of two pairs of districts to win $500,000 through a collaborative proposal. In their case, the money will go to support the creation of a “living laboratory” for students aged 18 to 22 who need additional support mastering activities of daily living and transitioning to the workforce. The house is located near downtown Bethel, with multiple job sites in walking distance.
Bethel’s director of special education services, Meghan Stabile, said the district already had a robust program before the grant, but the space it was using lacked important amenities for daily living activities, such as a full kitchen. Moreover, it wasn’t big enough to accommodate the growing need; Bethel, like most districts in Connecticut, has seen a steady rise in special education students in recent years.
“The community here in Bethel is pretty amazing and we have so many local businesses that employ our students, and so they’re going to be able to keep those job sites … it’s pretty amazing, actually,” Stabile said.
A full list of grant awardees can be found here.
Grant money aside, the issue of special education funding remains far from resolved in Connecticut. 
Special education is not factored into the state’s main funding system — a problem when the population of special needs students keeps growing. The SEED grant — also passed in 2025 — aimed to fill in the gap, but it remains underfunded by about $150 million. That’s far more than what the High-Quality Special Education Incentives Grant provides.
Lamont has signaled he’s aware of the problem. On various occasions speaking with educators and state leaders this year, he has brought up the idea that the state could step in to provide or negotiate for services with more leverage than individual districts can muster. 
His ongoing Blue-Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability is also looking at special education as part of its larger effort to reimagine the state’s relationship to its public schools.
The commission aims to release its recommendations at the end of the year, in time for the 2027 legislative session.
