name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Fewer e-cigarette sales in CT, but nicotine use is up
description: The amount of nicotine Connecticut residents purchase in e-cigarettes has increased, despite fewer unit sales, according to state data.
text:
Electronic cigarette sales hit record-low numbers in Connecticut this year — but this does not mean residents are consuming less nicotine.
The amount of nicotine Connecticut residents purchase in e-cigarettes has increased, despite fewer unit sales, according to state data. And nicotine pouches, which gained widespread national popularity in recent years, are a growing market in Connecticut.
In Connecticut in May, there were fewer e-cigarettes sold, including vapes, compared to any month in the past six years. Across the state, there were 440,000 sales.
As many as 1.2 million e-cigarette products were sold in a single month in recent years. The most sales were recorded in March 2022, when 1.24 million products were purchased.
While unit sales fell from March 2020 to March 2026, the amount of nicotine sold in e-cigarette products, not including products sold online or in vape shops, increased by more than 240% in Connecticut, according to an analysis by Monitoring Tobacco Product Use, an organization that works with the CDC Foundation and other national organizations.
Companies across the nation are making e-cigarettes larger and stronger. A study published in the National Library of Medicine in 2023 found that from 2017 to 2022, the amount of nicotine in most e-cigarettes increased. A similar study published in 2023 found that the products are both larger and stronger.
“Compared to just five years ago, today’s e-cigarettes deliver higher levels of nicotine at increasingly cheaper prices,” the CDC Foundation told the CT Mirror in an email. “E-cigarettes remain the most commonly used tobacco product among youth and young adults, and flavors continue to drive youth use.”
But the market is rapidly changing. Sales of nicotine pouches increased across the country over the past six years, and an industry that used to be worth less than $100 million is now a $600 million business.
A popular nicotine pouch brand called “ZYN” is owned by Philip Morris International, a tobacco company headquartered in Stamford.
There is currently no publicly available state-level data tracking nicotine pouch sales in Connecticut, but the rate of youth nicotine pouch use is 2.4%, or approximately 3,800 high school students, according to the state Department of Public Health.
Massachusetts, Rhode Island and New York have all seen dollar sales of nicotine pouches increase by tens of millions of dollars since 2020.
While national sales of nicotine pouches are increasing, Connecticut’s neighboring states are not experiencing the phenomenon as Connecticut regarding e-cigarettes. In New York and Massachusetts, nicotine sales have increased slightly, but unit sales of e-cigarettes have also increased slightly. 
Some states with no restrictions on flavored nicotine products, like Washington, have seen fairly steady numbers of unit sales but higher amounts of nicotine sold.
In Connecticut, around 16.8% of adults use any tobacco product, including e-cigarettes, according to the latest numbers from the Department of Public Health from 2024. This number has decreased since 2015, when nearly 20% of Connecticut adults used tobacco products. (Nicotine pouches were not included in this survey).
While the number of residents using tobacco products has declined, the American Lung Association rated the state’s legislative tobacco control an “F” in 2026. The state allocated $13.6 million and received $1.2 million federally in FY 2026 for tobacco control programs, but the CDC recommends spending $32 million on control programs.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware nuclear task force report could shape state energy policy for years, but…
description: Industry veteran says the state’s review lacked the technical depth needed as electricity costs rise and Delaware remains dependent on imported power DOVER, Del – Delaware’s Nuclear Energy Feasibility Task Force cannot approve a reactor, select a location or commit public money to a nuclear project.  Its influence, however, could be significant. The General[...]
text:
Caption: Kenneth J. Reuter Jr., a task force participant and longtime energy industry executive, contends the panel did not conduct the structured, technically intensive review necessary to support such a consequential decision.









Industry veteran says the state’s review lacked the technical depth needed as electricity costs rise and Delaware remains dependent on imported power
DOVER, Del – Delaware’s Nuclear Energy Feasibility Task Force cannot approve a reactor, select a location or commit public money to a nuclear project.  Its influence, however, could be significant.
The General Assembly created the task force to help determine whether small modular nuclear reactors could become part of Delaware’s long-term energy supply. Its findings could influence whether lawmakers authorize additional studies, investigate potential sites, revise state permitting laws or decide nuclear power is too costly or uncertain to pursue.
That makes the quality of the task force’s work important.
Kenneth J. Reuter Jr., a task force participant and longtime energy industry executive, contends the panel did not conduct the structured, technically intensive review necessary to support such a consequential decision.
In an Aug. 14 assessment, Reuter said the task force did not hear directly from willing nuclear manufacturers, adequately investigate possible Delaware sites or divide its work among specialized teams.
His criticism does not establish that the task force’s conclusions are wrong. It does raise questions about whether state policymakers have enough information to make decisions that could affect Delaware’s electricity supply, consumer costs and economic competitiveness for decades.
Panel assigned to study nuclear potential
The General Assembly created the Delaware Nuclear Energy Feasibility Task Force in 2025 to examine whether small modular reactors, commonly known as SMRs, could be developed in the state.
SMRs are designed to generate less electricity than conventional nuclear reactors. Supporters say they could be manufactured in sections, installed incrementally and placed on properties that cannot accommodate a traditional nuclear plant.
However, the technology remains commercially developing in the United States. Questions continue about construction costs, licensing schedules, financing and the risks utilities and customers could be asked to assume.
The General Assembly directed the task force to study nuclear energy’s economic impact, regulatory requirements, environmental implications and potential contribution to electric reliability. Its reporting deadline was extended to July 31, 2026.
The task force’s report is advisory. It does not authorize construction, approve a location or require the state to pursue nuclear power. But lawmakers could rely on it when considering future energy legislation and determining whether additional nuclear planning is warranted.
Delaware imports much of its electricity
Delaware generates substantially less electricity than its residents and businesses consume.
Reuter estimates the state currently imports between 45% and 55% of its electricity through PJM, the regional power grid serving Delaware and parts of 12 other states and the District of Columbia.
Importing electricity is a normal part of participating in a regional grid. It does not, by itself, indicate that Delaware faces an immediate shortage. PJM is designed to move power across state lines and allow utilities to purchase electricity from generators throughout the region.
But Reuter argues that Delaware’s dependence creates greater risk as regional demand grows, older generating plants retire and new projects face lengthy development and grid-connection delays.
Data centers, advanced manufacturing and other large electricity users are also adding to projected demand.
Delaware does not need to generate every unit of electricity it consumes. However, the state has limited control over when and where new regional plants are constructed, leaving its customers exposed to supply and price pressures elsewhere in the PJM market.
Intermittent power cannot carry the full load
Reuter argues that Delaware’s energy strategy relies too heavily on intermittent sources such as wind and solar.
Those facilities can contribute electricity when weather conditions permit, reduce fuel consumption and help meet emissions goals. But they cannot continuously produce power without storage, backup generation or other complementary resources.
An energy plan that depends heavily on intermittent sources without sufficient dependable generation would leave Delaware vulnerable during periods when the sun is not shining, the wind is not blowing or regional demand is particularly high, Reuter said.
He argues that Delaware should make the development of additional 24-hour generation a priority, including natural gas plants, nuclear power or a combination of the two.
Natural gas plants can generally be developed more quickly than nuclear facilities and can respond to changing electricity demand. Nuclear plants require longer development and licensing schedules but can provide large amounts of continuous electricity without direct carbon emissions.
Both carry costs and risks. Natural gas exposes customers to fuel-price volatility and future regulatory requirements. Nuclear projects require substantial upfront investment and can experience construction delays and cost overruns.
A responsible state plan would examine those risks without treating intermittent renewable resources as the equivalent of dependable, around-the-clock generation.
Rising electric bills add urgency
The debate is not limited to whether Delaware will have enough power. It also involves what residents and businesses will pay for it.
Residential and industrial electric bills are rising, placing additional pressure on household budgets and increasing operating costs for Delaware employers.
Reuter argues that those costs will continue climbing unless policymakers revise Delaware’s energy strategy and make affordability and dependable generation top state priorities.
Electric bills reflect more than the cost of producing electricity. They can also include transmission expenses, regional capacity charges, utility infrastructure investments, environmental compliance costs and other fees.
However, a tightening regional supply-and-demand balance can increase several of those costs. Delaware’s dependence on imported electricity leaves customers exposed to regional prices that state officials cannot directly control.
For households, higher electric bills reduce the money available for food, housing, health care and other necessities. For manufacturers and other energy-intensive employers, rising power costs can discourage expansion, weaken competitiveness and influence decisions about where companies invest.
Reuter’s position is that Delaware should not evaluate energy projects primarily according to environmental targets or political preferences. Each alternative should be measured by its total cost, reliability, construction schedule and ability to serve customers during periods of peak demand.
Participant questions task force’s approach
Reuter’s primary complaint is that the task force operated more like a broad discussion group than a technically organized panel working toward an actionable plan.
He said only a small number of the approximately 25 members and regular participants had direct experience with electricity generation.
Reuter recommended dividing the work among specialized groups focused on nuclear manufacturers, potential sites, technology selection, safety, environmental effects, permitting, government coordination and public communications.
Under his proposed structure, each group would have been assigned a leader responsible for investigating its subject and regularly reporting findings to the full panel.
Reuter said that structure was not adopted.
He also said no nuclear equipment manufacturer was invited to explain its technology, manufacturing capacity, construction schedules, costs or existing order commitments to the full task force.
According to Reuter, Westinghouse and another manufacturer were willing to make presentations but were not invited. He also said an offer to arrange a task force tour of the Salem and Hope Creek nuclear facilities in New Jersey was not accepted.
Manufacturers have a financial interest in promoting their products, and their claims would require independent scrutiny. However, direct presentations would have allowed task force members to question the companies about technological readiness, construction experience, pricing and financial risks.
Potential sites require closer examination
A complete nuclear feasibility review would eventually need to examine actual Delaware properties.
Potential sites would have to be evaluated for available land, transmission connections, water access, security, emergency planning and nearby development. The willingness of property owners and surrounding communities would also be important.
Reuter said the task force did not conduct sufficiently detailed discussions with potential site owners or determine whether particular properties could accommodate an SMR or a larger conventional reactor.
That distinction matters because a technology that appears promising in a general presentation may not be practical at an available Delaware location.
Preliminary site analysis would not commit the state to a reactor or a particular property. It would help determine whether nuclear power is a realistic Delaware option rather than a theoretical one.
Incomplete report could close the door prematurely
If the task force’s report is incomplete or overly negative, Delaware could abandon nuclear energy before fully understanding its potential.
That could leave the state more dependent on imported power from a regional market facing rising demand and generating-plant retirements.
Delaware could also lose time needed to examine sites, coordinate with federal regulators and develop a specialized workforce. Nuclear projects require years of planning, licensing, financing and construction, meaning a decision to delay preliminary work could have long-term consequences.
Dependable and competitively priced electricity also affects economic development. Manufacturers, health care facilities, technology companies and data centers consider energy availability when deciding where to invest.
A state without a credible plan for meeting future electricity demand could find itself at a competitive disadvantage.
Overly optimistic report also carries risks
A flawed report could create the opposite danger.
If the task force overstates the affordability or commercial readiness of SMRs, lawmakers could advance an expensive project without fully understanding the risks.
Nuclear facilities require substantial upfront investment. Construction delays and cost overruns can fall on customers if utilities are permitted to recover those expenses through electric rates.
Before advancing a project, policymakers would need to determine who would finance it, who would absorb the cost of delays and whether customers could be charged before a reactor begins producing electricity.
A responsible nuclear policy would protect ratepayers while allowing promising technologies to receive serious consideration. Private investors, utilities and manufacturers would need to bear meaningful performance risk rather than shifting every financial uncertainty to customers.
State plan must balance cost and reliability
The task force’s report does not need to provide a final verdict on nuclear power. The developing commercial market for SMRs makes absolute conclusions difficult.
A useful report should distinguish among what is known, what remains uncertain and what Delaware must investigate next.
Possible next steps could include independent cost studies, discussions with manufacturers, preliminary site reviews, federal regulatory coordination and comparisons among nuclear power, natural gas, renewable energy, storage and transmission investments.
Each alternative should be evaluated using consistent standards, including:

Total cost to residential and business customers
Dependable generating capacity
Development and construction time
Performance during peak demand
Fuel and transmission requirements
Environmental effects
Financial risks associated with delays or cost overruns

Wind and solar power can remain part of that mix. But policymakers must distinguish between electricity produced when weather conditions allow and capacity that can be counted on around the clock.
The central question is not whether task force members support or oppose nuclear energy. It is whether their process produced enough evidence to justify the panel’s findings.
A report that dismisses nuclear prematurely could cause Delaware to lose a potentially valuable source of dependable, carbon-free electricity. A report that is too optimistic could expose customers to years of higher rates and construction risk.
Delaware may ultimately choose to pursue nuclear power, continue studying it or reject it. But with electric bills rising, demand growing and regional supplies tightening, Reuter argues that revising the state’s energy plan should be a top policy priority.
That decision should rest on rigorous technical and financial evidence — not an incomplete process, assumptions about future regional supplies or a predetermined preference for any particular energy source.
TO-GO BOX:

The task force: The General Assembly created the Nuclear Energy Feasibility Task Force to study whether small modular reactors could help meet Delaware’s future electricity needs.
The concern: Participant Kenneth J. Reuter Jr. says the review lacked sufficient industry input, technical structure and analysis of potential sites.
The energy challenge: Delaware imports an estimated 45% to 55% of its electricity, while regional demand and electric costs are increasing.
What is at stake: A flawed report could cause Delaware to reject a dependable energy source prematurely — or pursue an expensive project without adequately protecting ratepayers.

name: VTDigger
title: Neema starts at Saint Michael’s College to pursue a career in social work
description:
Neema Isidore came to Vermont speaking Swahili and Kirundi, then rebuilt her life again after a traumatic brain injury a few years later. This week, she starts at Saint Michael's College on a full scholarship—determined to be like the social worker who was once there for her.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Neema starts at Saint Michael’s College to pursu[...]
text:
Neema Isidore will be the first person in her family to attend college. She’s the middle of five siblings, a 2026 graduate of Winooski High School, and she starts at Saint Michael’s College this week.
Neema has known she wanted to go to college since she started high school. The path was challenging; Neema was born in Burundi. She came to Vermont when she was in the 7th grade, speaking Swahili and Kirundi. As she got used to a new community and a new school, she was also learning a new language; then, halfway through high school, she experienced a traumatic brain injury.
Neema persisted, keeping her eyes on her goal. While at Winooski High School, she joined VSAC’s GEAR UP college and career readiness program, which, among other support, helped her visit several colleges. When she toured Saint Michael’s College, she says that she felt immediately connected to the school, the professors, and the campus. She describes it as a comfortable community for her, especially because she wants to attend a college with a smaller and more accessible student population. “They have great professors and it’s close to where I live,” she said. “Even after all the college visits I did, I always gravitated back to St. Mike’s in my mind.” 
Recovering from a brain injury taught Neema a lot about perseverance, and her own capabilities
When Neema was in tenth grade, she experienced a setback from symptoms related to a brain injury. The rehabilitation was tough and memorization was especially hard. “I would study for a test like I would have done before, and not remember anything,” she said. She worked with a social worker to get support and resources, and as she recovered, she began to think about how she could be that person for someone else. “I need my education to do that,” she thought. She decided to pursue a career as a social worker. 
“I love helping people,” Neema shared. “When I think about what interests me and where I like spending my time, it’s doing that.” Neema’s involvement in Peace Jam at Winooski, where she helps organize donations of clothing, food, diapers, and more for people in need, is one way she is connected to helping her community. 
Working one-on-one with her VSAC GEAR UP outreach counselor on her applications and financial aid 
As high school started to wrap up, Neema worked with her VSAC GEAR UP outreach counselor, Stevya Mukuzo, on her applications and her financial aid forms. “I struggled a lot because English isn’t my first language,” Neema noted. “But Stevya was helpful, making sure my mom and I knew what we were doing. I kept asking for help along the way and she kept encouraging me.” 
Stevya worked one-on-one with Neema, helping her understand the FAFSA federal financial aid forms and walking her through each piece of paperwork. “When I needed help, I went to my counselor,” Neema said. “It was hard, but she kept telling me it would be worth it. And now it is and I really appreciate that.” 
Stevya was impressed with Neema’s perseverance. “It’s been inspiring to watch her continue to develop both personally and academically despite challenges along the way,” she shared. “What stands out most to me is her growth in confidence, communication, and self-advocacy. Over time, Neema has become more comfortable speaking up for herself, asking questions, and pursuing opportunities that once may have felt intimidating. She consistently shows a willingness to learn, improve, and push herself outside of her comfort zone.”
Neema was delighted to receive a full tuition scholarship from Saint Michael’s College. She will also be able to leverage additional scholarships and grants, which will help cover some of her other expenses. “It was a happy moment,” she said, when she got the news about her scholarship. “Not everyone gets that opportunity and I was so excited and surprised. My family is very proud,” she added. 
Looking to her future with a positive outlook 
Neema is looking forward to starting at Saint Michael’s College this week. She knows college isn’t going to be easy, but she is strong and resilient. “If I can keep working hard, I can do anything in life,” she said. “It wasn’t easy coming to a place where I didn’t speak the language, and then to have a brain injury and feel like I had to learn everything all over again, it took a lot of hard work and determination to get through that.” 
Neema knows she can do it. A career helping others, as she’s been helped, awaits. 

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. Our grant, scholarship, and workforce development programs create opportunity, help students re-skill or learn new skills, and grow the economy. VSAC’s loan, loan refinance, and loan forgiveness programs provide competitive education financing to students and families. Find us at www.vsac.org or visit Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri placed diabetic teen in a foster home not licensed to take him. He died 24 days later
description: It was after 5 p.m. on May 13, and 17-year-old Korbin Papadopoulos sat in the Macon County office of the Missouri Children’s Division waiting for his next foster placement. Korbin had type 1 diabetes and autism, so his caseworker, another division worker and their supervisor searched the state’s foster provider database for a home licensed […]
text:
Korbin Papadopoulos poses before his first demolition derby competition in August 2025 in Macon. He chose his father's derby number, 13, for his car and added K for his first name (Photo submitted).It was after 5 p.m. on May 13, and 17-year-old Korbin Papadopoulos sat in the Macon County office of the Missouri Children’s Division waiting for his next foster placement.
Korbin had type 1 diabetes and autism, so his caseworker, another division worker and their supervisor searched the state’s foster provider database for a home licensed to handle elevated medical needs.
Between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m., they found what seemed like a match, according to a police investigative report obtained by The Independent. Korbin and two workers set off on the 300-mile journey to southwest Missouri with a brown paper bag containing his medications, arriving around midnight.
On May 19, Macon County workers learned they had made a mistake.
The foster parent was licensed only to care for his own relatives, who did not have diabetes, and could not take Korbin. Workers resumed searching for a foster home equipped for the teen’s medical needs. 
In the ensuing 18 days, the foster parent asked Macon County workers at least twice to move Korbin, according to police records. On June 6, a Children’s Division supervisor booked transportation to return Korbin to the Macon County division office two days later. 
He died that same day, 24 days after arriving in the office.
Autopsy reports list his cause of death as diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening build-up of toxins in the blood that occurs when the body does not have enough insulin. Though police records include a doctor’s note from April showing Korbin was struggling to manage his diabetes and “at high risk” of diabetic ketoacidosis, his foster parent said he didn’t show signs of being sick until a day and a half before his death. After a police investigation, no criminal charges were filed. 
Korbin’s father, Teddy Papadopoulos, told The Independent his son needed help “every step of the way” managing his diabetes — a primary reason he was in foster care.
Natisha Jett, Korbin’s mother, said that while her son knew how to use his blood sugar monitor and insulin pump, “he wouldn’t do it unless someone was there at all times” and needed help entering his carbohydrate intake to adjust his insulin dosage.
The Missouri Department of Social Services, which oversees the Children’s Division, declined to comment on Korbin’s case, citing state privacy laws. But in the months after his death, the Children’s Division issued new instructions addressing both problems that surfaced in his placement: placing children with foster parents who aren’t licensed to take them and responding when foster parents ask that a child be removed from their home.
When reached by The Independent, Korbin’s foster parent declined to comment beyond the contents of publicly available police records.
Missouri child abuse investigators are overwhelmed again as backlogs return

Korbin’s death comes as Missouri’s Children’s Division reckons with mounting caseloads among its child abuse and neglect response team and as workers increasingly struggle to finish investigations within the 45-day deadline in state law. 
Current and former division workers interviewed by The Independent over the last two months say the recent surge in caseloads is compounded by new rules and prescriptive policies that require more steps to close investigations or refer them to the court system. Additional layers of consultation, checklists and supervisory review, they said, are driving turnover and contributing to gaps in care, as remaining workers take on additional cases while training new colleagues.
A division worker involved in Korbin’s placement who was interviewed by police after his death said the teen “had multiple changes in case managers” in the months preceding his death. His current caseworker, according to the police report, had only been handling his case “maybe a week or two” when Korbin was placed in southwest Missouri. His previous case manager quit.
In July, the most recent month with available data, children who had been in foster care for at least a year in northeast Missouri averaged 3.86 workers for the duration of their time in the division’s custody, according to data from the Missouri Department of Social Services. Macon County exceeded that regional average, with 4.38 workers per child. 
Statewide, foster children in care for at least a year averaged 3.82 workers in July.
The division’s July monthly report on its implementation of a 2020 law on foster care, which reflects data through March, noted that “the number of workers assigned per child increases notably for children in care longer than 12 months,” with “potential impacts on continuity of care.”
While the department declined to comment directly on Korbin’s case, it released a statement saying that while the division “recognize(s) that policy enhancements can add steps to frontline work” and respects staff, “the questions that arise following critical incidents underscore leadership’s responsibility to strengthen safeguards when opportunities for improvement are identified.” 
An Aug. 18 message from Children’s Division Director Sara Smith instructs staff to get permission from a foster family’s licensing worker before placing a child in care. If workers need to make an emergency placement without prior approval, they must research the foster parent’s license status and notify the licensing worker within 24 hours of moving the child. 
“It is a violation of law and a significant safety risk to place a child in a home that is only licensed for relative placement when the child in need of placement is not a relative,” Smith wrote.
An Aug. 12 message from Smith to Children’s Division staff says that when foster parents request the removal of a child, “the worker must take immediate steps to locate a new placement within the timeframes given by the provider.” If the foster parent asks for immediate removal, workers “shall not delay making arrangements to move the child while a placement is being located.” 
 ‘Can you take these kids?’

Korbin first entered foster care in 2019. His father told The Independent he and Korbin’s mother approached Children’s Division for help after their son was diagnosed with diabetes and autism. They couldn’t afford the treatment their son’s doctors advised, Papadopoulos said, and the division indicated they could provide resources.
Jett said she and Papadopoulos went to the division because they “just wanted to get (him) the help he needed so he could have the life he deserves.”
Korbin “didn’t need a family,” Papadopoulos said. “He already had a family.”
Papadopoulos said Korbin had more than 15 placements in residential facilities and foster homes before his death.
“I don’t think we ultimately received the help that he really needed,” he said.
In August 2025, while splitting time between his parents, Korbin drove in his first demolition derby competition. He chose 13 for his car, which is his dad’s demolition derby number, with a K for his name — and he won. In a photo from that day, Korbin  is hefting a trophy half his height and his prize money for smashing the other drivers’ cars into submission.
Korbin Papadopoulos, shown here with his winnings, earned first place in his first demolition derby competition in August 2025 (Photo submitted).
A video from that day posted by Jett on Facebook shows the teen speeding past cars laid to waste on the dirt track, still delivering hits with smoke billowing from his car’s crumpled hood.
“Korbin had every single hit down and could tell you exactly what happened,”  Jett wrote.
Korbin spent about a year in a trial placement split between his parents, but re-entered foster care in May when aggressive behavior and problems managing his diabetes persisted.
Macon County staff searching for a placement for Korbin in May relied on the division’s foster family database. One worker called prospective foster parents, while the supervisor searched for licensed medical foster homes, according to police reports.
After Korbin’s death, the worker who made the phone call told police she did not ask the foster parent in southwest Missouri if he was a medical provider.
“I did not ask him specifically if he was a medical provider because (the supervisor) had clicked those selections,” she told police.
The worker told police she informed the foster parent “that Korbin was a type 1 diabetic, that he managed his medications pretty well on his own, that he’d done that for years.”
The phone call wasn’t the first time division workers asked him to take in children with medical needs, the foster parent told police. Previously, he had refused to accept a placement of a teenaged brother and sister who had autism and were nonverbal.
Smith’s Aug. 18 memo acknowledges that when workers search for “elevated medical needs homes,” the foster provider database “will return both licensed relative and foster homes.”
The worker told police on June 23 that she was aware the database returned both kinds of homes.
Relative foster parents, she told police, are “going to get calls a lot. ‘Can you please take these kids?’ But their training and their contract states you cannot take other children.”
The foster parent told police he thought workers wouldn’t have called him about a placement he wasn’t allowed to accept. That was also what he told his licensing worker when she called him saying Papadopoulos couldn’t stay at his house.
“I didn’t know,” he told police. “Children’s Division called me. I thought they’re all looped together.”
 ‘They should have trained me better’

During the nearly three weeks Children’s Division workers in Macon County were struggling to find a medical foster home, Korbin remained in southwest Missouri. 
Korbin’s foster parent told police the teen spent time at the pool, and that he dropped him and his girlfriend off at the movies and to get burgers.
By early June, however, Korbin was getting sick.
The foster parent told police that Children’s Division workers never explained to him exactly what Korbin needed to do to manage his diabetes or how he could help. He didn’t know when Korbin was supposed to check his levels or how often.
The battery on Korbin’s insulin pump died before his death and was never recharged. The device, which is worn externally and delivers insulin under the skin, was still dead when his belongings were returned to his parents, according to data his father downloaded from the device and shared with police.
Korbin’s foster parent told police that the teen ran out of replacement Dexcom blood sugar monitors, which can take continuous glucose readings using a sensor under the skin. They called the pharmacy, the foster parent told police, but were notified that Korbin’s prescription had expired and that he would need a new prescription from a diabetes specialist.
On June 2, the evening after Korbin’s check-up with the nurse practitioner, the teen called emergency medical services to check his blood sugar because he was feeling hot, which can be a sign of high glucose levels. Korbin’s levels were elevated, according to police records, but he told his foster parent he’d be fine if he took his insulin shots.
A day and a half before Korbin died, he started throwing up. His foster parent’s youngest grandkid was also sick, so he told police he thought it might have been a stomach bug.
On June 6, the foster parent thought Korbin might be improving because he was throwing up less, though the teen had been unable to keep much food down. 
The foster parent told police he kept asking Korbin whether he needed to go to urgent care, but the teen said he was alright. When the foster parent tried to wake Korbin so he could take him to urgent care, he told police, the teen’s fingernails were already blue.
“They should have trained me better,” he told police, “and they should only take him somewhere where they could have known something about diabetes.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Shark populations ‘increasing slowly’ in Long Island Sound, CT biologist says
description: Certain shark species native to Long Island Sound are increasing in population, according to CT's Department of Energy and Environmental Protection.
text:
Certain shark species native to Long Island Sound are increasing in population, according to scientists at the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (DEEP).
DEEP fisheries biologist David Molnar said that’s based on shark sighting reports made using the agency’s new coastal shark reporting app.
“Currently, with the reporting app, where anglers, boaters, charter boat captains can report, we believe the populations of some species are increasing slowly,” Molnar said.
Those species include brown sharks, dusky sharks, and sand tiger sharks.
Molnar attributes the population increase to fisheries management practices that protect sharks, as well as the warming waters of the Long Island Sound.
“Animals, especially fish, they don’t recognize political boundaries,” Molnar said. “If Connecticut’s a great place to live and thrive, they’re gonna go there, and if it’s not, they’ll go somewhere else.”
David Cochran is senior director of fish and invertebrates at Mystic Aquarium. He said increases in shark populations on the sound is good news.
“The more abundance there are of sharks, it gives you a better picture of the overall health of the ecosystem,” Cochran said. “So when top predators are present, that means that there’s generally a healthy population of prey animals to sustain them, which builds the foundation for a healthier ecosystem.”
“The other thing they do, because they tend to go after the slower and the weaker or the sicker prey animals, they’re removing those from the populations,” Cochran said, “which actually can help strengthen the genetics of those prey populations and help keep those populations sustained.”
Molnar and Cochran both said the sharks commonly seen in the waters of the sound are not cause for alarm.
“These shark species do not feed on humans, attack humans,” Molnar said. “They’re primarily fish eaters.”
Cochran agrees.
“The risk of having an impactful interaction with these animals is very low,” Cochran said. “They’re not out there marauding and looking for anglers or swimmers or anything like that. They’re just out there living their lives.”
He did say situational awareness is important.
“The best thing to do is just kind of be aware and be mindful of your surroundings,” he said. “If you see a shark out there, give them space.”
While white sharks, commonly referred to as great white sharks, have been spotted increasingly off the coast of Maine, Cochran said they typically don’t spend much time in Long Island Sound.
“Great whites will, or can, make their way into the sound,” Cochran said. “They generally don’t stay for very long. There’s not much for them to eat or to do.”
“It’s not necessarily a typical sighting that you would have,” he said.
This story was first published Aug. 21, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Lincoln, Elmo and the Lizard Man: KY voters to choose next ‘I Voted’ sticker at state fair
description: Lizard Man, Elmo, Abraham Lincoln and more are on the ballot for a heated race to decide which Kentucky student’s “I Voted” sticker will be available during November’s election.  Kentuckians can vote for their favorite design at the Secretary of State’s Office’s booth during the Kentucky State Fair this week. Polls opened Thursday with the […]
text:
Raelynn Short, of Allen County, casts a ballot in the 2026 "I Voted" sticker contest at the Kentucky State Fair with help from her mom, Stacey Simmons.  (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)Lizard Man, Elmo, Abraham Lincoln and more are on the ballot for a heated race to decide which Kentucky student’s “I Voted” sticker will be available during November’s election. 
Kentuckians can vote for their favorite design at the Secretary of State’s Office’s booth during the Kentucky State Fair this week. Polls opened Thursday with the start of the fair in Louisville. 
Drawings from eight finalists appear on the ballot from students across the state. Much like during Kentucky’s regular elections, voters may use a paper ballot to mark their choice and return it to a scanner. 
Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams told the Lantern his office received “several hundred” submissions and he “spent an afternoon doing nothing but going through these.” 
“We try to find ones that we think people will like. Obviously, we try to have a variety of representation around the state. … Creativity is a factor. A lot of kids just use AI, and that’s not interesting. We want to actually see kids with crayons,” Adams said. 
A poster at the Kentucky State Fair shows the eight designs on the ballot in the 2026 “I Voted” sticker contest. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
Kentucky’s first “I Voted Sticker” contest was in 2024. Adams said the idea came from another design in another state’s contest going viral. In recent years, other states have announced a contest for students to submit designs for upcoming elections. 
During the first Kentucky contest, a design from Fleming County student Cash Litzler featuring the Lizard Man, a Spiderman villain, got a lot of attention online. However, another design won that year. Cash is back with another iteration this year with “250,” a nod to the nation’s semiquincentennial. 
Several of the students’ designs this year feature classic Kentucky elements — a cardinal dropping a ballot into a box, a very detailed drawing of the state seal and a portrait of President Abraham Lincoln. Others capture the American duty of voting by using the American flag and an eagle. 
Two are hard to place in the aforementioned categories. Walden Fox, of Fayette County, submitted what looks like a yellow emoji face with “voting time” beneath it. Suzy Heichelbech, of  Woodford County, embodies what many feel when looking at the current political state of the U.S. — a drawing of the meme with Elmo standing in front of fire with the words “I voted.” 
Adams said he loves when a family comes to the booth to vote together. This election has no age restrictions, so any Kentuckian may vote. The adults tend to love the funny ones, like the green monsters and Elmo memes, but the kids are “super serious about this.” He attributed the votes of kids last year wanting “to present a good image of our state” to the winning sticker last year from Alyson Marinich, of Bluegrass Middle School in Hardin County. 
Secretary of State Michael Adams holds the winning design from the 2025 “I Voted” sticker contest. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
Alyson, now in eighth grade, told the Lantern she entered the contest after hearing about it from one of her teachers. Her winning design — a portrait of her grandmother’s horse and a garland of roses — was available during the May primary to voters. Alyson and her family helped pass out stickers at a polling place in Hardin County. The experience “taught me the importance of voting,” she said. 
“Just be creative,” Alyson said for students who want to enter a future contest. “Put whatever you want on that sticker that you want to design. Don’t be scared to do anything.” 
Alyson Marinich holds a roll of stickers with her winning design from the 2025 “I Voted” sticker contest. (Photo provided by Heather Marinich)
Adams said his office’s state fair booth also shares information about other services, such as notary, but the sticker election gains the most interest. 
“It’s really great to see people literally take time out of their day, stare at this poster thoughtfully, and make a decision,” Adams said. “That’s really encouraging.”

title: With almost all Alaska primary election day ballots counted, only a few races remain in question
description: The gap between the fifth and sixth-place finishers in Alaska’s 17-way governor race closed to fewer than 300 votes on Thursday as the Alaska Division of Elections published more results from Tuesday’s primary election. As of noon Thursday, fifth-place finisher Treg Taylor had 9,775 votes and sixth-place finisher Click Bishop had 9,489.  Ordinarily, a change[...]
text:
Supporters of various candidates, including Democat Mary Peltola, who is running for the U.S. Senate, her opponent, incumbent U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, and independent gubernatorial candidate Meda DeWitt are gathered on the afternoon of Aug. 18, 2026, at the busy intersection of Northern Lights Boulevard and the Seward Highway. The intersection is a favored spot for sign-waving on primary and general election days. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The gap between the fifth and sixth-place finishers in Alaska’s 17-way governor race closed to fewer than 300 votes on Thursday as the Alaska Division of Elections published more results from Tuesday’s primary election.
As of noon Thursday, fifth-place finisher Treg Taylor had 9,775 votes and sixth-place finisher Click Bishop had 9,489. 
Ordinarily, a change in order between fifth and sixth place doesn’t matter, because only the top four candidates advance to November’s general election. 
But if one of the top four finishers withdraws from the race by Aug. 31, the fifth-place finisher will be promoted and advance to November. 
Ahead of the primary, some candidates for governor said they were considering their options, depending on this week’s results. 
Only one election day precinct remains uncounted — votes from Koliganek in southwest Alaska had not been reported by the end of Thursday — but thousands of absentee and early votes also remain unreported and could change the result.
Voting precincts for the villages of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok in southwest Alaska also reported no results, but those communities were almost entirely destroyed by Typhoon Merbok in 2025 and did not host polling sites.
Counting is expected to wrap up by Aug. 28, the deadline for mailed absentee ballots to reach the Division of Elections.
Democratic frontrunners Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich, who are on track to finish first and second in the primary, have since issued statements implying that they will remain in the race. Third-place Republican finisher Bernadette Wilson has said she will remain in the race if she is the top Republican. 
Fourth-place finisher Dave Bronson issued a statement Wednesday that said in part, “Once the final tabulation of early votes are reported next Tuesday and we have the full picture of where this race stands, our campaign will make the decision that best advances that goal and gives Republicans the strongest path to victory in November.”
In other races, the newly counted ballots confirmed existing trends. In the U.S. Senate race, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola has 48.1% of the vote, and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan has 42.7%. In the No. 3 spot is Republican challenger Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg, with 2.4%. The fourth spot is currently held by progressive Democrat David Leslie, with 1.1%.
If Leslie withdraws or if late-counted votes alter election-day trends, his spot would be taken by conservative Republican Gerald Heikes, who sat just 17 votes behind Leslie on Thursday. 
In the U.S. House race, Republican Rep. Nick Begich III has 46.1% of the vote, ahead of independent challenger Bill Hill, with 30.9%. 
Democratic challenger Matt Schultz was in third with 8% and federal inmate Eric Hafner, a Democratic candidate, was in fourth with 3.8%.
Schultz has already suspended his campaign and is expected to withdraw, which would elevate fifth-place finisher John Williams, a Fairbanks Democrat with 2.6% of the vote. Republican Clay Strickland was in sixth with 2.4%.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas insurance department assists with $29M in consumer recoveries, a 147% increase
description: Kansas Department of Insurance's report for 2025 reveals an increase in money recovered for consumers based on complaints against insurance companies.
text:
Vicki Schmidt, the state's commissioner of insurance, says the Kansas Department of Insurance's investigation of more than 3,000 complaints led to a substantial increase in the amount of money recovered from companies on behalf of consumers in 2025. In this image, Schmidt takes the oath of office Jan. 9, 2023, at the Capitol in Topeka. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Kansas Department of Insurance assisted consumers with recovery of $29.2 million from insurance businesses in 2025 to more than double the amount the agency retrieved for policyholders during the previous year.
The office of Insurance Commissioner Vicki Schmidt said the department worked with consumers and companies in 2024 to recover $11.8 million for Kansans. In the 2025 annual report released Thursday, the agency documented a 147% year-to-year increase in cash recoveries for consumers.
“Complaints and inquiries equip the Department to hold insurance companies accountable and better serve Kansans,” said Schmidt, who chose not to seek reelection this year to a third term as commissioner. “I am proud to advocate on behalf of our consumers to ensure they receive the services and protections outlined in their policies.”
Schmidt said the department relied on consumer complaints to identify insurance companies or agents that warranted investigation for violations of state insurance laws or regulations.
The department’s latest annual “complaint index” was compiled by tracking the top 20 premium-writing companies operating in Kansas and taking into account companies with 10 or more closed complaints for a specific type of insurance during calendar year 2025.
The agency’s report says more than 3,000 complaints were submitted in relation to auto, accident and health, home, life, annuity and long-term care insurance last year. One-third of those requests were tied to vehicle insurance, the report said, while one-fourth related to homeowner or insurance policies.
Overall, the department said, 69% of insurance complaints submitted to the state agency were related to claims handling.
When a consumer submits a written complaint to the department, an insurance company was required by state law to respond to the department’s inquiry within 15 business days. The insurance department retains a record of each complaint filed by a consumer for up to three years.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Why are political insiders so afraid of giving voters more choices?
description: This November, Massachusetts voters can decide whether our elections are working for them, or whether they are mostly working for the people already in power.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS POLITICIANS LOVE talking about democracy. They love reminding voters how sacred the process is, how important participation is, and how deeply they value every voice.  
Then a reform comes along that might give voters more competition and more meaningful choices, and suddenly everyone in the political class starts clutching their pearls. It’s so typical. 
In November, Massachusetts voters will be asked whether they want to adopt an important reform to our election system by approving Question 3, which would institute all-party primaries in state elections and races for congressional offices. Under the proposal, all candidates for an office would appear on one primary ballot, regardless of party, and the top two vote-getters would advance to the general election. 
Maybe you love that idea. Maybe you do not. There are fair arguments to have about how it would work, what it would change, and whether Massachusetts should move away from traditional party primaries. The most important point is simple: voters should get to decide. Whether they would be able to do so was in question until June, when the Supreme Judicial Court rejected an effort by two Democratic Party insiders to have the measure thrown off the ballot.  
The opposition from insiders has been very telling. Both major parties have reasons to feel uncomfortable about this proposal, and honestly, that may be the best argument for taking it seriously. Party insiders like systems they understand, control, and benefit from. They like predictable primaries, protected incumbents, and races where the real decision is made before most voters are even paying attention. 
The problem is that the current system is not working for many voters. Massachusetts has some of the least competitive elections in the country. Roughly three in five legislative races this cycle have only one candidate on the ballot. In a state that loves lecturing everyone else about democracy, too many voters show up to find what amounts to a very expensive coronation. 
That is not healthy, and it is certainly not surprising that the people who benefit from it would prefer to leave it exactly as it is. When elected officials do not have to compete, they do not have to listen. They do not have to defend their records. They do not have to explain why housing is unaffordable, why families are leaving, why taxes keep climbing or why Beacon Hill seems allergic to basic accountability. They can simply survive another cycle, smile for the picture, and carry on. 
All-party primaries would not magically fix every problem in Massachusetts politics. No ballot question can do that. But the proposal puts forward a question worth asking: What would happen if more voters were brought into the process earlier and more candidates had to actually earn support? 
As the former Massachusetts Republican Party chair, I understand the concerns about weakening party identity or changing the traditional path to the general election. Parties matter. Clear political differences matter. Voters should know what candidates believe and what they stand for. But parties should serve voters, not the other way around. 
Too often, our current system seems designed around the comfort of insiders instead of the needs of the public. Massachusetts has a huge number of unenrolled voters, frustrated taxpayers, young families, small business owners, and residents who feel politically homeless. They do not fit neatly into the boxes political professionals keep trying to preserve, which is probably why the professionals get annoyed by them. 
If an incumbent is doing a great job, wonderful. That person should have no trouble making the case to voters. If a challenger has better ideas, voters should get to hear them. If two Democrats, two Republicans, or two candidates with no party label earn the most votes in an all-party primary, voters can make the final call in November. That is not chaos. That is competition. There is a difference, even if Beacon Hill sometimes acts confused. 
The funniest part of this debate is watching insiders pretend their concern is really about protecting voters. Voters are perfectly capable of hearing arguments, comparing candidates, and deciding what kind of system they want. The real fear is not that voters will be confused. The real fear is that voters might finally have more choices. 
This November, Massachusetts voters can decide whether our elections are working for them, or whether they are mostly working for the people already in power. 
No wonder the insiders are worried. 
Jennifer Nassour is the co-founder of the Pocketbook Project, host of the Political Contessa podcast, and former chair of the Massachusetts Republican Party. She serves as the co-finance Chair of the Mike Minogue for Governor campaign.

 Catching Our Eye

• $40 trillion in debt. The New York Times reports, “U.S. Debt Hits $40 Trillion as America’s Borrowing Binge Continues.”
America’s gross national debt topped $40 trillion for the first time on Wednesday, an ominous milestone for an economy that sits on a shaky fiscal foundation after decades of borrowing to pay for the rising costs of the military, social safety net programs and President Trump’s tax cuts.
This year alone, the United States is on track to borrow more than $2 trillion to help pay for its obligations, including spending on the war in Iran and the sweeping tax cuts that Republicans enacted in 2025. Soaring interest payments to investors who have purchased America’s debt now make up about half of that red ink, pushing the United States into a deeper financial hole.
• Trump’s “clean, beautiful coal.” Louisville Public Media reports, “Black lung rates in Appalachia are high as the 1970s, with thousands of miners sick.”
NIOSH researchers found that working veteran underground coal miners in central Appalachia are suffering from the incurable and fatal lung disease at the highest rates in nearly 50 years.
Ohio has only around 15 active coal mines today, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. But, at its peak in the early 1900s, there were hundreds, employing tens of thousands of Ohioans underground.
Miners working in Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia who’ve had at least 25 years underground have the worst rate of coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease. One in three — 32.5% — tested positive in X-rays conducted by NIOSH during the last five years.
• The forever target for corporate and industrial exploitation: Appalachia. The Athens County Independent’s Amanda Pirani reports, “Appalachian Ohio a target for data centers.”
Athens County is just the latest community in Southeast Ohio to be shaken up by data center proposals.
Some public officials and residents hope the centers will bring long-awaited economic development — or at least substantial tax revenue. However, researchers at the Georgia Institute of Technology found that data centers can have positive economic impact — but mostly in metropolitan areas. Rural counties see “negligible gains,” they wrote.
• Disability rights. NPR reports, “They grew up with disability rights. Now, they’re fighting to keep them.”
(A) lawsuit brought by several Republican-led states, Texas v. Kennedy, is working its way through the courts. The plaintiffs argue that the federal government cannot require states to provide disability services in the community rather than in institutions. Then, in June, the Department of Justice (DOJ), which enforces the integration mandate, issued a legal opinion taking a similar position — essentially aligning itself with the plaintiffs in the case. “Congress has not imposed an integration mandate on states,” the memo reads. It goes on to say the Olmstead decision “held only that a state cannot institutionalize such patients without justification. … What counts as adequate justification remains an open question.” In July, the DOJ also clarified that it would no longer enforce Olmstead in the same way it had in the past.
• School attendance. The Cincinnati Enquirer’s Grace Tucker reports, “Why parents might get more calls about student attendance this year.”
Changes in Ohio state law require schools to respond sooner when students are absent. It also removes the condition of medically excused absences, which means doctor appointments can now count toward a student’s chronic absenteeism. The legal definition of truancy, which is based on unexcused absences, has not changed.

title: After 2 Lombardo vetoes, lawmakers plan to again send him a bill capping senior rent increases
description: State lawmakers plan to reintroduce legislation that would limit rent increases for seniors after two previous bills were vetoed by Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo.  Measures to prevent cryptocurrency scams, allocate money to food banks for senior anti-hunger programs, and require more support for deaf and hard of hearing individuals were also included as propo[...]
text:
In his 2025 veto message, Gov. Joe Lombardo said capping rents for seniors could create “ripple effects that disrupt the rental market as a whole.” (Photo: Richard Bednarski/Nevada Current)State lawmakers plan to reintroduce legislation that would limit rent increases for seniors after two previous bills were vetoed by Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. 
Measures to prevent cryptocurrency scams, allocate money to food banks for senior anti-hunger programs, and require more support for deaf and hard of hearing individuals were also included as proposed bill draft requests at Monday’s interim Committee on Senior Citizens, Veterans, and Adults with Special Needs. 
The high cost of living, exacerbated by the lack of affordable housing in Nevada, has made it difficult for seniors living on fixed incomes to afford rent, putting them at risk of eviction and potentially experiencing homelessness. 
A number of older adults are seeing rent hikes they can no longer afford with their Social Security Income or retirement benefits, said Donna Clontz, a retired attorney and volunteer with AARP Nevada.
“They’re forced to choose between paying their rent and having medicine or having food,” she said. “We all see the information online and on television about the fact that about one out of five or one out of six of our kids are going hungry. The same number is true for our seniors. It is really a terrible situation for all of us.” 
The bill draft request approved Monday revives previously failed legislative efforts to offer some rent stabilization for seniors by capping rent from increasing more than 10% for a five year period.
Though the proposal was supported by members AARP and other seniors speaking during public comment, they warned lawmakers even if the cap is approved it could still put people at risk of unaffordable rents. 
Some seniors are “already paying $1,500 a month in rent or $2,000 a month in rent,” Marcy Cooper Smith told lawmakers Monday. “If you’re letting us get a 10% increase on that amount, that’s still a pretty good increase we’re getting hit with.” 
Democratic Assemblywoman Sandra Jauregui first introduced legislation in 2023 seeking to place a one-year 10% rent increase cap rent for people older than 62 or who rely on disability insurance benefits. 
The legislation, which also required landlords to refund fees if they don’t screen a tenant who applied for the unit, was supported by the Nevada Association of Realtors at the time.
Lombardo vetoed the legislation. 
When Jauregui introduced the bill with identical language in 2025, it no longer had the support of the Nevada Association of Realtors. Jauregui later strengthened the legislation by amending the 10% cap down to 5%, saying the association “did not negotiate in good faith.”
Lombardo, once again, vetoed the bill. 
He wrote in his 2025 veto message the legislation could create “ripple effects that disrupt the rental market as a whole.” 
“By prohibiting landlords from increasing rent by more than 5% for certain tenants, the bill may inadvertently encourage preemptive rent hikes before the cap takes effect, making housing less attainable in the short term,” Lombardo wrote. “In the long run, potentially as soon as this biennium, the cap could discourage investment in rental properties, especially as owners struggle with rising costs while being unable to adjust rents to match.” 
At the committee meeting this week, state lawmakers also approved a bill draft to address the rise of cryptocurrency scams by banning the installation, placement, and operation of crypto kiosks and cashier-facilitated cryptocurrency exchange transactions. 
Often located in grocery stores and convenience stores – where ATMs are also typically found –  the kiosks allow people to convert cash into Bitcoin or another cryptocurrency.
The kiosks have become vehicles for scammers, who extort or con victims to deposit cash into a crypto kiosk and transfer it to the scammer’s digital wallet, never to be seen again by the victim, state lawmakers were told in March.
Clontz told lawmakers Monday this has led to people being defrauded out of thousands of dollars, with most of those victims being seniors.
Nevada has 447 bitcoin kiosks, 336 of which are in Southern Nevada, according to a public listing by Bitcoin Depot.
The committee also approved a request to allocate $330,000 to support and expand senior and veteran anti-hunger programs administered by the Three Square Food Bank and the Food Bank of Northern Nevada.
State lawmakers also asked legislative counsel to draft  a bill requiring the administrator of the Division of Human Resources Management to employ a veterans coordinator to oversee a new veteran hiring program and peer mentor program.
Another subject of a bill draft request would require the Nevada Health Authority to maintain a list of assisted living and senior living committees specializing in services for deaf or hard of hearing and require medical intake forms to include an option for individuals to indicate their preferred language to include American Sign Language.

title: ‘Got to play the game’: Missouri doctors group jumps into state politics with $1.5M PAC investment
description: Missouri’s oldest business association is the state’s newest big political donor. On Aug. 14, the Missouri State Medical Association split $1.5 million between two newly created political action committees, Asclepius PAC, named for the hero god of medicine in Greek mythology, and Patients First PAC. The association, which represents doctors and doctors in tr[...]
text:
(Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)Missouri’s oldest business association is the state’s newest big political donor.
On Aug. 14, the Missouri State Medical Association split $1.5 million between two newly created political action committees, Asclepius PAC, named for the hero god of medicine in Greek mythology, and Patients First PAC.
The association, which represents doctors and doctors in training, already has a committee, MO Medical PAC, for pass-through contributions from members. But until this year, the association had used its own funds to contribute only $19,625 to political committees since 2001, Missouri Ethics Commission records show, and has made no donations since 2014.
The money will be contributed to candidates in this year’s legislative elections, said Jeff Howell, executive vice president of the association. The association supports legislation to put limits on prior authorization for medical services and ending the use of managed care for the state’s Medicaid recipients.
“We’re interested in ensuring that Missourians have access to the highest quality healthcare and to reinvest in that through those two PACs,” Howell said.
The donations immediately put the two PACs among the ranks of the best-funded political action committees representing lobbying interests. Only two donors, Michael Rayner, part of the family that owns the agribusiness firm Cargill, and retired investor Rex Sinquefield have contributed more to non-ballot issue committees.
And only four PACs have contributed or spent more than $1.5 million to influence this year’s elections.
The donations got the attention of other big contributors, who wonder how the money will be used.
“Anytime anybody drops that kind of money into a couple PACs, the light bulb kind of goes off, and you’re kind of trying to figure it out,” said Andy Arnold, a long-time lobbyist who donates client funds to candidates from an entity called Paladin PAC.
Paladin PAC has contributed $579,700 to candidate committees and other PACs since the start of 2025 as Arnold pursues legalization of video lottery terminals. All of the money came from J&J Ventures, an Illinois game vendor.  
The medical association already drew notice in the political world when it gave $100,000 to the PAC supporting Dr. Ellen Nichols in her unsuccessful campaign against incumbent state Sen. Jill Carter in the 32nd District Republican primary.
The donation was unusual for the association, Arnold said, but didn’t necessarily signal a change in legislative races statewide.
“She’s a physician. She was running against somebody that wasn’t a physician, and they apparently had some beef with Sen. Carter,” Arnold said. “I don’t know what the beef was, but apparently they did because you don’t just drop $100,000 into a campaign against an incumbent just to do it.”
In this year’s legislative session, the association supported Republican state Rep. Melanie Stinnett’s bill limiting the use of prior authorization for common medical treatments and making other changes intended to make prior authorizations more transparent.
The bill passed the House and stalled in the state Senate. Stinnett is a candidate for state Senate in the 30th District.
The association wants to end or limit the use of managed care in Medicaid, Howell said.
Missouri has paid private insurers to manage parts of the program since the 1990s and expanded their role in 2015 to cover all recipients except people with disabilities and those 65 and over.
“We’d prefer to have it be fee-for-service the way it used to be,” Howell said. “There’s a reason they passed that in the middle of the night.”
A September report by Physicians for a National Health Program, which advocates for a single-payer system, estimated Missouri could save up to $259 million a year in general revenue if the state managed Medicaid directly. Managed care companies refute those findings, arguing their services are necessary to ensure there are financial incentives for care that makes enrollees healthier.
Ed Weisbart, Missouri chair of Physicians for a National Health Program, said the decision to use association funds for politics is long overdue.
“I’ve always thought they were not doing enough,” Weisbart said. “The challenge has been finding the common ground that I thought they should work on that they wanted to work on.”
In 2013, Democratic Gov. Jay Nixon wanted the Republican-controlled General Assembly to expand eligibility for Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act provisions that capped Missouri’s share of the program at 10% of the cost.
The effort failed, and Missouri did not expand eligibility until a 2020 ballot measure mandating coverage. 
Weisbart was on the association’s legislative committee.
“The committee voted to support that initiative, but leadership above the committee didn’t seem particularly interested in prioritizing that as something that they were going to really fight for,” Weisbart said.
The association’s MO Medical PAC, used to accumulate modest donations from physicians, has raised $113,364 since the start of 2025 and made $123,275 in contributions.
The Missouri Health Plan Association PAC, which backs keeping Medicaid recipients in managed care programs, has raised $180,000 and contributed $204,700.
The decision to create the two new PACs is part of being a lobbying interest in Jefferson City, Howell said.
“If other people are going to play the game, you’ve got to play the game,” he said.
The medical association was founded in 1850 and predates the Missouri Chamber of Commerce and Industry by more than 70 years. 
“People have acted a little bit surprised by this,” Howell said. “They really shouldn’t be. We’ve been around forever.”
