name: Maryland Matters
title: There are good reasons to back redistricting reform. ‘They started it’ isn’t one of them
description: The schoolyard excuse for bad behavior, “He started it,” is the worst possible justification for amending the Maryland Constitution to perpetuate the practice of partisan gerrymandering, writes Gary Hodge, who says voters have a choice this fall.
text:
"I voted” stickers rest on a counter at the Pennington County Administration Building during early voting on Jan. 19, 2026, for a municipal election in Rapid City, South Dakota. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Assuming it survives court challenges, the looming question is whether Maryland’s voters will approve the proposed constitutional amendment on congressional redistricting.
It has never been shown that a majority of Marylanders support mid-census redistricting, extreme partisan gerrymandering, or the political objective of redrawing congressional districts to defeat the lone Republican in Maryland’s 10-member congressional delegation.
As a lifelong Marylander, a Democrat, a public servant and former elected official, I could never support an unworthy cause just because other states choose to compromise their principles under pressure from President Donald Trump.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Maryland should be a leader, not a follower, and do what’s right, fair and just, based on our enduring principles of representative government. The schoolyard excuse for bad behavior, “He started it,” is the worst possible justification for amending the Maryland Constitution to perpetuate the practice of partisan gerrymandering.
Maryland should be setting the standard for good government. Congressional districts should reflect registered Republican and independent (unaffiliated) voters’ share of the Maryland electorate. Silencing their voices, whether deliberately or as an indirect result of this amendment, is wrong.
While the vote tally in the Maryland House of Delegates and Senate was sufficient to put this amendment on the ballot, on Nov, 3, all Maryland voters — Democrats, Republicans and independents — will have a chance to be heard and to accept or reject the proposal.
A strong case has been made for urgent action to block and roll back the Trump administration’s policies, but if this amendment is approved, it won’t have any effect on the election of Maryland’s representatives in Congress for two more years, when Trump’s term of office will be ending.
It remains to be seen whether Maryland voters will turn out to support or defeat this Amendment. Will they seize this opportunity to call for a halt to extreme gerrymandering and the partisan Congressional gridlock it has caused? Will voters demand electoral reform and the creation of an independent redistricting commission?
In the November election, in 2028, 2030 and beyond, we should be focused on winning by challenging our political adversaries with the power of our ideas and our commitment to deliver results that improve the lives of our people, not by attempting to redraw election district boundaries for the sole purpose of gaining a temporary partisan political advantage.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Governor Race: Vivek Ramaswamy spent nearly $700,000 leasing private jets for campaign events
description: Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy has spent nearly 700,000 dollars leasing a private jet since the start of his campaign, according to campaign finance records.  Ramaswamy has spent, at least, nearly $690,000 leasing aircrafts since the start of his campaign, according to campaign finance reports.  The Republican candidate spent nearly $[...]
text:
Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy. (Photo by WEWS.)Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy has spent nearly 700,000 dollars leasing a private jet since the start of his campaign, according to campaign finance records. 
Ramaswamy has spent, at least, nearly $690,000 leasing aircrafts since the start of his campaign, according to campaign finance reports. 
The Republican candidate spent nearly $560,000 leasing a private jet from V Leasing LLC, whose address listed for the company is a house owned by Ramaswamy, according to campaign finance reports from July 2025, January 2026, April 2026, and June 2026. 
He has also spent nearly $130,000 leasing a private jet from TVPX Aircraft Solutions in Salt Lake City, Utah, according to campaign finance reports.. 
Ramaswamy’s campaign did not respond to questions sent multiple times by the Ohio Capital Journal. 
“I love long drives,” Ramaswamy said in May when talking to a Youngstown news station.
“You think about the time we spend in Trumbull County, and you think about the time we even spend just going for a nice jog. You think about Cuyahoga National Park, not far from where we are. I’m a nature guy.”
Ramaswamy has loaned his campaign more than $25 million, according to campaign finance reports. The Ohio Capital Journal reported earlier this year that Ramaswamy’s campaign has put more than a half of million dollars on credit cards.
“If he is basically fronting money to rent a plane from himself, and then if he does not forgive the loans but reimburses himself, he’ll essentially be using donor funds to pay himself,” said Jordan Libowitz, vice president in communications for the nonprofit watchdog Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington. 
Ohio Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton often talks about how she drives a Jeep. 
“As life becomes even more expensive for Ohio families, Vivek Ramaswamy is spending hundreds of thousands of dollars flying around the world to luxury destinations on his private jet, treating Ohio like a flyover state,” said Addie Bullock, spokeswoman for the Acton campaign. “Ohioans know they can’t trust a billionaire who looks down at us from 30,000 feet to understand the challenges we’re facing or to fight for us.” 
David Cohen, political science professor and director of the Applied Politics Program at University of Akron’s Bliss Institute, said he can’t think of another candidate running for Ohio office that has used a private jet as their main mode of transportation for campaign events. 
“The fact that Ramaswamy has spent two years flying around on his own private jet is really a bad look,” he said. “I mean, let’s face it: Ohio is not California or Texas. You can drive from border to border in Ohio in a few hours.”
Ramaswamy flights 
Federal flight records show Ramaswamy flew his private jet, operated by Talon Air LLC, to at least six campaign events in Ohio, Washington D.C., and Salt Lake City in April and May. The flights within Ohio lasted about 30 minutes. 
Ramaswamy flew to a campaign event in Lakeside on April 7, taking his private jet from Ohio State University’s airport in Columbus to Port Clinton. 
The next day, Ramaswamy used his private jet to fly from Columbus to Cleveland for a campaign event for the Cleveland Police Patrolmen’s Association.
Ramaswamy took his private jet from Columbus to Youngstown for an April 15 meeting with the Fraternal Order of Police at the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office. 
After winning the primary, Ramaswamy took his private jet from Columbus to Cleveland for an event in Brecksville in Cuyahoga County on May 21. 
“He’s flying between Columbus and Akron for crying out loud, and Columbus and Cleveland,” Cohen said. “That’s a two hour drive. Get in the car.” 
Ramaswamy flew on his private jet from Columbus to Washington, D.C. for a campaign event with Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz on May 13. 
Ramaswamy took his private jet from Columbus to Salt Lake City for a data center energy conference on May 22 and flew back to Columbus on his private jet on May 25.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio immigrant group adds to its list of criminally charged federal agents
description: A count of those working for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security who have been charged with sex crimes or violence against women and children took a big jump on Tuesday.  The vast majority of the accused worked for Border Patrol or Immigration and Customs Enforcement — the agencies tasked with President Donald Trump’s controversial […]
text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer watches a crowd of protesters at Delaney Hall in Newark, New Jersey, on May 25, 2026. (Photo by Ben Ackman/New Jersey Monitor)A count of those working for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security who have been charged with sex crimes or violence against women and children took a big jump on Tuesday. 
The vast majority of the accused worked for Border Patrol or Immigration and Customs Enforcement — the agencies tasked with President Donald Trump’s controversial mass deportations.
The Ohio Immigrant Alliance started searching court records after it was revealed last year that an ICE supervisor in Cincinnati had a lengthy history of violence against a woman with whom he lived. His history included 23 police visits to his house. 
A year earlier, a federal jury convicted an ICE deportation officer in Cincinnati of extorting sex from women over whom he held power.
An earlier version of the report listed 59 Homeland Security employees who had been charged or convicted. The newest version lists 152.
Some of the cases stretch back to the 1980s. But Lynn Tramonte, founder of the Ohio Immigrant Alliance, pointed out that criminality appears to be accelerating as Trump rapidly adds agents to his border-enforcement operation.
Just under one-fourth of the charges and convictions Tramonte and her team found happened since the beginning of the second Trump administration. Fifty-six percent of those on the updated list have been sentenced for their offenses.
About 90% of all cases involve allegations of sexual abuse or gender-based violence, Tramonte said, adding that just over half involved sexual abuse of children. In just under 45% of cases, agents were alleged to have abused their official authority as they committed crimes, she said.
Questions about agents’ vetting and training grew intense last winter when ICE agents in Minneapolis shot two U.S. citizens to death under questionable circumstances.
In July another ICE officer, David Brouillette, shot and killed a Columbian man in Maine. His ex-wife and some former friends told NPR that Brouillette had a long history of racism and violence. 
In an email, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said it vets new agents adequately and holds them accountable when they commit abuses.
“The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors,” the spokesperson said. 
“We take allegations regarding misconduct seriously and cherish the public’s trust. We work tirelessly to uphold the rule of law and hold ourselves accountable.”
Peter L. Markowitz, a professor at Yeshiva University’s Cardozo School of Law, said the list published by the Ohio Immigrant Alliance proves otherwise.
“One of the things that really stood out to me in this report is how plainly it exposed the hypocrisy of the federal immigration authorities,” he said during a virtual press conference. “We’re hearing the claims over and over again from ICE, from the White House about how they’re going after the worst of the worst. 
“But we’ve known for a while that the data just doesn’t match the rhetoric. The most recent data is that about 2% of the most recent immigration court filings involve any criminality at all. Meanwhile, this report is documenting that some of the worst of the worst are in fact employed by ICE. I don’t think this is going to come as a huge surprise to the American public because we’re seeing daily the brutality on our social media feeds.”
Markowitz and Tramonte said that an obvious reform would be to acknowledge that the government is seeking to deport less than 2% of the 66,000 people detained by ICE and Border Patrol based on allegations of criminality. In other words, the overwhelming majority are being held under civil and not criminal law.
Markowitz said “cooperative enforcement strategies” should be employed with documented immigrants.
“ICE is a federal agency that enforces civil law, just like the IRS, the” Securities and Exchange Commission and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, he said. “All these other agencies enforce their laws without using handcuffs and putting people behind bars.”
Those agencies can start a process that leads to criminal charges, “but their first instinct is not to initiate punitive enforcement actions to bring the harshest penalty possible. Instead they try to help the regulated entity to come into compliance.”
Markowitz said immigration authorities have pathways to do something similar.
“Unfortunately, ICE is doing exactly the opposite,” he said. “They’re creating enforcement problems instead of solving enforcement problems.”

title: Ohio Supreme Court allows certification of out-of-state wind farms
description: The Ohio Supreme Court gave the go-ahead for the sale of wind energy in a Tuesday decision regarding out-of-state vendors of the renewable natural resource. Six wind farms in the Midwest were certified to sell wind energy in the state in a supreme court decision that upheld a ruling by the Public Utilities Commission of […]
text:
Wind turbines rise up above farmland.  (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)The Ohio Supreme Court gave the go-ahead for the sale of wind energy in a Tuesday decision regarding out-of-state vendors of the renewable natural resource.
Six wind farms in the Midwest were certified to sell wind energy in the state in a supreme court decision that upheld a ruling by the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio.
The PUCO decision was challenged by Carbon Solutions Group, who has renewable energy clients in Ohio. The group argued that the energy company Avangrid did not meet the criteria to be certified for sales in Ohio, and that the commission didn’t act appropriately in the process of certifying the entities.
The challenge related to wind farms in four different states, each being certified as “a qualifying renewable-energy resource,” as is required in state law for the farms to be able to sell energy in Ohio.
The farms are located in states that don’t connect directly to Ohio, including Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Iowa.
In order to qualify as an energy resource, out-of-state facilities have to prove the energy can be delivered to the state, via a commission-adopted test that determines if energy coming from a noncontiguous state can be sent here.
The commission uses certain power-flow studies to determine whether energy sources sent from other states “have an impact on power flows over transmission lines within Ohio,” according to the supreme court decision.
The company challenging the certifications didn’t argue that the test was unreasonable, but instead that the test was “erroneously applied.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While the utilities commission approved the certifications for three different reasons, the only reason challenged by the Carbon Solutions Group was whether Avangrid had proven they could deliver the wind energy to Ohio.
The group challenging the certifications argued to the supreme court that the commission “erred” in finding that the energy was deliverable, and that the wind farms had “failed to provide sufficient evidence demonstrating” that fact.
The Ohio Supreme Court reviewed reports and multiple pieces of testimony by members of the commission who determined the deliverability requirement had been met, and the majority decision noted a previous decision in which the justices ruled that “if the commission finds that a staff recommendation contains sufficient factual findings and conclusions of law, it may adopt the same.”
“In light of (the staff testimony and analysis) … we find no merit in CSG’s contention that the evidence does not support the staff’s deliverability findings and recommendations,” the majority wrote in the Tuesday decision.
Judge Julia Dorrian of the Tenth District Court of Appeals sat in for Justice Jennifer Brunner on the case, and wrote the majority opinion, joined by Chief Justice Sharon Kennedy and justices Patrick DeWine, Dan Hawkins, and Megan Shanahan.
Dorrian and the majority also said the evidence in the record of the PUCO decision didn’t show “misapprehension, mistake, or willful disregard of duty.”
“Although the commission in its order could have articulated its reasons in a more methodical manner, the commission did address its reasoning as well as the facts on which it relied…,” Dorrian wrote for the majority.
While the court sided with PUCO in saying the commission had the authority to determine if the tests proved the energy could be delivered, justices held back from setting a precedent for future cases that might ask for further study of electricity load, “or other evidence as it determines may be necessary when considering whether the deliverability standard is met.”
Justice Patrick Fischer agreed with part of the majority’s decision, but disagreed with his colleagues in siding with the commission’s decision that the energy could be delivered to the state. Fischer went so far as to say the majority opinion “ignores the commission’s clear violation” of state law as it pertains to record-keeping in contested cases.
“Furthermore, the majority errs in determining that sufficient evidence exists in the record to support the commission’s decision,” Fischer wrote. “In affirming the commission’s order, the majority has acted far beyond the scope of our appellate authority in reviewing commission orders.”
Fischer was joined in his opinion by Judge John Williamowski, a Third District Court of Appeals judge sitting in for Justice Joe Deters.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Voting rights are under fire in Ohio. Casting a ballot is how you fight back.
description: Ohio voters are heading to the polls this November amid a wave of coordinated efforts to sow doubt about the very organizations that help eligible Americans register to vote and turn out to vote. At a moment when voters deserve clear, accurate information about how to participate in our democracy, they are instead being met […]
text:
Getty Images file photo of a voter registration form.Ohio voters are heading to the polls this November amid a wave of coordinated efforts to sow doubt about the very organizations that help eligible Americans register to vote and turn out to vote.
At a moment when voters deserve clear, accurate information about how to participate in our democracy, they are instead being met with efforts to intimidate and confuse them.
Recent actions by state and federal officials have cast an unwarranted shadow over decades of nonpartisan voter registration work, in an attempt to create a climate that risks discouraging eligible Ohioans from exercising one of their most fundamental rights.
Just weeks ago, more than 100 FBI agents raided the Cleveland offices of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative (OOC), a nonprofit that has spent nearly two decades helping register eligible Ohioans. Agents searched employees’ homes and questioned staff for hours, with insufficient public explanation for the raid.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose recently warned voters to be suspicious of voter registration groups like OOC — and mine, the Voter Participation Center (VPC) and Center for Voter Information (CVI). He falsely claimed these organizations don’t actually help unregistered voters and urged Ohioans to ignore our mailers.
Not all outside mail is the same. Legitimate voter registration groups, including VPC and CVI, use the same official forms as state election officials. We also share our materials with election officials in advance.
We’ve worked closely over the years with Ohio election administrators who are entrusted to run free and fair elections. Bad actors don’t do that.
There’s a broader context for Ohioans: the same secretary of state who’s raising alarms about voter registration groups is the one who handed the personal information of eight million Ohio voters over to the Trump administration’s Justice Department.
The state official warning Ohioans not to trust groups that help them register is also cooperating with a federal government building lists of voters and intimidating the organizations that reach them.
With the midterms just months away, Ohioans are being hit with misinformation from multiple directions. No matter the source, the message lands the same way — don’t trust the mail, don’t answer the door, don’t bother casting a ballot.
This confusion is designed to do one thing: keep eligible voters from turning out.
That’s exactly why nonpartisan civic organizations matter. Groups like VPC and CVI help fill the gap left by under-resourced election offices, giving eligible voters official registration applications and accurate information about upcoming elections.
Since 2003, VPC and CVI have helped more than 7 million Americans register to vote nationwide. This year alone, we sent more than 350,000 registration applications directly to unregistered Ohioans.
Helping eligible voters register isn’t a partisan act. It’s a partnership with the state and local officials responsible for elections, built on a simple principle: voters should choose their politicians, not the other way around.
This campaign of confusion succeeds only if Ohioans get discouraged, tune out, or decide it isn’t worth the hassle to vote. Democracy is weakened every time an eligible citizen stays home because they no longer know who to trust.
The answer isn’t to sit out. It’s to show up anyway.
If you’re eligible to vote, confirm you’re registered. If you’ve moved, update your registration. When Election Day arrives, cast your ballot — and help your neighbors to do the same.
The most powerful response to confusion and intimidation is participation.
Democracy doesn’t depend on the people trying to discourage engagement. It depends on the people who show up anyway.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lowering CTs electric bills takes more than political promises
authors: Pete Harrison, Rob Freudenberg and Kyle Mason
description: CT should increase the percentage of renewables in our energy mix by switching to more stable, alternative power sources.
text:
To anyone looking at their electricity bill, it comes as no surprise that Connecticut has some of the highest electricity prices in the country. In 2025 CT ranked second overall with rates expected to rise further. 
In this year’s governor’s race, voters will hear several perspectives of what should be done to lower energy costs. Our organization, Regional Plan Association, would like to offer another: make the shift to renewables, reduce energy demand, and ensure transparent and efficient utility practices.
The unfortunate reality is that there is little a governor or legislature can do to immediately lower energy costs. Transmission rates are set by federal legislators, and supply rates are determined by regional market costs. However, concrete actions can be taken to reduce long-term costs and price volatility. But as election season ramps up, we must resist gimmicks, easy scapegoats, or short-term thinking that could undermine this important work.
Last year, RPA released an electricity bill explainer to help demystify the cost of power, and just published a deep dive into the permitting process in Connecticut as well. Electricity bills consist of four parts: supply (38-42% of your bill), transmission (12-15%), local delivery (30-37%), and public policy fees (12-14%). We need to consider what drives the rates in each section to understand what steps can be taken to lower them.



Let’s start with the public policy fees, which have come under political fire, but are not easily or wisely removed. Forty percent of public policy fees are federal and state contracts that cannot be repealed via legislation. 
The remaining 60% is the Public Benefits Charge (PBC), which includes funding for low-income ratepayer relief as well as incentive programs for energy efficiency and renewable energy. 
We don’t cut off power for people struggling in Connecticut, but someone has to pay for it. Removing this fee would only transfer it to our taxes (and would likely cost more). The remaining incentive programs within the PBC are actively helping reduce energy consumption and supply costs, and accelerating the shift to renewables, including funds going to the Green Bank that have catalyzed nearly $7 of private investment for every public dollar.
Transmission and delivery charges are what utilities collect to enable the movement of power from points of generation to large substations and then onto homes, businesses, and critical facilities. New England has the highest transmission costs of any other region in the country, which can be attributed to geographic constraints in the northeast, population concentrating along the coast, labor costs, and high developer return on equity set by federal and state regulators. Federal regulators recently lowered utility return on investment to around 9.5%, which Eversource and Avangrid have appealed.
The supply charge is the cost to produce electricity, affected by market prices within a competitive auction controlled by the region’s nonprofit grid operator, ISO-NE. Supply, demand, and fuel costs are the largest contributors to price fluctuations in this portion of your bill. 
While Connecticut generates over 40% of New England’s electricity, most of this comes from natural gas. As a recent report from Connecticut LCV and UCONN’s Connecticut Center for Economic Analysis point out, Connecticut significantly expanded its natural gas footprint over a decade ago. While the move eliminated costly, aging, and heavily polluting coal plants, it made the state  more reliant on a fuel source subject to fluctuating prices, as we’ve seen through cold winters and international conflicts.



So what can be done to stabilize and reduce energy costs in Connecticut?
First, we should dramatically increase the percentage of renewables in our energy mix by switching to more stable, alternative power sources that will ultimately reduce the supply charge on bills. 
Spurring the growth of solar and wind – paired with battery and energy storage – is our best bet, and Connecticut should increase solar incentives and expand decentralized solar on existing public infrastructure, while positioning the state for additional offshore wind projects, once federal opposition inevitably ends. 
We should also explore the opportunities for geothermal, and determine whether nuclear energy is worth the environmental, capital, and operating costs. Importantly, we must also increase interstate and interregional transmission capability to connect to renewable sources beyond Connecticut’s border.
The good news is, this shift is already underway, albeit slowly. Revolution Wind – an offshore wind project – is expected to come fully online later this year, and is forecast to save ratepayers over $500 million by reducing our reliance on price-volatile natural gas, particularly during the winter months when the wind blows strongest and fuel prices are high.
Second, we must continue to reduce our energy demand. Since electricity rates are tied to usage, the lower the demand, the lower the bills. Connecticut’s next governor should prioritize energy efficiency programs and commit to a development strategy around transit-oriented communities with higher-density housing, walkability, and transit – all proven to reduce household energy consumption.
Finally, we must require greater transparency and efficiency from our utility companies. As rates have risen steadily over the last few years, utility profits have also skyrocketed. At the same time, there is a need to combat over-investment by utilities that yields them a higher return on equity–a practice known as “gold plating.” 
Steps to achieve greater transparency and efficiency could be achieved either through reforming the Public Utility Regulatory Authority (PURA) rate assessment process, changing the incentive structure to ensure we are building only what we need; or by reconfiguring rate classes to ensure large energy users pay their fair share and better align utility incentives with customer benefits, as Nevada did. Other pathways could include allowing the expansion of municipal utilities.
A healthy focus by gubernatorial candidates on ways to reduce energy costs is welcome, but there are no easy fixes. Instead, Connecticut needs a comprehensive energy strategy that expands energy supply, with a focus on renewables; reduces energy consumption through smart public programs and high-efficiency transit-oriented communities; and holds utilities to best practices and transparency.
Taking these steps can ensure reliable, more affordable power that will allow you to open your electric bill without fear of what’s inside.
Pete Harrison is the Connecticut Director, Rob Freudenberg is the Vice President of Energy and Environment; and Kyle Mason is an Associate Planner Energy and Environment, all for the Regional Plan Association.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bombs failed, deals failed, try supporting the Iranian people
description: The Iranian people reject both the current religious autocracy and a return to past monarchical dictatorship. They want a modern, secular, democratic republic.
text:
The Strait of Hormuz is closed. Then open. Then closed again. Confused? Welcome to 47 years of failed Western policy toward Iran. 
For 47 years, Western leaders have played a high-stakes game of trial and error with the regime in Tehran, trying almost everything to keep the peace. The only problem? Nothing has worked.
For most of these five decades, Washington and European capitals defaulted to economic concessions and diplomatic indulgence, punctuated only by the occasional threat of force. When direct military strikes hit Iran’s state and military infrastructure over the past year, it merely proved what many of us have known all along: whether you sign treaties or drop bombs, neither will ever turn a religious dictatorship into a peaceful neighbor.
The foreign policy establishment fell for a dangerous myth. They believed sanction relief would somehow nurture moderation inside the ruling elite. Instead, Tehran took those financial lifelines and bankrolled domestic repression and regional proxies. On the flip side, military strikes can shatter hardware, but they can’t construct a free society. By constantly choosing between negotiating with the mullahs, threatening them, or bombing them, global leaders completely ignored the real key to Iran’s future: the Iranian people.
Right now, Tehran is in absolute panic. The regime is crumbling from within, wrecked by economic collapse and widespread public anger. To stay alive, it is turning its violence inward on its own citizens in a desperate, bloody spree. Execution rates are skyrocketing, with scores of political prisoners, activists, and dissidents hanged on fabricated security charges. The regime is even carrying out secret executions and burying young protesters in remote deserts, denying families a final goodbye just to prevent funeral gatherings from turning into fresh uprisings.
Make no mistake: this relentless killing spree is not a display of power. It is pure panic. Tehran doesn’t fear foreign diplomats, and it has learned to maneuver around military strikes. What terrifies this dictatorship to its absolute core is its own population, organized and rising up against tyranny.
Decades of appeasement failed, and military action cannot build a democracy. The only viable path left is the one Western powers have ignored for nearly half a century: backing the Iranian public and their right to fight for a free country. Iranians across every city and region have made their demand loud and clear. They reject both the current religious autocracy and a return to past monarchical dictatorship. They want a modern, secular, democratic republic.
That democratic alternative already exists. The National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI) and their Ten-Point Plan for a free Iran offer a clear roadmap as the only viable alternative—calling for a non-nuclear nation, the complete separation of religion and state, gender equality, the abolition of the death penalty, and peaceful coexistence with the world.
It is time for Western governments to throw out 47 years of failed policy. That means maintaining maximum economic pressure to choke off the regime’s terror budget, holding human rights violators accountable on the global stage, and formally recognizing the Iranian people’s struggle for freedom and the legitimate resistance of the Resistance Units of the National Council of Resistance of Iran. 
Neither concessions nor air strikes will bring freedom. The time has come to pursue the only strategy left: standing shoulder-to-shoulder with the Iranian people as they reclaim their nation.
Jila Andalib of Storrs in a member of the Organization of Iranian American Communities – CT.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Board of Elections votes along party lines to reject most Sunday early voting hours
description: The Republican majority on the state Board of Elections voted against including Sunday hours as part of early voting plans in most counties where local boards could not agree on weekend schedules.  Republicans on county boards who presented their early voting plans to the state board on Thursday said it’s not worth opening polling sites […]
text:
Jay Pavey, a Republican member of the Jackson County Board of Elections, told GOP members of the state elections board on Aug. 20, 2026, that if they voted for a plan that received a single positive vote through coercion, it would hurt their party. (Photo by Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)The Republican majority on the state Board of Elections voted against including Sunday hours as part of early voting plans in most counties where local boards could not agree on weekend schedules. 
Republicans on county boards who presented their early voting plans to the state board on Thursday said it’s not worth opening polling sites on Sundays because too few people vote that day, and that Sunday should be reserved for church and family.  
“By having Sunday voting, we are requiring people to work on the Lord’s day,” said Matthew Longworth, a Republican member of the Anson County elections board. “I do believe that the downfall of this country will be contingent on what we do with God.” 
Elections board members on the state and county boards who wanted Sunday hours said they provided access to people who work long or irregular hours, have long commutes, or have care-taking responsibilities. They said some religions observe Saturday as a day of rest. 
Most of the 20 early voting plans the state board considered were adopted along party lines with Republicans in the majority. The other 80 counties in the state had unanimous agreement on their plans and so did not come before the board.
The contentious daylong meeting was held against the backdrop of state Auditor Dave Boliek and his staff having worked to influence local county decisions on voting locations and hours, as NC Newsline has reported.
Boliek hired Dallas Woodhouse, a GOP operative and former executive director of the North Carolina Republican Party, to work with local boards as an elections liaison. In that role, Woodhouse urged county elections chairs to drop Sunday hours and establish early voting sites in certain towns. 
Though Board of Elections Chair Francis De Luca said he never wanted to hear Woodhouse’s name again, the Woodhouse name was tattooed across the board’s proceedings.
NC auditor’s office liaison invoked state GOP wishes in some county early voting plans

“Even though Mr. Woodhouse resigned last month, his fingerprints are all over these plans,” said Siobhan Millen, a Democrat on the state elections board. “They want to tailor who votes by tweaking the sites and the hours.”
The state Board of Elections approves counties’ early voting plans if the five-member local boards do not unanimously agree on dates, locations, or hours. The state board can adopt any of the local plans, or come up with its own. The early voting period stretches from Oct. 15 through Oct. 31. Early voting locations must be open on weekdays and on the final Saturday, under state law. Otherwise, weekends are optional. 
Most of the local disagreements involved Sunday hours because Democrats wanted to provide them and Republicans didn’t. 
Woodhouse’s influence
The state board approved 20 early voting plans Thursday. Most of those votes were along party lines, with Republicans often voting for plans that Republicans on the county election boards wanted.  
Board member Jeff Carmon, a Democrat, asked county board chairs what interactions they had with Woodhouse. Some said they had a few quick discussions. 
Jay DeLancy, a member of the Lee County board, volunteered that Woodhouse called to ask his opinion on Sunday voting. 
“I thought the issue was moot,” Delancy. “In Lee County, we had three hours of Sunday voting. That’s the way it was. I didn’t think we could get rid of it.”
Woodhouse discussed the U.S. Supreme Court’s Louisiana vs. Callais decision and how it affected the issue, DeLancy said. The Callais decision significantly weakened the federal Voting Rights Act.
“He suggested that we add two hours on Saturdays and get rid of Sundays,” DeLancy said. 
The Lee County majority plan has no Sunday voting hours. The state board adopted a minority plan for the county that included three hours of voting on Sunday, Oct. 18. It was one of a handful of votes that was unanimous.
Most of the county elections board chairs whom Woodhouse is known to have contacted about early voting plans did not show up at the state board meeting to explain or defend them. 
That was the case for Jackson County, home to Western Carolina University. 
The Jackson elections board landed in the spotlight this year when its Republican members revealed they were subject to “pressure from Raleigh” not to approve an early voting site on the university’s campus. 
One Republican member on the Jackson board, Jay Pavey voted with Democrats for the campus site, saying it was the best choice. Pavey said he was threatened with removal from the board if he approved the campus site. 
Pavey and the Democrats who voted for the campus site came to Thursday’s state board meeting. The Jackson elections board Chair Bill Thompson, who cast the only vote against the campus site, did not attend. 
Pavey told Republicans on the state board that if they backed a plan “obtained through pressure and obtained through coercion, you’re going to hurt our party.”
Public records revealed that Boliek’s office worked to delay a vote on Jackson’s early voting plan and instructed Thompson to “stand strong” and vote for a plan without the campus site. 
The state board voted unanimously to include the campus site and the Cullowhee Recreation Center, the location that Thompson wanted, as two of four Jackson County early voting sites. 
A compromise in Granville
The state board adopted a compromise plan in Granville County where the local board had not been able to agree on locations. 
Again, Republican members of the Granville Board did not attend the meeting to defend their plan to close one of the county’s most-used sites and move another heavily-used site away from downtown Oxford, while opening a new early voting location in northern Granville.  The Republican plan and the Democrats plan agreed on an early voting site at the Tar River Elementary School in Franklinton.
Granville County elections board fails to adopt unanimous early voting plan after heated meeting

The sites Republicans wanted to move or close were those Black voters used most. 
Democrats want to keep those sites and the Franklinton elementary school, and open the new site in northern Granville.  At a contentious meeting last month, Republican members rejected Democrats’ proposals for four sites, even though the Board of County Commissioners approved the expense. 
After defeating a proposal in a 3-2 vote to adopt the sites Granville Democrats wanted, the state board voted 4-1 to keep the South Branch Library site rather than close it, keep the elementary school and the northern Granville site, but to move a fourth site from central Oxford to the Granville County Convention & Expo Center, which is outside downtown. 
Republican state board member Stacy “Four” Eggers IV, presented the four-site plan as a compromise, but Carmon didn’t think it was a good one. 
“If they’ve said that [central Oxford] area is heavily populated with Black and brown individuals, how can we say it does not disproportionately impact them?” Carmon asked. 
A controversial 2024 law stripped power to appoint the State Board of Elections from governor-elect Josh Stein, a Democrat, and gave it to Boliek, a Republican. It also allowed the board to flip from a Democratic to a Republican majority. Before 2025, the majority of election board members belonged to the governor’s party. Boliek appoints the chairs of the majority-Republican local elections boards. Stein and then Gov. Roy Cooper sued over the law. After conflicting lower court rulings, the state Supreme Court allowed the law to take effect while Stein appeals.

title: South Dakota airport directors seek additional funding for construction projects
description: The directors of the Rapid City and Sioux Falls airports urged the state Thursday to provide additional financial support for their construction projects. The two projects are already each set to benefit from $15 million in low-interest state loans, which the Legislature and Gov. Larry Rhoden authorized from a state housing infrastructure fund earlier this [[...]
text:
A rendering of the completed Sioux Falls Regional Airport expansion project. (Courtesy of Sioux Falls Regional Airport/South Dakota Aeronautics Commission)The directors of the Rapid City and Sioux Falls airports urged the state Thursday to provide additional financial support for their construction projects.
The two projects are already each set to benefit from $15 million in low-interest state loans, which the Legislature and Gov. Larry Rhoden authorized from a state housing infrastructure fund earlier this year. The loans carry 2% interest over 20-year terms, with repayments returning to the housing fund for future development projects. 
Rapid City Regional Airport Executive Director Patrick Dame and Sioux Falls Regional Airport Executive Director Dan Letellier briefed the South Dakota Aeronautics Commission about the expansion projects. They asked the commission to form a subcommittee to tour their facilities and discuss funding in more depth. 
Rapid City Regional Airport
Dame reported a record 452,195 passengers boarded commercial flights in Rapid City last year, up 5.8% and the airport’s third consecutive year of growth. 
He said gate congestion is a problem, including passengers standing in hallways due to a lack of seating. A shortage of overnight parking is also discouraging airlines from adding routes, he said.
Airport expansion loans cleared for takeoff despite turbulence in legislative committee

“We actually do get notifications of upwards of 45-minute wait times to get through TSA,” Dame said, in addition to baggage being moved largely by hand and gate areas designed for 76-seat jets handling aircraft carrying up to 115 passengers.
A $70.6 million project to rebuild the Transportation Security Administration checkpoint, baggage screening, and ticketing areas is funded roughly 70% by federal sources, 25% local and 5% state. Dame said the new TSA checkpoint is scheduled to open in October.
The larger project is a $121 million addition of five gates. Forty million dollars is expected in federal funding. The rest of the funding is state and local, including the $15 million state loan.
“So there is a considerable amount of local funding going into this project, because our community views us to be a very important project and very instrumental to the future development of western South Dakota,” Dame said. 
However, Dame said inflation is taking a toll on project costs. He declined to name a specific amount of extra money he’d like to receive from the state, saying he’d rather work through a subcommittee, but when pressed he estimated “$5 million between the two airports.“
Sioux Falls Regional Airport
Letellier’s Sioux Falls Regional Airport presentation centered on its $135 million project to expand the terminal, runways and taxiways, and to relieve capacity and gate constraints. 
“We’ve seen consistent passenger growth, really for the last 25 years, averaging 3.5% per year,” Letellier said. 
He said gate areas built for 50 to 60 people are now serving flights carrying 180 passengers, and that the existing concourse is “grandfathered” against current fire code standards and would fail them if rebuilt as-is.
The airport has secured $83.9 million in federal funding, with another $5 million requested. State funding stands at $3.5 million, plus the anticipated $15 million loan. Local funding is projected between $47 million and $50 million. Although Lettelier’s presentation described a $135 million project, the various requested and obtained funding sources add up to almost $160 million.
Separately, Letellier said talks earlier this year with Southwest and American Airlines about new routes cooled after fuel prices spiked amid the Iran war, causing airlines broadly to reassess their schedules.
Beyond that, Letellier asked the commission to support additional state funding — either as a match for federal grants already received, or toward an $8.5 million terminal reconstruction project that is $5 million unfunded.

title: Nicholas Gluba ‘confident’ Libertarians will be allowed on election ballots
description: Nicholas Gluba is “very confident” that he and other Libertarian candidates will make it onto election ballots this fall, he told reporters after making his case for governor at the Iowa State Fair. The Libertarian gubernatorial candidate took to the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox stage Thursday afternoon to speak with fairgoers about his priorities [[...]
text:
Nicholas Gluba speaks to fairgoers at the Iowa State Fair on Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Nicholas Gluba is “very confident” that he and other Libertarian candidates will make it onto election ballots this fall, he told reporters after making his case for governor at the Iowa State Fair.
The Libertarian gubernatorial candidate took to the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox stage Thursday afternoon to speak with fairgoers about his priorities should he be elected as the state’s leader, including restoring election integrity, overhauling property tax policy, ending eminent domain and improving the quality of both Iowa education and water.
Gluba is running with lieutenant governor candidate Charles Aldrich. They were selected Aug. 12 by the Libertarian Party after the State Objections Panel ruled in June that Gluba and previous running mate Jules Cutler were not qualified after Cutler failed to submit an affidavit of candidacy in time.
However, according to a petition Gluba and fellow Libertarians filed in Polk County District Court on Wednesday, Pate refused to accept the convention certificates to place Gluba, Aldrich and congressional candidate Jacob Heard on the ballot. The “petition for writ of mandamus” states the filers are seeking to have Pate accept and process the Libertarian candidate filings, certify them as nominees and place them on ballots. A hearing for the case is set for Aug. 21.

The Libertarian Party’s issues with entering into Iowa elections need to be faced head-on by ensuring election integrity and “allowing the candidates that want to run and by allowing the people that want to vote for those candidates to have that choice,” Gluba said.
Despite receiving 8,300 nominating petitions for his campaign for governor, Gluba said the Secretary of State’s Office disregarded those Iowans’ ability to choose in removing him. The Secretary of State’s Office has not yet responded to the latest petition.
“We have a party that is actively suppressing Iowa’s ability to choose,” Gluba said. “What we need to do is suppress their ability to suppress us.”
Gluba turned to existing, proposed and enacted, policies in Iowa and other states in how to triumph over some of Iowa’s most pressing problems, he said, like eminent domain abuse and worsening water quality.
Minnesota and Wisconsin have both passed “water clarity acts” that Gluba said he pulled from in crafting his own policy for Iowa, which would include expanding fines for parties illegally dumping in Iowa water and placing restrictions on how close pesticides and other products can be used in relation to moving waterways. As “pesticides are necessary” in farming he said spraying fields won’t stop, but it shouldn’t be done next to open, non-private waterways.
When it comes to eminent domain, Gluba said he would bring back legislation written by fellow Libertarian candidate Thomas Laehn in 2025, which saw approval in the Iowa House and Senate but was vetoed by Gov. Kim Reynolds. Gluba said he would be “the governor that says yes” if it makes it through both chambers again.
“We will end eminent domain abuse in the state of Iowa. We will end it now, and we will end it permanently.”
Gluba also wants to change property tax policy in the state to have it based on the last fair-sale purchase price of the property or land rather than relying on what price county assessors place on them.
After buying his home for $180,000, Gluba said the county assessor assessed the property at $230,000 despite buyer and seller agreement on its worth, and then raised it later to $250,000. This means he’s “paying taxes on a $250,000 assessment for a house that (he) could never possibly sell for that amount.”
While Gluba said it might seem strange for a Libertarian to advocate for continuing property tax collection, he recognizes the reality that Iowa needs that line of funding for things like education, which he hopes to bring back to the highest quality in the state by simply asking teachers what they need and providing it for them.
“Property taxes are inherently immoral, and we should get rid of them, but this is Iowa. We don’t have the ability to right now,” Gluba said. “We do still have to fund some things, so we have to have some property taxes, but what we can do is make that system logical.”

title: Court rebuffs attempt to ax ballot statement on WA income tax measure’s budget effects
description: A citizen activist lost his bid Thursday to keep a one-sentence statement off ballots that summarizes how an initiative to repeal Washington’s new income tax on high earners would affect the state budget. State Supreme Court Commissioner Michael Johnston denied Arthur West’s request for a preliminary injunction to block a state law requiring inclusion of […]
text:
The Temple of Justice in Washington state. (Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)A citizen activist lost his bid Thursday to keep a one-sentence statement off ballots that summarizes how an initiative to repeal Washington’s new income tax on high earners would affect the state budget.
State Supreme Court Commissioner Michael Johnston denied Arthur West’s request for a preliminary injunction to block a state law requiring inclusion of the “public investment impact disclosure” for Initiative 645, which voters will consider in the Nov. 3 election.
Johnston said he was “not persuaded” that West “makes such a strong argument for unconstitutionality as to overcome the public interest” in voters seeing the statement.
In his seven-page ruling, Johnston said he was “mindful of the public’s interest in finality with respect to the ballot” for the 2026 election and found “no compelling basis” for disrupting the process.
The legal fight isn’t over. 
In addition to seeking an injunction, West has asked the state Supreme Court to directly review his appeal of the Aug. 7 ruling by Thurston County Superior Court Judge Chris Lanese that upheld the statute.
Justices will decide later this year whether to take up the case or transfer it to an appeals court.
“I am disappointed but look forward to contesting the constitutionality of the law directly as this appeal proceeds,” West said Thursday.
Initiative 645 would repeal the 9.9% tax on individual and household wage income above $1 million a year that Gov. Bob Ferguson signed into law in late March. The tax is slated to take effect Jan. 1, 2028, with payments due the following year. The state Department of Revenue estimates it would bring in roughly $2.7 billion in its first year.
Under the 2022 law, when a proposed measure would repeal, levy or modify any tax or fee in a way that affects public investments, the ballot must include a “neutral, nonprejudicial disclosure” of how funding would increase or decrease.
The statement for I-645 drafted by Attorney General Nick Brown’s office reads: “This measure would decrease funding for public K-12 education, higher education (including universities and community colleges), and human services (primarily healthcare).”
The attorney general’s office filed a brief opposing West’s request for an injunction, saying it would “deprive the people of information that they are entitled to receive on their ballots.”
West had argued that the 2022 law requiring public investment impact disclosures is unconstitutional. He asserts that it violates the state’s separation of powers doctrine that protects the legislative, executive and judicial branches from each other’s overreach.
The law, he wrote in legal briefs, allows the legislative and executive branches to intrude unfairly on the people’s power to make laws via initiatives. It does so with Initiative 645 by requiring information written by government officials to be put on the ballot. He believes the statement is not written with neutral language and will cause voters to reject the measure.
West also said it is not needed because a separate four-page fiscal impact statement for Initiative 645 will be posted online and put in voter pamphlets.
The Washington State Budget and Policy Center and the Economic Opportunity Institute jointly filed a brief opposing West’s request for an injunction. The two groups, which are against the initiative, point out several states require similar information on ballots.
The Washington State Republican Party, initiative promoter Tim Eyman and the Citizens in Charge Foundation filed separate briefs in support of the West’s request.
In its brief, the GOP did not argue on the constitutionality of the statute. Rather, it contended that the disclosure statement is not required because the income tax is not in force and I-645 only withdraws the state’s authority to collect the tax.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Researcher reports Wisconsin hospitals charge more, but trade group rejects finding
description: Hospital costs in Wisconsin are about 26% higher than in Illinois, according to a new study comparing the two states, but a hospital trade association questions the report’s methods and disputes its conclusions. The reason for the difference isn’t certain, says the report’s co-author, University of Wisconsin economist Anthony Lo Sasso. But he says it […]
text:
(Getty Images)Hospital costs in Wisconsin are about 26% higher than in Illinois, according to a new study comparing the two states, but a hospital trade association questions the report’s methods and disputes its conclusions.
The reason for the difference isn’t certain, says the report’s co-author, University of Wisconsin economist Anthony Lo Sasso. But he says it could be because most metro areas in the state have one dominant hospital and healthcare system.
For hospitals, “it’s not a monopoly market, but it’s a consolidated market,” Lo Sasso said in an interview.
Illinois metro areas appear to have more evenly matched competing healthcare systems — in Chicago, but also in smaller communities around the state, he suggested.
Lo Sasso said the consolidation in Wisconsin appears to give hospital systems more power to negotiate smaller discounts with health insurance plans.
Lo Sasso is based at the UW-Madison La Follette School of Public Affairs. The report was produced jointly with Capital Policy Analytics in Washington, D.C., and was released by the Center for Research on the Wisconsin Economy at UW-Madison.
The report uses data hospitals and health insurers report to the federal government. Hospitals must report their charges for each service. Insurers must report the rates for each service that they’ve negotiated with hospital systems.
In both states, the report focuses on the rates paid by two health insurers, UnitedHealthcare and each state’s Blue Cross plan — Blue Cross Blue Shield of Illinois, and in Wisconsin, Anthem Blue Cross. Both United and Blue Cross have a substantial group of fixed, negotiated rates in both states, the report found.
While Wisconsin has “a handful of large, vertically integrated systems with extensive control over physician supply, service lines, and affiliated health plans,” the report states, Illinois “maintains a more competitive landscape.”
The Illinois sample included 67 hospitals throughout the state, while Wisconsin’s consisted of 58 hospitals. The study compared the charges for services in 26 billing codes that were found in both  states.
“We use 26 high-volume procedures,” Lo Sasso said, that included heart surgery, maternity, orthopedic surgery and trauma procedures. He said the hospitals in the study were “highly representative of each state.”
The report states that Wisconsin hospitals’ 26% higher prices were consistent through a variety of analyses. In addition, at one hospital chain with operations in both Illinois and Wisconsin — Advocate Health, which is Advocate Aurora in Wisconsin — Wisconsin prices were 23% higher, the report found.
Christian Moran, senior vice president for finance and payment at the Wisconsin Hospital Association, said he didn’t believe the report adequately supported its conclusions. 
The hospitals included were “not a representative sample,” accounting for less than half of all Wisconsin hospitals, he said.  He also took issue with the use of two dozen billing codes when there are more than 700 codes to choose from.
“I just don’t believe it’s appropriate to draw conclusions based on that sample and without looking at the broad array of things that are driving healthcare costs,” Moran said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Two family members describe recent ICE arrests in Santa Fe
description: Two relatives of people whom federal immigration agents arrested Wednesday in Santa Fe spoke out at a news conference Thursday, during which New Mexico elected officials decried the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency’s tactics in what they described as a spree of immigration arrests in the city this week.
text:
Madelinie Pernillo, 18, spoke during an Aug. 20, 2026 news conference regarding the recent federal immigration arrest of her uncle in Santa Fe, one of a string of as many as a reported 16 recent arrests in the area in recent days. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
Two relatives of people whom federal immigration agents arrested Wednesday in Santa Fe spoke out at a news conference Thursday, during which New Mexico elected officials decried the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency’s tactics in what they described as a spree of immigration arrests in the city this week. 
Madeline Pernillo, 18, and Yajaira Gutierrez, 19, described ICE’s arrests of their relatives in two separate events Wednesday. Their relatives are two of as many as 16 arrests that local immigrant advocates have identified in Santa Fe and surrounding communities recently, according to the American Civil Liberties Union of New Mexico. 
Pernillo’s description matches one of the more high-profile arrests this week in the parking lot of La Familia’s Alto Street clinic, which resulted in the father of an 11-year-old girl being arrested.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A U.S. Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told Source NM on Thursday that agents “conducted a targeted enforcement operation” against a man they identified as Edgar  Chacon-Miranda when they saw him park at the medical center. 
Pernillo said the man ICE arrested is her uncle. He had just stepped out of the car Wednesday with his 11-year-old daughter before a medical appointment at La Familia’s Alto Street clinic when ICE agents approached their car.
“Just as they were getting out of the car, they were surrounded by ICE agents,” Pernillo said in Spanish. “The agents began questioning the girl, asking for her father’s name, how many siblings she had and if she knew her mother’s name. When she innocently gave her mother’s name, she became upset and started crying.”
After that, agents began threatening to break the car’s windows if Chacon-Miranda did not get out of the car. Chacon-Miranda complied and agents arrested him, Pernillo said. 
“As the agents handcuffed him, my 11-year-old cousin was left traumatized,” she said. “She now wakes up crying at night.”
The statement from the unnamed DHS spokesperson described Chacon-Miranda as a “criminal illegal alien” with an extensive criminal history, including arrests for battery against a household member, criminal sexual penetration, child abuse and child abandonment. 
Court records show Chacon-Miranda was accused of those crimes in Santa Fe in 2018, but the charges were later dropped due to the case not being prosecuted within time limits. 
Immigration attorney Allegra Love, who is representing Chacon-Miranda, blasted ICE in a phone interview with Source NM for suggesting her client was violent or a criminal when he’s never been convicted. She noted he successfully applied to receive lawful permanent resident status after the charges were dropped. 
“He actually qualifies for a green card in the United States despite these charges because he was never convicted of them,” Love said. “That has to mean something, but it doesn’t mean something to ICE. It doesn’t mean anything to ICE.”
The arrest at the clinic parking lot has sparked outrage from local elected officials, who said ICE  should not make immigration-related arrests at medical facilities, as well as other community locations such as churches and schools. U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), who convened the Thursday news conference, has introduced legislation to prohibit ICE from arresting people at what she referred to as “sensitive places” like the clinic. 
“ICE should stay away. They used to stay away under the Biden administration. They used to stay away when it was Obama,” Leger Fernández said. “It was Trump and his cruel and corrupt policies that have decided, ‘No, there is no safe and sacred place from their raids,’ and so we are also calling upon ICE to start respecting the Constitution.”
Pernillo said her uncle, a father of three, was “simply fulfilling his duty as a father” when ICE arrested him. 
“At that moment, my cousin should have been thinking about school, not the moment her father was torn away from her,” she said. 
As for the second arrest, Gutierrez said she was with her mother-in-law, whom she identified as 43-year-old Adriana Ruiz, on the way to a medical appointment for Gutierrez’s 2-month-old baby, who was hooked up to an oxygen machine. 
Gutierrez said they were getting into their car when ICE agents approached. 
“We asked for the paperwork required for such stops, but they refused to show it and gave us false information,” Gutierrez said in Spanish. “They claimed they were looking for a car that didn’t even match my mother-in-law’s vehicle. We tried to reason with them, but all we got were threats.”
Ruiz stepped out of the car and agreed to be arrested “for the sake of my daughter,” Gutierrez said. 
New Mexico U.S. Rep. Leger Fernández denounces ICE arrest in Santa Fe healthcare clinic parking lot

“She did it for her granddaughter because we want safety for our families. We just want to live a normal life like any other human being,” she said. “No one is different, and everyone has rights, but apparently, that doesn’t apply in this case.”
A DHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment about Ruiz’s arrest Thursday. Gutierrez told Source NM after the news conference that she is very concerned about her mother-in-law, who has health problems. Gutierrez said she and other relatives still do not know where ICE agents took Ruiz or whether she is receiving medical care.
“We are just worried,” she said. 
State House Majority Floor Leader Rep. Reena Szczepanski (D-Santa Fe) and advocates Somos Un Pueblo Unido, an immigrant advocacy organization, also spoke at the news conference. Szczepanski touted the state Legislature’s recent enactment of a bill that bans public entities from helping ICE detain immigrants, and she said lawmakers are actively considering more immigration-related proposals.
All speakers said they are working on fighting back against Trump’s mass deportation efforts. 
“No one in Santa Fe or in New Mexico or in this country should have to decide between taking their children to school or to a medical appointment for fear of exposing their families to immigration enforcement,” said Gabriela Ibańez Guzman, an attorney with Somos Un Pueblo Unido.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Appellate court rules LSU has to make employee investigation records public
description: A state appellate court has ruled LSU must release its investigative records about a former administrator accused of catfishing students to the former editor of its student paper.
text:
LSU’s Memorial Tower pictured on March 20, 2023. (Matthew Perschall/Louisiana Illuminator)Editor’s note: Lawyers with the Tulane First Amendment Clinic have represented the Louisiana Illuminator. The plaintiff in this story, Josh Archote, edited the work of this author when they both were on The Reveille staff. 
A state appellate court has ruled LSU must release its investigative records about a former administrator accused of catfishing students to the former editor of its student paper. 
The case was filed in 2023 by Josh Archote, then editor-in-chief of The Reveille, LSU’s student newspaper. He was seeking records about Donald Abels, a former Greek Life administrator who the university investigated for allegedly creating multiple fake Snapchat accounts and using them to entrap fraternity pledges in violations of university policy and state law for underage drinking. 
The ruling from the First Circuit Court of Appeals affirms that the university’s internal investigations are subject to the state’s public records law. 
“This is a big win for transparency and accountability in our state,” said Annie Cleveland, the attorney with the Tulane First Amendment Clinic who litigated the case. “Disclosure of completed investigations encourages diligence and institutional accountability.” 
Archote could not be reached immediately for comment.
In a statement, LSU spokeswoman Meg Sunstrom said LSU is evaluating the court’s decision and considering whether it will appeal. 
In the case, LSU maintained it could not release the Abels documents for privacy reasons, citing their own policies. In their ruling, the appellate judges said no reasonable expectation of privacy existed for Abels. 
“The mere introduction of LSU’ s [policy], wherein LSU deems employee personnel files as ‘confidential,’ does not prove that an LSU employee has a reasonable expectation of privacy as to every document in his personnel file,” the opinion reads. “If such were the case, a public body could shield any public document regarding an employee from public disclosure by merely filing it away in his personnel file.”
The three-jurist panel — Chief Judge Page McClendon with colleagues Hunter Green and Tess Stromberg — ruled unanimously for Archote.
“We are grateful the First Circuit confirmed what was already established by state law: public institutions, like LSU, cannot create their own extra-legal exemptions to the public records law by secreting public documents in employees’ personnel files,” Cleveland said. 
The ruling Thursday from the Louisiana First Circuit Court of Appeals reversed a 2024 trial court decision.
Archote’s lawsuit is nearly identical to a case state Rep. Dixon McMakin, R-Baton Rouge, filed against LSU — and lost — in 2021, before he was in the legislature. The case was not appealed beyond the trial court.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: After data center debacle, Gov. Cox says MIDA has had ‘mission creep’ and needs ‘major reform’
description: Utah Gov. Spencer Cox said Utah elected leaders have delegated much of their land use and taxing authority to the non-elected Military Installation Development Authority — the powerful independent state body that went from obscurity to infamy this summer after it gave an initial green light to the highly controversial Stratos data center project in […]
text:
Community members protest ahead of a special Box Elder County Commission meeting to discuss the Stratos project, a massive data center proposed for an unincorporated area in Box Elder County, Utah, on May 4, 2026. (Photo by Alixel Cabrera/Utah News Dispatch)Utah Gov. Spencer Cox said Utah elected leaders have delegated much of their land use and taxing authority to the non-elected Military Installation Development Authority — the powerful independent state body that went from obscurity to infamy this summer after it gave an initial green light to the highly controversial Stratos data center project in Box Elder County. 
When asked about data centers during a televised news conference hosted by PBS Utah on Thursday, Cox said the process surrounding the Stratos project “was not good, and the MIDA process especially.” 
That’s why the governor said he’s supportive of changes to MIDA.
“I think we need major reform when it comes to MIDA, and I will be pushing for that reform again,” Cox said. 



The governor told reporters that he proposed changes to MIDA nearly two years ago, in 2025, but they never passed. A spokesperson for the governor did not immediately return a response to a question asking for more details about those past proposed changes. 
When asked what specific changes he would like to see for MIDA, Cox said state leaders, the Office of Economic Development and the governor “should play a bigger role in understanding what projects are going through.” 
“We have a lot of independent entities in this state, and they’re great. They play a very important role. But we’ve also delegated a lot of authority there, and the people are going to hold us accountable for what those entities do,” Cox said. “We need to make sure that we have insight and some say in what it is they’re doing, what projects they’re taking on. And are they the right projects for our state?”
Utah lawmakers get a primer on data centers after a summer of protests and political fallout 

Cox pointed to other independent agencies the Utah Legislature has created, including the Point of the Mountain Land Authority — which is tasked with overseeing the development of 600 acres of prime real estate at the site of the former Utah State Prison in Draper. He also pointed to the Utah Fairpark Area Investment and Restoration District, which has taxing, bonding and land use authority to facilitate development of a Major League Baseball stadium in and around Salt Lake City’s Fairpark neighborhood. 
“There are a lot of these authorities that have come up to do really important projects,” Cox said. 
But he said MIDA “in particular” has seen “a little mission creep with what their initial responsibilities were and goals were.” 
“And that may be OK,” Cox added. “We may support all of that. But we, the elected officials of the state, should be able to have a little bit more of a say in what happens there.” 
In June, Utah State Auditor Tina Cannon launched an online dashboard showing financial activity and other publicly available information about MIDA. It also painted a picture showing how since lawmakers first created MIDA in 2007, its powers have grown, enabling it to create project areas across the state — some with a clear tie to its original mission to facilitate military development, but also some public infrastructure districts with a focus on recreation, tourism and hospitality. 
New website sheds light on MIDA amid data center controversy. Here’s what it shows

While it’s not clear exactly what past legislative changes Cox was referring to when he said he previously pushed reforms to MIDA, there was one bill considered in 2025 and backed by the governor that would have created the Beehive Development Authority. 
That bill stalled amid bipartisan pushback and concerns around too much consolidation of government power. But had it passed, the Beehive Development Authority would have been tasked with “coordinating” with other state bodies that had broad land, bonding and taxing authority, including MIDA, the Utah Inland Port Authority, the Point of the Mountain State Land Authority, and others. 
In response to Cox’s comments Thursday, Kristin Kennedy Williams, a MIDA spokesperson, issued a prepared statement welcoming any discussion on future reforms. 
“As a State-created entity formed in 2007 to further military initiatives and economic development, MIDA is not a policy maker, and MIDA is of course subject to state statutes,” Kennedy Williams said. “We’re always happy to engage with the Governor and his team.”
Amid outrage over the Stratos project — backed by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary of TV’s “Shark Tank” — MIDA officials have said they’ve pushed pause on the Stratos project. Litigation over a referendum challenging the Box Elder County Commission’s vote to consent to the MIDA project area has also complicated the future of the data center — but O’Leary said in June “we are full steam ahead on the project and even more optimistic about the economic benefits it will bring to Utah,” The Salt Lake Tribune reported at the time.  
‘Power grab?’ Despite cross-party outcry, bill to create mighty new state agency moves forward

Currently, MIDA is governed by an eight-member board with seven voting members and one none-voting member from the Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity, meant to represent sectors ranging from military affairs, the Legislature, economic development and local government. 
Under Utah law, the governor currently appoints five members, while the Utah Senate president and Utah House Speaker each appoint one board member. 
Senate President Stuart Adams, R-Layton, has long served as a MIDA board member and chair. Outrage over the Stratos data center project was a key factor in his primary election loss in June against his Republican challenger, Stephanie Hollist. 
In an interview with Utah News Dispatch last month, Adams said “I’m not sure” when asked whether he would continue serving on the MIDA board after he exits the Legislature at the end of the year.

Rep. Lindsay James speaks at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair on Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic congressional candidate Lindsay James told Iowa State fairgoers Thursday she would focus on lowering healthcare costs and bringing money back to Iowans rather than spending it on foreign conflict or letting it be used for politicians’ own gain.
James, speaking at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair, said federal policies like those in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” are forcing Iowans to make “impossible choices” between healthcare, food and other necessities. James, Dubuque’s representative in the Iowa House, is running for the state’s 2nd Congressional District seat.
Across the 2nd District, which spans counties in northeast Iowa, James said people and organizations have been feeling the hurt of Affordable Care Act cuts and rising healthcare, grocery, gas, agriculture and other costs. Iowans have shared with her stories of having to choose between paying for utility bills or winter clothing, rent or food, and even rent or insulin.
“These are the kinds of impossible choices that people are making, and they’re doing it in the wealthiest country in the world,” James said. “And I think all of us can agree that that is not right.”
