title: Prickly Pear announces protection of 198 acres near Fort Harrison
description: Prickly Pear Land Trust announced 198 acres at War Eagle Hill have been “permanently protected” through an agreement with the Montana National Guard and Double L Family Land. The parcel is located six miles west of Helena behind Fort Harrison, which is a training facility and also hosts a United States Veteran Affairs Medical Center. […]
text:
The War Eagle Hill property is pictured. (Prickly Pear Land Trust photo - Kevin League / Cassie Solberg)Prickly Pear Land Trust announced 198 acres at War Eagle Hill have been “permanently protected” through an agreement with the Montana National Guard and Double L Family Land.
The parcel is located six miles west of Helena behind Fort Harrison, which is a training facility and also hosts a United States Veteran Affairs Medical Center. War Eagle Hill contains grasslands, old-growth forest and riparian habitat, a press release said. Additionally, it will help with winter ranging and movement of large animals, including elk, moose and bears.
The area is, in part, intended for hunter usage, and it’s close to Helena-Lewis and Clark National Forest, as well as Bureau of Land Management holdings and state land, as well.
“We treasure many memories made with family and friends on this land from time spent exploring its topographical and ecological diversity. These experiences were a gift that only time spent outdoors can cultivate,” Laurie Cox, a representative of Double L Family Land, said in a press release. “We are thrilled that this land will be available for people to enjoy. Collaborating with PPLT was a perfect way to do right by the land, ensuring that it is protected from development and included in a master plan of open spaces for the benefit of our ecosystems.”
Additionally, the move conserves open space around the military base, which the release said supports “local ecosystem health and military readiness.” Funding from the Department of Defense’s Readiness and Environmental Protection Integration Program was used in the project.
“For 31 years, PPLT’s strength has come from dedicated private landowners and visionary community partners who recognize that Montana’s open spaces are worth protecting forever,” Mary Hollow, executive director of Prickly Pear Land Trust, said in a press release. “By partnering with Double L Family Land and the National Guard, we are securing a wildlife gateway to the Continental Divide, supporting military readiness at Fort Harrison, and keeping public hunting access intact for central Montanans.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa lawyer accused of defrauding cancer patients and their insurers
description: A former public defender who won the support of judges and a member of the Iowa Legislature after a 2023 arrest for shoplifting now stands accused of defrauding Medicaid and cancer patients. Attorney Cassi Wigington, who will be sentenced next month on a charge of healthcare fraud, has agreed to pay $445,455 as restitution in […]
text:
(Main photo by simpson33 via iStock / Getty Images Plus; seal courtesy State of Iowa)A former public defender who won the support of judges and a member of the Iowa Legislature after a 2023 arrest for shoplifting now stands accused of defrauding Medicaid and cancer patients.
Attorney Cassi Wigington, who will be sentenced next month on a charge of healthcare fraud, has agreed to pay $445,455 as restitution in the case. That agreement comes 13 months after Wigington told the Iowa Supreme Court she had shoplifted alcohol and other items from a grocery store due to her struggles to meet her “family’s basic needs.”
Court records show Wigington was first licensed to practice law in Iowa in January 2020. Last year, she admitted in court filings that in August and September 2023, she committed the crime of theft by shoplifting from a Hy-Vee store in Gretna, Nebraska.
Court records show Wigington admitted that during 13 trips to the Gretna store between Aug. 6, 2023, and Sept. 13, 2023, she stole more than 300 items worth a total of $2,721.
After being criminally charged with felony theft by shoplifting, Wigington entered into a diversion agreement with the Sarpy County Attorney’s Office in which she agreed to pay restitution and the theft charge was dismissed.
In court filings, Wigington acknowledged she initially claimed to have been falsely accused of shoplifting, stating that when she made those statements, she “did not have the surveillance footage of my actions.”
Prior to the Iowa Supreme Court’s June 2025 decision to suspend her license for six months, Wigington argued for a 30-day suspension, noting that northwest Iowa was in serious need of public defenders.
“Any lengthy suspension of me will result in considerable disruption in the Second Judicial District,” she told the court. “I currently have approximately 700 cases assigned to me — several cases are companion charges pending against one defendant. It is extremely difficult to get lawyers to take these cases.”
In October 2025, Wigington applied for reinstatement of her Iowa law license. Buena Vista County Attorney Paul Allen wrote a letter to the Iowa Supreme Court supporting her application, as did Patrick Tott, chief judge of Iowa’s Third Judicial District in northwest Iowa, and Iowa Rep. Megan Jones, a Republican from Clay County.
District Court Judge Adam Miller also wrote in support of Wigington, calling her an “attorney of exceptional character and competence” and arguing she was “indispensable” to the Third Judicial District.
In December 2025, the Iowa Supreme Court agreed to lift Wigington’s suspension, making her fully qualified to resume the practice of law in Iowa.
Fraud involved patients’ breast prostheses  
Six months after her license was reinstated, on June 18, 2026, a federal grand jury in Nebraska charged Wigington with healthcare fraud.
That same day, Wigington entered a plea of guilty to the charge, acknowledging she could face up to 10 years in prison and agreeing to forfeit $445,455 in proceeds from an alleged scheme to overbill Medicaid and other insurers for devices used by cancer patients.
Prosecutors alleged that beginning in 2012, Wigington sold medical equipment such as custom-made breast prosthetic devices for women who had undergone mastectomies. In some cases, she allegedly had customers sign, in advance, receipts for the delivery of prostheses that had yet to be provided. In other cases, prosecutors alleged, she forged the customers’ signatures. She then sent bills for the undelivered devices to various insurers, including Medicaid, Blue Cross-Blue Shield, Aetna and United Healthcare.
“Twenty-five patients were identified wherein their respective healthcare benefit program was billed for products that were never received or provided,” prosecutors alleged. Losses incurred by individual patients and their insurers were alleged to be as much as $28,000.
Sentencing in the criminal case is scheduled for Sept. 10, 2026.
Recently, the Iowa Supreme Court Attorney Disciplinary Board asked the court to impose a temporary suspension of Wigington’s law license due to her guilty plea in the fraud case.
In its written request, the board stated the case, when considered in conjunction with Wigington’s prior disciplinary suspension for shoplifting, “reflects a troubling, years-long pattern of dishonesty and fraud, including repeated theft accomplished through deception.”
The court has yet to rule on the matter and Wigington’s Iowa law license is currently in good standing.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to Wigington for comment Thursday.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: USC among top college users of ChatGPT, renews OpenAI contract for $2.5M
description: University of South Carolina gobbled up 30 million credits on Chat GPT last school year, one of the top college users in the country
text:
The McKissick Museum on the University of South Carolina campus. (provided by USC)COLUMBIA — University of South Carolina students and staff gobbled up 30 million credits on Chat GPT last school year — 30 times what it was contracted for — making it one of the top college users on the platform in the country.
“The use has been through the roof,” said Brice Bible, the schools chief of information technology.
As a result, students will now find guardrails on how often they can use the more advanced features of this developing technology as they return to campus this fall.
“I can tell you the (USC) president loves it. The provost and the deans are like, go get ‘em. Our faculty are really at the cutting edge of using these tools,” Bible said. “We didn’t want to stop that.”
But as the school inked a new contract with ChatGPT, developer OpenAI had to make some changes.
Some 25,000 USC students and employees have signed up for a school ChatGPT Enterprise account.
That comes to about half of the school’s combined 40,000 students and more than 8,000 staff.
Most of the use involved basic prompts entered into the artificial intelligence-powered chatbot. Users of the platform’s free version can make 10 of those types of queries every five hours.
But between 3,000 and 5,000 users, about three-fifths of them students, used ChatGPT to conduct what’s known as “deep research,” Bible said.
For those users, USC had to pump the brakes on what was unfettered use.
“We wanted to make sure that, certainly, general users still had what they needed, but that the heavy users still could experiment and learn,” Bible said.
The deep research function is for complex, multi-step tasks, according to OpenAI.
For example, a business student studying whether a new product might do well on the market can ask the platform to conduct a complete competitive analysis against existing products. Or graduate students working on their thesis or dissertation could ask it to run a review of all previously published books and journal articles related to their topic.
“We had everything from science and business faculty conducting very detailed analytical experiments with large data sets to students using Codex, the software development platform OpenAI put out, to develop code and practice their troubleshooting for coursework or projects,” Bible said.
USC’s usage was up there with colleges such as Arizona State University and schools in the California and Pennsylvania state systems, Bible said.
Luckily, because USC was an early adopter of OpenAI’s college program, the technology company was willing to forgive the $1 million bill these heavy users had racked up above its one-year contract.
USC signs $1.5M contract with OpenAI to train students, faculty on responsible use

Instead, the company kept USC to the $1.5 million originally agreed upon for 1 million credits.
“They did not want to lose us,” Bible said. “We are not only a user, but we are pushing the envelope, and I think it’s helping them figure out the best way to work with any other university. Because if we have the challenge with these credits and the use of the different deep research areas, every research university ultimately will.
“OpenAI has been using our growth and our opportunities to help guide the way, quite frankly, as they position themselves in the higher ed market,” he added.
This year, the school will pay $2.5 million for the license and 40 million credits.
The new sole-source contract is for one year, starting with the fall semester.
As to why the contract didn’t go through the normal procurement process, Bible said the school looked at rates offered by other platforms, such as Claude and Gemini, and the costs were much higher.
“Plus, our faculty and students were already deeply embedded in (ChatGPT),” he said.
That reliance on sole-source also could change next year, Bible added.
Under the new system, USC students will each be allowed 60 credits a month. That’s enough for one “deep research” prompt and creation of two images, according to OpenAI.
Faculty will get 500 credits a month by default.
And the dean of each college or administrator of each department also will have a bucket of extra credits they can dole out if a professor puts in a special request. Deans also will receive monthly usage reports, Bible said, so if there are any unused credits, they can reallocate them to more heavy users.
A button in the platform allows students to put in individual requests to their professors for extra credits if they have a project due that requires them.
Clemson becomes second SC university eyeing Open AI contract. Here’s how schools are using the tech.

Starting next month, USC’s IT department is opening up a help desk, manned by students with specialized training who can answer questions by phone, online or in person about how to use credits efficiently to stay below the new limits.
And, all freshmen will receive AI fluency training as part of their entry-level university 101 class this fall.
Plus, USC’s journalism and communications school is hosting a conference Oct. 9-10 about how newsrooms, corporate communications and marketing agencies are using AI.
“Our goal is to create meaningful conversations that help professionals, educators and students better understand how AI is reshaping journalism, advertising and public relations while reinforcing the importance of creativity, ethics and human judgment,” dean Tom Reichert said in a statement.
Three student teams also will have the chance to earn up to $7,500 in a competition using artificial intelligence “to solve a real-world communications problem.”
While USC was the first in the state to adopt the technology, Clemson University also signed a $3 million, one-year contract with ChatGPT in February.
So far, the Upstate school has not run into any issues with availability of credits, according to spokesman Joe Galbraith.
At Clemson, the school is “investing in deeper, custom AI capabilities that go beyond what other universities have purchased, positioning the campus to lead in teaching, operations, and research innovation,” according to a filing with the state’s procurement office.
Last fall, Galbraith said those added tools are why Clemson would spend twice what the technology company originally charged USC. He has not yet responded to questions sent earlier this week seeking details on credits in the contract and usage.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Former records clerk sues Oak Park for alleged discrimination, harassment
description: A former records clerk for Oak Park is suing the city for alleged discrimination against her as a Muslim woman, as well as harassment and privacy violations, according to a lawsuit filed Wednesday in Oakland County Circuit Court. Tammara Saloum, who is represented in her lawsuit by attorneys with the Michigan chapter of the Council […]
text:
Getty ImagesA former records clerk for Oak Park is suing the city for alleged discrimination against her as a Muslim woman, as well as harassment and privacy violations, according to a lawsuit filed Wednesday in Oakland County Circuit Court.
Tammara Saloum, who is represented in her lawsuit by attorneys with the Michigan chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR-MI, alleged in the complaint that the harassment and discrimination she faced was “so pervasive and severe that it created a hostile working environment,” to the point that “it interfered with her ability to perform the functions of her job appropriately.” 
Specifically, Saloum alleges that her supervisor and multiple other city employees discriminated against her due to her Muslim faith, as well as harassing her with details of a previous sexual assault that the lawsuit says she was the victim of.
“Public employees should never have to choose between their livelihood and their right to be treated with dignity and respect,” Amy V. Doukoure, CAIR-MI lead staff attorney, said. “When an employee is allegedly subjected to religious hostility, sexual harassment, and the disclosure of deeply private information—and the employer has notice yet fails to take meaningful corrective action—the harm extends beyond one individual. Public institutions must be held accountable for ensuring that discrimination and harassment are not permitted to become part of the workplace culture.”
Brittany Toth, Oak Park’s director of communications, said in a written statement that the city takes all allegations regarding privacy, professionalism, workplace conduct, and discrimination very seriously. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.clerk sues Oak park
“The City maintains a zero-tolerance policy for discrimination and expects all employees to adhere to the highest ethical and professional standards,” Toth said. “The City of Oak Park previously addressed allegations made by Ms. Saloum in a Michigan Department of Civil Rights Investigation. The Michigan Department of Civil Rights determined that there was insufficient evidence and dismissed Ms. Saloum’s complaint.”
Toth added that, as of Wednesday afternoon, the city had not been formally served with the lawsuit, and that they do not comment on pending litigation. 
Saloum’s complaint acknowledges the Michigan Department of Civil Rights complaint, which was filed in July 2025 and dismissed in February 2026 due to “insufficient evidence to proceed.”
Saloum began working for the city in June 2024, according to the lawsuit, and began reporting her complaints to the city’s human resources department in early May 2025. The complaint alleges that no substantive action to stop the discrimination or harassment was taken, and that by August 2025, the toll on her mental health was so severe that she went on extended medical leave. 
“There is something deeply painful about dedicating your career built around safety and protection, only to discover that you do not feel safe or protected within it yourself,” Saloum said in a press release from CAIR-MI. “My experience in Oak Park made me reconsider not only my career choices, but my trust in the system I had believed in. I entered this profession believing doing the right thing mattered. I left questioning whether I still belonged in it.”
Her supervisor, according to the complaint, “made a series of derogatory and discriminatory comments” regarding Saloum’s faith and her ability to perform her job duties while fasting for Ramadan, allegedly also saying in front of Saloum that “a lot of Islamics [sic] had caused problems in Oak Park.”
The city’s human resources department acknowledged, according to the lawsuit, that Saloum’s supervisor had been the subject of multiple prior discrimination complaints — but imposed no formal discipline and required only two days of training. 
“In total, the City took no action that was reasonably calculated to actually stop the discriminatory and harassing conduct,” the lawsuit states.
In addition to Saloum’s supervisor, one coworker in the city allegedly called imams “creepy and pedophile-like.”
Saloum, who the complaint states was the victim of a sexual assault while working for the Dearborn Police Department, alleges that her Oak Park supervisor accessed a secure police-records database to search for and then share details of Saloum’s assault with other employees of the city. That then allegedly led to further harassment from her coworkers specifically about the assault.
Michigan legal protections for victims “reflect a settled public policy: a sexual-assault survivor’s identity and connection to the assault are intensely private matters that should not be exposed, circulated, or used without legitimate need,” the lawsuit states.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Appleton area could lose more than $800,000 per year in revenue following government prison purchase
description: APPLETON — The federal government’s purchase of a 1,600-bed prison in Appleton for an immigrant detention facility could deal a major blow to city, county and school finances.  The prison had been owned and operated by CoreCivic since 1996 until its closure in 2010, which led to significant job loss and population decline. Even as […]
text:
A member of the Appleton VFW speaks at the beginning of a roundtable discussion over the Department of Homeland Security's purchase of the Prairie Correctional Facility on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)APPLETON — The federal government’s purchase of a 1,600-bed prison in Appleton for an immigrant detention facility could deal a major blow to city, county and school finances. 
The prison had been owned and operated by CoreCivic since 1996 until its closure in 2010, which led to significant job loss and population decline. Even as the prison sat empty, however, CoreCivic regularly paid property taxes on the facility, generating 30% of Appleton’s tax revenue. 
In 2026, CoreCivic paid more than $800,000 in property taxes, with the majority — more than $500,000 — going to the city of Appleton, according to property tax records. Swift County received more than $100,000, and the rest was split between the local schools and state government. 
While the prospect of more than 500 new jobs is expected to bring new residents and economic activity to the area, it’s not clear how much that will offset the decrease in property tax revenue, especially given new pressures on the local police and infrastructure.
One analysis of 911 calls to an immigrant detention facility in Texas, for instance, revealed near daily calls for medical crises and detainees expressing suicidal thoughts, the Associated Press reported earlier this year.
Appleton Mayor Justin Koepp said the city anticipates higher demand on its water and sewer services, and doesn’t yet know how to pay for the higher operating costs.
Swift County Commissioner Gary Hendricks said the county is in negotiations with CoreCivic over a memorandum of understanding that would reduce the impact of the revenue loss. 
“Nothing’s been signed yet, but hopefully that will happen,” Hendricks said Thursday afternoon at a packed roundtable discussion at the Appleton VFW. He added that the impact wouldn’t be felt until the 2028 budget.
Around 150 people attended the Thursday afternoon event. Elected officials provided updates on the reopening, took written questions from the audience and read statements provided by CoreCivic. 
Down the street from the VFW, dozens of protesters held signs in opposition to the opening of the facility and President Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts. 
When Koepp read a question about what could be done about the protesters, and whether they could be moved from their post at the Flags of Honor, which is a public memorial site, the elected officials on the panel looked at each other and the crowd laughed. (Trump won Appleton by 27 percentage points in 2024.)
“As you know, First Amendment rules — there are certain areas that individuals can protest, and that is an area that they can protest in right now,” Koepp said. 
Some of the questions, however, underscored concerns held even by supporters of the Trump agenda: How much would the city have to raise taxes to fill the budget gap? Where will the employees live? Will detainees be released into the community? What would local officials do about an influx of protestors and negative press? What happens if this facility is sold again — as with a number of warehouses the Department of Homeland Security purchased last year? Or if the Democrats take the presidency in 2028?
“This is brand new. We don’t know a lot of information,” Swift County Sheriff Mike Hoffman said, adding that his department was working to understand the detention center’s potential impact on the local emergency management system. 
Statements provided by CoreCivic said detainees would be given transportation to their local airport or bus stop, and that they would not be released in Appleton; that the facility will not hold minors; and that the company anticipates 525 jobs.
One questioner stood up at the end of the meeting to express concerns about the lack of empathy for the people who will be detained at the prison.
After a lengthy pause from the elected officials on the stage, Republican state Rep. Paul Anderson took the microphone. Residents have honest disagreements over federal immigration policy, and immigration reform is needed, he said.
But: “That is way beyond what we are here for, which is to discuss the impact on the city of Appleton,” Anderson said.
The reopening of the prison fulfills a longstanding goal for area Republicans, who had lobbied the state to reopen the facility until the DFL-controlled Legislature banned private prisons in 2023. 
“I think it’s great news for the community — let’s just work through the stresses that go with it,” said state Sen. Torrey Westrom, R-Alexandria.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah governor says he’s ‘deeply troubled’ by Flock cameras, calls for review to protect privacy
description: Amid growing apprehension around license plate cameras across the country — especially those that are part of the Flock Safety network — Utah Gov. Spencer Cox told reporters he shares concerns around privacy and whether those cameras are being misused.  Cox’s comments came Thursday during a news conference hosted by PBS Utah, after a Utah […]
text:
Flock Safety license plate readers are typically mounted on tall poles, with a camera and solar panel on top. The company says its technology is used in more than 6,000 communities across 49 states in partnership with thousands of law enforcement agencies nationwide. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)Amid growing apprehension around license plate cameras across the country — especially those that are part of the Flock Safety network — Utah Gov. Spencer Cox told reporters he shares concerns around privacy and whether those cameras are being misused. 
Cox’s comments came Thursday during a news conference hosted by PBS Utah, after a Utah News Dispatch reporter asked him about a recent investigation by the Utah Civic Compact. The nonprofit found that records of 10 Flock cameras installed in one Utah county — Weber County — were searched more than 5 million times between February 2022 and July 2026, with the vast majority of those searches (nearly 97%) coming from police agencies outside of Utah, from 45 states. 
The top agency responsible for the largest chunk of those searches was Houston Police Department in Texas, with more than 423,000 searches or more than 26%.
Most of this Utah county’s license plate camera data is searched by out-of-state law enforcement  

Cox said he was “deeply troubled” by the issues raised by the Utah Civic Compact investigation, which has called on lawmakers to address the issue of out-of-state agencies making a large amount of requests to Utah-based Flock cameras with no systems in place to verify whether those searchers follow Utah’s existing laws that regulate how automatic license plate reader data can be used. 
Automatic license plate reader cameras, including those in the Flock Safety network, have been used by law enforcement agencies all across the country for years to help investigate crime. But concerns over privacy and misuse have surfaced in recent months, with reports from agencies across the U.S. where some law enforcement officials have accessed the cameras’ data for personal reasons.
“I think Americans should be deeply concerned about that,” Cox said.
He said Utah has been on “the forefront of really trying to put guardrails around the use of those types of technologies to protect citizens’ privacy, that it can only be used in the most extreme circumstances to protect life and safety.”
But the governor added, “I don’t think we should say, ‘hey, just trust us.” 
So he said he’s asked the Utah Privacy Governing Board and the Utah Privacy Commission to “do a review of all of our rules and regulations around these cameras, especially how they’re being used with local agencies to make sure that they are not being abused, to make sure that the public understands how and when they can be used, and if there are abuses taking place, people are held accountable.”



Cox noted Utah already has laws regulating Flock cameras, but “the question is, is the legislation being followed?”
So that’s why he said he’s asked the Utah Privacy Commission to look into whether lawmakers can do anything more to ensure Flock cameras can’t be misused. 
“If there are some gaps, then yes, I would absolutely support legislation,” he said, “but I think the legislation we have in place should allow us to protect people’s privacy.”
After the governor’s comments on Thursday, Clark Dice, communications director of the Utah Civic Compact, applauded Cox for saying Flock cameras are an issue Americans should be concerned with, and he praised the governor for asking state privacy officials to see if there are any gaps in enforcement of existing laws. 
“What we want to emphasize is to make sure that the governor understands that we have found documented cases of where the enforcement of Utah privacy laws are getting muddled with respect to how outside agencies access our data,” Dice said, pointing to the more than 5 million searches in Weber County alone, mostly from out of state. Dice said, “we can’t say” that anytime an outside agency requests to view that data “those were 5 million instances of malfeasance, but from what we can tell, there is very little data on whether or not these outside agencies had to adhere to Utah privacy laws before they accessed the data.”
In other words, there’s no way to tell if they’re following Utah law. 
Menasha officer sentenced for abusing Flock as statewide reckoning continues

“There’s no system for it,” Connor Radcliffe, president of the Utah Civic Compact, told Utah News Dispatch. 
Of the thousands of law enforcement agencies in the U.S. that use the cameras, he said “I’m willing to bet a significant amount of them have actual procedures in place (but) as we’ve seen in different parts of the country, protocols and such seem to be insufficient to stop abuse of a personal nature from police officers.”
“So we have no way of knowing if we’re being exposed to some cop searching his ex-girlfriend across state lines, for example,” Radcliffe said. “We can’t tell if that’s not happening because we can’t audit them, obviously.” 
As backlash against the cameras has grown, the company Flock Safety earlier this month announced changes to its platform to address privacy concerns and “documented abuses of its system by some members of law enforcement.”
Radcliffe said he’s hopeful, “based on the governor’s reaction,” that Utah’s Republican-controlled Legislature “will kind of rally around this and decide that it’s something we need to get a handle on.”
“This technology is going to get more pervasive, and it’s going to get more intrusive and more advanced,” he said, “and it’s really important that we get ahead of this.”
Utah’s existing laws on Flock cameras
Utah already has laws regulating automatic license plate readers, with a default ban on them unless they’re used by a law enforcement agency to access captured license plate data in four instances: as part of an active criminal investigation, to apprehend someone with an outstanding warrant, to locate a missing or endangered person, or to locate a stolen vehicle. 
The data, Utah law says, can’t be used or shared for any other reason, and misuse is a crime punishable with a class B misdemeanor. 
Flock Safety tightens safeguards as states, cities question surveillance network

However, there’s no way for Utah law enforcement to verify whether other agencies — including out-of-state agencies — are adhering to Utah’s license plate reader law, the Utah Civic Compact pointed out on its website showing the results of its investigation. 
“The statute sets a requirement that no administrative apparatus was ever built to carry out,” the nonprofit’s website says. “Utah requires each search to be logged with a crime type and incident number, and requires those logs to be kept for five years, but no office collects them, no format is specified, and no agency reports them to anyone. Whether the requirement is being met is left to each agency to determine for itself, and whatever it determines stays with that agency.”
The Utah Civic Compact warned that county and city police budgets are already tight, and they don’t have the manpower or structure to audit their records. That’s not a “failure” of the agencies, the nonprofit said, but a “predictable structural outcome.”
“That infrastructure does not exist inside Utah, for Utah’s own agencies,” the Utah Civic Compact said. “It certainly does not exist for the 3,343 agencies across 45 states that have searched this network. Meaningful accountability would mean auditing every one of them, and no authority in Utah has the power or the tools to do that.”
While raising these concerns, the Utah Civic Compact has called for a legislative audit of Flock cameras in Utah, and a mechanism that would allow a law enforcement agency sharing residents’ location data to determine whether the recipients of the records are following Utah law. Today, there’s no way to do so. 
The nonprofit has also called on every Utah agency operating automatic license plate readers to publish its network sharing configuration. 
And the Utah Civic Compact wants to see lawmakers pass tighter restrictions around Flock cameras, noting that three bills focused on reforming automatic license plate reader laws have failed since 2025. 
That included HB468, which passed the House but died in the Senate. That bill would have added reporting requirements and created standards for the data obtained from the cameras, among other measures.

title: National group releases cover crop tool modeled after Iowa ‘batch and build’ program
description: An Iowa program that deploys conservation practices across an area, rather than one at a time, served as a model for a cover crop adoption program launched by American Farmland Trust.  The conservation agriculture group released a guide to help producers follow the “batch and grow” cover crop program, which it said removes barriers, lowers […]
text:
A local effort to "batch" cover crop implementation can help lower barriers to entry, according to an ag conservation group. (Photo by USDA)An Iowa program that deploys conservation practices across an area, rather than one at a time, served as a model for a cover crop adoption program launched by American Farmland Trust. 
The conservation agriculture group released a guide to help producers follow the “batch and grow” cover crop program, which it said removes barriers, lowers cost and streamlines cover crop adoption for participants. 
The program follows the “batch and build” model initiated in Polk County to install water quality edge-of-field practices, like bioreactors and saturated buffers, in batches across a neighborhood or community. Now the batch and build model has been adopted by the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship for water quality projects in counties across the state. 
Similarly, the batch and grow model, which was first initiated in Dubuque County, enrolls “batched” acres in a region and a local farmer-led group initiates contracts for cover crop seed and application. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the Batch and Grow Roadmap from American Farmland Trust, this method “removes several barriers of adoption for farmers” like part of the financial risk, uncertainty about seed mixes, lack of technical experience and the lack of time during harvest season. The roadmap is meant to support other organizations around the country as they look to implement similar systems. 
Midwest Senior Program Manager Julie Larsen with American Farmland Trust said the roadmap helps interested groups initiate these programs without having to “recreate the wheel.” 
“It draws on those lessons learned and is filled with practical information to help organizations launch their own Batch and Grow program, ultimately putting more cover crops on the ground to improve water quality and soil health,” Larsen said in a news release. 
Cover crops are a conservation method in which a farmer seeds a second crop into their standing cash crop so that once the corn or soybeans, for example, have been harvested from a field, a different crop has already taken root. This helps to keep roots in the ground, which in turn help soil and nutrients from washing off of what would otherwise be a bare field. 
The Dubuque County project resulted in nearly 16,000 acres seeded with cover crops across land from 125 farmers in 2025, according to the Sand County Foundation, which partnered with Dubuque County Watersheds on the initiative.
The effort started in Dubuque County in 2024 and in 2025, American Farmland Trust helped expand the batch and grow model to areas of Illinois with funding assistance from the U.S. Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Conservation Service. 
According to the roadmap from American Farmland Trust, “batching” cover crop seed purchases and applications resulted in savings between 3% and 56% depending on the seed mix, as compared to per acre Environmental Quality Incentives Program payment rates – a popular USDA conservation funding program. 
The first step to bringing a batch and grow program to an area, according to the roadmap, is to identify potential farmer-led groups, like the county conservation district or local grassroots farmer groups, to gauge the interest in starting a batch and grow program. 
Farmer-led groups are a “critical component” of the program, as these groups make decisions on things like seed mixes, dealers, application methods or contractors, project geography and more. 
Putting these decisions on the farmer-led group, versus an individual farmer, is part of how the batch and grow system removes barriers of cover crop adoption. The trust also recommends the groups work with a local support organization, like a nonprofit, local municipality or small business that can help coordinate the effort. 
Next, the group should establish goals and timelines for the project, before it can create applications for interested farmers and initiate contracts with seed dealers and applicators. The project in Dubuque County utilized drone contractors to seed cover crops, a practice that is growing in Iowa. 
Once farmers have enrolled and the farmer-led group has approved applications, they can work with USDA’s NRCS and Farm Service Agency offices to try to secure funding that will support the projects. Alternatively, farmers could also pool resources for the cover crop costs. According to the roadmap, the program in Dubuque County asked farmers to pay $10 per acre enrolled to “stretch” public funding. 
Finally, the group can coordinate cover crop implementation with enrolled farmers. Having a central group plan and execute contracts with dealers helps the farmers who might otherwise not have time to do these things during harvest season, according to the roadmap.
In addition to streamlining the logistics of adding a cover crop, the roadmap said the collaboration among participating farmers allowed them to ask for advice and learn from one another. According to the roadmap, more than a quarter of participants in existing batch and grow programs were implementing the practice for the first time. 
More specific information and tips on the batch and grow process can be found in the American Farmland Trust roadmap.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: As back-to-school prices rise, donations fill the gap for North Carolina teachers, families
description: There is perhaps no clearer sign that summer is drawing to a close than the arrival of school supplies in big box stores and school supply drives in most counties. On Wednesday, Gov. Josh Stein delivered school supplies collected over the summer to W.M. Irvin Elementary School in Concord. It’s the eighth year the governor’s […]
text:
In the state's largest public school district, Wake County teachers are invited to fulfill their back-to-school wishlist for free at the Tools4Schools store near downtown Raleigh. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)There is perhaps no clearer sign that summer is drawing to a close than the arrival of school supplies in big box stores and school supply drives in most counties.
On Wednesday, Gov. Josh Stein delivered school supplies collected over the summer to W.M. Irvin Elementary School in Concord. It’s the eighth year the governor’s office has partnered with the State Employees’ Credit Union, the North Carolina PTA, the Boys & Girls Clubs of North Carolina, and Communities in Schools of North Carolina to distribute supplies to students in need.
Gov. Josh Stein delivers school supplies to W.M. Irvin Elementary School in Concord on August 19, 2026. (Photo: N.C. Governor’s Office)
“This year’s state budget had a lot of good news for education, but to truly support our public schools and our students’ futures, we need to better support teachers who pay for school supplies out of their own pockets,” Stein said in a statement.
The state budget Stein signed in July provides the largest average teacher pay raise in 20 years, the governor said. It also provided a 3% raise and a bonus of at least $1,000 for all other school staff and non-certified employees.
But that modest boost in pay diminishes quickly when teachers dip into their own pocket to pay for school supplies. A 2025 study by CouponBirds revealed teachers in the Tar Heel state shell out more than $1,600 annually to outfit their classrooms, the second highest average in the country. Only Pennsylvania teachers spent more out of pocket than North Carolina teachers.
In the state’s largest public school district, Wake County teachers are invited to fulfill their back-to-school wish list at the Tools4Schools store near downtown Raleigh.
The idea of a free supply store just for public school teachers was created four years ago by the nonprofit WakeEd Partnership. Since then, about 6,000 of the county’s 10,000 public school teachers have taken advantage of the assistance.
WakeEd CEO Keith Poston said the goal is to remove some of the financial pressure that educators feel at one of the most important times of the school year.
“Regardless of political perspective, folks understand intuitively that a teacher trying to teach children should not also have to worry about bringing in classroom supplies. We’re talking about the things they need to do their job,” said Poston in an interview with NC Newsline.
Poston said the “good-heartedness” of teachers prompts them to use their own money to make sure all the children in their classroom start the year on a level playing field.
GOP leaders say the NC budget offers ‘historic’ raises. A top education panel says it’s not enough.

A survey by the nonprofit found in 2025, Wake County teachers were spending on average $1,200 on back-to-school supplies. With inflation, many teachers are able to afford less than they did just a year ago.
“We’re gonna try to take that burden off as much as we can. It’s not a substitute for adequate funding, but I like to think we’ve made a difference,” said Poston.
On Wednesday, the storefront, designed to look like a small Staples, opened its doors to Wake County teachers, who scanned the well-stocked shelves for items their students might need.
Highlighters, pencils, glue sticks, backpacks, and hand sanitizer are among the most sought-after items. Laptops and Chromebooks are provided by the school district, but Poston says teachers need a lot of basic supplies for their students to start out the school year.
“I remind folks, this is a classroom supply store for teachers, but these are going to students,” said Poston. “Something that we are keenly aware of here is that not every family can afford to go out and make sure that their child has a new backpack full of all the things they are supposed to have or need to have when they walk in the door.”
A recent analysis from the Groundwork Collaborative and The Century Foundation, two progressive think tanks, finds a typical basket of school supplies will cost families 7.7% more this year, outpacing inflation.
According to new data released by Intuit Credit Karma, more than half of parents with kids under 18 are entering back-to-school shopping season with credit card debt. Nearly two-thirds of those parents (63%) expect that they will add to their existing balance to cover this year’s school purchases.
Corporate sponsors and community groups can help make sure students have what they need to start the school year, but individuals can also play a role. Poston said an Amazon wishlist makes it easy to see which items are the highest priority, and people can then donate at any level that fits their budget.
The average price of a school backpack this year is $30-$60. At WakeEd Partnership’s Tools4Schools store, teachers can grab a free backpack for students in need. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Fazio promises to find a ‘grand bargain’ on housing, zoning reform
description: Ryan Fazio's concept of a "grand bargain" includes state-mandated zoning reforms in return for significant revisions to 8-30g and H.B. 8002.
text:
Republican Ryan Fazio had two reasons to choose Simsbury to pitch a “grand bargain” on housing reforms Thursday: The town is roiled by a proposed 689-unit housing development, and it is a prime example of a former GOP suburb that Fazio must recapture if he is to compete with Gov. Ned Lamont. 
The GOP gubernatorial nominee opened with a familiar attack on the Democratic governor and legislators, accusing them of undermining local control by passing an omnibus housing bill without repealing 8-30g, a decades-old law that can negate some local zoning rules in communities with less than 10% affordable housing.
“People across Connecticut are engaged in their communities,” Fazio said. “They love their town and city. They want to preserve all that is wonderful about it — the history in our neighborhoods, the open space and greenery — and they want input in the decisions that are made about their neighborhoods.”
Then he pivoted to his concept of a “grand bargain”: state-mandated zoning reforms in return for significant revisions to 8-30g and H.B. 8002, the housing bill Lamont signed last year after vetoing a similar measure in the face of opposition centered on suburbs that have become crucial to the Democratic base.

Republican nominee for governor Senator Ryan Fazio speaks during a a press conference highlighting the impact of state statutes on housing and development at Pinchot Sycamore Tree Park in Simsbury on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

His bargain is more framework than a plan, offering unspecified reforms to building codes and mandating that municipalities “streamline permitting processes to make them more rules-based, speedy and predictable.” But, in theory, that represents a willingness to consider some intrusion into local control.
Currently, fewer than two dozen Connecticut communities allow buildings with more than three housing units as a matter of right under local zoning. A few ban them outright, and the majority will consider them only under a special permit process that can be lengthy and expensive.
In fact, Fazio was told at a housing roundtable he hosted the previous day that the special permits can add 20% or more to the cost of multifamily housing.
So, would that streamlining potentially include curbing the use of special permits?
“Yeah, I think that that would be part of the trade — that if we streamline the zoning and permitting decisions, then we get more local control back. We get a rollback of 8-30g and 8002,” Fazio said. “And that’s what I’ve heard, not just from the gentleman who talked about it yesterday but from developers across the state.”
The revisions to the 8-30g would include height and size limits on projects that could employ the law’s provisions and give municipalities an indefinite reprieve from 8-30g if they took other actions towards promoting new housing, such as adopting “housing growth zones” in commercial areas or near transit.
Simsbury is one of the Farmington Valley suburbs that once reliably voted Republican. In 2018, when Lamont narrowly won his first term, Simsbury split nearly 50-50, giving Republican Bob Stefanowski the slightest advantage. In 2022, Lamont beat Stefanowski by 23 percentage points in Simsbury.

Harwinton First Selectman and candidate for state Senate Mike Criss speaks during a press conference highlighting the impact of state statutes on housing and development at Pinchot Sycamore Tree Park in Simsbury on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Fazio is using the housing issue in two ways: claiming that Democrats are more likely to impose on local zoning and development issues and faulting the governor for not being more involved in House Bill 5002 — the version he vetoed after his administration had signed off on the details.
In suggesting a grand-bargain approach, Fazio is positioning himself as a Republican willing and able to negotiate with a Democratic legislative majority.
Lamont has countered that his veto of the first bill opened the door to negotiations with municipal officials and produced a bill that keeps the pressure on cities and towns to permit affordable housing while listening to their concerns about what they found objectionable, such as limiting parking requirements.
He noted that the second version of H.B. 8002 passed by a larger margin than H.B. 5002. Rep. Melissa Osborne, D-Simsbury, was among the Democrats who opposed the first and voted for the second.
Fazio said neither version made the changes to 8-30g that cities and towns demand. 
He spoke under the Pinchot Sycamore, the state’s largest tree, on the bank of the Farmington River, downstream from the 689-unit project proposed on the site of an office park once occupied by The Hartford. By making 30% of the units affordable, the developer could sue under 8-30g to overturn the recent rejection of the proposal.
“The potential 8-30g project for over 600-unit apartment complex without local zoning control here in Simsbury is one of many cases across the state of local control being totally disregarded by this governor and state government,” Fazio said.
He believes the issue will resonate with voters in the valley.
“They live in wonderful, beautiful communities with a rural aspect to it, a bucolic aspect to it, and those considerations deserve respect and deserve to be considered in the type of policy that we create in Hartford,” Fazio said. “And under Gov. Lamont and supermajorities, that hasn’t been the case.”
A recent Sacred Heart University poll found 67.1% of voters identified housing costs and housing affordability as among the most important issues influencing their vote in the gubernatorial election. But preserving local control over housing development issues was a priority of only 7.2%.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RIPTA board votes to move ahead on new Providence bus hub
description: A 4.4-acre plot of land used to host Providence’s World Cup festivities next to the city’s Amtrak station is the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority’s choice for its state-of-the-art transit center. On Thursday, RIPTA’s board of directors voted 6-0 to direct contractor Next Wave Partners to move ahead with drafting bid specs and cost estimates […]
text:
Station Park in Providence is the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority’s preferred location for its new transit center. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) A 4.4-acre plot of land used to host Providence’s World Cup festivities next to the city’s Amtrak station is the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority’s choice for its state-of-the-art transit center.
On Thursday, RIPTA’s board of directors voted 6-0 to direct contractor Next Wave Partners to move ahead with drafting bid specs and cost estimates for the proposed bus hub that will eventually replace operations at Kennedy Plaza.
“We need the bus hub,” board member treasurer Normand Benoit said before the vote. “I don’t think Kennedy Plaza does the job.”
RIPTA has used the city-owned Kennedy Plaza as its centralized bus depot since the early 1980s. While the location has served the agency well over the last four decades, agency CEO Christopher Durand said the existing hub has become operationally inefficient.
“You’ve got buses on the main plaza, you’ve got buses up on Exchange Terrace,” he said in an interview before the board meeting. “It’s a lot of streets you’ve got to cross.”
RIPTA’s vision for the new transit center is to make it like an airport: climate-controlled and well lit with a dedicated busway outside passengers would see through a glass wall. Bus service would continue using to Kennedy Plaza as a stop if there’s a new depot.
“We want to do something better for our riders,” Durand told the board. “This is part of an anchor toward bigger and bolder things.”
The plan to improve or create a new bus hub has been in the works for years. In 2014, Rhode Island voters approved $35 million in bonds for mass transit center infrastructure — $22 million of which went to RIPTA.
Numerous sites have been studied by the agency and Rhode Island Department of Transportation, but nothing ever stuck.
A decade later, RIPTA approved a nearly $16.9 million contract with Next Wave Partners to finally get the wheels in motion. In May 2024, RIPTA narrowed down seven possible sites — including the two near the train station.
Then last December, planners turned their attention to the empty lot west of the Amtrak station fronting Francis and Gaspee streets. The land served as the PVD FanZone during the World Cup this summer.
Durand said the agency ultimately chose the site since it had the biggest available footprint in the area for its new transit center.
A preliminary map attached to the RIPTA board’s information packet shows a central passenger services area surrounded by bus bays, with the proposed transit center stretching between Francis Street, Finance Way, Gaspee Street and Railroad Street.
RIPTA planned to include residential housing on the upper floors, but Durand said the housing component no longer remains the project.
“It’s really not the right time in the market,” he told Rhode Island Current. “The interest rates are high. Costs are escalating.”
Reducing the scope of the project also means about $10 million in savings. But Durand said no final price tag has been set yet, noting construction costs will be finalized during the design and engineering phase.
The informational packet provided to the agency’s board of directors estimates the cost of the still “very preliminary” project at $70 million.
RIPTA has committed $77 million to the bus hub project, including $46 million identified in the State Transportation Improvement Program, a $25 million U.S. Department of Transportation BUILD grant awarded last month, and $6 million in state matching funds.
A preliminary schematic shows the proposed location of the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority’s new Providence transit center. (Courtesy of the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority)
‘Buses continue to be packed’ 
Transit advocates and riders have long been critical of the agency dedicating millions of dollars to a new bus hub, especially since RIPTA’s board approved sweeping service cuts nearly one year ago.
The service cuts were made after Gov. Dan McKee declined to fill a $32.6 million deficit for fiscal 2026. The General Assembly eventually propped up RIPTA with nearly $15 million in annual revenue from upping the agency’s share of the gas tax and highway maintenance fund. RIPTA administrators working with McKee’s office found other savings, but not enough to stave off service reductions.
“Buses continue to be packed,” Dylan Giles, operations manager for the Providence Streets Coalition, told the board. “Your current riders, future riders deserve a service that is dependable, reliable, and competitive with driving.”
Durand too would like to see RIPTA’s service grow. But restoration won’t be coming anytime soon, even after the agency was provided a favorable fiscal 2027 budget from the General Assembly. 
Lawmakers rejected a plan from McKee that called for a $9.3 million annual increase to RIPTA’s share of the state’s Highway Maintenance Account, $1 million revenue from raising fees on cruise ships visiting Newport, and reallocating $3.5 million in capital funds toward agency operations.
Instead the General Assembly chose to increase RIPTA’s share of the Highway maintenance account by an additional $4.2 million beyond McKee’s proposal. Those changes meant RIPTA received $553,000 more for operating expenses than it had requested, Durand confirmed.
“We’re not expecting any changes to service this year,” he told Rhode Island Current. “But we’re but likewise, we’re also not looking at reducing any further.” 
Durand said the agency is looking for ways to generate revenue in the future. He noted the funds for the hub cannot be used toward the agency’s operating expenses.
“If we could pay for service with this, we would,” he told board members and transit advocates.
 McKee released a statement Thursday afternoon “heartily” supporting the board’s vote.
“The new hub will help grow ridership and create new opportunities for RIPTA’s future,” McKee said. 
Board members Bernard Georges and Heather Schey were absent from Thursday’s meeting.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Atlanta left off the shortlist of 2028 DNC host cities
description: The Democratic National Committee has narrowed its list of host cities for its 2028 national convention — and Atlanta did not make the cut. The Democratic and Republican national conventions are held every four years, during which delegates officially select that year’s presidential nominee. Both Atlanta and Chicago made it to the Democrat’s list of […]
text:
DNC Chairman Ken Martin visited Atlanta in April as part of the city's bid to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention. Jill Nolin/Georgia RecorderThe Democratic National Committee has narrowed its list of host cities for its 2028 national convention — and Atlanta did not make the cut.
The Democratic and Republican national conventions are held every four years, during which delegates officially select that year’s presidential nominee. Both Atlanta and Chicago made it to the Democrat’s list of final five host cities before being eliminated. Boston, Denver and Philadelphia were selected as finalists for the 2028 convention.
Georgia Dems push for ‘28 national convention, Ossoff tries to tamp down presidential talk and more

Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin, who visited Atlanta in April as part of the selection process, said the event would be “a critical step” toward electing a Democratic president in 2028.
“Boston, Denver, and Philadelphia all presented incredibly strong bids to host the convention,” he said in a statement. “We look forward to continuing to work with them as the DNC makes a final selection in the coming months.” 
The announcement came as a disappointment to many Atlanta Democrats, who were hoping to break the nearly four-decade hiatus since the city last hosted the convention in 1988. Georgia has never hosted a Republican national convention.
In a letter obtained by the Recorder, Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens accused Martin and other national Democrats of being “unwilling to do the bare minimum to support the base of the party,” highlighting GOP efforts to redistrict that critics say will dismantle Black voters’ electoral power across the South.
“They are afraid to leave their comfort zone and blind to the fact that the South is the answer,” he wrote. “They are abandoning Atlanta, abandoning the South, and once again abandoning Black voters.”
State Sen. RaShaun Kemp, an Atlanta Democrat, also expressed disappointment with the decision.
“Georgia is the cradle of the Civil Rights movement and ground zero where Republicans are going to try again to disenfranchise and silence Black voters, and the Democratic Party made a horrible decision in excluding Atlanta,” he said. “They had an opportunity to show that the base of this party is respected and their voices need to be heard, and Atlanta should have been at the top of their list.”
The Democratic National Committee declined to comment on Dickens’ letter.
But Charlie Bailey, chair of the Democratic Party of Georgia, said his organization would continue working to elect Democrats during the midterm elections, regardless of where the convention is held.
“Georgia is the premier battleground state in the country,” Bailey said. “The road to the White House in 2028 will come straight through Georgia whether or not the Democratic National Convention does.”

name: VTDigger
title: Don’t punish Vermonters who split their time here
description:
Before taxing part-time residents more, Vermont should look at regulating short-term rentals and making businesses pay their fair share.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Don’t punish Vermonters who split their time here.
text:
Dear Editor,
I read the recent opinion piece by Donna Brown about second-home owners, and I totally agree with her. We bought our house in 2004, and as I was a teacher, we spent the summer and my vacation in Vermont. During the pandemic, we were here for a year and a half. We spend as much time here as we can, sometimes up to six months at a time. Does that mean that our other house is also a second home? 
We pay our taxes but are on a fixed income, so increases are a concern. What about short-term rentals like Airbnbs, which need to be regulated and taxed at a higher rate? Wouldn’t it be more meaningful to try to attract more businesses to Vermont and make them pay their fair share of taxes?

READ MORE

How will the taxing authorities identify who comes to Vermont once in a while versus those of us who come regularly and spend our money at the general stores, restaurants and many recreational establishments?
Without discussing these issues, the proposed legislation is harmful to many of us who love Vermont.
Lew Holzman
West Wardsboro, Vt., and Amesbury, Mass.

title: Jackson says he will cancel newly extended state contract if elected Georgia’s next governor
description: Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson says he will terminate his companies’ contracts with the state if he is elected in November, but he did not rule out extending contracts before the election and then pulling out if he wins. Jackson is set to face Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in […]
text:
Georgia Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson speaks at an Atlanta barbershop. Jackson reiterated his pledge to terminate his companies' contracts with the state if elected, but would not rule out extending contracts into his potential term and then pulling out if he wins. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderRepublican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson says he will terminate his companies’ contracts with the state if he is elected in November, but he did not rule out extending contracts before the election and then pulling out if he wins.
Jackson is set to face Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in less than three months.
Companies owned by Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive, have brought in nearly a billion dollars from state agencies since the 2020 fiscal year, according to a Healthbeat Atlanta analysis in February. The bulk of that money comes from medical personnel staffing services with the state Department of Community Health.
Jackson’s rival in the GOP primary contest, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, sought to make those contracts a campaign issue, taking the rare step of criticizing Jackson Healthcare from the Senate dais. A Senate bill stalled that would have barred anyone who has a financial interest in a state agency, including state contracts, from running for office – a measure that was largely seen as a swipe at Jackson.
Jackson responded in March by pledging to “unwind” all of his financial ties to the state government if elected, but on Tuesday, an 11Alive report found that the state Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Disabilities extended a contract with Locum Tenens, a Jackson Healthcare subsidiary, through the end of next June – six months into the next governor’s term.
Locum Tenens provides temporary healthcare workers to the department.
Speaking with reporters at a campaign stop Thursday, Jackson said continuing the contract does not amount to a contradiction of his pledge.
“There’s a 30-day out,” he said. “I can get out of that contract any day I want to. If I’m elected on Nov. 3, the next day, it will be terminated, and so it will not even be in existence on the day I arrive.”
Jackson added that he plans to exceed legal requirements to avoid even the appearance of impropriety and, if elected, he will push lawmakers to pass the most “strenuous ethics bill that’s ever been known.”
“We will have the highest of ethics,” he said. “You’ve never heard anybody in 43 years ever claim that I have ever done anything unethical, and we’re going to maintain that value going forward.”
Jackson said he could not say whether his companies would extend other contracts into the next governor’s term and pull out if he wins the election.
“I don’t know what all my companies are doing,” he said. “When they call us and they (have a) severe staffing shortage for mental health and some of these things, they’re going to respond.  We’re not assuming I’m going to win this election. I’ll deal with that at the time.
“Here’s what I can tell you. On Dec. 31, we will not have a contract if I’m the governor-elect at that point in time,” he added.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Democrats said that’s not good enough.
In a statement released Thursday afternoon, Bottoms called on Jackson to disclose more information about past contracts and suspend any new contracts or extensions while he is running for governor.
“Georgians deserve transparency and have a right to know how much money Rick Jackson is making off the taxpayers,” Bottoms said. “There’s no reason to trust him when he won’t provide the basic facts of how he’s made his fortune and continues to profit off Georgians all while opposing Medicaid expansion that would lower healthcare costs and ensure hundreds of thousands of Georgians get healthcare coverage.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Of wilderness, springtails and Donald Trump
description: Like many modern humans, especially those of us who are regularly bombarded by various technologies, I spend way too much time being distracted by “stuff” that doesn’t really matter, from news feeds to emails and text messages and what we’ve come to call social and streaming media—not to mention more traditional forms of the entertainment […]
text:
Bill Sherwonit's tent near Summit Lake in Alaska's Brooks Range. (Photo courtesy of Bill Sherwonit)Like many modern humans, especially those of us who are regularly bombarded by various technologies, I spend way too much time being distracted by “stuff” that doesn’t really matter, from news feeds to emails and text messages and what we’ve come to call social and streaming media—not to mention more traditional forms of the entertainment industry.
Fed by all these distractions, along with the details and concerns of busy lives, our minds are often filled with internal chatter that disconnects us from the real world we inhabit.
Long ago, I discovered that trips into “the wild” help to take me out of my head and ground me in the present moment; to be more mindful, more aware of my surroundings, my relationships with place and people and the other life forms with whom I share the world. At the same time, I become more attuned to what my physical senses and emotional body are experiencing.
This can be true even on short walks into the “nearby wild,” for instance local parklands. But the effect is deepened by longer stays in more remote wilderness, particularly on solitary sojourns.
I was recently reminded of all this during a 10-day solo adventure in Alaska’s Brooks Range wilderness, within Gates of the Arctic National Park.
Dropped off by floatplane at a place called Summit Lake, I chose to explore the Arctic landscape in modest fashion. Instead of backpacking or river-running many miles, I set up a base camp and did day hikes in assorted directions.
With an aging body and arthritic shoulders, this approach made sense. It also allowed me to move more slowly across the tundra and pay closer attention to my immediate surroundings and the multitude of life forms with whom I shared my temporary home.
Several days into my adventure, one experience in particular helped me to realize just how deeply I’d moved into a different—and I would say healthier—state of being.
It began with tiny creatures that are commonly called “springtails.” In certain circumstances, notably northern winters when the ground is covered by snow, these relatives of insects are also known as “snow fleas.”
There’s good reason for that: dark in color, and not much bigger than grains of ground pepper—small enough to fit on the head of a pin—springtails from a distance resemble fleas. And, like fleas, they hop around, though the mechanism of their movement differs.
I should also mention that while fleas have flattened and hard-shell bodies, springtails have more rounded, softer bodies that are easily crushed. And they don’t bite.
There’s considerably more to be shared about the nature of springtails, but for now I’ll end with this: when threatened, springtails jump away from the perceived danger by using a rigid, forked tail that folds under their body like a jackknife blade. A catch that normally holds the tail in place is released, allowing the springtail to propel itself into the air, out of harm’s way. Thus, springtail.
To see springtails leaping about the snow is an amazing—and to me, delightful—sight to behold, and this ability has contributed to my fascination with the species. But because they are dark and tiny and blend well with ground not covered by snow, I’d never noticed them in summer. Until my recent trip to the Brooks Range.
The springtails appeared following a stormy night in the mountains. Presumably seeking shelter from that storm, large numbers of them had begun crawling—or springing—from the soaked tundra onto my tent. And, eventually, into it, through a tiny slit that serves as an air vent along the tent’s bottom.
Hundreds, if not thousands, of them eventually infiltrated the tent and I wondered what the heck they could be, until I saw some of the dark forms jumping about.
Though I knew they wouldn’t bite or sting or otherwise harm me, I didn’t fancy the idea of them crawling all over my gear, not to mention my body. Softly blowing on them, I managed to keep most in the back of the tent. But some inevitably spread elsewhere.    
Springtails gather in the corner of Bill Sherwonit’s tent in Alaska’s Brooks Range. (Photo courtesy of Bill Sherwonit)
 
One morning I simply sat in the tent awhile, observing the springtails and contemplating the remarkable nature of those miniscule beings, which move about the world largely ignored or unrecognized by our kind.
Eventually my thoughts turned toward the notion that all life forms have value in and of themselves, irrespective of their relationship to humans, an idea and attitude that I embrace.
I further reflected that, as far as I can tell, only one species inhabiting the Earth considers itself more important than all the rest. And as I considered the egocentric nature of Homo sapiens, Donald Trump slipped into my thoughts, he being the epitome of human narcissism, in my opinion.
And in that moment I realized I’d gone more than a week without Trump entering my thoughts. That, like the springtails occupying my tent, seemed a rather astounding—and wonderful—thing, considering his overwhelming presence in the “normal” world of American culture that I’d temporarily left behind.
I encountered many other wonders during my days in that Arctic wilderness, but the juxtaposition of springtails and Trump—or more accurately, “no Trump”—reveal, as much as anything I experienced, the marvelous nature of the real world we humans inhabit and are truly part of: the wild, wild Earth.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Top federal highway official stops in Rhode Island to cheer on ‘Missing Move’ project
description: Earlier this year, as part of his department’s “Freedom to Drive” initiative, which aims to lessen the time Americans spend “staring at a car bumper,” U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy asked states to single out their most congested roadways. An unfinished plan to directly connect Route 4 and Interstate 95 in all directions was at […]
text:
U.S. Federal Highway Administrator Sean McMaster, center, and Rhode Island Department of Transportation Interim Director Robert Rocchio, right, tour construction on the $144 million 'Missing Move' project in East Greenwich on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Earlier this year, as part of his department’s “Freedom to Drive” initiative, which aims to lessen the time Americans spend “staring at a car bumper,” U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy asked states to single out their most congested roadways.
An unfinished plan to directly connect Route 4 and Interstate 95 in all directions was at the top of Rhode Island’s list. 
Planned over 60 years ago but deferred continually and never completed, the missing links have forced motorists to detour off the highways and onto secondary, local roads and through traffic lights before they can get back on the freeway.
The pair of turns, one to allow easy access from I-95 North to Route 4 South, and the other from Route 4 North to I-95 South, were set aside even as the rest of the highway became operational in 1972. Now the missing links are finally starting to take shape as part of the Rhode Island Department of Transportation’s (RIDOT) $144 million “Missing Move” project. 
It was an excellent choice, as far as the feds are concerned.
“These new alignments…it’s going to be absolutely fantastically transformational from a congestion management standpoint,” U.S. Federal Highway Administrator Sean McMaster said Thursday after a tour of the future link between I-95 North to Route 4 South.
McMaster was in Rhode Island to join Gov. Dan McKee and members of the state’s congressional delegation for a firsthand look at one portion of the two-part project. 
“These ‘missing moves’ were deferred,” Rhode Island Department of Transportation Interim Director Robert Rocchio said at the start of the tour. “They were planned. They were pushed out to a later date, and I don’t think they ever anticipated it would be this much later.”
Rocchio was standing in a large valley alongside I-95 in East Greenwich, addressing a crowd of officials, department employees and media, all donning hardhats and fluorescent safety vests. The site is visible evidence of the in-progress connection from I-95 North to Route 4 South, carved through a stretch of ledge that would have taken two years to dismantle with hammering techniques, Rocchio said. 
“So, we decided to go with 30 days of blasting,” Rocchio said. “We did a lot of blasting.” He added that much of the blasted bedrock will be put to good use elsewhere on the project. 
The future at-grade link between I-95 North and Route 4 South will be paired with what Rocchio described as a roughly 600-foot-long elevated bridge that will eventually carry Route 4 northbound traffic over the interchange and onto I-95 South. I-95 will be slightly realigned to accommodate the structure, Rocchio said, and the bridge’s support columns will rise from the median.
Currently, motorists must detour off the highway and onto secondary, local roads and through traffic lights before they can get back on the freeway.
“This eliminates all that,” Rocchio said.
Gov. Dan McKee, left, speaks with U.S. Federal Highway Administrator Sean McMaster during a tour of the ‘Missing Move’ construction site in East Greenwich on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Route 4 connects Route 102 to I-95 and carries about 63,000 vehicles each day, according to RIDOT. 
When RIDOT broke ground on the project last year, an agency press release noted “numerous adjustments” the department had made to traffic signals in the surrounding area, all to compensate for the missing connections at the interchange. 
Increased development and traffic at the nearby New England Institute of Technology campus only heightened traffic issues in the area, and the department noted about 60 crashes per year at the Division Street/South County Trail intersection to which travelers often resort without the missing moves.
Fixing the two missing connections has been on the state’s wishlist for years. A 2003 assessment took note of “No fluid movement from Route 4 North to I-95 South or I-95 North to Route 4 South,” with the missing moves noted as a problem for commuters and trucks traveling to and from Quonset’s Davisville area.
An additional portion of the project will add three ramps on Route 403 in North Kingstown and link the Quonset Business Park to the West Davisville area via a limited-access highway.
RIDOT began construction in winter 2025 and is expected to finish in fall 2027.
“This was the top project that was identified from Rhode Island, and you can see why when you see the amount of traffic right now on 95 and traffic behind us on 4,” McMaster said.
An $81 million federal grant awarded in January 2024 under the Joe Biden administration is covering more than half of the project’s costs, which were estimated at $135 million in RIDOT’s original grant application. 
McMaster told reporters that President Donald Trump’s administration is “happy to support” the initiative, adding that the “amount of investment is justified.” McMaster pointed to the defense industry in Quonset as one example of why the project is worth subsidizing, because the new turns will help improve freight access.
A Rhode Island Department of Transportation staffer reviews a script during of a tour of the ‘Missing Move’ construction site off Interstate 95 in East Greenwich on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
“The freight movement along this corridor has been growing over the last couple of decades,” McMaster said. “This project is going to absolutely enhance that, and save not only Rhode Islanders tremendous pain from sitting in congested corridors, but it’s going to also have a positive net impact on the national economy.”
“From the federal government’s side, when we invest and when we support with American taxpayer dollars, this is exactly the type of charge and the impacts we would like to see,” McMaster added. 
He estimated that the new connections could save motorists a combined 1 million hours in congestion each year, plus $1 billion annually in economic savings from reduced congestion.
“I’m looking forward to seeing the completion and maybe getting an invite back when this goes live here in another year,” McMaster said.
