name: Alaska Beacon
title: Ruling overturns land trade in Alaska wildlife refuge, casts doubt on road plan
description: A federal judge has overturned the land exchange intended to enable the state to build a controversial road through the Izembek National Wildlife Refuge, possibly halting plans for construction to start in the coming weeks. U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason ruled Tuesday that the Department of the Interior violated three laws when it approved […]
text:
Pacific black brant fly above Izembek Lagoon at Izembek National Wildlife Refuge on Dec. 27, 2013. The refuge is used as a migratory stop for nearly the entire global population of Pacific black brant. Road supporters say the access route is needed for emergency evacuations, while road opponents say brant and other important birds and wildlife would be harmed by the project. (Photo by Kristine Sowl/U.S. Fish and Wildlfie Service)A federal judge has overturned the land exchange intended to enable the state to build a controversial road through the Izembek National Wildlife Refuge, possibly halting plans for construction to start in the coming weeks.
U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason ruled Tuesday that the Department of the Interior violated three laws when it approved a trade of Native-owned land for acreage within the Izembek National Wildlife Refuge. The state plans to appeal the decision.
In approving the land trade between the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the King Cove Corporation, the local for-profit Native village corporation, the Trump administration’s Interior Department violated three laws, Gleason ruled: the Endangered Species Act, the Refuge Act and the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

The road has been promoted for decades as an emergency route connecting the village of King Cove, with about 750 residents, to an all-weather airport at the much-smaller village of Cold Bay. The Cold Bay airport is a military legacy dating back to World War II; it has a runway extending over 10,000 feet, allowing it to accommodate large jets.
The 18.9-mile road, as planned, would cross a narrow isthmus that separates the refuge’s Izembek Lagoon on the north from Kinzarof Lagoon on the south. Both lagoons are important to migratory birds and other wildlife.
The Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities, which has mobilized equipment and materials to start building a section of the road, intends to begin construction despite Gleason’s ruling.
This year’s construction “is still on track,” Sonny Mauricio, a public information officer with the department, said by email. 
Road-building equipment mobilized at King Cove is seen in August 2026. The equipment is itended for use on a road to connect King Cove with the all-season airport at Cold Bay. The road would cross through Izembek National Wildlife Refuge. (Photo by Karolina Zakravska/Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities)
“That work is on King Cove Corporation’s own land, which is separate from and outside the land addressed in Judge Gleason’s ruling, so the decision doesn’t affect this year’s construction plans,” Mauricio wrote.
Justin Shelby, operations manager for the department’s central region, said construction is intended to start sometime after Sept. 1.
And Alaska’s acting attorney general reiterated the state’s desire to build the road quickly.
“Although we are sorely disappointed that the court ruled more process was necessary after years and years of endless review, the construction of this life-saving road remains a priority. We will appeal this decision and move forward with helping the community build the portions of the road that we can while we work on our appeal to overturn this ruling,” Acting Attorney General Cori Mills said in a statement.
But attorneys for the environmental and tribal plaintiffs who oppose the road and sued to overturn the land trade said construction of any part of the project would be illegal.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers permit issued to the state on July 9 covers the entire 18.9-mile road planned to link King Cove to an all-weather airport at the tiny village of Cold Bay, not just a piece of it, the plaintiff attorneys said. And that permit is predicated on the land exchange, they said.
“Our position is that there is no way that the road construction can legally proceed,” said Michelle Sinnott, an attorney with Trustees for Alaska, an environmental law firm representing the conservation groups that sued to overturn the land exchange.
The plaintiff attorneys said one part of Gleason’s ruling is particularly relevant to the state’s road construction plans.
The ANILCA violation the judge cited concerns a required analysis for any contemplated road in an Alaska conservation unit, which the department failed to carry out before it approved the land trade.
 

The view from Izembek Lagoon to Cold Bay is seen on May 24, 2006. Izembek Isthmus has been part of a designated wilderness area. The Trump administration-approved trade gave some of the wilderness acreage to the King Cove Corporation to enable a road to be build between King Cove and Cold Bay. (Photo by Kristine Sowl/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)
 

	Gleason shot down the argument from the Trump administration and the state that the land trade negated the need to do the analysis, called the Title XI provision, which is named for a section in the sweeping conservation law that relates to road construction and utility corridors.
The Interior Department “cannot rely on the Exchange’s removal of the corridor from the Refuge — the very action alleged to require Title XI compliance — as the reason why Title XI does not apply,” Gleason wrote.
Rebecca Noblin, an attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity, a co-plaintiff with three Yup’ik tribal governments, said it would be unlawful for the state to designate part of the planned road as not falling under those Title XI requirements.
“If any part of a road goes through a refuge, it all has to go through Title XI,” she said.
If the state were to proceed with construction, “that would be a pretty bold violation of a court order that just voided the land exchange under Title XI,” Sinnott said.
Three lawsuits, now consolidated, challenged the trade, while two additional lawsuits, also now consolidated, are challenging the Corps of Engineers wetland-fill permit that was granted to the state last month to enable road construction.
In addition to suing to overturn the land trade, road opponents have sued to overturn the Corp’s permit.
Debate over the road has divided Alaska Native groups.
The residents of King Cove and the Aleut Corp., the regional corporation that includes the village, are strong advocates for the road and the land trade that would enable it. But many Western Alaska Yup’ik residents, including those who are members of the three tribal governments that have sued to block construction, oppose the project because of threats to migratory birds that depend on Izembek’s wetlands and are also important sources of subsistence food.
 

A black oystercatcher forages on June 7, 2008, in Kinzarof Lagoon in the Izembek National Wildlife Refuge. (Photo by Kristine Sowl/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)
 

	The refuge, especially the lagoon area that has been protected as designated wilderness, is the gathering site for hundreds of thousands of birds, including most of the world’s population of Pacific black brant, a type of goose. The refuge also holds one of the world’s largest beds of eelgrass, a plant that supports birds and marine life.
A representative of one of the tribal governments that sued to overturn the land trade cited Izembek’s importance to migratory birds.
“Our community depends on the brant and emperor geese and subsistence use to eat, so I’m relieved the court decided to protect Izembek from a road that could hurt our harvests,” Chief Edgar Tall Sr. of the Native Village of Hooper Bay, said in a statement. “I started learning how to find and save food like the birds, salmon and moose at a very young age from my elders, and that’s still how a lot of us get enough food. It’s getting harder to make our voice heard and protect our right to live off the land and the sea, but if Izembek is safe, that will help.”
Even before Gleason issued her ruling voiding the land trade, the plaintiffs were seeking an injunction barring the start of road construction. That request was filed on July 24 as part of the lawsuit seeking to overturn the Corps permit.
Sinnott said the 2.8-mile road section, though it is planned for King Cove Corporation-owned land and not land within refuge boundaries, would cause environmental harm. The plan calls for a dozen culverts, a bridge and other disturbances, she said.
But the Alaska Department of Law, in a brief filed in opposition to the motion for an injunction halting road construction, has argued that Corps permit is not relevant to the construction work planned on the initial 2.8-mile section of road.
Rather than cause harm, the state and King Cove parties “assert that this initial construction phase will not only render significant benefits to the community of King Cove but is also environmentally beneficial,” the Department of Law argued in its Aug. 6 response to the injunction request.
“Construction of the initial 2.8 miles of road seeks to reestablish the historical means of access for King Cove residents to subsistence use lands on the Kinzarof Lagoon bookends and consolidate off-road vehicle (ORV) access onto a consolidated route to prevent compounding impacts caused by dispersed use,” the department’s response said.
The opposing parties were scheduled to file reports in court Thursday detailing the status of road construction and how the latest legal decision is expected to affect it.
A brown bear walks by a bird on Aug. 3, 2008, in Kinzarof Lagoon at the Izembek National Wildlife Refuge. The lagoon habitat supports several wild mammal species as well as bird populations. (Photo by Kristine Sowl/U.S. Fish and WIldlife Service)

title: Oklahomans head to the polls for first day of early voting in primary runoff
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahomans braved the scorching heat Thursday and began casting their votes to narrow down which candidates will make it to the general election ballot in November.  Voters throughout Oklahoma, including Darla Gragert in Oklahoma City, turned out for the first of three days of early voting in the statewide election despite temperatures […]
text:
Voters exit their cars and head into the Oklahoma County Election Board Thursday in Oklahoma City to vote in the primary runoff election. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahomans braved the scorching heat Thursday and began casting their votes to narrow down which candidates will make it to the general election ballot in November. 
Voters throughout Oklahoma, including Darla Gragert in Oklahoma City, turned out for the first of three days of early voting in the statewide election despite temperatures that by midday had already topped over 100 degrees. 
Gragert, a retired teacher, said the Republican governor and superintendent runoffs drew her to the polls. Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond is facing off against financial adviser Mike Mazzei for the Republican gubernatorial nomination. Retired educator Robert Franklin is challenging teacher James Taylor.
“I never like messy,” Gragert said. “I like positive, I don’t like negative, I don’t like mudslinging. We have to look past all the ads and look at their record of what they’ve actually done.”
Voter Guide: 2026 Oklahoma Primary Runoff Election

She said because she was a teacher for 27 years, education issues are important to her because she knows the impact it has on society as a whole. 
Multiple major partisan offices are on the Aug. 25 runoff election ballot. Republican voters will decide on party nominees for governor, state superintendent, and labor and insurance commissioners. Democrats can vote in a runoff between two candidates for the U.S. Senate. 
Lawmakers also placed two nonpartisan state questions on the ballot. One would give lawmakers the power to recalculate the amount paid under a manufacturing tax incentive program while the other would enshrine voter identification in the state Constitution. All voters are eligible to vote on state questions regardless of party affiliation.
While there were no lines at Oklahoma County’s polls, a steady flow of people came in and out of Oklahoma County’s early voting location. Nobody lined up outside, but voters through Election Day on Aug. 25 expected to face temperatures of over 100 degrees.
The Oklahoma County early voting site is air conditioned. But relief from the heat could vary by county because local county election boards determine early voting polling locations, although a spokesperson with the State Election Board said most county boards choose their offices. 
The National Weather Service in Norman issued a warning Thursday afternoon that “dangerous heat” would continue to bring high temperatures with heat indexes expected to be between 105 and 110 degrees across much of Oklahoma. They advised people stay hydrated and indoors when possible. 
David Robertson said while he usually likes to vote on Election Day, he would be out of town Tuesday, so he decided to vote early at the Oklahoma County Election Board on Thursday. 
He said the Oklahoma County Commissioner race drew him, and he voted for Democrat Jason Lowe because he’s been impressed by what Lowe has done for the community. 
“I think a person should vote whenever there’s an issue to vote on because one way or another, it’s gonna affect you,” Robertson said. 
The state questions on the ballot were difficult to understand, he said. But Robertson said he “did his research” before voting. 
Both state questions were added to the August ballot by state lawmakers this past session. 
State Question 844 asks voters to amend the state constitution to allow lawmakers to to recalculate how much it should pay for a five-year property tax exemption offered to manufacturers with new operations in Oklahoma. Supporters say the program’s cost has grown beyond the fund dedicated to support it as qualifying criteria have changed, but critics argue changes to the program could shortchange local schools and governments millions in property tax revenue. 
While identification is already required to vote in Oklahoma elections, State Question 846 asks voters to amend the state constitution to include voter ID requirements and give lawmakers the ability to enact laws to specify what forms of identification are acceptable. 
Genny Lytle, a retired teacher, said education issues and the superintendent’s race were top of mind when she voted Thursday. She said she was going to be unavailable to vote next week. She said she voted ‘no’ on State Question 844 because she was concerned it would affect education funding.
“I encourage people to vote early because it was easy and fast with no lines,” Lytle said. 
Oklahoma’s primary elections are closed, meaning voters can only vote in primaries for their registered party. All voters, including independents and Libertarians, can vote on the state questions. 
Polls are for early voting from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Thursday and Friday and from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Saturday. Oklahomans can cast their ballots on Tuesday at their local precinct from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. 
Early voting locations can be found at the Oklahoma Voter Portal. Voters must cast ballots in the county in which they are registered. 
The State Election Board did not yet have an estimate of how many ballots had been cast during early voting as of Thursday afternoon.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mail-in ballots have cut into popularity of early in-person voting
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: As voters this election cycle weigh ballot questions allowing people to register and vote on Election Day, and substituting an all-party primary in for the traditional party-based primaries, early in-person voting remains an enduring and often utilized election reform in Massachusetts.
text:
WHEN VOTERS BEGIN casting their ballots at the polls this weekend ahead of the September 1 primary, they’ll be partaking in an early voting method that hit the Bay State a decade ago — the relevance of which some locals clerks now question.
Early in-person voting became an option for voters in 2016, after Gov. Deval Patrick signed a law in May of 2014 applying the practice to biennial state elections only. The law dictated that the early voting period begin 11 business days preceding the election, and required municipalities to have at least one voting site open during normal business hours.
In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the state introduced mail-in voting for all voters — not just for those who fell under the specific requirements necessary to receive an absentee ballot. 
Those temporary pandemic-era methods changed the way people approached voting, especially after Gov. Charlie Baker in 2022 signed a law permanently expanding early in-person and mail-in voting to primary and general elections. 
The popularity of early in-person voting has decreased over the years, particularly in primary elections, in part due to the surging popularity of mail-in voting. But as voters this election cycle weigh ballot questions allowing people to register and vote on Election Day (Question 4), and substituting an all-party primary in for the traditional party-based primaries (Question 3), early in-person voting remains an enduring and often utilized election reform in Massachusetts.
Local Impacts
While Massachusetts Town Clerks Association President and Easton Town Clerk Danielle Sicard called it “exciting” to see more voting options, she described early in-person voting as “a mini election every day” that includes the preparation, counts, and balancing of voting lists for what could be a very small team of election officials in each municipality, while they’re preparing for a 13-hour Election Day and managing mail-in ballots. 
“I look at finances and data, and when I see a 3.4 percent turnout in early in-person voting, that means town halls were open for six hours and saw 20 voters,” Sicard said, referring to the September 2024 primary early voting turnout. 
“Staffing for the potential for hundreds because you don’t know and you have to be prepared. And I’m talking about primaries,” Sicard, who has been a clerk for 16 years, said. “I don’t think we should eliminate choices when we’re talking about November elections, but we should limit the number of days so we cut the cost in half.”
Still, 28,908 voters took advantage of early in-person voting to make their voices heard in the 2024 primary elections.
Once early voting takes place this fall, municipalities will be reimbursed for their efforts, Galvin spokesperson Deb O’Malley said, though the exact process has varied over time. In recent years, the secretary of state’s office has a line item within its budget meant for the reimbursements. The reimbursement stems from former Auditor Suzanne Bump’s determination in 2017 that a  2014 early voting law signed by Gov. Deval Patrick was an unfunded mandate. Though in 2018 lawmakers were still hesitant about implementing early voting for primary elections with worries about cost. 
The amount that each municipality receives is based on an auditor’s office survey of local officials about costs for things like staffing and postage, O’Malley said. The early voting line item in the current state budget is $6.8 million.
MIT Elections Data and Science Lab Director Professor Charles Stewart told the News Service that early in-person voting “creates administrative burdens for municipalities that have to implement it. Elections are administered by the 351 cities and towns. You have to have early voting set up in every little town, which is problematic given the demand for early voting.”
“There is so little early voting in the primaries and the midterm elections that I’ll go out on a limb and say if Massachusetts only had early voting for presidential years I don’t think it would be tragic. And it would not reduce turnout and it would give relief to the cities and towns of the commonwealth,” Stewart said.
Referring to association data, Sicard said that since the onset of the permanent vote-by-mail method in 2022, early in-person voting for primary elections have seen a 3.4 percent to 4.6 percent turnout rate with a median reimbursement cost of $720,000 to communities.
“I like to use this analogy as an example. Let’s look at a fire department. Let’s say we’re going to ask the same two to four firefighters to put out a brush fire for 11 days straight. They can’t tag team, they don’t get a day off, while they’re planning for their largest fire that they get every two years or four years,” Sicard said. “Wouldn’t we expect that at some point there’s going to be a problem?”
While 520,056 voters cast mail-in ballots in the 2024 primaries, early in-person voting remains “a very important element of our elections,” Common Cause Massachusetts Executive Director Geoff Foster said.
“It ensures people can vote at a time that works for their schedule,” he said. “It includes a weekend and weeknight option. People aren’t always working conventional hours.” 
“It’s really important that our voting laws can meet people where they’re at in the 21st century,” he said. “I do think if there are conversations around the impact early voting processes might be having on local election officials, that conversation needs to be more about resources and not whether we should be rolling back our voting rights.”
Compared to mail-in voting, early in-person voting also gives voters a longer period of time to study up on candidates, absorb their advertising, and hear directly from them before casting their ballots. 
While only briefly, early in-person voting also creates de facto same-day registration in Massachusetts for the primaries, Foster said. Saturday, August 22 is the last day voters can register for the primary and is also the first day of early voting, giving them a one-day window to complete both tasks. In the November 3 general election, there’s a week where the two overlap; the early voting period begins October 17 and runs through October 30, and the voter registration deadline is October 24.
“I think what’s really important is that we continue to see an increase in participation in democracy. You’re hearing, you know, countries overseas where they’re decreasing participation in democracy, and I think it’s really important, regardless of your political persuasion or where you’re at, that we give the most access to people to vote,” Sen. Barry Finegold, who led early voting negotiations in 2014, reflected. “People have incredibly busy schedules, there’s a lot going on, and the easier we can make it for people to participate, I think it’s a win for democracy.”
Looking Back
Gov. Deval Patrick in 2014 said the early voting law, which also instituted online voter registration, “makes our democracy better.” He was backed by Galvin, who pointed out that the law would mean “you don’t need a reason” to vote earlier, as was required under absentee voting prerequisites. 
Lawmakers agreed in 2014 to limit early voting to general state elections every two years. The law also authorized 16- and 17-year-olds to pre-register to vote, and required post-election audits of voting equipment. During negotiations, conferees dropped a Senate-approved plan to let people register and vote during early in-person voting or on Election Day.
Finegold, then-Senate chair of the Election Laws Committee, said in 2014 that “we focused where we thought the highest turnout would be.”  
“It was super hard because, you know, you were really negotiating with five different groups. You had the House, the Senate, the secretary of state, you had the Republicans, you had the governor,” Finegold said. “And then you had all the outside interests.”
Voters cast over one million ballots in the first-ever early in-person voting period leading up to the Nov. 8, 2016 state election, accounting for 30.7 percent total ballots cast, according to the secretary of state’s website. Voters were able to vote early in a midterm election without providing a reason for the first time in the Nov. 6, 2018 election. Of 2.7 million ballots cast, 21.2 percent, or over 584,000 of them, were early voting ballots, per state voter statistics. 
“Massachusetts, like every other state in New England, had a very conservative set of laws about voting, and New England in general had been very slow to embrace convenience voting, and that was because of constitutional constraints,” Stewart told the News Service. “So the early voting law was an attempt to get around constitutional issues.”
“Voters immediately gravitated towards it because they were already getting around the restrictions,” Stewart said of early in-person voting. “In 2016, and even into 2018, there was quite a lot of usage of it. But once the pandemic came and no excuse absentee voting arrived, voters flooded into voting by mail as opposed to voting early.” 
During the pandemic, voting methods “underwent a dramatic change” due to temporary voter laws, per Galvin’s office. Bay Staters could vote in person on Election Day, in person during an early voting period, or by mail. “No-excuse voting by mail” was available for the September primary election and the November general election — a different method than by absentee ballot, which required that voters be either away from their city or town on Election Day, have a religious reason they couldn’t vote at the polls on Election Day, or have a disability that prevented them from voting in person. 
Of 1.7 million ballots cast for the September 1, 2020 primary, voting early in-person accounted for 12.2 percent, mail-in voting sat at 47.7 percent, and Election Day voting accounted for 40.1 percent of ballots. Galvin’s statistics show his office accepted over 814,000 ballots by mail and over 208,000 ballots early in-person.
In November 2020, 23.1 percent, almost 844,000 voters, cast their ballots early in-person; 41.7 percent, more than 1.5 million voters, mailed their ballots; and 35.2 percent cast them on Election Day, totaling to over 3.6 million ballots. 
When Baker signed an elections reform bill in June of 2022, he ushered into law a permanent system of no-excuse early voting by guaranteeing the right to vote early or by mail in state elections and state primaries. The law requires that early voting begins 17 days before the election for state biennial elections — lasting for 14 days — and 10 days before the election for presidential or state primaries. The law also moved the deadline for prospective voters to register from 20 days before Election Day to 10 days out. 
“Early voting has generally dropped significantly since people started voting by mail,” O’Malley told the News Service. “It’s just shifting. People who want to vote before Election Day are just doing it a different way. It’s become less common to vote on Election Day since they have all the options.” 
“It could still change, we’re still learning,” O’Malley continued. “This is our first, really, post-COVID midterm election, and I can’t compare a midterm election to a presidential election — the equivalent would be four years prior, and four years ago we were still changing our laws.” 
While people may not be voting in person early as much as they once did, Finegold said, “When it comes to participation in democracy, I still believe we want to give every avenue possible for people to participate. Could there be some tweaks in the future? Sure. But I do believe the fact that we allow people to vote early, that we allow people to vote by mail, has enhanced democracy, and improved people’s ability to participate in the process.” 
Mail-in and early in-person voting also has an impact on campaigning, Suffolk Poll Director David Paleologos noted.
“Early voting rewards the candidates who are most organized at the local level, at the precinct level,” Paleologos said. “We have a Senate race coming up. One of the things we’ll be tracking is how early are voters breaking? Because a large share of voters vote early either by mail or in person.” 
Even though most voting will take place on Election Day, “if some candidate banks an early lead, there’s no persuasion left,” he said. “There’s nothing you can do to change that person’s vote, they’ve voted. So it becomes a smaller pool of persuadables.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Bureau for Social Services commissioner out, limited details from Morrisey administration
description: Lorie Bragg is no longer the commissioner of the state’s Bureau for Social Services, a position tasked with overseeing the troubled foster care system.
text:
Lorie Bragg has resigned as commissioner of the state’s Bureau for Social Services. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Department of Human Services)Lorie Bragg is no longer the commissioner of the state’s Bureau for Social Services, a position tasked with overseeing the troubled foster care system.
Bragg officially stepped into the role in May of last year within Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s administration. She confirmed the exit to West Virginia Watch on Wednesday. 
“I was grateful for the opportunity to do that, to even step up into commissioner,” Bragg said. “It really was a privilege to work with the people that I worked with … I’m closing a chapter, and I’m just looking forward to what comes next, new opportunities and still making a difference with children and families. This has been my heart my whole career.”
Bragg had more than two decades of experience in child welfare and social services, including previously serving as Child Protective Services case aide. 
There are more than 5,600 children in West Virginia foster care. More than 500 of those children are living out of state due to West Virginia’s shortage of in-state care options, and the Department of Human Services continues to house foster children in hotel rooms.
DoHS Secretary Carl Ayers also confirmed Bragg’s exit this week.
“We can confirm that Ms. Bragg is no longer an employee of the Department of Human Services. This is a personnel matter, therefore, we cannot provide further information or comment,” he wrote in an email.
Former Department. of Human Services Secretary Alex Mayer resigned from his position earlier this year, marking another major turnover in child welfare under Gov. Patrick Morrisey. Mayer now works in the private sector. 
Bragg emphasized the hard work of the Bureau of Social Services’ staff during her tenure.
“I really have tremendous respect for them. Our providers, like our foster families, kinship families, the community partners that we work with, I feel like all of them truly do work together to support West Virginia’s children and families,” she said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Marketplace: What’s ahead for Mississippi farmers?
description: Will Maples, an agricultural economics professor at Mississippi State, said producers are “way ahead of where we were this time last year” with China promising to buy around 25 million tons of soybeans this year. But Maples cautions that input costs are still a huge drag on profit.
text:
Demand for soybeans has improved since last year but Mississippi farmers still face high input costs. 
Agriculture remains a top industry for the state with soybeans being the most valuable row crop, valued at over $1 billion a year. Last year, China, the world’s largest soybean purchaser, did not buy any soybeans until late fall due to the Trump administration’s trade war tariffs. This led to economic uncertainty for farmers who were already coping with years of rising costs. 
Will Maples, an agricultural economics professor at Mississippi State, said producers are “way ahead of where we were this time last year” with China promising to buy around 25 million tons of soybeans this year. But Maples cautions that input costs are still a huge drag on profit. He said that input costs are the biggest concern he hears about from farmers. 
Katherine Lin
During the 2026 legislative session, state lawmakers tried to ease pressure on farmers by passing a bill exempting lime used for farming from sales taxes and reducing the sales tax on fencing materials used for containing livestock. However, prices are often driven by global forces. The ongoing war with Iran has led to increased prices for fuel and fertilizer. 
Duane Dunlap of DNS Commodities, an agriculture and renewables consulting firm, said that things are not yet where they need to be for growers to turn a profit. 
Dunlap and Maples both said that the industry is grappling with how to become less susceptible to trade disruptions. 
“What’s the next step in terms of demand?” Maples asked. 
Dunlap said that much of the strength in the commodities market is driven by high biofuel targets set by the federal government. For Mississippi, Dunlap believes the biggest opportunity is encouraging soybean processing within the state. He points out that soybean meal is a major food ingredient for livestock and that helping feed the state’s robust poultry industry could also provide an opportunity to strengthen the domestic market.
In addition to dealing with market forces, farmers are waiting on a new farm bill from Congress. The House passed its version in April but the bill is stalled in the Senate Agriculture Committee over the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program for poor people. 
Other news

Time named the University of Southern Mississippi’s Gulf Blue Navigator as one of the best accelerators in the U.S. The program focuses on blue-tech startups with the “substantial potential to impact ocean health, economic development and innovation.”
Nissan is using AI to monitor workers at its Canton plant over video. The company said that it is using video monitoring to save millions of dollars in worker safety, to train new workers and keep workers safe. Nissan told Business Insider that the system has only been deployed in its Canton plant.
Southwire, a wire and cable manufacturer, is investing over $250 million in Starkville to expand its operations. The investment is expected to create 128 new jobs. The Golden Triangle continues to be an attractive region for development with the head of its development agency recently saying that there has been interest from data center and defense companies in the region.
In Mississippi, almost all alcohol flows through the state-owned warehouse in Gluckstadt. A new article in the Mississippi Law Journal compares Mississippi’s alcohol laws to other states and makes recommendations about opportunities for reform. The Department of Revenue reported that it collected $108 million last year through its Alcoholic Beverage Control operation.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho attorney general appeals court order allowing abortions to protect health, prevent self-harm
description: Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador announced Thursday his office is appealing a recent federal court ruling allowing abortions to protect the mother’s health or prevent her death from self-harm. Labrador is asking a federal appeals court to block the decision, allowing the near-total abortion ban to be enforced as written.  Labrador argued that U.S. Distri[...]
text:
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador speaks at a press conference outside the U.S. Supreme Court on April 24, 2024, in Washington, D.C.  (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador announced Thursday his office is appealing a recent federal court ruling allowing abortions to protect the mother’s health or prevent her death from self-harm.
Labrador is asking a federal appeals court to block the decision, allowing the near-total abortion ban to be enforced as written. 
Idaho judge ruling allows abortion if it protects mother’s health, prevents self-harm

Labrador argued that U.S. District of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill’s ruling defied the U.S. Supreme Court decision Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health, which overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, according to a press release from Labrador’s office. 
The legal battle stems from a lawsuit from Dr. Stacy Seyb, a Boise maternal-fetal medicine specialist, who argued that Idaho’s abortion bans were unconstitutional because they didn’t allow abortions to protect a mother’s health, her future fertility or if her mental health put her at risk of self-harm. 
Labrador said Winmill’s ruling “has replaced Idaho’s law with his own abortion standard,” and that Idaho’s law does allow for pregnant patients with medical emergencies to be treated in the state.
“Dobbs made clear that abortion policy belongs to the people and their elected state representatives, not the judiciary,” Labrador said in a press release. “We have appealed to the Ninth Circuit, and we will fight until this ruling is reversed and Idaho’s law is restored.”
Seyb is represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice.
“The Attorney General’s utter disregard for the health and welfare of pregnant Idaho residents is appalling,” Stephanie Toti, executive director of the Lawyering Project, said in an email. “We look forward to continuing to litigate this case with the goal of making it safer for people to be pregnant in Idaho.”
Idaho’s criminal abortion ban allows abortion to prevent the death of the mother, to treat ectopic or molar pregnancies, and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester, if there’s been a police report filed. Doctors who provide abortions that don’t fall within those exceptions face two to five years in prison and revocation of their medical license. 
Idaho also has a civil-enforcement ban on abortion, allowing family members to sue abortion providers for a minimum of $20,000 if an abortion occurs after six weeks or after fetal heartbeat activity is detected. 
Winmill’s 81-page decision said the U.S. Constitution protects access to abortion in certain high-risk cases that went beyond the exemptions outlined in Idaho’s ban. 
A voter-led initiative will appear on November ballots this year that, if approved, would overturn Idaho’s abortion ban and enumerate protections to women’s reproductive healthcare and privacy into law. 
Labrador’s appeal also argues that Winmill’s decision should not be applied to every doctor in the state, but only Seyb because he is the one who challenged the law. He said the Winmill’s decision violates the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that said federal courts cannot in most cases issue “universal injunctions,” which broadly block enforcement of laws for everyone, not just the parties to the lawsuit.

title: Cox Communications becomes part of the Spectrum brand, affecting 1,000 Kansas employees
description: TOPEKA — Charter Communications finalized its $34.5 billion deal to acquire Cox Communications on Thursday, and Kansans will soon see their Cox products marketed under Charter’s Spectrum brand.  Along with its Cox transaction, Charter announced completion of its purchase of Liberty Broadband Corp.  Now the largest cable company in the country, with services[...]
text:
Cox Communications trucks in Kansas will soon be sporting Spectrum branding after Charter Communications purchased the company. (Submitted by Charter Communications)TOPEKA — Charter Communications finalized its $34.5 billion deal to acquire Cox Communications on Thursday, and Kansans will soon see their Cox products marketed under Charter’s Spectrum brand. 
Along with its Cox transaction, Charter announced completion of its purchase of Liberty Broadband Corp. 
Now the largest cable company in the country, with services across 45 states, Charter will rebrand Cox services to the Spectrum name, said Chris Winfrey, CEO and president of the Connecticut-based company, in a media call. 
Winfrey said he expects frontline employees to see few changes. There are more than 1,000 Cox employees in Kansas. 
“The thing I want to make really clear is that from a frontline employee perspective, which is probably 90% of what each of these two companies have, there’ll be very little change, and we’re actually out hiring additional people today for sales positions,” he said. 
Charter plans to move all customer service to the United States, which is a “job creation opportunity,” Winfrey said.
The company will be hiring for 1,000 new sales positions, said spokeswoman Christine Martini in an email. The company’s new release said all employees would be paid a minimum of $20 an hour.
Cox’s Atlanta headquarters office will see some reorganization, Winfrey said, but part of the acquisition negotiations included maintaining a “significant presence” in the city. 
“Across many of our locations, the composition of the different types of employees is going to change to optimize for the footprint that we have and the talent that we have,” Winfrey said. “There’ll be certain functions that come out of Atlanta, and there’s certain functions that are already being moved into Atlanta.”
Charter’s southeast region is being moved to the Atlanta headquarter campus, Winfrey said. 
Cox customers will see the brand name shift to Spectrum beginning in September, which includes changing all building and truck signage.
However, cost changes will occur immediately, Winfrey said. Internet pricing will be “better” and new Cox Mobile customers can receive a free mobile line for a year, he said. 
“The value is higher for Spectrum products with more apps included, often better internet pricing,” Winfrey said. “The average pricing of internet is much lower with Spectrum, and mobile is lower, and video is also lower, but also has more value with the app.”
Winfrey said no Cox customers will be forced to switch but can elect to do so once Spectrum pricing and packages are launched in mid-September. 
Charter is a publicly traded company on the New York Stock Exchange. Cox Communications was a privately held company.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Stein touts historic teacher pay raises as NC students return to school
description: The spending plan includes more funding for North Carolina’s Principal Recruitment Supplement Program.
text:
Gov. Josh Stein speaks with reporters on Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)As North Carolina students and teachers head back to school, Gov. Josh Stein highlighted the state’s commitment to education during a Thursday press conference. 
North Carolina’s 2026 budget delivers the largest average teacher pay raise for the state in 20 years, Stein said, and the largest increase in starting teacher pay in about 50 years.
Stein said the budget strengthens public schools by investing in teacher recruitment and retention through apprenticeships and professional development. It also enhances training for early math educators, helping to set students up for success later on in their education and careers. 
“When we invest in our kids, we invest in their future,” Stein said. “We invest in our future, so I am proud that we’re sending our kids back to school this year with a budget that higher prioritizes them.”
The spending plan also includes more funding for North Carolina’s Principal Recruitment Supplement Program, initially launched in 2019, aimed at attracting high-performing principals to low-performing schools through a $30,000 annual salary supplement.
In Charlotte, Tuckaseegee Elementary School’s performance grade rose from a D to a B in two years under the leadership of LaTresha Wilson, the state’s 2026 Southwest Region Principal of the Year and a speaker at Stein’s event.
Wilson’s story in public education began well before she became a principal, she said. It started when she was a little girl sitting in a public school classroom. 
Wilson said she sees her younger self in the eyes of her students, and it reminds her of the importance of education. 
Great leaders and teachers rely on investments in teacher pay, literacy, mathematics, student wellness, and school facilities, she said. 
“We aren’t just funding schools. We are funding possibilities. We are funding potential. We are funding the next generation for North Carolinians,” Wilson said. “When we invest where the need is greater, we don’t just change schools. We change trajectories.”
GOP leaders say the NC budget offers ‘historic’ raises. A top education panel says it’s not enough.

Jeremiah Tucker, student body president at Broughton High School in Raleigh, said his mother has been an educator for 27 years. It’s given him a deep appreciation for teachers everywhere, especially their dedication to their students and their families.
He said educators are the backbone of society. 
“My mother’s pay doesn’t represent her sacrifices,” Tucker said. “It doesn’t account for the long hours she spent designing lesson plans for her kids. It doesn’t represent the money toward school supplies that sometimes even comes out of her own pockets.”
That’s where the budget comes in. While it’s a starting point, there’s still room for improvement, Tucker said, especially in raising pay for veteran teachers.  
The raises move the state’s ranking for overall teacher pay from 47th in the country to 40th.
“I see this budget as a launching pad, not a landing spot,” Stein said. 
Republican lawmakers spent more than a year debating over the budget, disagreeing on income tax cuts and teacher raises. 
House Republicans wanted to boost teacher salaries, especially for those new to the classroom. The Senate, on the other hand, wanted smaller raises for teachers.
Upon releasing the spending plan, House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, said the budget included “historic raises” for teachers. 
Hall’s and Senate Leader Phil Berger’s offices did not immediately respond to NC Newsline’s requests for comment.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: When 100% of students get tuition vouchers, there’s almost no accountability
description: This story first appeared in ProPublica. At some point, my reporting colleagues and I began referring to them as the “100% schools.” We were following the money that flows from states’ public coffers into private schools through vouchers when we noticed a subset of educational facilities where tax dollars cover all or a big part […]
text:
Indiana and Ohio give tax-funded vouchers to just about anybody, regardless of income, so the vast majority of voucher money is enriching families whose children already attend private church schools, writes columnist John Schaaf. (Getty Images)This story first appeared in ProPublica.
At some point, my reporting colleagues and I began referring to them as the “100% schools.”
We were following the money that flows from states’ public coffers into private schools through vouchers when we noticed a subset of educational facilities where tax dollars cover all or a big part of the tuition for every student.
In essence, these were schools that were funded like public schools but didn’t operate with the same oversight or transparency.
Our reporting found that these types of private schools exist throughout the country and that in Wisconsin — where I’m based — there were 39 that fell into that category during the most recent school year. Together, they were educating 7,923 children and taking in roughly $87 million from vouchers offered by the state.
Atlas Preparatory Academy in Milwaukee was a 100% school in my city that had low test scores and declining enrollment while also receiving more than $4.3 million in voucher money for 357 students in grades K-12. It was one of the first schools I dug into, and immediately some of the facts I unearthed in public documents made me curious.
There was, for instance, the money being made by its board chair, who also appeared to serve as a school administrator. His compensation was more than $150,000 in 2024.
This dual role would be prohibited at a traditional public school in Wisconsin, though there are no such rules for private schools.
In another transaction that would raise alarm in a public school setting, the same board chair’s accounting firm received tens of thousands of dollars from the school for accounting and consulting.
During my reporting, it became clear that the school’s operations were not only discordant with public school policies but with basic governing standards for nonprofits, experts told me.
More than a decade ago, a Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction research paper on what it called “choice schools” asked: “When is a private school really a public school?”
Though that question still resonates today, public officials supporting vouchers have yet to provide a clear answer.
Nor has there been any progress in Wisconsin or elsewhere in lining up the standards of private and public schools on a range of issues, even with the spectacular growth of private schools funded by taxpayer dollars.
Voucher schools, for instance, are not required to serve all children with disabilities. Public schools are.
Another major difference is transparency. In Wisconsin and elsewhere, information about public schools — good, bad or mundane — can be gleaned through open meetings, district YouTube channels and robust websites with detailed agendas, minutes, reports, statistics and information about enrollment, curriculum, special education services and more.
Districts have to abide by Wisconsin’s open records law, meaning that reams of records are available to anyone who formally requests them. Not so for the private schools. Voucher schools must, by law, have at least two opportunities a year for parents to meet with the governing board. But the schools do not have to make those meetings accessible to the general public.
In many states, private schools also don’t have to administer standardized tests or report those scores — in sharp contrast to the mandates for public schools. Wisconsin is different because it does require both students using vouchers and public school students to be tested, though parents can and do opt out.
In recent years, Atlas Prep has fared poorly on the state’s report card for schools, garnering the lowest rating: “fails to meet expectations,” or one star out of a possible five.
Not far from Atlas, Bay View High School, a public school, also has earned only one star on the state report card. Its website connects the public to the school’s improvement plan — its strategy to reduce dropouts and improve school culture — as well as information about local school council meetings and discipline methods, and about its science, technology, engineering, arts and math programming.
The Atlas Prep website includes a tab labeled “Build Your Own Curriculum.” When you click on it, nothing loads.
Though every student at the 100% schools we looked at relies on public funds for tuition, the money does not necessarily make up the institution’s total budget. The schools can take in additional revenue from investments, fundraising, grants or other means, but they are heavily dependent on tax dollars to maintain operations.
“If the choice schools are really some kind of quasi-public schools, then in keeping with national efforts to turnaround struggling schools, it may be necessary to subject low-performing choice schools to financial sanctions, turnaround efforts or even closure,” the state Department of Public Instruction suggested in its research paper.
That was back in 2011. Those types of accountability measures still do not exist.
Supporters and opponents of Amendment 2 made their opinions known at the Fancy Farm Picnic, Aug. 3, 2024. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)
Some key financial documents are available, however, for Wisconsin voucher schools — if you know where to look.
Annual IRS information filings for many nonprofit schools are easily obtainable through ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer page. And independent financial audits, required by the state, are available through the state Department of Public Instruction. I requested those for a handful of Wisconsin’s 100% schools, and I visited four.
One warm day in June, I stood in the lobby of one such school in Milwaukee, near a large fish tank. I’d sought days earlier to contact the woman running the school. An audit showed she was paying her own company rent for the building ($128,000 in one recent year). She put me off. “I’m not interested, ma’am,” she said via a phone in the foyer. “Please do not call us back again.”
On the other side of town, I rang the bell at Atlas Prep’s high school building and asked to speak to the executive director, Michelle Lukacs. I was informed she was headed to a meeting and could not speak with me.
By then, I was digging into Atlas’ finances, a process that would last several weeks and continue into July.
Over multiple emails, I shared with Lukacs what I was learning, including the compensation of the board chair, Steven E. Menden. A licensed certified public accountant, Menden had compiled the school’s IRS filing since its formation in 2001.
At times since then, Menden has been listed on the school’s website as “board advisor.” His daughter, Kaitlyn Menden, was also among the school’s most highly compensated employees in 2024. Her package was $127,674 in salary and benefits for a job in “business services.” (In an email to me, she described her role as wearing “many hats” beyond that, citing human resources duties, “oversight of the school’s technology hardware and cloud resources” and “special projects.”)
In the past couple of years, records show, Steven Menden has taken on the role of board chairman. The fiscal year 2025 IRS form showed Menden putting in a 40-hour workweek for Atlas and earning $132,505 in pay plus $19,916 in additional benefits. What’s more, his accounting firm, Menden & Associates, had an $87,250 contract.
Lukacs defended the school’s compensation practices, noting in an email: “Every person on our team, regardless of their role, earns their compensation and is not overpaid.”
She explained that Menden is not compensated for his board service but for “Executive Management Services.”
It would be forbidden for a public school board member in Wisconsin to also have a district management job under a legal doctrine regarding roles that are “incompatible.”
“In essence, one cannot supervise oneself, which would include hiring and firing and disciplining oneself,” said Dan Rossmiller, executive director of the Wisconsin Association of School Boards.
State law governing public officials also prohibits school board members from having a private interest in any contract over $15,000 that they bid for, vote on, negotiate or participate in. Violators can be charged with a low-level felony. There is no similar law that pertains to private school operators in Wisconsin.
In an email to me, Menden explained how the Atlas board handles potential conflicts of interest.
“Any conflicts of interest for either related or unrelated parties are resolved in favor of Atlas Preparatory Academy as outlined in our IRS mandated Conflict of Interest Policy,” he wrote. “This means that conflicted persons recuse themselves from the situation and do not vote or participate and the final decision that is made is strictly in the best financial interest of the school.”
This organizational structure does not comport with best practices for the governance of a nonprofit organization, experts told me.
“Board members are volunteers, and best practice is unambiguous that they should not simultaneously hold paid staff positions at the school they oversee — doing so collapses the separation between governance and management that gives a board its purpose in the first place,” said Chelsea Cross, a vice president at City Forward Collective in Milwaukee.
City Forward is a nonprofit group that champions high-quality school options for students and has been critical of the performance of the Milwaukee Public Schools.
Atlas Prep’s IRS filing indicated that Lukacs, the full-time executive director, earned $175,000 in salary and benefits and also had a board position. A third board member is listed as working only one hour a week for no pay.
In a public school setting, Lukacs’ situation would be akin to a district superintendent also sitting on the school board — an arrangement that would raise issues over proper checks and balances since superintendents typically are hired by and report to the school board.
Said Cross: “With 2/3 of its governing board also on the payroll — including the very executive the board exists to evaluate — Atlas Prep’s board cannot meaningfully hold its own leadership accountable.”
Lukacs disagreed with that assessment. “This is a false statement,” she wrote in an email, saying that Atlas board members “model strong personal leadership showing integrity, confidence and consistency in their actions and decision making.”
She told me she does not vote to approve her own salary “or vote in any other situation where a conflict of interest exists.” And she noted that countless hours have been invested at Atlas Prep in improving curriculum and student support. “While our standardized test scores do not yet reflect the level of achievement we aspire to, our staff has remained steadfast in its commitment to continuous improvement,” she wrote.
I had asked Atlas Prep twice for a copy of the school’s conflict of interest policy, which Menden had mentioned. As of mid-August, I had not received it.
I also requested a copy of the school’s contract with Menden’s accounting firm. I did not receive that either.
At a public school, such contracts would be subject to open record laws. I easily found a link on the Milwaukee Public Schools website to a decade’s worth of contracts for school nurses, mental health services, fitness instructors, interpreters, color printers, portable toilets, busing, professional development and so on.
But Atlas does not post those records online. It doesn’t have to.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Bill proposal puts a target on expired renewable energy requirement
description: A couple of sections of Utah code mandating electric utilities to procure 20% of their energy portfolio in renewables expired in 2025. Lawmakers want to ensure the requirement is scratched for good.   St. George Republican Rep. Colin Jack is drafting a bill ahead of the 2027 legislative session that would repeal a carbon emission reduction […]
text:
A solar installation in Emery County, with PacifiCorp’s Hunter coal-fired power plant in the background, is pictured on Wednesday, July 31, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A couple of sections of Utah code mandating electric utilities to procure 20% of their energy portfolio in renewables expired in 2025. Lawmakers want to ensure the requirement is scratched for good.  
St. George Republican Rep. Colin Jack is drafting a bill ahead of the 2027 legislative session that would repeal a carbon emission reduction requirement for both electrical corporations and municipalities, which prescribed 20% of electric sales to come from renewable sources — as long as it is a cost effective practice. 
Jack, who is also the chief operating officer at Dixie Power, said the electric cooperative had never followed the requirement since “renewable energy on the market was always more expensive than our regular energy portfolio.” However, he was still required to present regular reports on the utility’s energy portfolio.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I foolishly assumed then that the section of code just kind of evaporated and went away. Turns out it doesn’t work that way. We have to have a bill to repeal laws as we get finished with them,” Jack told the Public Utilities, Energy, and Technology Interim Committee on Wednesday. 
But, that move has a little more nuance than a regular legislative proposal to undo expired code. 
“We always had the caveat in this law that said it was subject to economic viability, but by repealing it, it could prevent some future group, our successors, from maybe making it a mandate, repealing the sentence about economic viability,” Jack said, “and we may be preventing future rate increases by our successors.”
Making the renewables provision an absolute requirement would be expensive for ratepayers, Jack said. Because of the way the law was written, it didn’t have that effect while it was in place. But, electricity providers “were forced to look at it each year to evaluate what we had bought and to evaluate what we might have bought.”
While Democratic lawmakers had questions about whether this legislation would undermine the procurement of more renewable resources, the full committee ended up voting unanimously to advance the bill, giving it a faster path to approval next year.



Let us know what you think...


 


“We as a state, not everybody is in agreement that we should disenfranchise renewable energy necessarily and I’m not sure if that’s exactly what this bill addresses, but I just wanted to state that,” Murray Democratic Rep. Rosalba Dominguez said during the discussion.
Utilities had been drafting cost-benefit analyses before the original law passed in 2008, Jack said, and he’s confident the practice will remain moving forward. 
“It will just give them more surety that this report is finished as it currently stands in code,” he said.
Representatives from associations representing rural cooperatives, municipal power systems and Rocky Mountain Power, the largest commercial utility in the state, spoke in favor of the draft, saying it would help ensure that customers can turn their lights on when they need them, and that at the end of the month, they can afford to pay their utility bill. 
Energy cooperatives supporting the repeal had taken issue with the law because it prescribes a specific type of fuel, when the state’s recently established energy policy is “agnostic to fuel types,” said Nathaniel Johnson, executive director of the Utah Rural Electric Cooperative Association.
“Repealing this would make it so that the state energy policy, that again, that is agnostic, allows for market-driven solutions, not a mandate on a specific fuel source,” Johnson said.
Thom Carter, vice president of government affairs at Rocky Mountain Power said the legislation “may not necessarily change how we do business because, at the end of the day, as the sponsor has indicated, it is about affordable, reliable, and safe.”
“And because this has always talked about putting the economics first, we are going to put the economics first,” Carter said. “And ensure that people have the ability to pay their bill, or more importantly, keep their lights on.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Gov. Sherrill signs shield law aimed at protecting reproductive, transgender healthcare
description: The law aims to protect doctors performing reproductive and transgender health care, and their patients, from criminal and civil penalties.
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) signs a shield law to protect reproductive and gender-affirming healthcare in New Jersey outside Planned Parenthood in Montclair on Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation on Thursday that criminalizes interference with reproductive and transgender healthcare while barring a range of officials from aiding investigations spawned by states where such care is illegal.
The bill, which cleared both legislative chambers in party-line votes this June, bars the state from extraditing individuals facing out-of-state investigations over reproductive or gender-affirming care, expands existing confidentiality protections to such care, and expands safeguards for doctors and others who provide it.
Sherrill, a Democrat, took a shot at the Republican governors of Texas and Florida in her remarks during a bill signing ceremony outside a Planned Parenthood location in Montclair.
“If Greg Abbott or Ron DeSantis tries to investigate someone who came to New Jersey to access care, we will protect anyone seeking care that is legal here in New Jersey from investigations in other states,” she said.
State Sen. Teresa Ruiz (D-Essex), a chief sponsor of the bill and the Senate’s majority leader, said the bill signing shows that New Jersey is “a beacon of hope for everyone who understands democracy.”
“You can’t tell us what we can read on a library shelf but want to be up in our uterus in an exam room,” Ruiz said.
The new law, which became effective immediately upon its signing, creates a new criminal charge for individuals who physically block access to health care facilities that offer reproductive or transgender healthcare or who intentionally intimidate individuals away from such clinics.
Violators face criminal penalties ranging from up to 18 months to up to five years in prison if their obstruction caused a victim serious bodily harm. Such individuals would also be exposed to civil suits from the victim and the state.
Individuals who prevail in those suits could win at least $1,000 per violation, plus attorney’s fees, injunctive relief, and — if they can prove willful or reckless disregard for the law — punitive damages.
If the suit comes from a local, state, or county prosecutor, violators face a fine of up to $10,000 for a first offense and $25,000 for subsequent ones.
Simone Kraus, a transgender woman from Sussex County, called the new law “a profound milestone” for the fundamental right to bodily autonomy and human dignity. For too long, Kraus said, the lives of transgender people have been subject to shifting executive orders that left them wondering if a new governor would “pull the rug out from under us.”
“As a trans woman who has walked this path, who knows the deeply personal and necessary journey of receiving gender-confirmation surgery, this hits home in a way policies and legal briefs rarely can capture,” she said, adding, “New Jersey is making it clear today that what happens in a doctor’s office is strictly between the patients and the doctors. Politicians do not have a say.”
The new law’s supporters said the provisions are needed to blunt the Trump administration’s bids to block those seeking abortions and transgender healthcare. Among other things, the administration has sought to force the release of deanonymized emergency room records, subpoenaed the health records of transgender youth, and sought to gain access to systems that hospitals use to swap identifiable patient health records. It has also sought to block funding to hospitals that provide certain types of healthcare to transgender individuals.
“This isn’t just about abortion. Republicans in Washington are trying to control people’s lives. That’s why the White House has relentlessly attacked our transgender community as well,” Sherrill said. “They’ve pulled tactics straight out of the Red Scare playbook to restrict transgender people’s healthcare.”
The new law further bars state and local law enforcement from arresting or assisting in operations to arrest individuals seeking or providing reproductive or gender-affirming care unless their conduct also broke New Jersey law. It places similar limits on court-issued search warrants, wiretaps, and bounty hunters and expands a statutory bar on extradition for charges related to reproductive health services to include gender-affirming care.
It also bars state licensing boards from disciplining providers solely for providing such care.
On Thursday, the new law’s supporters framed its passage as a sorely needed boon for New Jerseyans and their health care providers.
“This is not a law that’s abstract. It has faces attached to it: the parent who postponed a visit who wasn’t sure it was safe; the nurse who second-guessed her own charting, thinking that maybe she was going to be caught up in a lawsuit at some point in time; the family doing the math about risk instead of thinking about their health,” Ruiz said, tearing up. “This is for all of you.”

name: WyoFile
title: One Wyoming lawmaker with criminal history loses reelection bid. Another ekes out a victory.
description:
Cheyenne Rep. Gary Brown, who served time in prison for felony intimidation, lost his reelection bid. Meanwhile, Natrona County Rep. Bill Allemand, who pleaded guilty to drunk driving last month, defended his seat in the Wyoming House. 
The post One Wyoming lawmaker with criminal history loses reelection bid. Another ekes out a victory. appeared first on W[...]
text:
Rep. Gary Brown, a Republican lawmaker from Cheyenne with a criminal history including felony intimidation and harassment, lost his seat in the Wyoming House by a landslide in Tuesday’s primary. 
Brown mustered about 28% of the vote, while his Republican opponent Erin Edwards won 72%. 
Meanwhile, Rep. Bill Allemand, R-Midwest, who pleaded guilty to drunk driving a month before the election, successfully defended his seat, narrowly clinching a victory with 50% of the vote to his opponent’s 48%.  
Both incumbents have criminal histories that surfaced in the run-up to the primary elections. 
In December, a Johnson County sheriff’s deputy stopped and arrested Allemand in Buffalo after a caller reported a possible drunk driver. The deputy then watched Allemand abruptly stop just short of hitting a passing vehicle at an intersection, authorities said at the time. Allemand, who faced Bar Nunn Mayor Peter Boyer in the primary, pleaded guilty to driving under the influence of alcohol on July 15. 
Allemand’s DUI case surfaced previous domestic battery and trespass charges from when the lawmaker lived in Kansas in the 2000s. 
The domestic battery charge stemmed from a 2001 incident in which Allemand allegedly “unlawfully, willfully and intentionally [caused] physical contact with another person … in [a] rude, insulting or angry manner,” according to court documents. The charge was dismissed after Allemand, a member of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, completed a one-year diversion program, according to court documents. 
Allemand told WyoFile in July that the charges were dismissed because the incident “never happened.” 
Then in 2009, Allemand was accused of violating a protection order after he was charged with criminal trespass for allegedly appearing at an address that was off limits to him by court order, and with harassment for allegedly calling the victim 27 times the same day, according to court records. 
He pleaded no contest — meaning he didn’t admit guilt but nonetheless accepted the court’s punishment — to the protection order violation and was sentenced to six months in jail and a $200 fine. The other charges were dropped. Instead of serving jail time, he was granted 12 months of “non-reporting” probation requiring him to avoid contact with the victim, to obtain a domestic violence assessment and to follow any resulting recommendations, the plea deal states. Allemand told WyoFile in July that he knew “nothing about” the incident and charges. 
Allemand’s Republican opponent, Boyer, is originally from Alabama and moved his family to Wyoming in 2016 because of “low taxes and less regulation,” he wrote in response to WyoFile’s candidate questionnaire. He works in the oil industry transporting crude. Though initially political allies, Allemand and Boyer clashed last year over a proposed nuclear microreactor manufacturing project that divided the Natrona County community. 
Brown, meanwhile, served prison time in Colorado for felony intimidation, according to court documents and police records. Court documents show that in 1991, Brown was charged with two felony intimidation counts stemming from alleged harassment of an ex-girlfriend and a friend of hers in Larimer County, Colorado, where he lived at the time. 
Prosecutors later brought additional charges against Brown — one felony count of criminal attempt to commit first-degree arson and one felony count of second-degree burglary of a dwelling. Police reports indicate that the property at the center of the case was Brown’s ex-girlfriend’s house in Loveland.
Three of the four charges were dropped in 1992, according to court filings, when Brown agreed to plead guilty to one felony count of intimidating a witness and victim. He was sentenced to four years and six months in prison. Wyoming restored his right to vote and hold public office, according to a copy of a certificate issued on Nov. 8, 2023. 
Brown had other brushes with the law, including a 2013 conviction for misdemeanor harassment. 
While Brown is not listed as a member of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, he regularly votes alongside the caucus and co-sponsors legislation with its members. 
Brown’s Republican opponent, volunteer firefighter Edwards, ran on a platform that focuses on limited government, personal responsibility, supporting law enforcement and protecting constitutional freedoms, according to Cap City News. She vowed to support Wyoming industries such as agriculture and energy while protecting public lands. 
Both Edwards and Allemand face Democratic opponents — Cheyenne Democrat Stacy Becker and Bar Nunn Democrat Keenan Morgan, respectively — in November’s general election. 
WyoFile reporter Maggie Mullen contributed to this story.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s housing shortage is the real obstacle to growth
description:
Outdated zoning is keeping industry from expanding in Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s housing shortage is the real obstacle to growth.
text:
Dear Editor,
I mostly agree with a recent letter to VTDigger about second-home owners, but for one statement. The author says Vermont should encourage industry, but I can tell you that industry cannot survive without workers, and workers cannot survive without a place to live, and there are no places to live. 
I have lived and worked here for all my 55 years. I currently own and manage five rental properties and work as a robotics specialist at a local factory. My perspective cuts across a few aspects of this discussion. 
First, there is very little housing available. I know this as a landlord. My occupancy rate is 100%, plus I have a long list of people waiting to get in. Second, I work in a factory for a business that would love to hire more people so it can expand, or even enough people to meet current demand — but alas, there is no place for these workers to stay. A big cause of this constant problem is the obsolete zoning rules in this and many other states. These rules make it difficult to develop housing for enough workers to support the current workload, let alone an expansion. 

READ MORE

In addition, Vermont’s hilly geography only gives us so many places to live or develop for agriculture. And there is a large swath of the population that has aged out of the workforce, is too old and is uninterested in creating a granny flat for someone else, even if their property is zoned for a huge lot. These poor veterans of the workforce in America are not able to help with the housing crisis, even if they wanted to. 
So tell me, where do second-home owners fit into all this nuanced chaos?
Tray DuClosRandolph, Vt.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Roadless no more? Feds eye rule change in areas of national forests.
description: This story was originally published by Carolina Public Press. U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins announced a proposal Tuesday to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, commonly called the Roadless Rule, opening tens of thousands of Inventoried Roadless Areas within the Pisgah and Nantahala national forests to future road development. The[...]
text:
View from Sam Knob in the Pisgah National Forest in southern Haywood County. (Photo: Jack Igelman/Carolina Public Press)This story was originally published by Carolina Public Press.
U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins announced a proposal Tuesday to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, commonly called the Roadless Rule, opening tens of thousands of Inventoried Roadless Areas within the Pisgah and Nantahala national forests to future road development.
The federal designation restricts road building and logging in undeveloped portions of national forests.
The proposal advances the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s August 2025 notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement to evaluate the effects of rescinding the rule.
Reversing the 25-year-old Roadless Rule is intended to return some land management decisions to local Forest Service officials. Critics of the rule argue that in addition to limiting local control of federal land, it hinders wildfire management, restricts access to timber and complicates the active management of public forests.
“For too long, outdated restrictions have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities,” said Rollins in a press release. “Today, we filed a proposal to restore authority to local forest managers who know the land best, removing the barriers that have kept them from doing the work the land demands.”
The U.S. Department of Agriculture said the proposed rescission does not mandate timber cutting or road construction.
A dramatic reversal on Roadless Rule
However, supporters of the Roadless Rule said the designation protects wildlife habitat, safeguards water quality, preserves scenic landscapes and supports the Western North Carolina outdoor recreation economy.
“The Roadless Rule is one of the biggest conservation wins of the modern era and it has reliably delivered the benefits it was designed to year after year,” said Kristin Gendzier, a senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center.
“The Forest Service’s misguided proposal will clear the way for reckless projects that can permanently scar these spectacular roadless landscapes and do long-lasting harm to countless communities that depend on our national forests for tourism, recreation and clean drinking water.”
The Pisgah and Nantahala national forests contain nearly 152,000 acres of IRAs within their 1 million acres. Under the Pisgah-Nantahala Forest Plan, IRAs are managed primarily as “backcountry” or under more restrictive designations such as the Appalachian Trail Corridor, Heritage Corridors or designated Wilderness.
The move returns authority over those lands to local Forest Service officials, who will decide whether to allow new roads or timber harvests in areas once largely off-limits.
Will Harlan, Southeast director at the Center for Biological Diversity, told CPP that rolling back the Roadless Rule would be “the largest evisceration of public lands in American history. It’s especially heartbreaking for Western North Carolina, which has some of the highest concentrations of roadless areas in the country. These are some of the wildest places we have left, and the public overwhelmingly supports their protection.”
Gendzier said roughly 99% of comments received by the USDA last fall opposed its rescission.
A public comment period on the proposal and on a draft environmental impact statement is expected to open on Aug. 19 and end on Sept. 21.
Once the comment period closes, the USDA will review comments and decide whether to proceed, modify or withdraw the proposal.
