name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Republicans appeal to Nebraska Supreme Court regarding overseas voter law
description: LINCOLN — The Republican National Committee appealed a district judge’s ruling to the Nebraska Supreme Court that upheld the validity of a state law allowing certain overseas voters to vote. The RNC and two Lancaster County voters filed the appeal Thursday afternoon. The case involves a state law dating back to 2005 that allows U.S. […]
text:
National GOP Committeeman JL Spray speaks during the Nebraska Republican Party's 2024 annual convention on May 18, 2024. (Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Republican National Committee appealed a district judge’s ruling to the Nebraska Supreme Court that upheld the validity of a state law allowing certain overseas voters to vote.
The RNC and two Lancaster County voters filed the appeal Thursday afternoon. The case involves a state law dating back to 2005 that allows U.S. citizens who have never resided in Nebraska but have a parent registered to vote in one Nebraska county to register in that county. It would be a felony to register or vote in multiple states or counties.
The RNC argues the law “dilutes the votes of lawful Republican voters” and violates Article VI, Section 1 of the Nebraska Constitution, which defines a qualified voter as a U.S. citizen who “has resided within the state and the county and voting precinct for the terms provided by law.”
Judge dismisses lawsuit from RNC challenging Nebraska voter law

Lancaster County District Judge Ryan Post ruled Aug. 12 that there was at least one constitutional application for the law so it couldn’t be challenged as unconstitutional on its face.
“A statute is presumed to be constitutional, and all reasonable doubts are resolved in favor of its constitutionality,” Post wrote in a 13-page order.
Attorneys for Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen, from Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers’ office, offered a hypothetical scenario of a voter who was born in South America to Saunders County missionaries who had every intention of returning home.
As of July, 116 overseas Nebraska voters were registered under the targeted statute, six of whom voted in the May 12 primary, according to data from Evnen’s office.
In a statement last week, an RNC spokesperson said the organization was “exploring all available legal options” to fight Post’s decision.
“We will never stop working to protect the ballot box and ensure Nebraska elections are decided by Nebraska voters,” said Ally Triolo, the RNC’s election integrity communications director.
Attorneys for the RNC have made clear they do not intend to challenge the voting rights of any Nebraskans — military, diplomats or otherwise — who have lived in Nebraska first.
The clock is ticking for a court ruling this election cycle as ballots are sent out next month.
Special ballots with space for any not-yet-finalized races must be mailed to some voters registered under the challenged law by Sept. 3. The deadline for Evnen to certify the ballot is Sept. 11. Certified ballots are mailed to all other military, diplomatic and overseas voters by Sept. 18. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska GOP, Dems appeal to state Supreme Court to stop other political parties
description: Nebraska’s two major political parties have asked the state Supreme Court to overrule a decision allowing two new political parties to form.
text:
The state's two largest political parties, the Nebraska Republican Party and Nebraska Democratic Party, are fighting the official formation of two new political parties. Republicans are opposed to creation of the America First Party, while Democrats oppose the proposed Nebraska Working People Party. (Logo photos courtesy of the party websites | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s two major political parties have asked the state Supreme Court to overrule a judge’s decision allowing two new state political parties to form. 
The Nebraska Democratic and Republican parties filed their appeals Thursday morning. The two cases are in the hands of the Nebraska Supreme Court, but there had been no indication whether the high court had accepted them as of 1:30 p.m. 
Lancaster County District Court Judge Darla Ideus rejected both major parties’ objections earlier this week. In her order regarding the Nebraska Working People Party, she wrote that the state Democratic Party — and the national Working Families Party — filed their objections too late.  Regarding the challenge to the America First Party, she ruled that state law doesn’t address the “confusion” that the Republican Party alleged the party’s name would cause for voters. 
Nebraska will have two new political parties after efforts meet signature threshold

GOP lawyers had asked Ideus to give Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen more authority to reject a party or candidate. In its lawsuit, the GOP called John Cartier’s effort to establish the America First Party “political sabotage.” Attorneys for the Nebraska Democratic Party and the national Working Families Party had sought to compel Evnen to remove the Nebraska Working People Party because its name is similar to the Working Families Party.
An emergency injunction delaying their certification was lifted Wednesday. It is unclear whether any of the new political parties have already submitted the organizational documents required to name candidates for the Nov. 3 general election.

title: Frijoles Fire grows to roughly 14,000 acres, creates smoke concerns
description: The lightning-caused Frijoles Fire burning in the Pecos Wilderness as of Thursday morning had grown to just under 14,000 acres, with officials reporting 31% containment.
text:
Smoke rises Aug. 15, 2026, from the Frijoles Fire, which has grown to nearly 14,000 acres in the Pecos Wilderness. Ongoing smoke from the fire prompted state officials to issue another air quality warning Aug.19, 2026. (Photo courtesy Inciweb)
The lightning-caused Frijoles Fire burning in the Pecos Wilderness as of Thursday morning had grown to just under 14,000 acres, with officials reporting 31% containment.
A news release said Wednesday’s weather had influenced fire behavior and pushed smoke into nearby communities, particularly in low-lying areas. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state health and environment departments on Wednesday issued a smoke advisory, and announced two additional air monitors at the Nambe Community Center and the Harold L. Runnels Building, along with a third planned for Mora to measure the fine particulate matter associated with wildfire smoke.
In a statement, Dr. Chelsea Langer, NMDOH bureau chief of the environmental health epidemiology bureau, said given the decreasing air quality in the area of the fire, officials were encouraging residents “to stay indoors and set up a clean room, which is a place designed to keep inside air as clean as possible. To keep indoor air clean, limit how much outdoor air is coming inside, and keep air that is already inside clean by not burning candles or incense, not using air fresheners or other strong scented products, and not smoking or vaping indoors.”
Residents can also monitor the Air Quality Index, in which higher numbers indicate more pollution and health risks, online at fire.airnow.gov. As of Thursday morning, monitors showed unhealthy air quality throughout Santa Fe.
“We have been proactively working with government partners to ensure communities have the most up-to-date information available through our monitoring system,” New Mexico Environment Department Air Quality Bureau Chief Cindy Hollenberg said in a  statement. “Fine particulate matter from wildfire smoke can contribute to respiratory issues and other health impacts with higher risk community members, which is why we want to provide as much data as possible.”
Fire officials say they have 866 personnel on the fire, with “steep, rugged terrain in the wilderness” continuing to “challenge firefighters’ ability to safely access remote areas and use direct extinguishment strategies along the fire’s edge.”
While evacuation orders are limited to an area of the small village of Cundiyó, residents in the rest of Cundiyó, as well as Cerro Piñon and Borrego Mesa area, remain in “set” status, meaning they should keep tabs on emergency alerts and create a plan to safely flee the wildfire. 
Internal situation reports that the California incident command team in charge of the fire show that 11 people have evacuated due to the fire, and three others are sheltering in place. 
The reports also show that no structures have yet been burned in the fire. However, they identified more than 100 structures at risk at the nearby Gorham Boy Scout Ranch, Canyon Chimayó and the rest of Cundiyó. 
In addition, more than 1,000 structures in Truchas, which is nine miles north of the wildfire’s northern edge, are at risk, the reports show. 
The report, known as an ICS-209 report, which Source NM reviewed Thursday, also describes staffing and other challenges firefighters face as they seek to build containment lines and allow residents to return home. 
The report says “steep terrain and poor access” are increasing time required to complete containment lines. In addition, “limited crews qualified to work in these areas” are slowing progress, as the most-specialized teams, known as Type 1 crews, are regularly being shifted between areas of the fire to try to contain the fire in difficult terrain. 
“This, in turn, is preventing cohesive line construction that can gain containment and shorten the duration of public displacement from their homes,” an incident commander wrote Wednesday afternoon. 
In addition, the team’s window for weather conditions favorable for tackling the blaze is “narrowing as a return to unseasonably high temperatures and record-low relative humidities is expected to affect the area and drastically increase fire behavior,” the commander wrote. 
The ongoing fire behavior, as well as prolonged smoke exposure and forest closures, are “significantly reducing” economic activity in the area, including fairs, festivals, camping and “once-in-a-lifetime” draw hunts for bighorn sheep in the Pecos Wilderness, the commander wrote.

title: DeSantis announces cancer grants applications are open, touts increased research dollars
description: Florida is accepting applications for $70 million in cancer “innovation” funds. During a press conference in Orlando Wednesday, Gov. Ron DeSantis announced the availability of cancer innovation grant funds for next year and the latest list of researchers chosen to receive grants. During a lengthy press conference, the governor touted his administration’s foc[...]
text:
First Lady Casey DeSantis and members of the Cancer Connect Collaborative. (Photo via the Cancer Connect Collaborative)Florida is accepting applications for $70 million in cancer “innovation” funds.
During a press conference in Orlando Wednesday, Gov. Ron DeSantis announced the availability of cancer innovation grant funds for next year and the latest list of researchers chosen to receive grants.
During a lengthy press conference, the governor touted his administration’s focus on increasing cancer research funding during his tenure in office, an interest inspired by First Lady Casey DeSantis’ cancer diagnosis and treatment.
DeSantis successfully pushed for increasing funds to the “National Cancer Institute (NCI) Centers Program,” created in 2014 by former Gov. Rick Scott and later renamed for Casey DeSantis, who disclosed in October 2021 she had breast cancer. The governor announced she was cancer free in March 2022.
The $127.5 million Casey DeSantis Cancer Research Program provides research dollars to NCI facilities: Moffitt Cancer Center; University of Florida Health Cancer Center; Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center; and Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center.
A push by the DeSantis administration to steer dollars away from the NCI-designated facilities and to a larger number of  cancer hospitals and healthcare providers was repeatedly rejected by the Legislature. Although unwilling to go along with the DeSantis push for change, lawmakers did provide for cancer innovation grants as well as money to establish a pediatric cancer research incubator.
In all, DeSantis said Wednesday that since 2019 when he took office Florida has invested more than $1.4 billion in cancer research and treatment, and funding for cancer research programs  increased by more than 175% under his administration.
The American Cancer Society estimates there will be 2,114,850 new cancer cases nationwide in 2026. Also nationwide, the society projects that 626,140 people will die from cancer in 2026. More than 50,000 deaths are projected in Florida.
Although California is projected to have the most new cases with 206,500, Florida is projected to have 183,100 new cases, ranking it second highest in the nation. The cancer society says the biggest caseloads will involve prostate cancer diagnoses (26,970) followed by breast cancer (24,700).
Since 2019, Florida has invested more than $1.4 billion in cancer research and treatment under DeSantis. In Fiscal Year 2026-27 alone, Florida committed nearly $228 million to cancer research and innovation.
“Gov. DeSantis and First Lady Casey DeSantis have shown tremendous leadership in making cancer research a priority in Florida, and I’m incredibly grateful for their continued commitment,” Department of Health Secretary and State Health Officer Joseph Ladapo said. “These investments give researchers the freedom to ask important questions, explore new ideas, and follow the evidence wherever it leads.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: High court rules against Quincy mayor on Catholic saint statues
description: The statues will be kept in storage and off the building while litigation continues at the lower court level. The visages of a winged Michael and towering Florian extinguishing fire await further judgment, but the ruling signals a rough legal road ahead for Quincy.
text:
IN THE END, there was no divine intervention for the City of Quincy. 
After a lower court judge temporarily blocked the city from installing 10-foot-tall bronze statues of Catholic patron saints on the facade of its new public safety building, siding with the residents who sued to stop it as impermissible government support for religion, the city appealed to the Supreme Judicial Court.  
On Thursday, the state’s highest court upheld the judge’s injunction, deciding that he ruled correctly that the city’s actions likely violated the state’s bar on government favoring a particular religion. 
In 2023, without seeking city council approval or making a public announcement, Quincy Mayor Thomas Koch commissioned two statues — St. Michael the Archangel, patron saint of police officers, and St. Florian, patron saint of firefighters — that would cost an estimated $850,000 and frame the entryway of the $175 million, four-story, 120,000-square-foot building replacing the city’s old police station. 
In a unanimous decision, the SJC held that a Norfolk Superior Court judge was in the right to halt installation of the statues. A group of residents had standing as taxpayers to sue over the use of public funds, according to the court, and the judge applied the correct test to determine whether the statue approval and installation was constitutional. 
The lower court record, SJC Justice Scott Kafker wrote, “reflects that the statues are large and will stand alone, they are brand new rather than long standing, they are closely affiliated with a particular religion, and they thus may convey to observing members of the public implicit government support for that religion and, as a result, subordination of other religions.” 
This means the statues will be kept in storage and off the building while litigation continues at the lower court level. The visages of a winged Michael and towering Florian extinguishing fire await further judgment, but the ruling signals a rough legal road ahead for Quincy. 
Statues of St. Florian (at left) and St. Michael the Archangel (at right) are barred for now from appearing on the public safety building of Quincy, Massachusetts. (Photo courtesy of Office of Mayor Thomas Koch)
Koch did not initially bring the statue plan to the city council, which had already approved funding for the public safety building, or disclose it publicly. The Patriot Ledger first reported on the statues in February 2025, kicking off intense public backlash that included a petition with more than 1,600 signatures and a joint statement from an interfaith coalition of South Shore clergy. 
Fifteen Quincy residents, represented by the ACLU of Massachusetts along with the Freedom From Religion Foundation and Americans United for Separation of Church and State, sued Koch and the city in May 2025. Their suit argues the statues violate Article 3 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights, which bars government favoritism toward any religious sect. 
“The contested practice here raises concerns at the core of the text, purposes, and history” of Article 3, Kafker wrote. That is, “whether the city is singling out a particular religion for special treatment.” 
During oral arguments in May, an attorney for Quincy pointed out the irony of the court weighing in on the actions of the “City of Presidents” — birthplace of John Adams and John Quincy Adams — from within the John Adams Courthouse, which is adorned with a statue of Moses.  
Kafker took the implication to task in a footnote in the ruling. The statue of Moses in the courthouse’s Great Hall, he wrote, is one of 16 allegorical statues representing not religion but “virtues and concepts” like law, justice and reason. This sort of installation, he wrote, is “part of a continuing tradition that started in antiquity.” 
Koch has said the saints were chosen for their association with first responders, not their religious meaning.  
But Judge William Sullivan granted a preliminary injunction blocking the installation in late 2025, which at that point had already cost the city about $761,000 of public funds.  
He concluded that, based on the depiction of the figures and the remarks of some city officials directly referencing prayer and that the statue might “bless” first responders, the allegations were enough to “suggest the decision to erect these particular statues was ‘motivated wholly by religious considerations,’ and that the statutes cannot not be separated from their religious symbolism.”  
The plaintiffs, he wrote, were likely to succeed in showing the display violates Article 3. 
The city appealed and sought direct review from the SJC, which the resident group supported so the constitutional question could be resolved without a detour through the Appeals Court.  
The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, representing the city, filed a 62-page brief in February arguing the residents lack standing, that Article 3 doesn’t entirely bar religious imagery on public property, that Sullivan applied the wrong legal test, and that blocking the statues amounts to unconstitutional hostility toward religion under federal law. 
Becket senior counsel Joseph Davis argued for the city that the two saints carry meaning beyond Catholicism. 
 “Firefighters and police officers across the Commonwealth and the country understand the figures of Florian and Michael to symbolize the values of courage and self-sacrifice that they seek to embody in their professions,” he told the justices in May. “The city of Quincy does not violate [the state constitution] by honoring its first responders with statues of these figures.” 
Quincy Firefighters Local 792, the National Association of Police Organizations, and the International Association of Fire Fighters submitted briefs in support of the statues. 
“The proposed statue of Florian is important to me and Quincy Fire because it depicts what we do every day, the virtues that are most important in our work: honor, courage, bravery,” wrote Thomas Bowes, president of Quincy Firefighters. 
On behalf of the residents, ACLU of Massachusetts legal director Jessie Rossman told the high court that the statues may have some secular significance but cannot be separated from their Catholic origin. 
“The purpose, the inspirational power of these two statues is inextricably intertwined with its religious underpinning.” She added: “If there was a statue that directly reflected another religion — if there were two ten-foot-tall Jewish stars, or two ten-foot-tall moon and crescent and stars that are outside the building, it would pose the same issue.” 
The current US Supreme Court has been particularly concerned with laws that might be hostile to religious freedom, SJC justices noted. 
But the court ultimately concluded that protections on the free exercise of religion simply do not apply to the city. The government cannot impose restrictions on the religious exercise of “affected citizens,” Kafker wrote, but preventing the statues from being erected is halting city action, not a person’s.  
Claire Fitzmaurice, a resident of Quincy and the main named plaintiff, said in a statement that she was “thrilled” and “relieved” by the ruling.  
“As a Unitarian Universalist, I cherish the principle of religious pluralism,” she said. “To have these imposing religious statues looming over the entrance of the public safety building would fly in the face of that pluralistic ideal — especially as our city continues to grow more diverse. I look forward to our next day in court.” 
The ruling, though not the final word on the matter, is the latest blow to Koch, Quincy’s longest serving mayor and something of a swaggering political figure.  
A public dust-up and legal action unfolded after the city council in 2024 approved Koch’s request to raise his salary from $159,000 to $285,000, which would place him among the highest-paid mayors in the country. Last November’s election ushered six Koch critics into City Council offices, and the new council voted to rescind the raise. 
In a statement, the mayor’s office said the SJC decision was “disappointing” but “preliminary.” 
“Quincy’s firefighters and police put their lives on the line for this city every day, and these statues were chosen to honor their bravery, service, and sacrifice,” a spokesperson for the mayor said. “We will continue to fight for the ability to commemorate our first responders as the law permits.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Proposed repeal of ‘Roadless Rule’ could open Michigan national forests to logging, roadbuilding
description: Thousands of acres of currently protected national forest land in Michigan could be opened to road construction and logging under a proposal from the U.S. Forest Service to rescind a 25-year-old rule. The 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, which restricts road construction and timber harvesting in designated roadless areas, currently protects about 16,000[...]
text:
Overlook from the Trap Hills within the Ottawa National Forest, Western U.P. (Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)Thousands of acres of currently protected national forest land in Michigan could be opened to road construction and logging under a proposal from the U.S. Forest Service to rescind a 25-year-old rule.
The 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, which restricts road construction and timber harvesting in designated roadless areas, currently protects about 16,000 acres of roadless forest land across the Huron-Manistee, Hiawatha and Ottawa national forests in Michigan. They are among nearly 45 million acres of inventoried roadless areas nationwide which would see protections eliminated under the proposal to rescind the rule, filed Wednesday for publication in the Federal Register.
“For too long, outdated restrictions have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities,” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement.
Hiawatha National Forest (Susan J. Demas/Michigan Advance)
Environmental advocates dispute that assertion and say new roads would actually increase opportunities for human-caused fires.
A 2025 study by The Wilderness Society determined that the “highest wildfire-ignition density was in lands within 50 meters of roads,” and that “building roads into roadless areas is likely to result in more fires.” Additionally, Ellen Montgomery, Great Outdoors campaign director for Environment America Research & Policy Center, noted earlier this year that less than 1% of wildfires in the lower 48 states since 2010 have started in roadless areas of national forests.
“As Americans are planning how to spend their time outside in our public lands this fall, the Forest Service is proposing to open our wild forests to logging and new roads,” Montgomery said in a statement issued Wednesday. “We call on all Americans to submit public comments over the next 30 days. To keep America beautiful, let’s ask the Forest Service to keep our wild forests wild.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the proposed rescission, the Forest Service estimates that permanent roads could potentially be built across 18.2 million acres currently covered by the Roadless Rule, while temporary roads could be built across another 11.3 million acres.
Calvin Floyd, conservation advocate for Environment Michigan, said the proposal could affect some of Michigan’s remaining mature and old-growth forests.
“Spread across the Huron-Manistee, the Hiawatha and the Ottawa National Forests on both peninsulas, Michigan’s roadless forests protect some of the last mature and old-growth trees in the Midwest,” Floyd said in a statement. “These forests filter headwater streams that flow into the Great Lakes, which hold 20% of the world’s fresh surface water.”
Floyd added that the areas in question also provide critical habitat for wild animals such as bobcats, martens and deer. 
“If we lose our roadless forests, we lose part of our heritage as Michiganders,” he said.
The public has until Sept. 21 to comment on the proposed rescission.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Applications to open early for workforce program grants
description: Chef Lashante Cox, center, teaching a culinary arts class at Hinds Community College, Tuesday night, Jan. 20, 2026 in Jackson.
text:
Applications are expected to open this week for a financial aid program aimed at helping adult students pay for an associate degree or professional credential at one of the state’s community colleges. The application deadline is Sept. 15. 
The launch of the Upgrading Priority Skills for Key Industry Learning and Labor, or UPSKILL, Mississippi Grant Program is happening earlier than expected thanks to $1 million in funding from the Mississippi Works Fund, said Courtney Taylor, executive director of AccelerateMS, the state’s workforce development office. The original UPSKILL program launch was slated for spring 2027.
The Legislature created UPSKILL during the last session to cover eligible students’ remaining tuition costs after other financial aid and scholarships are applied. Lawmakers did not allocate funding for the program, which launches as a pilot effort.  
Eligible adults — applicants should be at least 24 years old — can receive up to $500 annually for books and other materials. The Mississippi Office of Student Financial Aid will oversee the distribution of grants for the program. 
The state’s workforce investment board selected 28 eligible programs based on workforce demand and available enrollment for job training courses. The options include plumbing, construction engineering and emergency medical technician courses. 
Read more: New law creates grant program that covers some college costs
“By focusing scholarships on priority occupations, we can help more Mississippians move into good careers while addressing some of our state’s most critical workforce needs,” Taylor said. 
Jennifer Rogers, who leads the state financial aid office, said AccelerateMS and the state’s financial aid office are finalizing a contract to distribute funds to students.
To qualify for UPSKILL, students must have lived in Mississippi for at least two years. Students must also have a high school diploma, a GED or an equivalent. Students must also be enrolled at least half time in an eligible certificate or associate degree program and have completed the Free Application for Federal Student Aid and the state financial aid application. UPSKILL grants will be awarded on a first-come, first-served basis. Community colleges will also have to provide additional support for students. 
The pilot program will also offer support services for students to work with an adviser or success coach at community colleges, according to the legislation rules. The coaches will help students navigate the program’s course enrollment process and apply for financial aid and will support them with career planning. 
The Mississippi Office of Student Financial Aid plans to request $1.5 million from the Legislature in January to fund UPSKILL for the 2027-28 academic year.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Federal judge orders release of parent, child held by immigration authorities
description: A federal judge has ordered the U.S. government to release a Billings father and child from a facility in Havre and described their detainment as “disturbing.” U.S. Customs and Border Patrol arrested Adrián Espinoza De La Cruz and his 9-year-old child on Aug. 11 without a warrant and detained them at the Havre Border Patrol […]
text:
The emblem of the United States federal court of Montana (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan). A federal judge has ordered the U.S. government to release a Billings father and child from a facility in Havre and described their detainment as “disturbing.”
U.S. Customs and Border Patrol arrested Adrián Espinoza De La Cruz and his 9-year-old child on Aug. 11 without a warrant and detained them at the Havre Border Patrol Station.
In a court filing on Tuesday, Upper Seven Law, representing De La Cruz and his child, said arresting  the father and child was unlawful and called for their immediate release.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office acknowledged on Wednesday the arrest took place without a warrant. But the lawyers said the parent and minor are in the United States without legal permission, and the government did issue a warrant after the arrest.
In a decision late Wednesday, U.S. District Court of Montana Judge Brian Morris ordered the release of Espinoza De La Cruz and the child within 24 hours citing the violation of their constitutional rights.
“The court finds this case particularly disturbing considering the government’s lack of regard for the rights of a father and minor child,” the order said.
Citing another case, the order said the government does not have “free-ranging ability to arrest and detain people, and figure out the reasons later, like they apparently did here.”
The judge said nothing in the record shows the parent and child have any criminal history or any earlier encounters with law enforcement or immigration authorities.
The judge also noted the child’s special medical needs for a gastrointestinal issue and raised concerns about the conditions the parent and child face at the facility in Havre.
“The court has been informed that De La Cruz and (the child) are being held in a family holding room but remains concerned about the alleged lack of proper bedding and basic amenities typically found in long-term detention facilities which the Havre Border Patrol Station lacks,” the order said.
Attorneys for the plaintiffs said they tried to negotiate relief with the U.S. government before filing for their release in court, but officials refused.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office earlier told the Daily Montanan it does not typically comment on pending litigation.
Upper Seven filed the petition against acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche; Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials, including Utah Field Office Director Michael Bernacke; and Havre Chief Patrol Agent Zachary Crosson with CBP.
The Daily Montanan did not receive responses to questions asked Wednesday to ICE, CBP and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, or Crosson at the Havre station, about the conditions under which the child was being held.
In the order, the judge said the legal way to arrest noncitizens under the relevant statute is to issue a warrant in advance or determine they are violating the law being in the country and also are a flight risk.
He said “unadmitted noncitizens” in the interior of the country can be detained but not automatically; a bond hearing must be held to determine if they are at risk of escape or a danger to the community.
“The government’s recent practice of subjecting such people to mandatory custody … proves unlawful,” the order said.
In this case, the judge said, nothing in the record shows the government met the lawful conditions to detain the father and child, and the government’s assertion the law offers flexibility on the timing of warrants is incorrect.
The judge said the government’s interest is “legitimate,” but it is outweighed by the liberty interests of Espinoza De La Cruz and his child.
The judge disagreed with the government’s argument the plaintiffs must first seek administrative relief. That’s because the process was deficient from the start, he said, and the court already reprimanded the government for a similar problem with the warrantless arrest of Jesus Verde Hernandez of Yellowstone County.
The father and child are part of a possible class-action case with Hernandez, also released after being detained unlawfully and represented by Upper Seven Law. In the case, the lawyers argue 17 people are being illegally detained in Cascade County jail, and others in Montana are in a similar situation.
A hearing is set for Sept. 4, but Upper Seven filed the separate petition to release Espinoza De La Cruz and his child because of the “exceptional circumstances” of a minor being incarcerated in a temporary facility. The petition said minors are entitled to specific provisions, including suitable living conditions, proper food and a reasonable right to privacy.
In the decision, Morris ordered the government to release the father and child “under appropriate conditions of release” and return their property, including any personal identification and employment authorization documents.
The order also said the government may not redetain them during their current removal proceedings until after an immigration hearing is held to determine if detention is appropriate.
The judge said the lawyers for the plaintiffs may pursue attorneys’ fees and costs by filing a separate motion.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Taxation with retaliation in Colorado
description: Coloradans for a long time have understood that the Trump administration is punishing their state out of political spite. Now there’s proof. It was always shocking to think that an American president could so subvert democracy as to use taxpayer money to extort a whole state, but direct evidence demands the victim move beyond disbelief […]
text:
President Donald Trump looks on during a Cabinet meeting at the White House on May 27, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images/Illustration by Colorado Newsline)Coloradans for a long time have understood that the Trump administration is punishing their state out of political spite.
Now there’s proof.
It was always shocking to think that an American president could so subvert democracy as to use taxpayer money to extort a whole state, but direct evidence demands the victim move beyond disbelief to action. The founders of the United States based a war for independence in part on their complaint that George III imposed taxation without representation. The Trump administration has one-upped the king. It imposes taxation with retaliation.
Like the colonies, Colorado doesn’t have to take tyrannical abuse sitting down.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As first reported by The Denver Post, the “smoking gun” came during a discovery hearing last week in federal court, where the disclosure of a White House email made the administration’s calculated attack on Colorado explicit. The purpose of the email, sent as President Donald Trump was raging about the incarceration in Colorado of election denier Tina Peters, was to convene a “brainstorm call” among federal agency officials about what they could do “with respect to Colorado.” They were to discuss “grants and federal support” to the state.
The fallout was immediate. In the following days, the administration was reported to be cutting $615 million in green energy funds and $109 million in green transportation grants. It denied the state disaster recovery funds for wildfire and flooding. It moved to dismantle the world-renowned climate science hub NCAR in Boulder. It froze federal funds in Colorado for food and childcare. Trump vetoed a bipartisan bill to fund a clean water project in the rural southeast part of the state.
The lawsuit that disgorged the email was brought by the state to address a previous act of illegal federal hostility: Trump’s decision to move Space Command out of Colorado, which Trump himself tied to his dislike of Colorado’s universal mail ballot system when he announced the move in September.
Upon learning of the email, the judge in the case, R. Brooke Jackson, spoke for us all when he said, “I’ve never seen anything like it. I’ve never even imagined something like it.”



The administration is treating Colorado as enemy territory. How should the state respond?



In truth, other evidence had been trickling in. In other court documents, the administration admitted it had cut off funding to Colorado and other states led by Democrats for purely political reasons, The New York Times reported last month. No less an authority than ultra-MAGA U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert of Windsor told a podcaster in early August that Trump vetoed the clean water project bill over Peters’ incarceration.
This is not how a republic functions. The administration is treating Colorado as enemy territory. How should the state respond?
U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper of Colorado has called for an investigation by federal inspectors general. That’s a good start, but it’s the bare minimum.
Christopher Armitage, a Substack writer, has spearheaded the idea of a coordinated effort in states led by Democrats to keep federal tax revenues in escrow until the federal government aligns its behavior with constitutional principles. Here’s how it would work: For most Americans, employers take federal taxes out of worker paychecks and send that money to the IRS. But legislatures in multiple states outraged by Trump’s attacks and corruption could make laws that channel those taxes to the states, which would hold onto the funds until state officials are assured the federal government will manage them lawfully.
A key point of leverage for Colorado and many Democratic-led states, and a major reason for their grievance, is that every year they send billions more to the federal government than they get in return, according to IRS data analyzed by the nonprofit USAFacts. 
The legality of this scheme is uncertain. But its deployment would come in answer to immeasurable lawlessness by an administration that’s checked by virtually no meaningful accountability (and led by a man the Colorado Supreme Court ruled is an insurrectionist). The law is less a determinant than is the momentum of enough states willing to take a stand.
A multistate tax escrow is just one form of “soft secession” Colorado can pursue in resistance to an enemy federal government. The alternative is for Coloradans to do nothing while the administration retaliates against them with their own tax dollars.

text:
Voting booths await voters in the general election on Nov. 5, 2024, at North Junior High in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Boise School District voters can hear directly from board of trustees candidates at a public forum organized by local youth.
The candidate forum, which is hosted by the youth-led, nonprofit BABE VOTE organization, will feature candidates from the district’s only contested race this election.
The event will be held from 6:30-8 p.m. Tuesday at the Boise High School auditorium, 1010 W. Washington St.
“Andy Hawes and Kirt Naylor, who are running for the same seat in the only contested race in this election, will participate,” a BABE VOTE press release said. “The other two candidates, Dr. Alejandro Necochea and Krista Hasler, are running unopposed in their respective races. Both have been invited, and Dr. Necochea will participate.”
Kevin Richert, longtime education and state politics reporter at Idaho Education News, will moderate the discussion.
“Since students are the primary stakeholders in our education, we wanted to provide our classmates and the community the opportunity to hear from people who may be making decisions that affect us,” said Mona Schwartz, a BABE VOTE board member and junior at Boise High, in the press release. “We are excited to hear from all the candidates.”
Due to the school district’s original charter, trustee elections in Boise take place outside of the state’s other election cycles. The election will take place Tuesday, Sept. 1, and voters can find polling information online. Polls will be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.

The candidate forum, which is hosted by the youth-led, nonprofit BABE VOTE organization, will feature candidates from the district’s only contested race this election.
The event will be held from 6:30-8 p.m. Tuesday at the Boise High School auditorium, 1010 W. Washington St.
“Andy Hawes and Kirt Naylor, who are running for the same seat in the only contested race in this election, will participate,” a BABE VOTE press release said. “The other two candidates, Dr. Alejandro Necochea and Krista Hasler, are running unopposed in their respective races. Both have been invited, and Dr. Necochea will participate.”
Kevin Richert, longtime education and state politics reporter at Idaho Education News, will moderate the discussion.
“Since students are the primary stakeholders in our education, we wanted to provide our classmates and the community the opportunity to hear from people who may be making decisions that affect us,” said Mona Schwartz, a BABE VOTE board member and junior at Boise High, in the press release. “We are excited to hear from all the candidates.”
Due to the school district’s original charter, trustee elections in Boise take place outside of the state’s other election cycles. The election will take place Tuesday, Sept. 1, and voters can find polling information online. Polls will be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.

title: Arkansas launches online wildfire tracker as drought continues
description: The Arkansas Department of Agriculture launched an online dashboard detailing active wildfires across the state this week, as a months-long drought has left a third of the state at a high risk for wildfires and nearly the entire state under burn bans. The dashboard shows the current number of wildfires and acres affected by them, […]
text:
Firefighters work under an orange sky at the Rowe Creek Complex Fire in Oregon in late July. As fires spread rapidly across the Pacific Northwest this summer, wildfire veterans say extreme conditions and aggressive fire suppression could put crews in danger. (Photo by Brett Deedon/Oregon State Fire Marshal)The Arkansas Department of Agriculture launched an online dashboard detailing active wildfires across the state this week, as a months-long drought has left a third of the state at a high risk for wildfires and nearly the entire state under burn bans.
The dashboard shows the current number of wildfires and acres affected by them, as well as details about individual fires and their location. 
Year-to-date data about wildfire numbers and acreage is also included. According to the dashboard, as of Thursday, there have been 1,097 wildfires, with 27,182 acres burned so far this year. One wildfire is currently burning.
The agriculture department has warned that fire risk is expected to go up across the state in the coming weeks. The department has 175 wildland firefighters and other equipment and resources used to fight fires on the 15 million acres of non-federal forest it protects.
“This new resource is designed to provide timely, reliable information to Arkansans and support public awareness during periods of elevated fire risk,” the department wrote in a press release earlier this week. “While the Department encourages the use of this dashboard to stay informed, it is critical that Arkansans follow established safety guidance.”
The department said people should “never attempt to approach or investigate a wildfire on your own” due to conditions that can change rapidly when a wildfire is burning.
While drought conditions have improved compared to how they were in the spring — 92% of the state was in a state of severe drought, at a minimum, at the beginning of April — 71% of Arkansas is at least in moderate drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor, with 40% of the state in severe or extreme drought.
Relief isn’t likely to come soon. While the National Weather Service in Little Rock noted on its website that next week will bring better chances for relief from the extreme heat baking the state in recent weeks, “widespread beneficial rainfall doesn’t look promising at this time” even with higher rainfall chances.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippians share stories of unaffordable healthcare as national campaign comes to Jackson
description: Dorothy Triplett jots down her concerns regarding the current condition of healthcare during the One Nation Overcharged event held at Smith Park, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
As Jacksonians gathered at the public green space of Smith Park Wednesday, they connected over rising healthcare costs, enjoyed free food and live music and plugged into the “One Nation, Overcharged” national campaign network. 
The healthcare affordability campaign is an initiative of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, a health policy nonprofit research organization. Several state groups co-sponsored the block party styled event, including the Mississippi chapter of the NAACP, the health-oriented Care4Mississippi Coalition, Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable, Mississippi Urban League and a maternal health group, Six Dimensions.
Early Wednesday, members of the Urban League tucked campaign pamphlets into blue cotton bags filled with canned goods and fruits during their monthly food distribution. Then, volunteers headed over to Smith Park to talk with 150 registered attendees.
The healthcare rally drew the interest of people from different walks of life. Office workers strolled through the event during their lunch break. College students looked up resources and grabbed plates of catfish from food trucks that served over 200 meals during the event. Some visitors, like longtime Jackson resident Dorothy Triplett, were invited by friends. 
Dorothy Triplett jots down her concerns regarding the current condition of healthcare during the One Nation Overcharged event held at Smith Park, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
At 87 years old, the retired civic advocate said she is still physically active and volunteers with community organizing groups. From the One Nation, Overcharged community participation table, she chose a large yellow sticker to inscribe her frustrations with the healthcare system. A volunteer helped her add the sticker to the growing board of local voices. 
“People on Medicaid don’t have equal access to excellent care,” she wrote, punctuated with several exclamation points. Triplett knows, she said, because of how her son has struggled to obtain care in California. 
“Healthcare is in need of CPR,” she told Mississippi Today. 
Cassandra Welchin, executive director of the Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable, said her conversations at the event reinforced the importance of advocating for more affordable healthcare nationwide. 
She said she spoke to one woman who couldn’t afford paying $1,000 a month for her prescription and was instead waiting until her checkups to collect samples, which last about a month. 
“She goes like two months at a time without the prescription because her insurance won’t cover it,” Welchin said. “And she said the cost is just too expensive.”
Welchin hopes people who attended the block party will push Mississippi lawmakers to expand Medicaid. 
“The state of Mississippi really needs to care about what families are going through and not play politics with people’s lives,” she said.
Jalyn Owens, left, with Six Dimensions, a non-porofit health and advocacy organization that focuses on Black maternal wellbeing, explains literature to those attending the One Nation Overcharged event held at Smith Park, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
As coverage shrinks, costs loom larger 
Expanding Medicaid would give Mississippians more health insurance options as premiums increase for plans in the Affordable Care Act Marketplace.
Those rising costs may be linked to people losing coverage. For the first time in over a decade at the Mississippi Insurance Department, Life and Health Actuarial Division Director Bob Williams is seeing the number of people covered by Marketplace plans go down. 
After COVID-19-era subsidies that reduced health premiums expired in December, around 200,000 Mississippians lost their Marketplace coverage, Williams said. From a peak of about 335,000 people enrolled in 2025, he estimates around 125,000 are still making payments as of August. 
Comedian Rita Brent hosted the One Nation Overcharged event held at Smith Park, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Those numbers may continue to drop. Williams said enrollees in the ACA Marketplace can expect to see an average rate increase of 18% next year, depending on their carrier and plan. 
The jump may be tough to handle for Mississippians like Madison-based poet Steven Randle, who performed a healthcare-oriented spoken word piece under the domed Smith Park stage. In it, he reflected on his childhood fear of doctors, with their sharp needles and strange chalky medicines. Now, he’s afraid of how much their services cost. 
After leaving his public policy career to pursue poetry full time last year, Randle realized the prices for individual healthcare plans are “astronomical.” To manage the costs, he said he tried to ignore his pain, including flare-ups from an old hip injury and severe migraines. 
Marsha Credit spins a wheel with each slot asking a health related question for a prize during the One Nation Overcharged event held at Smith Park, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Randle recently took on a new job solely for the health insurance benefit. But some costs, including the screenings he’s hoping to get due to a family history of cancer, still come out of pocket. 
“That’s a fear of mine,” he said. “It’s not only just if they say yes. It’s also, will I be able to afford to live?”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: State health department gives UL Monroe $2 million to address rural nursing shortage
description: The Louisiana Board of Regents projects the state will have a shortfall of approximately 6,000 nurses by 2030.
text:
The University of Louisiana Monroe library, photographed from Northeast Drive. (Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)The Louisiana Department of Health is awarding the University of Louisiana at Monroe more than $2.1 million for programs to mitigate the state’s shortage of nurses. 
The Louisiana Board of Regents projects the state will have a shortfall of approximately 6,000 nurses by 2030. The problem is particularly acute in rural areas in Northeast Louisiana, which the health department has designated professional shortage areas. 
The investment in UL Monroe will help an additional 40 nurses per year to graduate and fund the creation of a Nurse Residency Hub serving rural hospitals in the region. 
“This investment is a critical part of Louisiana’s broader Rural Health Transformation strategy to strengthen our workforce pipeline and ensure rural communities have access to health care professionals where they live,” Louisiana Department of Health Secretary Bruce Greenstein said in a news release. 
“Ultimately, this is about bringing better care closer to home and improving health outcomes for rural Louisianans,” he added. 
In addition to funding nursing initiatives, the grant will also support development of a diagnostic medical sonography concentration under the school’s existing radiologic technology bachelor’s degree.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: A new day dawns for Providence Place as new owners close on $133M deal
description: On Aug, 20, 1999, crowds streamed through the Providence Place mall, ready to celebrate the long-awaited opening day of the downtown shopping destination.  On Thursday — exactly 27 years later — a much smaller and more muted celebration unfolded as the mall’s new owners gathered outside the first-floor Apple store to announce that they had […]
text:
Providence Place sits empty on the morning of Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026, after the end of the 50-minute ceremony to announce new owners had closed on the mall. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)On Aug, 20, 1999, crowds streamed through the Providence Place mall, ready to celebrate the long-awaited opening day of the downtown shopping destination. 
On Thursday — exactly 27 years later — a much smaller and more muted celebration unfolded as the mall’s new owners gathered outside the first-floor Apple store to announce that they had closed the sale.
“Never did I think I would be standing at a podium in the Providence Place mall as its owner,” said Joe Paolino Jr., former city mayor who now heads downtown real estate development group Paolino Properties. “Sometimes you end up right back where you began.”
Indeed, the $133 million, all-cash purchase by Paolino Properties and New York management firm Pyramid Management Group marks a poetic full-circle moment for both sets of new owners. Paolino helped craft the deal for the mall’s creation, setting the wheels in motion during his time as city mayor and cementing details later as state economic development director. Robert Congel, the late CEO of Pyramid, was majority partner for the company that built the landmark structure in the 1990s. His son Stephen Congel, now Pyramid CEO, sat in on early mall development meetings as a young employee for his dad’s company.
Their personal attachment to the 13.2-acre site and professional expertise won over the court-appointed receivers, who recommended the Paolino-Pyramid purchase offer to the courts. Their proposal was one of three bids submitted through the receivership process — not the highest, but the only one with local ties and without conditions attached. 
A Rhode Island Superior Court judge approved the transaction in June, awaiting finalization of a purchase and sale agreement. 


 Stephen J. Congel, right, CEO of Pyramid Management Group, one of the new owners of Providence Place, describe the 27-year-old mall as “well maintained and in very good condition” at a press conference announcing the sale on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. At left is Joe Paolino Jr., left, principal of Paolino Properties. (Video by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current) 
With the bank transfer completed late Wednesday, Thursday was the first day Paolino and Congel could call themselves mall owners. The timing, on the 27th anniversary of the mall’s opening, was “pure coincidence,” Paolino said.
But their plans for reviving the struggling shopping destination, plagued by store vacancies, reduced foot traffic, and, since November 2024, the state equivalent of bankruptcy, are deliberate.
“We love to manage properties that are complex, that have real idiosyncrasies, as this one does, and make them special,” Congel said. 
Congel, whose company manages nine shopping destinations totaling 12 million square feet and $2.3 billion in sales, wants to bring Pyramid’s “gold-standard” security system to Providence. He declined to offer specifics on the security protocol, but mentioned equipment and personnel.
Paolino also named security improvements as his “No. 1 priority.” Rare but high-profile incidents of violence in or near the mall — including a 2018 shooting outside Nordstrom — have sown safety concerns in shoppers and tenants. 
Also on the to-do list: technological upgrades to the parking garage. Problems with the parking management and payment system left shoppers stuck in the garage for hours on a Saturday in March 2025. Paolino said he’s still hearing from people “getting stuck” in the labyrinthian parking structure.
Much of the physical maintenance was put on the back burner under the previous owner and operator, Brookfield Properties. After Brookfield defaulted on the mortgage loan backed by the mall space, private lenders filed suit in state Superior Court, claiming the mall owner more than $259 million in principal and interest from the 2011 loan.
As the claims process played out in court, a pair of local attorneys designated as court-appointed receivers began the early stages of the makeover, bringing in a new management company to oversee daily operations, and investing nearly $100,000 in repairs and improvements to the shopping center and connected parking garage.
Paolino and Congel declined to comment when asked how much money they plan to invest in cosmetic and infrastructure improvements in the first year.
Joe Paolino, managing partner for Paolino Properties, announces the completed sale of the Providence Place mall at a press conference on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)
They were also tight-lipped about courtship of new tenants, though Congel touted multiple calls from prospective tenants who heard about the sale even before it was solidified. Meanwhile, Paolino continues his own pursuit of a Costco, though he admits the downtown shopping center does not offer the square footage or suburban environment the big box retailer typically looks for.
“I want Costco,” Paolino said Thursday. “I am not announcing it because we don’t have it.”
But, he’s talked to the company, whose board of directors includes former Gov. Gina Raimondo and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Helena Buonanno Foulkes.
“They haven’t thrown us out, and they haven’t signed anything,” Paolino said.
Separately, Paolino wants a supermarket, which he said is also a long-held desire of Providence Mayor Brett Smiley. Smiley, who joined the executives for the announcement, heralded the new ownership as a “bright horizon” for the capital city.
“It’s not the relationship we had in the past,” Smiley said, alluding to the global real estate firm, now known as BGRE, that formerly owned and operated the mall.
Unlike at least one of the competing bids for the property, Paolino and Pyramid have not sought any tax incentives from the state or city. At least, not yet.
An existing 30-year property tax agreement with the city is set to expire in 2028. Under the agreement, the mall pays $500,000 a year in city property taxes, rather than the $26.8 million it would pay if taxed at the full, fiscal 2027 city commercial tax rate. 
“There’s no reason to ask for something when we don’t know what we’re asking for,” Paolino said of tax incentives. “If something dramatic happens, then we’ll have to have that conversation.”
But, Paolino emphasized stability and predictability in the relationship with city and state officials. Smiley and Gov. Dan McKee are both locked in tough primary battles against Democratic challengers David Morales and Foulkes, respectively.
Paolino acknowledged when asked that he had concerns about leadership changes resulting from the 2026 election cycle, but declined to elaborate.
Morales has expressed public support for the new ownership and redevelopment plans, including the addition of a grocery store. 
The mall remains at 80% occupancy, Congel confirmed. He declined to comment on specific, existing tenants, including Apple, but said most seem assured by the stability provided by the sale.
DW Partners, a New York real estate investment firm, is also part of the partnership deal with Paolino Properties and Pyramid. Company representatives did not attend the announcement event.
Paolino and Congel declined to disclose the payment split between the three partners for the sale. 
The parking garage of the Providence Place mall is slated for improvements, the new owners said during the event on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)

description: Denver is one of three finalists the Democratic National Committee will consider to host its 2028 national convention.  If selected, Colorado’s capital would host the 2028 Democratic National Convention two decades after it last hosted it, when Barack Obama accepted the party’s 2008 presidential nomination in front of a crowd of more than 80,000 people […]
text:

Jared Polis and DNC Chair Ken Martin address delegates and the media at Denver's Ball Arena on May 6, 2026, during a visit to evaluate the city's bid for the 2028 Democratic National Convention. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Denver is one of three finalists the Democratic National Committee will consider to host its 2028 national convention. 
If selected, Colorado’s capital would host the 2028 Democratic National Convention two decades after it last hosted it, when Barack Obama accepted the party’s 2008 presidential nomination in front of a crowd of more than 80,000 people at what was then known as Invesco Field at Mile High.

title: Cyclospora ‘slowing down’ in Alabama, says state Department of Public Health
description: The Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH) said Thursday that cyclosporiasis, a parasite that causes intestinal illness, is slowing down after a nationwide outbreak.  “The cyclospora outbreak associated with lettuce, mostly we think, has now tallied about 117 cases confirmed in Alabama, (which) pales in comparison to sort of the upper Midwest are just un[...]
text:
Vegetables and lettuces at a grocery store in Michigan. Alabama State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris said Thursday that cyclosporiasis is "slowing down" in Alabama after a nationwide outbreak. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)The Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH) said Thursday that cyclosporiasis, a parasite that causes intestinal illness, is slowing down after a nationwide outbreak. 
“The cyclospora outbreak associated with lettuce, mostly we think, has now tallied about 117 cases confirmed in Alabama, (which) pales in comparison to sort of the upper Midwest are just under 10,000 confirmed cases, but about 16,000 or more other suspected cases that have been reported,” said Dr. Scott Harris, the state health officer.
According to ADPH data, there were 21 reported cases in 2025, 30 in 2024 and 139 in 2023 in the state. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As of Aug. 13, there have been 9,481 confirmed cases in 17 states, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Cases are likely under-reported, according to the CDC. There have been two deaths in Michigan and 398 hospitalizations. 
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services – where the outbreak is centered – has reported nearly 14,000 cases. The Ohio Department of Health has reported nearly 5,000 cases, another hub of the outbreak. 
Alabama’s outbreak was concentrated in the northern region of the state, said Ryan Easterling, director of communications for ADPH on Thursday. Seventy-three cases were reported in the Northern ADPH District – consisting of 12 counties mostly north and northwest of Birmingham; 10 in the Northeastern District; eight in the Southeastern District; seven in Jefferson County and in the Southwestern District; five in Mobile County and the West Central District; and two in the East Central District. 
“Even though that doesn’t sound like a lot compared to 20,000, it’s a lot for Alabama, so we’ll keep tracking that,” Harris said. 
Cyclosporiasis is caused by the parasite cyclospora. Symptoms include watery or “explosive” diarrhea, nausea and stomach cramps. It’s often contracted by eating or drinking something contaminated with the parasite, which lives in feces.
The illness is not contagious, and symptoms can develop within about 10 days and last for a few days to up to a month without antibiotic treatment, according to the CDC. 
The CDC linked the outbreak to iceberg lettuce from Mexico-based Taylor Farms. The company voluntarily recalled several of its bagged lettuce and Marketplace brand lettuce distributed to 31 states. The link was later retracted. The best buy dates on those products have passed.
About 94% of Alabama’s cases were laboratory-confirmed, Easterling said. About 34% of the state’s cases are associated with an outbreak.
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in collaboration with the CDC also recalled organic frozen blueberries distributed to Publix locations in the southeast in late July due to an E. coli risk. 
Many news outlets reported that the FDA upgraded the risk to Class I – meaning there is a reasonable chance that using or being exposed to a product will cause severe health harm or death. Easterling said on Wednesday that ADPH had not received any updated guidance from the FDA or CDC, and the FDA’s investigation page has not been updated since July 30. 
He also said Wednesday there have been no reported cases of E. coli in Alabama. According to the Mayo Clinic, symptoms of E. coli can begin within three to four days of eating a contaminated product and are similar to that of cyclospora.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Poor coordination, missing documents, mismatched training: Report analyzes prison releases in SD
description: South Dakota prisons struggle to prepare inmates for release, and the support systems meant to help them on the outside often fall short, according to a report from a national nonprofit. The assessment found consistent gaps in support, employment, housing and mental health and addiction treatment for people leaving prison. It also found the state […]
text:
A housing unit at the new women's prison in Rapid City, South Dakota. (Courtesy of South Dakota Department of Corrections)South Dakota prisons struggle to prepare inmates for release, and the support systems meant to help them on the outside often fall short, according to a report from a national nonprofit.
The assessment found consistent gaps in support, employment, housing and mental health and addiction treatment for people leaving prison. It also found the state lacks the data and oversight structure needed to track and improve outcomes.
The state paid the Council of State Governments Justice Center $160,000 to study reentry on behalf of the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force, which met Wednesday in Rapid City.

Ryan Brunner, senior policy adviser for the governor, speaks during the state Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force meeting in Sioux Falls on Oct. 29, 2025. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

Gov. Larry Rhoden created the task force to study ways of reducing repeat offense rates and improving rehabilitation programming. The task force came on the heels of a legislative vote to replace the oldest parts of the state penitentiary with a $650 million men’s prison in Sioux Falls, which is under construction. The state opened a new $87 million prison for women in Rapid City this summer, the state’s second for female inmates.
South Dakota’s recidivism rate is 50%, meaning half of all inmates released from state prison return within three years.
Ryan Brunner, senior policy adviser for Rhoden, told lawmakers at the meeting that the report will help guide the expansion and operation of treatment and programming at the new prisons.
The Department of Corrections, Brunner said, “is certainly taking this data and focusing on it, and it’s good for us to have that conversation.”
System inconsistencies
When someone leaves prison, the assessment says, coordination breaks down. Access to support depends more on personal relationships between inmates, staff members and outside organizations than on formal systems, said Megan Pfeiffer, deputy policy director with the Council of State Governments Justice Center.
“There are some deep challenges here,” Pfeiffer said. 
South Dakota State Penitentiary loses fourth warden in five years amid senior staff shake-up

The Department of Corrections has a reentry initiative in place to help people released from prison reenter society, but the assessment found people frequently leave prison without the transition support they need. Community handoffs are inconsistent and rushed, and inmates often leave without vital documents — identification cards, Social Security cards, birth certificates — that they need to find work or access services.
More than 80% of men and 95% of women serve two years or less in prison — a “narrow window” to address rehabilitative needs, Pfeiffer said. Many inmates leave without programming — 35% of people released in 2025 hadn’t had programming, the report found. Most of those people were incarcerated for less than a year.
The assessment recommends starting reentry planning the day someone enters prison, not weeks before they leave, and says the state should create a permanent reentry council and formalize how agencies share data and coordinate services.
Employment barriers
Participation in vocational programming inside prison is low. Structured referrals to such programs and job placement services are largely absent, and the state has no data on whether people find and keep jobs after release.
Even motivated inmates who get vocational programming in prison frequently lose connection with workforce services the moment they’re released, Pfeiffer said.
“We heard that there’s often competing appointments and needs, and people get lost in the shuffle where employment isn’t prioritized as one of their primary needs,” Pfeiffer said. “Transition can take a long time to walk through the assessment and appointment process, which leaves people unemployed for a longer period of time.”
State laws also restrict where people with felony convictions can work after release.
More than 250 legal and regulatory employment barriers can be triggered by any felony conviction in South Dakota, Pfeiffer said. South Dakota is one of fewer than 15 states without “fair chance” hiring laws, which limit when employers can ask about criminal history.

Rep. Bobbi Andera, R-Sioux Falls, speaks in the South Dakota House of Representatives on Feb. 9, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

Sioux Falls Republican Rep. Bobbi Andera said her “biggest concern” is putting state resources toward programming without considering how hireable people are when they’re released.
“Programming is great, but programming is only great if they get a job,” Andera said.
A 2025 Department of Labor and Regulation survey found that 84% of South Dakota employers cite finding skilled workers as their top challenge, but only 40% said they’d hire someone with a criminal record.
The Department of Corrections trains inmates in areas such as welding, electrical work, auto service, plumbing, machining and carpentry — but those skills don’t align with the state’s most in-demand jobs, which include heavy truck drivers, sales representatives, nurses and dental assistants. The gap is especially stark in healthcare, where workforce demand is highest. State laws and regulations for healthcare, however, create more employment barriers for people with felony convictions than in any other industry.
“There’s a real gap here that we talk about as an opportunity,” Pfeiffer said. “There’s the workforce need and there’s a population that wants and needs employment.”
Brunner told lawmakers the state is exploring more employment programming options, including a five-week commercial driver’s license program and a medical technician training partnership with Western Dakota Technical College and Sanford Health. Felons can be medical technicians in South Dakota.
Behavioral health, housing needs unaddressed
About 91% of men and 97% of women in prison were diagnosed with substance use disorder upon admission, according to the 2025 Department of Corrections statistical report.
Staff can coordinate treatment referrals before release, but provider shortages, lack of transportation and fewer options in rural areas often stymie access to care for inmates upon release. The state also doesn’t have enough residential mental health space.
State-ordered study says opioid settlement money should target treatment for incarcerated people

The assessment says the state should improve Medicaid enrollment for departing inmates and work to expand treatment access in rural and tribal areas.
Sen. Jamie Smith, D-Sioux Falls, said the assessment confirmed his belief that South Dakota shouldn’t be “punishing someone with illness,” and that the state needs to improve its mental health infrastructure as a whole. 
The behavioral health aspect of rehabilitation should not be the Department of Correction’s job, he said.
“We can look at all the programs we want in recidivism and all the things within our correction system that we want — and we need to do a better job, and I think there’s a lot of things we’re going to learn — but unless we look at it holistically and from all the different departments, we’re not going to do anything,” Smith said.
Insufficient affordable housing is also one of the “greatest barriers” to successful reentry, the assessment said, and the state should prioritize housing stability for people leaving prison.
Work, housing and staffing: How South Dakota’s corrections chief aims to keep inmates from returning

The state has some housing programs in place, but they don’t meet demand. Given employment challenges, a person earning a minimum wage would need to work 1.4 full-time jobs to afford a one-bed rental home, the report says. The gap in affordable housing options is worst in rural and tribal areas.
Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen chairs the task force and said the group focuses on programming within the prison system, even as the assessment revealed issues in the community that factor into recidivism.
“We’re obviously not going to solve the housing issue,” Venhuizen said. “But we can identify that as an issue and talk about some ideas for continuing work on that.” 
Venhuizen said he plans to have a “good idea” of recommendations for the governor and lawmakers by their October meeting.

title: Portland sees more immigration detentions as arrests increase nationally
description: Colleagues and community groups are pushing back on recent immigrant detentions in Portland as arrests nationwide hit a Trump-era high.   Federal agents detained a Cambodian man on Tuesday while he was working at Veranda Asian Market. Earlier this month, agents detained a Portland Public Schools transportation employee. These detentions are in addition to ot[...]
text:
Two protesters hold signs saying "No ICE on our streets" in Scarborough. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Colleagues and community groups are pushing back on recent immigrant detentions in Portland as arrests nationwide hit a Trump-era high.  
Federal agents detained a Cambodian man on Tuesday while he was working at Veranda Asian Market. Earlier this month, agents detained a Portland Public Schools transportation employee. These detentions are in addition to others outside court and at the jetport in recent weeks.
Over the past year, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has grown its staff by 44% in Maine, the first significant growth in the state in at least a decade, according to an analysis by the Portland Press Herald. 
Across the country, ICE arrests have been on the rise, reaching the highest on record in July. This increase has come as the White House pushes for the agency to meet a new target of 2,000 arrests per day, roughly double the pace from earlier this year. 
Many of these arrests have not been through dramatic sweeps or large-scale operations, like the one in Maine in January, but instead conducted more quietly during everyday encounters. 
For example, federal agents went into Veranda Asian Market around 9 a.m. Tuesday and asked to speak with the Cambodian man outside before detaining him, according to Marpheen Chann, executive director of Khmer Maine. Chann declined to share the man’s name.
Meanwhile, Simao Paulo, the van driver and bus assistant for Portland Public Schools who is originally from Angola, was arrested on Aug. 4 after Canadian border agents turned him over to U.S. Customs and Border Protection in Champlain, NY, according to a DHS spokesperson who said he was issued a final order of removal in July. 
“His detention by immigration enforcement has done nothing to make our community safer and makes it harder for our district to ensure transportation is available for all eligible students,” the school district shared in a statement. The Benefit Association of School Employees and the Portland Education Association have called for his release. 
Paulo’s detention is at least the second employee of the school district detained by ICE this year. Agents detained Micheline Ntumba, a facilities staffer, in January after she dropped one of her children off at Portland High School. A father of an elementary student was also detained outside Gerald E. Talbot Community School last September. 
The majority of the immigrants detained across the country continue to have no criminal convictions, contradicting the Trump administration’s continued statements that federal immigration agencies are targeting “the worst of the worst.”
