name: WyoFile
title: The Wyoming Freedom Caucus can blame itself for its resounding defeat
description:
Far-right legislators were convinced they had a forever mandate, but voters quickly put them in their place, writes columnist Kerry Drake.
The post The Wyoming Freedom Caucus can blame itself for its resounding defeat appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Freedom Caucus bristled whenever anyone, including yours truly, described it as “far right.” So, the media started using adjectives like “further right” and “hard-line conservatives.”

Opinion

Thanks to Tuesday’s shocking primary election results, we now know what to accurately call a huge chunk of these Freedom Caucus members, including its top leadership: “former legislators.”
Please note that I did not write “losers.” I am not a cruel man, just a very happy one. And I know the political winds can shift quickly, so I am definitely not counting on the electorate to prevent the Freedom Caucus from ever coming back.
As the (ahem) far-right caucus proved when it took control of the House in 2024, it all depends on which voters actually show up on Election Day.
But this was a trampling unlike any other election in the state’s history. The Freedom Caucus, with its never-ending gloating about its “mandate,” was led to the slaughterhouse without any idea of what was coming.
Thirteen House incumbents lost, plus nine other candidates. Voters spurned six Freedom Caucus members who tried to move to the Senate.



That leaves the caucus with likely just 10 reliable House votes. It’s an astounding turnaround from January, when the group could count on about 35 votes, give or take, in the House.
I realize there were Freedom Caucus survivors, like Rep. Tomi Strock of Douglas, whose winning margin was 121 votes. But they were few and far between, and sometimes inexplicable. 
How, for example, did Rep. Bill Allemand, R-Midwest, win after his embarrassing DUI arrest and plea deal was splashed all over the news for months? In unofficial results, he defeated Peter Boyer, Bar Nunn’s mayor, by 27 votes.
But look at some of the Freedom Caucus’ most eyeball-popping losses.
House Speaker Chip Neiman, R-Hullett, lost his bid to move to the Senate when he was defeated by Sen. Ogden Driskill, R-Devils Tower, one of the Legislature’s biggest Freedom Caucus disparagers.
Rep. John Bear, R-Gillette, former Freedom Caucus chair and co-chair of the powerful Joint Appropriations Committee, was pinned to the mat by challenger Douglas Moore.
House Majority Floor Leader Scott Heiner, R-Green River, who decided what bills would fall on the cutting room floor at the introduction deadline, was upset by Kenneth D. Roberts of Kemmerer, a Wyoming Game and Fish commissioner.
How about pundits who pooh-poohed the premise that “Checkgate” was a major scandal when it dominated the Legislature’s budget session?
Nine Freedom Caucus House members and a Senate ally were given campaign checks from a Jackson donor that were delivered — some on the House floor during a legislative session! — by conservative activist Rebecca Bextel.
Rep. John Bear, R-Gillette, left, speaks with Rebecca Bextel, second from left, Rep. Ken Pendergraft, R-Sheridan, right, and Rita Benson LeBlanc on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, on the third floor of the Wyoming Capitol during the 68th Wyoming Legislature’s budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
Bextel had been lobbying lawmakers on an anti-affordable housing bill under the guise of stopping local governments from infringing on private property rights. It was sponsored by Bear. 
Out of the 10 check recipients, only Rep. Christopher Knapp, R-Gillette, will appear on the general election ballot. Gone are Neiman and Bear, whose joint conduct during the Checkgate incident and investigation was appalling.
Bear, who had accepted his $1,500 check from Bextel, didn’t admit it when the issue first came up. Instead, he berated Rep. Mike Yin, D-Jackson, who had called out Bextel’s actions to the entire House without mentioning her name and diplomatically not identifying any check grabbers.
Bear said Yin was “making accusations of an individual that cannot be substantiated, and that accusation is offensive to this body.”
Neiman, who much later acknowledged Bextel gave him his check in his office, a few feet from the House floor, also objected to Yin’s claim and asked him to substantiate it.
Rep. Rachel Rodriguez-Williams, R-Cody, Freedom Caucus chair, said if what Yin said was true, it “essentially would be bribery and unethical.” She claimed Yin made a defamatory statement.
I think voters made a statement of their own when they rejected her bid for the Republican nomination for secretary of state.
Gone are Rep. Darin McCann, R-Rock Springs, who was famously photographed by Rep. Karlee Provenza, D-Laramie, accepting Bextel’s check on the House floor with Rep. Marlene Brady, R-Green River, standing nearby clutching her check.
At least McMann admitted what he did. Brady told reporters it was none of their business.
Other members of the Checkgate gang who lost their seats were GOP Reps. Joe Webb of Lyman and Tony Locke of Casper. Sen. Bob Ide, a Casper legislator endorsed by the Freedom Caucus, is also out. So is Mark Jennings, a former representative who was trying to win his House seat back. 
From right, Rebecca Bextel, Rep. Darin McCann, R-Rock Springs, Rep. Mike Schmid, R-La Barge, Rep. Joe Webb, R-Lyman, and Rep. Nina Webber, R-Cody, during the first meeting of the House Special Investigative Committee on Thursday, Feb. 26, 2026, at the Wyoming Capitol in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
Even Rep. Nina Webber, R-Cody, who had escorted Bextel on the House floor, lost her reelection attempt. Only Knapp escaped.
Two other Freedom Caucus defeats loom large in explaining why the devastating blows to the far-right movement were inflicted internally. They happened to two members of the caucus with extremely high profiles.
Former Rep. Jeanette Ward of Casper was the poster girl of the Freedom Caucus during her one term in the House. The self-described “political refugee” from Illinois, who couldn’t win an election there, made headlines by promoting the most red-meat issues one could toss in front of Wyoming voters.
Whether it was banning supposedly “pornographic” material from libraries, taking on the LGBTQ+ community or reproductive rights, she was always controversial.
Voters quickly tired of her act and replaced her with Julie Jarvis, a “traditional” Wyoming conservative who didn’t share Ward’s extreme views. Ward responded by watching her from the House gallery and making derogatory statements about Jarvis on social media.
The rematch was a test of whether the Freedom Caucus has any staying power. The verdict is in, and it doesn’t. The totals are unofficial until the state canvassing board meets, but Jarvis won, 685-496.
Rep. Jeanette Ward and challenger Julie Jarvis stand for the Pledge of Allegiance before the start of a Politics in the Park event on Wednesday, July 31, 2024, in Casper. (Dan Cepeda/WyoFile)
If we’re lucky, Wyoming will join Illinois as the next state Ward flees.
If you’re looking for a Freedom Caucus loss even more significant than the ones suffered by Bear and Neiman, examine what happened to Rep. Ken Pendergraft of Sheridan when he tried to succeed Senate President Bo Biteman of Ranchester, who left office to unsuccessfully pursue Wyoming’s U.S. House seat.
I will never forget sitting at Joint Appropriations Committee meetings and watching Pendergraft try to gut the University of Wyoming, the Wyoming Business Council, the Department of Health and Wyoming Public Media. He had no justification for taking a chainsaw to these budgets, just the vague belief that he knew money was being wasted and he would stop it.
The Freedom Caucus plan was to sic Pendergraft on the Senate, which saved all of these institutions from his wrecking ball last session. He was supposed to “educate” the chamber, which was only a vote or two away from being taken over by Freedom Caucus sympathizers, and show them how to responsibly work a budget.
If ever a man was totally unfit for that job, it’s Pendergraft, outpointed by Melissa Butcher in Senate District 21 by 17 percentage points.
People I spoke to ahead of the primary thought Pendergraft was a shoo-in for the nomination. It’s the perfect example of the “Peter Principle,” a concept that observes people in a hierarchy tend to rise to a “level of respective incompetence.”
In Wyoming, it should be forever known as the “Pendergraft Principle.” The architect of the Freedom Caucus’ plan for statewide political dominance went down in flames.
Rising from the ashes should be a Legislature with people who didn’t arrive at the Capitol hoping to burn everything down. 
With new legislative leadership and an executive branch likely headed by former Sen. Eric Barlow of Gillette, a level-headed man who has shown intelligence and compassion during his 14 years in the Legislature, hopefully Wyoming can close the chapter on the nightmarish past two years and head toward a much brighter future.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho law student writes bill to ban sale of human remains — before she can even practice law
description: When Desalyn Swank applied to law school at University of Idaho, she said she made it clear she wanted to reform the state’s laws. Before her first year at law school ended, she already had.  This year, the Idaho Legislature passed, and the governor signed, a bill she wrote to strengthen the state’s laws to […]
text:
More than a month after a bill she wrote to outlaw the sale of human remains took effect, University of Idaho law student Desalyn Swank walks down the halls of the Idaho State Capitol. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)When Desalyn Swank applied to law school at University of Idaho, she said she made it clear she wanted to reform the state’s laws.
Before her first year at law school ended, she already had. 
This year, the Idaho Legislature passed, and the governor signed, a bill she wrote to strengthen the state’s laws to criminalize the possession and sale of human remains. 
Inspired by her faith and her upbringing as the daughter of a mortician, she worked with coroners, law enforcement and others to craft a bill that didn’t receive a single no vote from any of Idaho’s 105 state lawmakers — all in the final few weeks of this year’s legislative session, when lawmakers often discourage new bills. 
But she doesn’t take all the credit.
“I don’t think that I really carved the path forward,” Swank said in an interview. “I think that it it carved the path for itself because … the human remains retail market is so heinous, and it’s so against what we stand for as a nation and as humanity and what we hold as our values.”
The law, which took effect July 1 through House Bill 856, makes it a felony to sell own,, buy or lease “any artifacts or any human remains taken from a cairn, grave, or burial site,” or to “sell or advertise the sale of any material advertised as real human remains.” The law carves out several exceptions, including actions to perform government duties, such as work done by law enforcement or coroners, or by licensed medical practices, mortuaries, cemeteries, or medical research facilities. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 ‘I am definitely a mortician’s kid,’ University of Idaho law student says

At 16, Swank started full-time college and earned a degree in communications. She got married soon after, and went on to get a master’s degree in communications and later worked at several companies, including Amazon Web Services in Seattle. 
But when she got divorced, she said she went soul searching.
“I kind of went into this midlife makeover, and thought, ‘OK, well, what did I want to be when I was little?’” Swank said. “I thought, ‘OK, well, I wanted to take care of dead people like my daddy.’”
Then she decided to go to law school — to help pass legislation and policy “to protect those that have passed that are being taken advantage of.”
Swank, who’s now 38, said her path became clear after prayer. She wanted to honor her father, and his foster dad, who were both funeral directors. 
She described herself as definitely being a “mortician’s kid.”
“I wave to graveyards as I drive by, and I say ‘Hi, everybody!’” Swank said. “When you’re raised in that industry, you’re taught the basic level of respect and honor for those that have passed that I think most people in our country, the majority — except for those that are working in human remains retail — have as part of our culture in America.”
“I don’t have that squeamish factor that some people might have when they talk about death or when they have to deal with death, because I was raised around it,” she said.
To prepare the bill, Swank has researched the human remains retail industry — pouring through websites that depict skulls turned into lamps, a skeleton lying in a coffin propped up for display, and skulls for sale on Facebook groups for $700 and $1,200.
“As far as human remains retail goes, we’re not just talking about old graves” that are the sources of human remains, she said, describing methods retailers might use to remove flesh from bones.
Desalyn Swank said she enrolled in law school to help pass legislation and policy “to protect those that have passed that are being taken advantage of.” (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
 How she prepped the bill

When she started law school at U of I, she got paired with a mentor: Richard Seamon, who’s taught prospective attorneys for 30 years. 
They started with a deep dive into how the state’s existing laws work, to find and fix the loophole that human remains retailers tap, she said. Then she drafted the bill, got feedback from Seamon, and reached out to various groups that had a stake in the issue, like law enforcement, coroners and academics. 
Seamon said he hadn’t ever taught a law student who’d written a successful bill while they were in school. 
“I have never known a student who had such a clear vision of what she wanted to accomplish and was so dedicated in pursuing it,” he said. “It really, from my perspective, is just so encouraging because this is really in the finest legal tradition. Lawyers have a professional responsibility to reform the law. It’s always in need of improvement, and lawyers are better situated than anyone else to make law and to advocate for it.”

He called Swank “exactly the kind of person who I think is going to make a wonderful lawyer, not only because of her skills, but also because of her integrity and her honesty and her passion for justice.”
When Swank had finished her bill and brought it to the Legislature, she said many lawmakers weren’t even aware of the issue. That includes Rep. Heather Scott, R-Blanchard, who was the bill’s original sponsor. 
 ‘We can try it and see:’ House Bill 856 in the Statehouse

With weeks left before the Idaho Legislature was set to adjourn for the year this spring, she reached out to Rep. Bruce Skaug, who chairs the House Judiciary and Rules Committee. He referred her to Scott, a North Idaho lawmaker who serves on that committee.
That late in the legislative session isn’t the best time to bring a new bill, Scott said. But because of Swank’s work, the bill seemed ready to go, Scott said. 
Idaho state Rep. Heather Scott, R-Blanchard, walks to the lectern to present a piece of legislation during the House State Affairs Committee on Jan. 7, 2025, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“I told her that I would carry it. Not sure, you know, it’s a new topic for a lot of legislators, so sometimes it takes several years to get something passed,” Scott said in an interview. “So I said, ‘We can try it and see what happens.’”
Within a week, it had passed both the House and Senate unanimously — a rare feat in the Statehouse. Scott credits Swank’s work. 
In the past, Scott said she’s had students bring ideas for bills to her. But, she said, “I’ve never had a student take such an initiative and take such an active interest in and then actually showing up and helping the bill work through the process.”
But Swank doesn’t think this bill will be the end. She said “tougher laws” are needed. 
“Laws are made because there’s bad actors, because somebody did something that harmed somebody else, and they weren’t able to — justice was not able to be served,” she said. “And so we fill those gaps as society, and when we bring forth those gaps to lawmakers, and lawmakers work with members of the community to ensure that justice will be able to be served in the future.”
“At least,” she added, “that’s one way laws are made. That’s the way this law was made.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee tabs road-building group for $9B toll lanes project
description: A Tennessee transportation board selected a road-building group Wednesday to fund and build toll lanes from the southeast Nashville area to Murfreesboro as part of a package in which the contractor locked up the bid by agreeing to pay the state nearly $25 billion over the life of a 50-year contract. The Transportation Modernization Board […]
text:
Members of Tennessee's Transportation Modernization Board met Wednesday to award a contract to build toll lanes from Southeast Nashville to Murfreesboro. (Photo: Sam Stockard/Tennessee Lookout)A Tennessee transportation board selected a road-building group Wednesday to fund and build toll lanes from the southeast Nashville area to Murfreesboro as part of a package in which the contractor locked up the bid by agreeing to pay the state nearly $25 billion over the life of a 50-year contract.
The Transportation Modernization Board voted unanimously to hire a six-company partnership called DriveTN made up of Transurban, an Australian global transportation company, Tikehau Star/Infra/Capital, a French infrastructure investment firm, Ferrovial, a Spain-founded infrastructure company, its U.S. subsidiary, Cintra, a highway management company, AECOM, a global engineering infrastructure company, and Webber, an American construction company. The group proposed to spend $9.2 billion to design, construct, operate and maintain lanes from downtown Nashville to Murfreesboro and along portions of I-40 east of downtown and I-440 south of downtown Nashville. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Transportation Department officials and Gov. Bill Lee endorsed the bid because the group said it would make nearly $25 billion in payments over half a century, in contrast to one bidder that asked for a subsidy to start the job and two other bidding groups that offered only about $7 billion in concessions. 
Officials said the amount the vendor is agreeing to pay the state has no relation to the fees it will charge. The group is taking on the risk that it will be able to collect enough in road-use fees to pay for construction and state concessions and still turn a profit.
Lee hailed the proposal as the largest and “most valuable” “choice” lane road building project in the nation and called it the new way to construct highways in Tennessee. 
Under the agreement, DriveTN will pay the state $1.5 billion up front and fund the project itself, then make the rest of the concessions over five decades as it collects payments from motorists who choose to use the lanes. Officials did not say how much might be charged but said it would depend on the amount of traffic and time of day.
Work on the road is expected to start in 2027 and take up to eight years for completion, though some portions of the toll lanes will be ready sooner, officials said.
Lawmakers challenge board control over “toll lanes”

“Not only will these partners fund 100% of the construction costs for these ‘choice’ lanes, but they’re going to offer the state an unprecedented concession payment that will provide billions of additional dollars beyond the project’s cost,” Lee said. The money is supposed to be used to improve the project’s corridor and to provide transportation funding statewide. 
Lee issued an executive order Wednesday creating a board of lawmakers and officials that will oversee toll-lane projects.
The legislature passed the Transportation Modernization Act in 2023, paving the way for the new funding and construction mechanism designed to look at major interstate-type projects over the next 25 years.
Toll lanes, which state officials refer to as “choice” lanes, also could extend through Murfreesboro along I-24 and part of I-840, farther out I-40 toward Lebanon and from downtown Nashville up the I-65/24 corridor. Those segments will have to go through more negotiations, officials said.
State officials could not say how many homes would have to be torn down to make way for lanes on both sides of I-24, but they said DriveTN’s plan is based on keeping that number as low as possible.
In its proposal, DriveTN agreed to avoid the Pan-Asia Supermarket in southeast Nashville and Noble Place Townhomes, which have been points of contention, in addition to eliminating the need to rebuild the Hickory Hollow Parkway bridge.
State Rep. John Ray Clemmons, a Nashville Democrat, told the board constituents and business owners in his South Nashville district oppose the project because of its impact on homes and neighborhoods, especially when construction forces traffic to detour.
Clemmons called Lee’s initiative a “boondoggle” and said he hasn’t received any data from the state showing how the “toll” lanes will reduce traffic. He said Nashville residents want passenger rail and more public transit, not toll lanes for which motorists are paying $20 to $47 in other states.
“This is not modernization. This is wrong,” he said.
During a public hearing, Nashville resident Gerald Stankevich said he has seen the “tsunami coming in slow motion” because it could affect his house, yet he has received conflicting signals from the Department of Transportation. If he had known he was going to have to put up with road construction for nearly a decade, Stankevich said he wouldn’t have bought his house. He encouraged the state to consider using “inverse condemnation,” a process in which the property owner sues the state to seek a fair price for the value of the property, instead of eminent domain in which the state sues the property owner.
Smyrna resident Connie Casha, who drove the I-24 corridor to work in Nashville from 1994 to 2016 and suffered through two widening projects, said the state is looking at the problem incorrectly.
“We’re saying we don’t have enough roads. I’m saying we have too many cars. We need to be looking at alternative transportation issues,” Casha said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Tuskegee students question focus on dress code changes
description: TUSKEGEE — If there are dress code issues with students at Tuskegee University, they weren’t apparent on Wednesday.  The first day of class at the Historically Black University saw many students in a range of outfits, from full suits to streetwear. Others dressed more casually in t-shirts and sweatpants. But few if any seemed to […]
text:
A banner hangs across the main road through Tuskegee University welcoming new and returning students on Wednesday, August 19, 2026 in Tuskegee, Ala. Tuskegee students Wednesday questioned the focus on dress code changes made over the summer. (Estela Muñoz for Alabama Reflector)TUSKEGEE — If there are dress code issues with students at Tuskegee University, they weren’t apparent on Wednesday. 
The first day of class at the Historically Black University saw many students in a range of outfits, from full suits to streetwear. Others dressed more casually in t-shirts and sweatpants. But few if any seemed to be in violation of a new dress code imposed by university officials over the summer.
“Students are prohibited from wearing revealing clothing in class, to the cafeteria or in official settings like Convocation,” Tuskegee University President Mark A. Brown wrote in a letter to students over the summer.  “They are also not able to wear bedroom shoes, bonnets, or (do rag) to class or the cafeteria,” the statement said.
It’s unclear how the policy will be enforced. The statement from Brown said “faculty will be empowered to respond to students who are inappropriately dressed based on these guidelines.” 
A Tuskegee University student handbook for the 2025-26 school year also gave guidelines for student attire, but did not mention rules of enforcement or penalties for violating the dress code.
The university declined to comment on the new policy. The announcement of the dress code was the subject of debates on social media and sparked conversations about respectability politics on college campuses.
A range of opinions
A car drives past the Tuskegee University entrance on Wednesday, August 19, 2026 in Tuskegee, Ala. (Estela Muñoz for Alabama Reflector)
Tuskegee students on campus for their first day of class seemed to have a range of opinions about the new dress code.
Serenity Mitchell, a junior at Tuskegee majoring in biology, said the public manner of sharing the dress code painted students in a bad light.
“I think that releasing it in the way that they did made it look like students were kind of walking around here looking any type of way, and that’s just not true,” Mitchell said. “We as a student population represent ourselves well, so I think publishing the dress code like they did just makes us look bad.”
Mitchell also disagreed with the university imposing the same dress code on the school cafeteria.
“It’s essentially our kitchen. For most people who are living in a dorm, you don’t have anywhere else to eat,” she said. “It’s not an everyday, common occurrence to see people with bonnets or pajamas on. And if you do see them in the (cafeteria), it’s because it’s either super late at night for dinner or super early in the morning for breakfast.”
Serenity Mitchell, a junior studying biology, answers questions with the Alabama Reflector outside Tuskegee University on Wednesday, August 19, 2026 in Tuskegee, Ala. (Alabama Reflector Photo by Estela Muñoz)
Jamari Blackmon, a freshman biology major, said he did not wear the items prohibited under the policy. But he also felt that the focus on clothing was misplaced. 
“They should just let students be as free as they want as long as they get their education in my opinion,” he said.
Nailah Ashi-Sulaiman, a sophomore political science major and legacy student at Tuskegee, said the new dress code prevented students from expressing themselves through fashion and that students’ clothes have never been a large issue on campus.
“A lot of students are actually required to wear business casual attire for their majors. So it’s not like we’re going around here wearing anything,” Ashi-Sulaiman said. “For the most part, as long as I’ve been going here, I’ve always seen students dressed for success.”
Some students said they didn’t see a real issue with the dress code. Jamiyah Jones, a junior transfer student and basketball player at Tuskegee, said she understood why the dress code is needed.
“I think it’s a little strict definitely because we’re in college, but you really got to think about it when you look at this campus,“Jones said. “I’m not mad at the dean or the person that’s over the school to change the dress code, because I wouldn’t want the students attending my school in bonnets or do rags, or they walk in there with their slides on or it looks like they just got out of bed.”
Nathan Sullivan, a freshman mechanical engineering major, called the policy a “good rule.”
“Your presence is very important in the world we are in today, so coming up to class (in) your best dress is definitely a good thing,” he said.
Sullivan said he understands why there might be controversy around the dress code, but that “anywhere you go, you want to be presentable.”
Ashi-Sulaiman said she hopes the university listens to the opinions about the new policy.
“I just hope they’re taking everything into consideration and having open ears about everything,” she said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: ICE changes location of Tennessee call center site from Adams to Nashville
description: The location of a planned U.S. Department of Homeland Security national immigration enforcement call center has changed from Adams to Nashville, a federal contract database shows. Last week, the database showed ICE had awarded a $63 million contract to Alaska-based company Koniag Government Services, and listed Adams, a rural town of about 600 people near […[...]
text:
ICE wants to open a call center in Nashville, awarding a $63 million contract in August. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The location of a planned U.S. Department of Homeland Security national immigration enforcement call center has changed from Adams to Nashville, a federal contract database shows.
Last week, the database showed ICE had awarded a $63 million contract to Alaska-based company Koniag Government Services, and listed Adams, a rural town of about 600 people near the Kentucky border, as the location of the new facility.
But an update to USASpending.gov now lists the contract location as Nashville, with a ZIP code covering the Donelson neighborhood near the Nashville International Airport.
The planned call center is intended to function as a 24/7 support center for local law enforcement across the county who have entered into cooperative agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ICE.
Call center employees will “analyze data, perform database cross-checks and confirm enforcement actions in the field,” according to the contract documents.
A Koniag Services spokesperson previously told the Lookout it was “not at liberty to discuss” the contract details or the call center’s precise location. The company has over two dozen open positions listed online, with the Nashville area listed as the job location.
The Lookout reached out to ICE to ask whether the listed location on the contract was precise or meant the Nashville area in general. Adams is about 40 miles north of Nashville.
Local officials in the dark about contract naming Adams as ICE call center site 

ICE did not respond.
Andrea Fanta, a spokesperson for Nashville Mayor Freddie O’Connell, said they were still “still in the process of getting a consistent depiction of what is planned.”
ICE has previously tried to keep local officials in the dark about its project for fear of community backlash.
Earlier this year, ICE announced plans to build a detention center in Lebanon, then canceled the project after local officials and U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn asked it to reconsider.
The contract documents also show Koniag will be tasked with a wider range of duties beyond a call center. The facility will track and report the locations of unaccompanied minors and find new technologies that increase the effectiveness of ICE’s work with local police and sheriff departments.
The call center expands President Donald Trump’s administration’s coordination with local law enforcement agencies. Federal immigration agreements with local enforcement, called 287(g), aren’t new but have drastically increased in Trump’s second term, as he’s made the deportation of non-citizens a top priority.
Lisa Sherman Luna, executive director of the Tennessee Coalition for Immigrant & Refugee Rights, characterized the call center plans to the Lookout last week as “trying to set up shop in middle Tennessee to facilitate this terror on a massive scale.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘We have nowhere to go’:  WV handicap-accessible housing in short supply for low-income residents
description: Upshur and other regional counties already have a shortage of subsidized housing units that are accessible for seniors and those with disabilities, according to the 2025 Statewide Housing Needs Assessment by the West Virginia Housing Development Fund.
text:
Sarah and Ricky Mathes have been living in a leaky camper while they wait for accessible housing in Upshur County. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)ROCK CAVE, W.Va. — Sarah and Ricky Mathes waited out July’s deadly storms in the only home they know — a 30-foot camper off of a gravel road in the rural community of Rock Cave in Upshur County, West Virginia. 
The trailer has been deteriorating since they bought it used in 2022 to put a roof over their heads. They’ve covered the top in a blue tarp, a futile attempt to keep out water. The windows and doors don’t seal anymore. 
“Every time it rains, (Ricky) has to clean the carpet, run fans across the carpet,” Sarah Mathes said. “Our mattress has been soaked countless times, the pillows. Because it’s all starting to come in the seams of the cabinet.”
Sarah has multiple sclerosis and uses a wheelchair. She needs handicapped-accessible housing, which is in short supply in her community, she said. 
“We have nowhere to go,” she said. “There is no emergency housing or housing for a disabled person.”
The camper was only meant to be a temporary housing solution for the couple — a step up from couch surfing and sleeping in cars. But they’ve been on waiting lists for subsidized housing since 2020. 
Heather Schnieder, the co-founder and coordinator of Appalachian Mutual Aid Collective, an Upshur County nonprofit organization that works with those struggling with housing, said the Mathes’ story is not unique. 
“When someone has disabilities in the community and is also low income, it’s very hard, as you can see, nearly impossible to get into one of the handicap accessible units in the neighborhoods that are also supposed to be income accessible for people who don’t have a lot of money,” she said. 
Several of the public housing projects in the area have units, she said, but only a small percentage have handicapped accessible housing. Once people get into these units, they tend to stay there, she said. 
“That’s where they live out the rest of their life,” Schneider said. “And I understand that, because they’re people who are on fixed incomes and also need that type of accessible housing. Why would they move? So it’s very hard for anybody who is needing to get into those units to get in, and they have been on lists. Some of them up to six years.”
A blue tarp covers the top of the Matheses’ camper in rural Upshur County, West Virginia. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)
‘Accessible units are desperately needed’
More than 60,000 West Virginians rely on federal rental assistance, and a quarter of those using assistance have a disability, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. 
Upshur and other regional counties already have a shortage of subsidized housing units that are accessible for seniors and those with disabilities, according to the 2025 Statewide Housing Needs Assessment by the West Virginia Housing Development Fund.
West Virginia is projected to lose more than a quarter of its federally subsidized low-income rental units due to federal changes, according to the report. 
April Dotson, the executive director of the Buckhannon Upshur Housing Development Authority, said their agency oversees one property with 84 units, 29 of which are handicapped accessible. All of the accessible units are occupied, she said. 
According to The Kelsey, a national organization that builds and advocates for disability-forward housing, less than 6% of housing stock in the United States is accessible to those with sensory and mobility disabilities. With so few options available, the organization says those units should be matched with people who really need them, but that’s often not the case. 
“Accessible units are desperately needed,” the organization wrote in an undated report. “However, local, state and federal governments and the housing field have failed to create and implement systems that track, affirmatively market and match accessible units to tenants who need them.  
“Municipalities can strengthen existing policies and practices and build out new ones to ensure that the limited supply of accessible units, regardless of the funding source, is matched to tenants who need them,” they wrote.
Schnieder said July’s deadly storms and flooding only complicated and worsened living situations for some Upshur County clients she works with. One family was living in a camper that floated away during the flood. They were able to get the trailer back and are living in it again, she said. 
Schnieder said any housing that’s built in the future needs to be accessible for those with disabilities. 
“Right now I may be able-bodied, but as someone who has been a caregiver for multiple family members throughout their life, I know that at any given moment, something can change your life drastically,” she said. “My father had a series of strokes at the age of 54, and that’s only 10 years away from my age.”
“If we’re building housing, ADA compliant right from the beginning, and anyone in our community should be able to use it,” she said. 
As for Sarah and Ricky Mathes, she is filling out an application for assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. 
Mathes said being in the small space has added to the mobility problems caused by her disease. 
“I don’t have the room to get up and move around any,” she said. “I mean, I can’t even propel my own self in my wheelchair, because there’s no room.” 
And as hard as the summer storms have been, the couple is also dreading the upcoming winter. They typically spend hundreds of dollars to keep their propane tank filled because the hot air flows through the trailer. 
She said her living situation is wearing on her mental health. 
“I’m to the point where I’m mentally breaking,” she said. “It’s where I think about all this and wonder why people want to keep sweeping us under the rug?”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: The University of Tennessee’s new civics degree should treat citizenship as a practice
description: This fall, students at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, will be able to major in Civic and Constitutional Thought. Approved in July by the Tennessee Higher Education Commission and the UT Board of Trustees, the degree is the first academic degree program offered through UT’s Institute of American Civics. Tennessee deserves credit for treating civic […[...]
text:
The University of Tennessee is offering a new major in Fall Semester 2026 on Civic and Constitutional Thought. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)This fall, students at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, will be able to major in Civic and Constitutional Thought. Approved in July by the Tennessee Higher Education Commission and the UT Board of Trustees, the degree is the first academic degree program offered through UT’s Institute of American Civics.
Tennessee deserves credit for treating civic education as worthy of sustained undergraduate study. Public life increasingly demands citizens who understand the institutions they will inherit, the forces shaping political judgment and the obligations citizenship places upon them.
UT has built a promising foundation. The curriculum includes American political thought, constitutionalism, governing institutions, political philosophy, political economy and American political development. Students may study democratic policymaking, public leadership, constitutional interpretation, law and civic thought. Each student must also complete a professional-development practicum through an internship, local-government fellowship, faculty research or career preparation.
The question now is what kind of citizen the program will produce.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
A student can read the Federalist Papers and still struggle to explain which level of government controls a local school policy. Someone can debate constitutional interpretation while lacking the tools to evaluate a misleading political claim online. A graduate can speak eloquently about democracy yet remain unprepared to work with neighbors who hold different values or to turn a community concern into effective public action.
Civic knowledge matters most when people can use it.
As a civic education researcher developing a Citizenship Empowerment Framework for higher education, I have organized that capacity around four connected pillars: foundational knowledge, media and information literacy, “Courageous Dialogue” and civic action. UT’s degree already contains elements of each. Its success will depend on how intentionally they are connected and practiced.
First, graduates should understand where governmental power resides. They should be able to distinguish federal, state and local authority, explain how public institutions interact and identify the officials or agencies responsible for particular problems. Knowing the Constitution remains essential. So does knowing whom to contact when a road is unsafe, a school policy changes or a state agency fails to deliver a service.
Second, constitutional education now requires media and information literacy. Citizens encounter public life through news organizations, social platforms, search engines, political campaigns and artificial intelligence. Students should learn to examine sources, distinguish evidence from assertion, recognize manipulated or synthetic content and understand how information systems shape political judgment. Modern civic competence joins knowledge of government with the ability to navigate the information environment surrounding it.
Third, the degree should make serious disagreement a learned civic skill. UT says the program will prepare students to reason carefully, communicate persuasively and “disagree civilly.” Civil disagreement begins with politeness and demands much more. Students should practice identifying the strongest version of an opposing argument, asking honest questions, defending principles with evidence and recognizing when compromise is possible and when conscience requires dissent. A constitutional system depends on people who can share institutions while taking their differences seriously.
Finally, students should translate learning into civic action beyond elections. Voting is indispensable, and citizenship also includes attending public meetings, serving in community organizations, conducting research for public use, communicating with officials, building coalitions and helping institutions solve problems. UT’s practicum and local-government opportunities provide an excellent beginning. Every graduate should leave with evidence that they have applied civic knowledge to a real institutional or community challenge.
This approach would strengthen the degree UT has created. The program already aspires to thoughtful citizenship, civil discourse and responsible public leadership. Connecting those ambitions to measurable civic capacities offers a clear test: Can graduates understand institutions, evaluate information, deliberate across difference and act constructively?
Tennessee has taken an important step by declaring civic education worthy of an undergraduate degree. It now has an opportunity to offer the country a model of constitutional education that is intellectually rigorous, politically pluralistic and closely connected to practice.
The American experiment needs citizens who can interpret its founding principles. It also needs citizens prepared to carry them into public life.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Lawmakers want public involved as they pursue nuclear power industry
description: North Dakota lawmakers are looking for ways to engage communities across the state to gauge interest in hosting a future nuclear power plant.  No facilities have been proposed, nor has a site been selected. But members of an interim committee studying the feasibility of advanced nuclear energy said having early conversations with local communities could […]
text:
Sen. Dale Patten, R-Watford City, and Rep. Dick Anderson, R-Willow City, listen to a colleague during a meeting of the Advanced Nuclear Energy Committee on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota lawmakers are looking for ways to engage communities across the state to gauge interest in hosting a future nuclear power plant. 
No facilities have been proposed, nor has a site been selected. But members of an interim committee studying the feasibility of advanced nuclear energy said having early conversations with local communities could prepare the ground for future development. 
“Without that success, I don’t think there’s a path forward,” said Sen. Dale Patten, R-Watford City, chair of the committee. 
North Dakota lawmakers to consider exception to nuclear waste storage ban

The Advanced Nuclear Energy Committee completed its work Wednesday but does not plan to sponsor legislation for the 2027 session. Committee members can introduce proposals on their own. 
Patten said he plans to sponsor two bills, including a proposal related to the state’s ban on storing high-level radioactive waste. Patten plans to introduce an exception that would allow temporary on-site radioactive waste storage for nuclear power plants. A draft of the bill was not available Wednesday.
In addition, Patten said he plans to propose combining the interim committee with the High-Level Radioactive Waste Advisory Council to continue evaluating the feasibility of nuclear power. 
Experts testifying in front of the committee emphasized the need for a bottom-up approach to determine which communities are open to nuclear power plants and to better educate the public on the industry, instead of a top-down directive from a company or government. 
Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, said he plans to work with Patten on the bill to ensure the information gathered by the interim committee is presented to communities across the state. He wants to avoid an inflamed public debate down the road because the public was left in the dark.
“We should direct an entity to either go to every county or eight regions of our state to hold some sort of meeting,” Mathern said. 
Ian Gilley, a farmer from Sheyenne who used to be a nuclear engineer in the U.S. Navy and has a master’s degree in the subject, urged lawmakers to continue their pursuit of nuclear power in the state. 
“You can guarantee North Dakota reliable electricity for the next 100 years, and the community that you pick will be the most prosperous county in the state of North Dakota for the next 100 years,” Gilley said during the public comment period of the meeting. “These are incredible jobs and incredible economic powerhouses.”
What other states have done
Wyoming is a state that has already gone through much of this process. TerraPower, a company backed by Bill Gates, broke ground on the construction of a small modular reactor in the state earlier this year. 
Wyoming State Sen. Cale Case said his state’s citizens have generally been supportive of nuclear energy. 
Missouri River is best source of water for nuclear energy in North Dakota, regulator says

“We view this as really protecting our future as an electricity exporter,” Case told North Dakota lawmakers. 
TerraPower selected a site in Kemmerer after four communities had expressed interest in hosting the project, Wyoming Energy Futures CEO Rita Meyer, who has been involved in TerraPower’s community engagement process, told lawmakers. 
“It needs to be good for the community,” Meyer said. 
She said the biggest obstacles for the project have been the broken supply chain, such as obtaining nuclear fuel, and the lack of education on nuclear energy in recent decades. 
Some states are working to change that through community engagement programs. Chase Blaeser, an analyst with Envoy Public Labs, said eight states have taken the lead: Wyoming, New York, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Nebraska, Connecticut and Utah. 
Utah’s effort is the most robust. Austin Blanch, Envoy Public Labs’ chief operating officer, said the state has committed to hosting at least one public engagement event in every county and has been advertising on billboards, radio and other forms of media.
“Utah has the first statewide nuclear energy education program of its kind in the country,” he said. “There’s a lot of partnership happening with chambers of commerce, economic development authorities, local elected officials, to get into the community and meet folks where they’re at.”
Nuclear education options
North Dakota State University is anticipating a growing demand for nuclear engineers, and is launching a new certificate program this fall to meet student demand. 
Alan Kallmeyer, dean of NDSU’s College of Engineering, said the certificate program will focus on producing the nuclear engineers that companies like Xcel Energy, which operates nuclear power plants in Minnesota, are wanting to employ.
He said 23 students are enrolled in the first class despite its late addition to the semester, showing clear interest among engineering students.
Kallmeyer said a long-term goal is to add a second certificate program. The college is also exploring a three-year bachelor of applied science degree to produce future nuclear technicians.
Alicia Uhde, vice president of academic affairs at Bismarck State College, answers a question from Senate Majority Leader David Hogue, R-Minot, during a meeting of the Advanced Nuclear Energy Committee on August 19, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Bismarck State College has an existing online associate degree program focused on training future nuclear technicians. Alicia Uhde, vice president for academic affairs, said the program emphasizes applied learning with a nuclear plant simulator.
“It’s an actual pressurized water reactor environment, and we are teaching our students how to start up, shutdown and to normally operate a nuclear plant,” Uhde said. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: With Idaho’s history, everyone should pay attention to evolving language of institutionalization
description: People with disabilities are hearing the words ‘institutionalization’ and ‘Olmstead’ daily. This shift in the way policymakers openly discuss the segregation of people with disabilities naturally follows nationwide budget cuts to home and community-based services. If people with disabilities cannot get the services and supports they need to live independentl[...]
text:
Members of the Idaho Legislature's Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee and their staff tour Southwest Idaho Treatment Center, or SWITC, in Nampa on Nov. 20, 2024. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)People with disabilities are hearing the words ‘institutionalization’ and ‘Olmstead’ daily. This shift in the way policymakers openly discuss the segregation of people with disabilities naturally follows nationwide budget cuts to home and community-based services. 
If people with disabilities cannot get the services and supports they need to live independently in their homes and communities, where are they to go?
As an Idaho historian and a person with a disability, it is clear to me that whether or not you or a member of your family has personally experienced disability, whether or not you have a friend or colleague who is disabled, or you work in the field of direct care for people with disabilities, everyone should be paying attention to the evolving language of institutionalization. 
Idaho has a long history with institutionalization and a shift back to overreliance on this practice by either federal or state policymakers presents the same constitutional and moral danger.
As federal protections fade, Americans with disabilities fear a return to institutions

Idaho statehood and the institutionalization of people with disabilities were entwined. The state of Idaho wasted no time getting into the business of institutionalizing people with disabilities whether those disabilities were intellectual or developmental, mental illness, verbal or non-verbal, in adults or adolescents. People with physical disabilities were not always immune from the practice. 
The question of whether these Idahoans were better suited for living independently in their communities with appropriate supports wouldn’t be asked for nearly a century. 
The Idaho Insane Asylum, the original name for what is now State Hospital South, was established in 1886, four years prior to Idaho statehood. It had an original capacity of 300 beds. In 1889 at the state constitutional convention, language was included to formally establish the hospital in Blackfoot. 
Idaho’s founders decided that institutionalizing people with disabilities was the only way to deal with the scourge of difference. Families were encouraged to lock away their family members with disabilities, and many did exactly that.
As the state grew, so did its institutions. The Northern Idaho Sanitarium at Orofino, now State Hospital North, would follow in 1905 with a 250-bed capacity. The Idaho Sanitarium for the Feeble-minded and Epileptic came in 1911 with an original capacity of 250 beds primarily for adolescent “inmates,” a term that was used for far too long in referring to Idahoans with disabilities residing in our state hospitals. It has had an array of names including the State School and Colony for the Feeble-minded, Idaho State School and Hospital and now the Southwestern Idaho Treatment Center. 
As slippery slope arguments go, the day the state opened these institutions was a slippery slope toward an expensive and morally dubious enterprise. While the state’s population grew, the population of these hospitals exploded. 
In the 1930s to 1950s, the population to capacity issue abounded at each of the hospitals. By 1955, 1,221 Idahoans were institutionalized by the state in hospitals rife with overcrowding, abuse, neglect and doctor to patient ratios that are horrifying by today’s standards. In 1970, a report found the adolescent residents of the Idaho State School and Hospital to be living in substandard conditions.
It was the independent living movement that forced the question of whether institutionalization was constitutional and if it was the best way to care for people with disabilities who had been locked away from society since the 19th century. 
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 required that people with disabilities be included in any program that receives federal funding. The Americans with Disabilities Act, signed into law in 1990, prohibited discrimination based on disability, similar to how prior civil rights legislation prevented discrimination based on race, religion and sex. 
Then came a 1999 ruling by the United States Supreme Court in Olmstead v. L.C.
The court in Olmstead decided that under the ADA, people with disabilities have a right to receive government supports and services in their homes and communities utilizing a three-part test. That test asks that a healthcare provider determine that home and community placement is appropriate for the individual, that the individual is not opposed to living in their home and community, and the placement is a reasonable accommodation. 
Of the third part of the test, it can be said unequivocally that placement in one’s home and community is more economical than permanent institutionalization in a specialized hospital run by the states. 
A state institution is not the same as assisted living or a nursing home. It is beyond skilled nursing. Institutionalization is all-encompassing. Every way a person requires support in their physical, mental and behavioral health must be accessible within the halls of that institution. 
In June, the U.S. Department of Justice released a slip opinion — a legal memorandum for the Counsel of the President — on the application of the Rehabilitation Act and Americans with Disabilities Act in the states. 
In that opinion, the DOJ submitted that neither Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act nor the ADA “imposed an integration mandate on the states in their treatment of mentally disabled individuals. Nor does either statute authorize the responsible Executive Branch agencies to impose such a mandate.” It goes on to say more plainly that Olmstead did not hold that the Rehab Act or the ADA “require states to treat mentally disabled patients in the most integrated setting appropriate to their needs.”
The instruction they are offering the White House is that the Supreme Court’s interpretation of the laws that have preserved the rights of people with disabilities to live in their homes and communities for nearly three decades is incorrect and the federal government no longer needs to abide by the previous flawed interpretation.
The current number of Idahoans receiving home and community-based services is 33,000. In the years since deinstitutionalization, a process of getting people out of hospitals and into homes and communities triggered by good advocacy and the Rehab Act, not only have the numbers decreased dramatically in our state hospitals, the number of beds available in those facilities shrank. 
If Idaho policymakers were to resume the practice of segregating people with disabilities, where would these Idahoans go? The state hospitals are no longer structured in a way to support this. 
The cost to Idaho taxpayers would be exorbitant. This would tax the Department of Health and Welfare. The facilities would be costly. The price to staff expanded facilities in a field with high turnover would be huge. 
These costs would be a pittance compared to the human costs. The mental and emotional cost to people with disabilities being ripped away from their communities, homes and families cannot be overstated. Families would be forced to travel to one of three locations in the state to see their family members. 
Every Idahoan with a disability, with a family member with a disability, with a business that employs people with disabilities, with an organization that utilizes volunteers with disabilities, or pays taxes would be impacted by this state choosing to follow the DOJ’s interpretation of Olmstead. 
In 2025, Idaho was found to be in violation of section II of the Americans with Disabilities Act for unnecessarily segregating people with disabilities to nursing homes. Is it advisable for this state to expand that violation to include the Rehab Act and the Supreme Court’s ruling in Olmstead? And at what cost?
If the legal implications aren’t reason enough to avoid the segregation of people with disabilities, consider the risk of abuse, neglect and death. Is there a line policymakers are willing to walk up to and not cross when it comes to the denial of civil rights? 
The abuse and neglect rampant in the first half of the 20th century in Idaho’s institutions did not go away with deinstitutionalization. An investigation of the state hospital in Nampa, SWITC, from 2017-2023 revealed systemic safety, abuse and neglect issues with danger to residents and staff. 
We are not as far removed from these practices as we would like to believe.
And still, if policymakers can’t find it in themselves to act based on these legal, moral and ethical considerations, they must consider the cost. If there is a policymaker concerned about the cost of home and community-based services whose answer is to put the consumers of such services in state institutions, they are not a serious thinker. The slippery slope of institutionalization will explode the budget.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Proposed changes to Head Start program could affect Alabama
description: Changes to the federal Head Start program could have major impacts across Alabama.   Earlier this month, the Department of Health and Human Services announced a proposal to revamp the Head Start program.  The HHS said the new rule, known as the Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs, would return power to the states to […]
text:
A group of children playing in a classroom. Earlier this month, the Department of Health and Human Services announced proposed changes to the federal Head Start Program. (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent)Changes to the federal Head Start program could have major impacts across Alabama.  
Earlier this month, the Department of Health and Human Services announced a proposal to revamp the Head Start program. 
The HHS said the new rule, known as the Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs, would return power to the states to allow them to fit the program to local needs, reduce administrative costs and increase access to the program.
Head Start is a federally funded program started in 1965 that allows three and four year olds from low-income backgrounds to prepare for school.
According to the National Institute for Early Education Research’s State of Preschool 2025 report, during the 2024-25 school year Alabama had 4,100 four-year-olds and 3,900 three-year-olds enrolled in Head Start. If the program loses funding, three-year-olds in the state could be left without early childhood education programs.
Amanda Stanford, director of communications and governmental relations for the Alabama Department of Early Childhood Education, said in a statement last week that the department is reviewing the proposal.
“Alabama has long prioritized research-based standards for quality across our early childhood programs,” she said. “As we review the proposed changes, we will look particularly closely at areas connected to the quality standards we know matter for children—including strong learning environments, qualified and supported educators, appropriate class sizes and teacher-child ratios, developmental screening and assessment, and systems for continuous quality improvement.”
Steven Barnett, founder and director of NIEER, located at Rutgers University in New Jersey, said in an interview last week he found the proposal to be confusing.
“If you really wanted to align with states, why wouldn’t you ask Alabama or Mississippi what they want?” he asked.
The HHS statement said the proposal “restores flexibility to programs to meet local needs, reduces regulatory burden and administrative costs, and aims to increase available slots and services for families.” 
Barnett said this proposal will make the program weaker.
“What Head Start’s guiding star was it was part of the War on Poverty, and it was to break the cycle of poverty,” Barnett said. “This is just like saying, nope, we’re just going to surrender in the war on poverty and give up because none of this moves in the right direction to make that happen.”
Tracye Strichik, executive director for VOICES of Alabama’s Children, said in a statement Tuesday evening the flexibility could give Alabama the opportunity to “respond to the unique needs of their communities and to make decisions about staffing and resources that support access and sustainability.”
“Research tells us that quality is driven by what children experience every day—a safe and language-rich environment, warm and responsive relationships, and meaningful interactions with skilled adults,” Strichik said. “Greater flexibility can give local Head Start leaders more ability to determine how best to deliver those experiences while remaining accountable for strong outcomes for children.”
Barnett said by forcing Head Start to align with state standards, it could increase the number of students in each classroom from 10 students to 18 students and if costs are cut for Head Start, it could leave the state to pick up the remaining funds.
“And if what this means is that the federal government’s only going to pay for a classroom that’s almost as big which you can translate that into almost half as much money. Then is Alabama going to have to make up the difference?” he asked. “So the choice in Alabama is now Alabama has to spend a lot more money to raise Head Start up to the state standards for Pre-K, or those kids are not going to do well, and Alabama’s going to pay the cost for that when it has to catch them up in kindergarten, first, second grade (and) when they’re drop out of school and are less productive. Alabama could be paying the cost of this for decades.”
Earlier this year, NIEER praised the quality of Alabama’s Pre-K program for the 20th consecutive year making it the longest-running state to meet all 10 of NIEER’s research-based quality standards. Barnett did not say if the state’s ranking would be affected if the proposal is approved.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky hospitals are helping turn the tide on the opioid crisis
description: When a Kentucky woman called an emergency department earlier this year, she wasn’t asking whether treatment was available. Through tears, she was asking whether anyone would judge her for needing it. She had been referred to the hospital for help managing opioid withdrawal but was afraid to walk through the doors. A peer support specialist […]
text:
Access to naloxone, or Narcan, has helped decrease overdose deaths in Kentucky. Naloxone, shown in this photo at the Louisville jail, reverses overdose effects. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)When a Kentucky woman called an emergency department earlier this year, she wasn’t asking whether treatment was available. Through tears, she was asking whether anyone would judge her for needing it.
She had been referred to the hospital for help managing opioid withdrawal but was afraid to walk through the doors. A peer support specialist assured her that asking for help wasn’t something to be ashamed of — it was one of the bravest things she could do. She came. She received treatment. And today, she remains in recovery.
Stories like hers help explain why Kentucky has seen overdose deaths decline for the fourth consecutive year. In 2025 alone, fatalities fell nearly 23 percent — a remarkable achievement that reflects years of determined work across the commonwealth. Thousands of families have been spared unimaginable loss because of it.
Success can create a dangerous temptation to believe the crisis has passed. It hasn’t. In 2025, 1,110 Kentuckians still lost their lives to drug overdoses. The decline in overdose deaths didn’t happen by chance. It reflects years of investment in prevention, treatment, recovery support and evidence-based opioid stewardship. The latest numbers should give us hope, but they should also reinforce a simple truth: the strategies that are working must be sustained, strengthened and expanded. 
Kentucky hospitals are a vital part of that work. Every day, hospitals care for patients affected by substance use disorder, acute and chronic pain, behavioral health needs and complex medical conditions. They also have an important opportunity to prevent opioid-related harm before it begins by improving prescribing practices, supporting safer pain management and connecting patients to treatment and recovery resources when they need help most.
One of the ways hospitals are putting those principles into practice is through the Kentucky Statewide Opioid Stewardship program (KYSOS), a partnership between the Kentucky Hospital Association and the Cabinet for Health and Family Services through the Kentucky Opioid Response Effort. 
KYSOS helps hospitals and health systems reduce opioid overprescribing, improve safe opioid use when opioids are warranted and demonstrate their commitment to patients and communities. The program supports hospitals where this work happens every day — inpatient units, hospital-owned outpatient primary care clinics and emergency departments. One key component is its Emergency Department Bridge Program, which helps connect patients with opioid use disorder to treatment when they need it most. 
For someone experiencing opioid use disorder, an emergency department visit may be the first — and sometimes only — opportunity to begin recovery. KYSOS’ Emergency Department Bridge Program helps ensure that opportunity isn’t missed. Patients are connected with Peer Support Specialists while they’re still in the hospital, giving them immediate guidance and a direct path to treatment and community resources.
Each interaction between a peer support specialist and a patient with substance use disorder is considered a “peer support touch.” This includes recovery or peer coaching from a peer support specialist, any intervention by a peer support specialist to help link or refer to treatment, referrals to other services like transportation and food, and providing harm reduction education such as offering naloxone in hand to patients. These meaningful interactions have totaled more than 2,000 “peer support touches” so far in 2026 across the state’s 17 Bridge Programs.
KYSOS also reflects what Kentucky’s overdose data makes clear: no single program, agency or profession can solve this crisis alone. This progress depends on collaboration among hospitals, clinicians, pharmacists, peer support specialists, behavioral health providers, public health leaders, law enforcement, policymakers, community organizations, patients and families. The decline in overdose deaths is a testament to that shared commitment.
Hospital opioid stewardship isn’t about denying appropriate pain relief. It’s about treating pain safely, prescribing responsibly and recognizing opioid use disorder early so patients receive compassionate, evidence-based care instead of falling through the cracks. Prevention, treatment and recovery aren’t competing priorities — they’re part of the same continuum of care.
The recent decline in overdose deaths should encourage every Kentuckian, but it should also sharpen our resolve. Kentucky hospitals, through programs like KYSOS, are helping turn that resolve into practical, measurable action every day.
The encouraging decline in overdose deaths proves something important: this crisis is not inevitable. When hospitals, public health leaders, first responders, policymakers and community organizations work together, lives are saved. Kentucky has shown what’s possible. Now we have a responsibility to keep that progress moving forward.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: November glut of school referendums signals necessity of taxing option in Virginia
description: A 2021 tour of the construction of the new Highland Springs High School in Henrico, which was estimated to cost about $80 million. (Photo courtesy of Henrico County Public Schools)
text:
A 2021 tour of the construction of the new Highland Springs High School in Henrico, estimated to cost about $80 million. (Photo courtesy of Henrico County Public Schools)If you wondered whether localities across Virginia desperately need another way to raise money to build new schools, take a look at the dozens of communities that will hold voter referendums in November. 
Cardinal News recently reported that more than 40 localities plan referendums this fall seeking a 1% sales tax increase for school construction and major renovations. Many of those school divisions are small and rural. Some are urban like Norfolk, Portsmouth and Newport News.
This is a Dillon Rule state, and some local taxes can’t be increased without the General Assembly’s blessing. Former Gov. Glenn Youngkin repeatedly vetoed similar sales tax legislation that reached his desk – his eyes more focused on his political future than fixing the state’s crumbling school buildings.
When current Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed the state budget this year, the tax increase clause – including a voter referendum – was part of the deal. The rest of the state will now enjoy an option that only nine localities previously had access to.
State lawmakers and education officials knew for years that school infrastructure statewide needed help. In 2021, the General Assembly’s own Commission on School Construction and Modernization placed the tab for new construction and major repairs at $25 billion for public K-12 buildings at least a half-century old. More than 1,000 Virginia public schools fit that category.
Recent news stories have noted the dire conditions and desired overhauls: HVAC and boiler upgrades in Franklin County. A layout design that isn’t as safe as it should be and an expensive roof replacement in Pulaski County. Broken pipes and busted air conditioning units in Newport News.
Money from the sales tax increase would put a dent in the bills for repairs and school-building.
In Norfolk, for example, “The City is estimating the additional annual revenue to be $40 million,” Kelly Straub, a city spokesperson, told me by email. The tax in Norfolk would expire in 2046.
It shouldn’t have taken so many years to give all localities this taxing tool. It would be no surprise if voters in many communities passed their referendums on Nov. 3.

title: USDA advances Roadless Rule repeal; advocates, lawmakers say it puts 400,000 acres in Va. at risk
description: The United States Department of Agriculture is nearing a full repeal of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule that protects millions of acres of virgin forestland nationwide. In Virginia, if the rule is repealed it would open up an estimated 400,000 acres of forest, largely across the Shenandoah Valley region, to development.  The Trump Administration […]
text:
A forest in Highland County during a prescribed burn by the Virginia Department of Forestry in 2021. (Photo by Sarah Vogelsong/Virginia Mercury) The United States Department of Agriculture is nearing a full repeal of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule that protects millions of acres of virgin forestland nationwide. In Virginia, if the rule is repealed it would open up an estimated 400,000 acres of forest, largely across the Shenandoah Valley region, to development. 
The Trump Administration has touted the move as a way to expand wildfire management and economic development to public lands.
“We filed a proposal to restore authority to local forest managers who know the land best, removing the barriers that have kept them from doing the work the land demands,” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement on Tuesday.
The rule was created decades ago as a way to protect the least-developed portions of the National Forest System and aid in preserving wildlife, clean drinking water, recreation and old-growth forests. 
While wildfire management is necessary, groups like the Southern Environmental Law Center said there are already fire mitigation rules under the Roadless Rule that provide that guidance. 
Kristin Gendzier with the SELC also said that federal budget cuts to the U.S. Forest Service and reorganization of the agency contradict the administration’s stated goal of bolstering wildfire fighting capabilities.
“They’re ignoring the reality that more roads lead to more fires. Their own reports show that. They are glossing over their ability to put out fires and also to address fire risks that they already have under the roadless rule,” Gendzier said.
Groups like the SELC are concerned that increased development in these will lead to degradation of the natural environment and impact the watersheds that millions of people rely on for clean drinking water.
Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Virginia, has been a staunch supporter of the rule. He has sponsored legislation in the past attempting to codify the Roadless Rule protection into law, but the measures failed.
“I strongly oppose the Trump-Vance Administration’s rollback of this rule, which would open the door to more development and increased logging in our national forests,” Kaine said in a statement Wednesday. “I’ll keep working to protect our roadless areas, which support outdoor recreation, tourism, and local economic growth in communities across the country.”
Hundreds of thousands of comments flooded in during the first public comment period for the proposed rule change last fall. Citizens now have a final chance to weigh in with their support or opposition of the repeal of the 25-year-old rule, with the current public comment period ending Sept. 21.
Once the period ends, the USDA will have the authority to repeal the rule.
