name: Georgia Recorder
title: Would Gov. Brian Kemp really shut down his Pathways Medicaid program?
description: Patient advocates reacted with alarm this week at the suggestion by the administration of Gov. Brian Kemp that it could end Georgia Pathways to Coverage, his signature Medicaid program that gives health coverage to about 18,500 poor Georgians.  Precious Andrews, an advocate who works for mothers’ and children’s health, said she was in shock when […]
text:
Gov. Brian Kemp, who is serving his last year in office, speaks at 2026 Eggs and Issues. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderPatient advocates reacted with alarm this week at the suggestion by the administration of Gov. Brian Kemp that it could end Georgia Pathways to Coverage, his signature Medicaid program that gives health coverage to about 18,500 poor Georgians. 
Precious Andrews, an advocate who works for mothers’ and children’s health, said she was in shock when she saw the news. 
“I was like, this is totally insane,” she said in an interview with the Georgia Recorder.
Gov. Brian Kemp answers questions from reporters at the state Capitol after unveiling his proposed Medicaid waiver plan in 2019. The program has become his signature healthcare policy. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
The state Department of Community Health said in documents filed last week that unless the federal government increases its financial support of Georgia’s partial Medicaid expansion, the program is “unsustainable.” The feds currently provide two-thirds of the cost to cover those 18,500 low-income people, the same amount it provides for the state’s general 2 million-plus Medicaid population, old and young. But Georgia wants a special increase to 90% federal support. Washington has previously said Georgia doesn’t qualify.
Georgia officials say that quirks in a new federal law change things. They say the law will increase the Pathways program’s patient load not just with more patients, but with patients who are more expensive to care for – too expensive, they argue, for the state’s budget.
“The financial burden of this federally-mandated coverage expansion is simply not sustainable for Georgia in the long run,” the state wrote in its application.  
A spokesman for Kemp, Carter Chapman, said Wednesday that the governor still “fully supports DCH’s efforts to ensure Georgia Pathways remains a national model for other states while maintaining the integrity of the first-of-its-kind program.” 
“While we cannot speculate on potential outcomes at this time with discussions ongoing” with the feds, Chapman said, “the governor is committed, as he always has been, to ensuring Georgians have access to quality healthcare while maintaining fiscal discipline for the state.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Federal changes would grow Georgia’s partial expansion program
The uproar is a result of the passage last year of President Donald Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. That law made massive cuts to Medicaid nationwide and in Georgia. One nationwide cut was made by adding new eligibility requirements for Medicaid enrollment for the 40 states that expanded Medicaid to all their poor. Anyone who doesn’t work or perform certain activities will be kicked off. 
However, for Georgia, which already did a partial expansion with its own requirements, those new requirements are more lenient. That specific rule is not a cut for Georgia, but a loosening of the rules. 
In one example, as a partial Medicaid expansion to the poor, Georgia now will be required to offer coverage to low-income parents who care for children as old as 13. Currently, Pathways covers those parents for kids up to age six.
The Kemp administration calculated that enrollment for the partial expansion group would increase by about 100,000, to a total of nearly 120,000 over 18 months. That’s not much more than the Kemp administration forecasted when it first launched the program. But Kemp aides say they’ll cost more per patient.
A spokeswoman for the department said the patients mandated for inclusion in the new federal law include more patients in expensive programs like active addiction recovery and the medically frail.
Is Pathways legally eligible for more federal funding? 
Allowing Pathways to expire on schedule at the end of the year would be a major development politically, putting an end to the foremost initiative of Kemp’s first year as governor and his policy response to the singular issue in his campaign to beat Stacey Abrams: dealing with Georgia’s uninsured poor.
Kemp created Pathways in a new law in 2019, the Patients First Act. Among other initiatives, it lifted the state’s ban on partial Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act, and created work and activity requirements for newly eligible Medicaid members. Such requirements had previously been banned in other states, but they were not banned under the new ideas of President Donald Trump and recent court decisions.
The first Trump administration partnered closely with Kemp to develop the programs and make them work. Trump’s administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, Seema Verma, in 2020 flew down to Atlanta to announce her approval in a celebratory ceremony beside Kemp at the Georgia Capitol. She said no one had done more to make use of the administration’s new flexibilities, and shook the governor’s hand as cameras flashed.
Then-Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Seema Verma traveled to Georgia in late 2020 to announce federal approval of the governor’s scaled-down version of Medicaid expansion. John McCosh/Georgia Recorder (2020 file photo)
Under the ACA, if Georgia had expanded Medicaid to all of its poor, it would already get that 90% from the feds for those patients. But federal law says that states that only do partial expansion don’t get the special rate. 
However, Georgia is making the case that Trump’s tax cut and spending law makes Georgia more like those other states even though it didn’t fully expand Medicaid. And they claim the federal law has created a dire situation for the state budget.
Joan Alker, executive director of Georgetown University’s Center for Children and Families, said that giving Georgia the extra federal money that goes to full expansion states when Georgia has not done full expansion simply wouldn’t comply with the law. Full expansion under the law means giving Medicaid to everyone under 138% of the federal poverty level, or about $22,025 for a single adult. Georgia only gives it to those under 100% of the federal poverty level.
But, she says, maybe the Trump administration could surprise everyone with its take on the law.
“From a legal perspective, waiving the match like this would be a bridge really, really far … The lawyers know that,” Alker said. “I expect them to turn it down. But who knows?”
State Senate Appropriations Chairman Blake Tillery, a Vidalia Republican who introduced the Patients First Act for Kemp in 2019, said he’s not surprised at the situation.
Sen. Blake Tillery, a Vidalia Republican, presents a budget proposal during the 2026 session. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
“I think that’s consistent (with) what you’ve been hearing from the Governor and Legislature since Nathan Deal,” Tillery said in a text message. Deal as governor rejected full Medicaid expansion when it was first created as an option by President Barack Obama under the Affordable Care Act. 
“Our two biggest expenses are education and Medicaid,” said Tillery, who was a floor leader for Kemp. “Our two largest annual increases are also generally education and Medicaid.  Georgians have been clear how they feel about the government – state and local – taking more of their money. The trend on these increases is unsustainable, much less with a change dictating more state funds.”
‘So what happens to those 18,000?’
Advocates for patients who raised the alarm about the Pathways announcement made clear that they still would prefer the state to do a full Medicaid expansion as laid out under the original Obamacare law. 
Andrews, who is director of special projects and innovations at Healthy Mothers, Healthy Babies Coalition of Georgia, spoke at a public hearing on the issue Wednesday. Speaking later with a reporter from her personal perspective, she said, “So what happens to those 18,000? Are we now living in a society where – you have to basically sacrifice a certain number in order for a certain number to survive?”
Georgians for a Healthy Future has advocated for full Medicaid expansion and released a written statement.
“More than 18,000 Georgians could lose the only health coverage available to them, not because of anything they did, but because state leaders are using their coverage as leverage in a funding dispute with Washington,” Laura Colbert, the group’s executive director, said in the statement. “Whatever happens with this request, Georgia should not be threatening to take health coverage away from the people who depend on it.”
Laura Colbert, executive director of Georgians for a Healthy Future, answers questions during a hearing on a Medicaid expansion proposal in 2024. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
Before new restrictions in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act, fully expanding Medicaid under the ACA would have given every low-income Georgian Medicaid. Estimates have varied over the years but it might have provided insurance to 200,000 uninsured Georgians. The new federal law passed last summer will lessen that number and experts aren’t sure yet by how much.
The 18,500 current Pathways enrollment figure comes from state records obtained by the Georgia Budget and Policy Institute.
The Georgia Hospital Association, which represents powerhouse health systems as well as teetering rural hospitals, didn’t comment on the claims that the state’s Pathways program is no longer sustainable. It supports the request for more federal money, though. 
“GHA supports affordable coverage options for Georgians and continues to support efforts by DCH and the state to expand those coverage opportunities in a cost-effective manner,” Anna Adams, the association’s chief government relations officer, said in an email.
Laurisa Barthen, executive director of the Georgia Council for Recovery, said people grappling with addiction recovery and mental health problems need health insurance to climb out. 
“Ending Pathways is not a feasible solution if the 90% match is denied,” Barthen said during Wednesday’s public hearing. “More than 18,000 Georgians currently rely on this coverage, and many more could potentially gain coverage under the new eligibility framework. So Georgia should be working towards reducing the need for preventable crisis services by expanding healthcare coverage, not creating the possibility that thousands of our friends and neighbors will lose it.”
Alker said that if the request is denied, it would mark the end of Kemp’s signature Medicaid program, which has carried huge administrative costs compared to its low enrollment. (Kemp has long argued that Pathways has been a major success because it left hundreds of thousands of Georgians free to choose not Medicaid but private Affordable Care Act plans.)
Legally, canceling the program would not be hard. It’s officially a pilot program set to expire at the end of 2026 unless Georgia and Washington agree to renew it.
“He very well understands the twists and turns behind this, and that this has been turned down before,” Alker said. “So, is this a face-saving way out? They get turned down, and then they can say, ‘Oh, we couldn’t do it,’ – rather than having to admit failure?
“That’s one possibility,” she said. “We’ll just have to see.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohioans criticize Ohio US Rep. Mike Carey for cuts to SNAP, Medicaid, and education
description: Ohio Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Carey’s constituents are speaking out against Congress’s cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Medicaid, and education.  More than a dozen people recently protested outside Carey’s Columbus office as part of the Center for Popular Democracy’s national “Care Over Cruelty” August Recess Month of Action.  The even[...]
text:
Susan Cavendish discusses how her children rely on services and therapies through Medicaid during a protest outside Ohio Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Carey’s Columbus office. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).Ohio Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Carey’s constituents are speaking out against Congress’s cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Medicaid, and education. 
More than a dozen people recently protested outside Carey’s Columbus office as part of the Center for Popular Democracy’s national “Care Over Cruelty” August Recess Month of Action. 
The event was also hosted by Progress Grove City, Parents United for Public Schools, and the Ohio Organizing Campaign.
“We’re here today to demand that Rep. Carey chose priorities that put people first,” said Kate Terenzi with the Center for Popular Democracy. 
“Health care, education, and food must come before tax cuts for billionaires, ICE, data centers, and another endless war. We need care over cruelty.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
More than 100,000 Ohioans — including more than 50,000 children — have lost their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits since the Republican “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” made the largest cuts to food stamps in the history of the program. 
Carey voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and represents Ohio’s 15th Congressional district.
“The One Big Beautiful Bill Act offers momentous tax relief that will help workers, families, seniors, farmers, and small businesses live the American Dream,” Carey said in May 2025.
Carey’s office did not respond to a request for comment by the Ohio Capital Journal. 
Medicaid work requirements part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act could cause 356,000 Ohioans to lose their healthcare coverage and about 113,000 Ohioans have already lost their coverage after tax credits expired. 
In Ohio’s 15th district, 220,200 residents rely on Medicaid, 12% of households receive SNAP, an estimated 33,000 people could lose health coverage by 2034, and $40.4 million in special education funding is at risk, according to event organizers. 
“We are calling on him to restore funding to the critical services like Medicaid, SNAP, fully fund the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act and end all funding to ICE, war, and his support to data centers,” Terenzi said. 
Ohio’s 15th district includes Madison county and parts of Franklin, Fayette, Clark, Shelby, and Miami counties. 
Susan Cavendish, a mom of four, shared how her children rely on services and therapies through Medicaid through public schools and publicly funded childcare. 
“My five-year-old son is autistic. There was a time when he was considered nonverbal … but in large part, due to the services and support he has received, he has made progress that at one time seemed unobtainable,” she said. 
“The slashing of public assistance and access to these critical services robs the opportunities, the skills, and the voices of the marginalized and underprivileged.”
As a mom of a daughter with special needs, Michelle Bolzenius has learned how to advocate for her daughter. 
“Public schools are asked to educate every child who comes through their doors,” she said. 
“That promise matters tremendously to families of children with disabilities. But we cannot expect schools to fulfill that responsibility without giving them the resources to do so.”
Cavendish’s family has seen cuts to their SNAP benefits. 
“It has become increasingly difficult to make up the differences and make sure my children are getting the nutrition they need,” she said. 
“When you cut SNAP, people do not suddenly need less food. Children do not suddenly become less hungry. The grocery bill does not suddenly become smaller as a suffering economy and rising food costs run rampant.”
Jen Belt, an organizer with Protect Grove City, had a question for Carey: At what cost?
“We hear about jobs,” she said. “We hear about economic development, we hear about winning the race for artificial intelligence, and yes, economic growth matters, jobs matter, investment matters, but Congressman Carey, our people matter too.” 
Mid-term election 
Republican Mike Carey speaks at a rally hosted by former President Donald Trump after receiving his endorsement, in Wellington, Ohio. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Carey will face Democratic candidate Don Leonard in the November election.
Leonard defeated former Ohio state rep. Adam Miller in the Democratic primary with nearly 53% of the votes. Miller lost to Carey in the 2024 election. 
Leonard, who previously taught regional and city planning at Ohio State University, was arrested during a March “No Kings” protest and was charged with obstructing official business.
“I’m a Medicaid kid,” Leonard said in an email.
“Those programs gave me a shot at the American Dream. Why would he take that same opportunity away from kids today?”
Carey first won his congressional seat in a 2021 special election and won the 2022 and 2024 elections. 
The Cook Political Report rates Ohio’s 15th Congressional District as “Likely Republican.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio’s future will be built by skilled hands
description: As cranes fill the skyline and new projects move from planning to construction, we must remember what makes all of this possible. It is not just the concrete, steel, or technology. It is the skilled men and women who install, power, maintain, and modernize the electrical systems that keep Ohio running. Whether constructing transmission lines, […]
text:
Crews work on a construction site. (Photo by Dan Koeck, States Newsroom.)As cranes fill the skyline and new projects move from planning to construction, we must remember what makes all of this possible. It is not just the concrete, steel, or technology. It is the skilled men and women who install, power, maintain, and modernize the electrical systems that keep Ohio running. 
Whether constructing transmission lines, maintaining substations, operating advanced manufacturing facilities, or connecting new energy resources to the grid, IBEW members play a critical role in supporting the systems that Ohio families and employers depend on.
A wave of investment unlike anything Ohio has experienced in recent decades is driving this demand. New energy projects, semiconductor manufacturing facilities, and utility infrastructure are creating opportunities across the state. 
Major projects like the Intel campus are already employing over 1,000 Building Trades workers, with that number expected to reach 1,600 by the end of this year. Ohio also added 8,100 new construction jobs over the last year, demonstrating both the scale of this growth and the benefits for working families.
But this growth also brings a serious challenge. Ninety-two percent of construction firms report having a hard time finding qualified workers, reinforcing the importance of the continued recruitment, training, and development for the next generation of tradespeople. 
The success of our state’s economic growth depends on ensuring we have the skilled and unionized workforce necessary to complete the work safely, reliably, and on time while supporting the manufacturing workforce that produces the equipment and technology energy projects rely on. 
For too long, a narrow narrative suggested that a four-year university degree was the only reliable path to the American Dream. The International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) and our partners across the Building Trades have long understood there is another proven route to the middle class. A career in the trades provides family-supporting wages, quality healthcare, and retirement security. Through apprenticeship programs, workers earn while they learn, receiving world-class training without taking on substantial student debt.
For the IBEW, the need for skilled electrical workers has never been greater. Grid modernization, electric vehicle infrastructure, renewable energy generation, semiconductor manufacturing, battery storage, and transmission upgrades all require a highly trained electrical workforce. These investments also bolster Ohio’s energy manufacturing base, creating and growing opportunities for IBEW members. Meeting this demand will require sustained investment not only in projects, but in the people who build, connect, manufacture, and maintain them.
That is why union apprenticeship matters so deeply. North America’s Building Trades Unions and their affiliates have built one of the most sophisticated workforce development systems in the country, combining classroom instruction, hands-on jobsite experience, safety training, and long-term career support. These programs do not just fill today’s jobs. They create durable career pathways and a pipeline of skilled workers ready to meet tomorrow’s infrastructure demands.
The rising demand for both infrastructure and labor requires bold partnerships that recognize the inherent value of union work. That is why the recent $100 million commitment from The BlackRock Foundation to support skilled trades training and workforce development is so significant. This investment reflects a growing recognition across the financial sector that a strong economy depends on a well-trained, well-supported workforce. It also reinforces the need to strengthen effective skilled trades programs and deliver them at scale, so the people building our future have the skills and support to thrive in a rapidly evolving industry.
Recent investments in AES present a significant opportunity for our state’s energy sector. AES Ohio is a vital part of our infrastructure, serving over 500,000 customers and maintaining and operating thousands of transmission and distribution lines across Ohio. This transaction will support continued investment in grid modernization, system reliability, and, most importantly, the skilled workforce responsible for keeping the lights on across the state. Moreover, it will strengthen the broader ecosystem of manufacturing jobs that supply and sustain our energy infrastructure.
As this transition moves forward, it should reinforce the clear standard that long-term infrastructure investors should work with the best contractors and the best-trained workforce available. In the energy sector, that means respecting the value of unionized workers, maintaining strong labor standards, and ensuring that modernization, reliability, and customer service are supported by people who know the system, understand the safety requirements, and serve the communities that depend on them.
Strong communities are built on strong careers. That is why partnerships among labor, responsible contractors, utilities, investors, and workforce organizations matter so much. When companies invest in reliability and training, when investors recognize that infrastructure depends on skilled people as much as capital, and when NABTU, IBEW, NECA, and the Building Trades expand apprenticeship pathways, Ohio gains more than projects. We gain safer jobsites, stronger communities, a more reliable grid, and careers that can support families for generations. 
The next chapter of Ohio’s growth must be built by the workers who know how to do the job safely, responsibly, and right. With the right partnerships and continued commitments to skilled union labor, we can strengthen our infrastructure, expand opportunity, and power Ohio’s future.

title: Passenger train upgrades heading to Wisconsin, neighboring states
description: Wisconsin rail service to Chicago and the Pacific Northwest will share in a $140 million upgrade from the federal government. The investment, awarded by the Federal Railroad Administration, will be used to overhaul 41 passenger locomotives that pull trains on the popular Hiawatha route connecting Milwaukee and Chicago and trains that pass through Wisconsin e[...]
text:
A $140 million grant to Wisconsin and other states will pay for upgrades to 41 Amtrak Charger locomotives used on passenger trains. (Amtrak photo/Copyright National Railroad Passenger Corp.)Wisconsin rail service to Chicago and the Pacific Northwest will share in a $140 million upgrade from the federal government.
The investment, awarded by the Federal Railroad Administration, will be used to overhaul 41 passenger locomotives that pull trains on the popular Hiawatha route connecting Milwaukee and Chicago and trains that pass through Wisconsin enroute to Washington state.
Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin) announced the award Wednesday. The contract was a joint application involving the Wisconsin Department of Transportation and corresponding agencies in Illinois, Michigan, Missouri, Oregon and Washington, all of which will also have passenger routes that will be served by the upgraded motive power.
“Investing in this rail line is an investment in the Main Streets that will get more customers, in families’ safety, and in our state’s future,” Baldwin said.
“This grant will help keep the locomotive fleet in a state of good repair, enhancing rail line resiliency, and preventing unplanned outages,” said Wisconsin DOT Secretary Kristina Boardman.
The funding came from the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law enacted in the first year of former President Joe Biden’s term. Baldwin’s office noted that the law was enacted without the votes of any Wisconsin Republicans in Congress.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida university’s plan for flight school in national forest is plane crazy
description: The Ocala National Forest is one of most magnificent ecosystems in the United States. More than half a million people visit it every year, many to relish its peace and quiet. Yet a Florida college wants to cut down a bunch of its trees and pave over part of it. That sounds plane crazy, doesn’t […]
text:
The Deep Woods Ranch has a 2,000-foot grass landing strip created in the 1980s. Now Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University owns it and wants to pave it, extend it and use it for lots of pilot training flights, despite it being amid the Ocala National Forest. (Photo via Louise Chen)The Ocala National Forest is one of most magnificent ecosystems in the United States. More than half a million people visit it every year, many to relish its peace and quiet. Yet a Florida college wants to cut down a bunch of its trees and pave over part of it.
That sounds plane crazy, doesn’t it?
But it’s all because of planes.
Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University in Daytona Beach is best known for training pilots. Flyboy U, as I like to call it, has bought 118 acres within the Ocala National Forest, an area called Deep Woods Ranch that contains a grass airstrip.
Embry-Riddle officials have proposed some big changes. Here’s the way the Orlando Sentinel described the plans: “turn the site into a new training facility by paving an existing private airstrip and developing a 10,000-square-foot aircraft hangar.”
The school wants to use the strip for lots of training takeoffs and landings. To make it work, though, school officials want to chop down nearly 40 acres of trees — but not on the college’s property. The trees are part of the national forest.
A few other people live in this enclave near the town of Paisley. They do not like this proposal and have made their objections plane — er, I mean plain. The same goes for people who enjoy the forest and are appalled at the idea of altering it.
The opponents have brought up the increased noise of the training flights, the pollution from all the fuel, oil, and rubber used by the planes, and the damage to wildlife habitat.
Susan Fetter via screen grab
“Nobody that’s heard about it is happy about it,” said Susan Fetter, president of the Lake County Conservation Council. She told me Embry-Riddle officials “think they can sneak something into a rural area and get away with it.”
One opponent with a front-row seat says the biggest risk lies with the precedent being set.
“If we allow our forest to be stolen from the public for private users,” warned Richard Graham, who lives at one end of the air strip, “there will soon be thousands of companies lining up to make their case on why the public lands should be made as an exception as well for them to utilize.”
 President Teddy Bear
It all started with the man who gave his name to the teddy bear.
In 1905, President Teddy Roosevelt created the national forest system. Then, three years later, he signed the order establishing the 387,000-acre Ocala National Forest, the largest national forest east of the Mississippi.
This forest contains the largest existing stand of sand pines in the world. It contains more than 600 swamps, lakes, rivers, and springs, not to mention the largest population of Florida scrub jays in the state.
President Teddy Bear would be delighted to see how popular it is now. About 650,000 people visit Ocala National Forest every year, according to the U.S. Forest Service.
Last year, National Geographic named the Ocala National Forest one of the best travel destinations in the world. The magazine praised its natural beauty, diverse ecosystems, and recreational opportunities like swimming in crystal-clear springs.
Although the forest is mostly owned by the federal government, there are a few privately owned enclaves. One sliver of private land, about 220 acres, was owned by a retired Illinois banker. He put in some cattle and named it Deep Woods Ranch.
The retired banker had a small plane. Even though the DeLand Municipal Airport was just nine miles away, he wanted to take off from his own yard. In 1987, he persuaded Lake County to grant him permission to create a grass-covered, 2,000-foot landing strip there.
The banker specified it was for family and friends — no outsiders. However, there are stories floating around Lake County that the airstrip was occasionally used by the Cocaine Cowboys transporting goods from South America. Either way, a plane used to take off or land there maybe once every couple of weeks, tops.
Richard Graham via screen grab
In subsequent years, the ranch was cut into three pieces, according to Graham, whose 55-acre parcel is one of them (more on that in a minute). Then, with no notice to the neighbors, Embry-Riddle popped up as the airstrip’s new owner.
Suddenly, sleepy Deep Woods Ranch was scheduled for a major makeover from the people for whom Tom Petty’s “Learning to Fly” is a school anthem.
 Up in the air
In the 1920s, a barnstorming pilot named John P. Riddle roamed around the Midwest putting on stunt shows and giving rides. One of his customers, entrepreneur T. Higby Embry, convinced him to start a flight school.
The Embry-Riddle college campus, now located at 1 Aerospace Boulevard in Daytona Beach, trains thousands of pilots a year. I assume they learn all the hand motions to “Up in the Air, Junior Birdmen” on the first day and after that it gets more technical.
Alan and Louise Chen via subjects.
A key part of pilot training is practicing your takeoffs and landings. From its Deep Woods Ranch property, Embry-Riddle expects to launch 300 or so takeoffs seven days a week, 50 weeks a year, according to an analysis by Alan and Louise Chen, two engineers working with Fetter who have pored over the plans.
Somehow, the Chens said, nobody has done a noise analysis about what that will do to the forest’s abundant wildlife. That includes such imperiled species as gopher tortoises, roseate spoonbills, and migratory swallowtail kites.
The Chens spotted scores of kites nesting three miles from the airstrip. Their foraging range is 15 miles, so they often fly over the runway.
“One day,” Louise Chen told me, “there were five of them circling above the runway.”
According to the Chens’ analysis, the Embry-Riddle planes will bathe up to 50,000 acres with the sound of Cessna 172s. It will be just as soothing as having a swarm of really big mosquitoes buzzing in both your ears.
Swallowtail kites over Deep Woods Ranch, via Alan Chen.
It’s not just wildlife that would be disturbed. Among Embry-Riddle’s neighbors is a 64-acre religious institution called Deerhaven Retreat and Conference Center in the forest near Paisley. It’s celebrating its 60th anniversary.
People seek out Deerhaven for its tranquility, said chairman Charles Greenberg. Embry-Riddle will ruin the very thing that makes it so appealing.
“The frequent drone of aircraft means groups using the center might not return, and Deerhaven would not survive,” he told me. “That would destroy our campgrounds.”
Deerhaven Retreat and Conference Center via Deerhaven.
 People in Smokey Bear hats
At this point you may be wondering: What does the U.S. Forest Service think of all this?
After all, that’s the federal agency managing our national forests. When the banker asked to build his airstrip, the feds specified that he wasn’t allowed to cut down any of their trees.
Now Embry-Riddle wants to chop down nearly 40 acres of trees that belong to the American people.
Surely, I thought, the folks in the Smokey Bear hats are jumping up and down screaming, “No way!”
The answer, I was surprised to learn, is nope. The Smokey Bear folks are not jumping at all, unless you count jumping to provide Embry-Riddle with whatever the college wants.
The U.S. Forest Service, much like other federal regulatory agencies, has been converted into a virtual rubber stamp by our profit-first, protection-last presidential administration.
In fact, just this week The New York Times reported that the Trump administration is trying “to open nearly 45 million acres of wilderness in national forests to road construction and logging, removing protections that had been in place for a quarter century.”
As for the Osceola National Forest, in April, a spokeswoman for the Forest Service promised WMFE-FM that the agency was studying Embry-Riddle’s proposal and would decide “once all environmental and regulatory reviews are complete.”
But in July, the agency decided it didn’t need any reviews, because Embry-Riddle was exempt from all that nitpicky stuff. If there are no requirements to meet, then there’s no problem meeting them, right?
“This whole thing is just odiferous,” Greenberg said with a sniff.
Fetter and the Chens met with a forest service supervisor Tuesday and presented some information that the agency folks were apparently unaware of, Fetter told me.
“The permit is now on administrative hold,” she said.
Among other things, they pointed out flaws in the college’s own cursory environmental report.
The forest supervisor “found it somewhat amusing that the report mentioned it wasn’t a suitable habitat for sandhill cranes, which we followed up with the picture of a couple families of sandhill cranes running across the grass runway,” Alan Chen told me.
However, Fetter said, the forestry official said, “the county is the only agency that can stop it.”
 The man with two hats
Lake County officials learned what Embry-Riddle wanted to do long before the neighbors or forest fans did.
In 2024, county records show, an Embry-Riddle vice president invited Commission Chairwoman Leslie Campione and other county officials to the college’s Daytona Beach campus to discuss the Deep Woods Ranch airstrip.
Rep. Tyler Sirois via Florida House of Representatives
Commission Chair Leslie Campione via Lake County.
The college vice president had an interesting sartorial distinction. He was wearing two hats. Tyler Siroise is in charge of “government relations” at Embry-Riddle. He is also a member of the state House of Representatives. In 2024, he was midway through his term as the House majority leader.
You can see how county officials would want to accommodate someone in the legislative leadership corps. The desires of Rep. Siroise would count for more than the desires of a bunch of tree huggers, rural neighbors, and religious campers.
There’s nothing wrong with county officials helping an economic development project, the Chens said. But “who was independently identifying and evaluating the risks to Lake County, neighboring property owners and the surrounding national forest?”
No one, that’s who.
The college initially submitted an elaborate plan that included not just paving the airstrip but also building hangars, classrooms, and research facilities. The county staff recommended approval. In its report, the county referred to the surrounding national forest as “vacant land.”
I can’t tell you how much I loathe hearing nature preserves referred to as ‘vacant” simply because they hold nothing manmade.
The college applied for a change in the zoning. The opponents lined up to point out the many flaws in its plans. But on the day the county was supposed to hold a public hearing, Embry-Riddle abruptly withdrew its application.
As a result, “there has never been a public hearing on this project,” Greenberg said.
What changed? The county attorney agreed with the college’s attorney that the main thing the college wanted, paving the grass airstrip, wasn’t expressly forbidden by the zoning already in place.
Presumably, they could use that justification for other questionable stuff. How about a Deep Woods Ranch shopping mall? Gas station? Nuclear plant? Hey, there’s nothing to forbid it!
Despite that abrupt turn of events, the Embry-Riddle plan has yet to take off. It’s been grounded, primarily because of Graham.
Graham, a former Navy Seal, has been using his property for a veterans’ charity and sniper training. It’s not that Embry-Riddle is afraid he’ll shoot down their planes. It’s that he’s repeatedly pointed out that Embry-Riddle has not considered the rights he holds to an easement across its property.
While they’re discussing that, though, I think the best point I have heard is one Louise Chen mentioned.
“I know we need to train pilots,” she told me, “but we need to find a better place for it than here.”
 What goes up
I tried repeatedly to get Siroise or someone else from Embry-Riddle to talk to me. The best I could get was a boilerplate response: “Embry-Riddle continues to work closely with Lake County and other regulatory agencies as we develop a limited footprint in the area.”
The main question I wanted to ask was: Why did the college need to build on THIS inappropriate site?
I’m no aviation expert. Most of what I know about airplanes comes from watching the movie “Airplane!” But surely (sorry!) there are better places to put an aviation training facility than the Ocala National Forest.
A quick Google search turned up 11 other airports in Florida that are for sale right now. I bet none of them have the same limitations that Deep Woods Ranch does.
What limitations? Why, all those trees, of course.
One major rule of aviation is, “What goes up must come down.” If an Embry-Riddle trainer goes down, there’s nowhere outside of that airstrip to land safely. A falling plane is going to collide with many, many pines.
Cindy Newton via subject.
“Why are they training kids in a forest?” asked conservation council member Cindy Newton. “It’s a safety issue. That’s baffled me.”
Maybe Embry-Riddle couldn’t see the trees for the forest.
I think if its leaders are smart, they will sell this property to the national forest and look elsewhere for training. Rather than try to fly a craft this flawed, they should just bail out.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The benefits of war?
description: For most of America, whether war still stimulates an economy is a historical question. For Connecticut, it is a paycheck.
text:
Violet Carol Moss, my grandmother, whom we affectionately called Big Mommy, packed up her two-year-old son and moved across the country to build the machines of war.
It was the 1940s, the height of World War II. My grandfather had been called to serve, and Big Mommy left Cleveland, Ohio for Tacoma, Washington, with my father, Nathaniel Gachette Moss Jr., a smiley, talkative baby boy.

Yvonne Renee Davis

She became one of the women the country would later romanticize as Rosie the Riveter. In the Pacific Northwest, they had their own name, the Wendy Welders. They were paid roughly 60 percent of what men earned for the same work. They built the war anyway.
Three generations later, I write from Connecticut, a state that still runs on exactly what Big Mommy built.
Consider the numbers, then decide for yourself what to feel.
Connecticut ranks sixth in the nation for aerospace and defense jobs, according to the Aerospace Industries Association: more than 113,000 jobs and $63.8 billion in economic output. Researchers at the Yale School of Management estimate that nearly ten percent of this small state’s entire GDP flows from the defense industry. On Pentagon spending per capita, Connecticut ranks at or near number one.
The machinery behind those numbers is familiar to anyone who lives here. In fiscal 2024 alone, the Department of Defense spent $18.7 billion at Connecticut contractors, most of it flowing through General Dynamics Electric Boat, building submarines in Groton, RTX’s Pratt & Whitney, building engines in East Hartford and Middletown, and Lockheed’s Sikorsky, building Black Hawk helicopters in Stratford.
Every F-35 in the American fleet, and in the fleets of allies from Norway to Israel, is powered by a Pratt & Whitney F135 engine built right here. The airframe is assembled in Texas; the heart is made in Connecticut. The older F100 engine powers the F-16s and F-15s of more than 20 air forces worldwide. When any ally goes to war, Connecticut’s economy hums.
This is not a recent arrangement. It is the state where Samuel Colt built the American gun in 1855, and Colt is still there, still in West Hartford, still making rifles for the military, a living passed down through generations of Hartford families, now under Czech ownership. War in Connecticut has never been distant news. It has been the employer.
I do not write this as an outsider. Before my State Department years, I was a communications consultant to the National Minority Supplier Development Council on the 51% Minority Ownership Rule Change, reporting to Shelley Stewart Jr., then United Technologies’ Director of Worldwide Sourcing, alongside former chairman George David. Years later, as a leadership and communications trainer for the U.S. Department of State promoting public diplomacy, I worked in the war zones themselves: Bosnia, Kosovo, Afghanistan. I knew this world from the corporate side, then met it in the field.
Which is why I want to be precise and fair. Even now, prosperity is uneven. Pratt & Whitney furloughed union machinists last year, and the union walked out in its first strike since 2001 before settling. But that pain sits on the commercial side of the house, the airliner engines that have grounded planes worldwide. The F135, the war engine, is surging, boosted by the new contracts in the fiscal 2026 defense bill Congress passed in December. The lesson is uncomfortable. It is the military work that holds steadiest here.
So here is the question I cannot stop turning over. On April 28, roughly 150 soldiers of the 192nd Military Police Battalion boarded aircraft at Bradley for Operation Epic Fury, the campaign against Iran, joining hundreds more from the state already deployed across the region. Maj. Gen. Francis J. Evon Jr., the Connecticut National Guard’s adjutant general, said most people will never fully appreciate “what it costs a person to step away from a job, a family, a routine, and the life they’ve built to answer that call.” In a state where one in ten dollars flows from defense, the same economy that sends these soldiers also feeds the families they leave behind. The dread and the dependence live in the same households. That is Connecticut’s paradox.
Big Mommy knew that tension in her hands. She built the instruments of a war her husband, my grandfather, was fighting in, and that work fed her child, my dad. Whether you are for or against this administration, in a state that leans the other way, the arithmetic does not care about your politics.
For most of America, whether war still stimulates an economy is a historical question. For Connecticut, it is a paycheck.
I will let you sit with the question mark; the same one Big Mommy carried in her hands.
Yvonne Renee Davis, of Avon, is Founder, President and CEO of DAVISIntelligence, a strategic communications and crisis management firm. A former Presidential Appointee under President George W. Bush, she served as a trainer and speaker for the U.S. Department of State across three Presidential Administrations, with assignments and business spanning 68 countries.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Trump announces plans to fill Alaska’s third federal judge position, vacant for over two years
description: President Donald Trump announced plans to nominate Kyle Reardon, a federal magistrate judge and former prosecutor, to fill the last of three federal judge positions for the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska. Trump announced the nomination on social media on Tuesday, as well as picks for federal trial courts in Texas, Florida, […]
text:
The east entrance of the James M. Fitzgerald United States Courthouse and Federal Building is seen on July 8, 2024. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)President Donald Trump announced plans to nominate Kyle Reardon, a federal magistrate judge and former prosecutor, to fill the last of three federal judge positions for the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska.
Trump announced the nomination on social media on Tuesday, as well as picks for federal trial courts in Texas, Florida, Oklahoma, Kentucky and Louisiana. The move largely clears the backlog of judicial vacancies in red states, Bloomberg reported, setting the clock for the U.S. Senate to confirm appointments before the midterm elections may shake up majority power.
The Alaska federal judge seat has been vacant for over two years, since July 2024, when former federal judge Joshua Kindred resigned in disgrace following a judicial panel finding he sexually harassed and created a hostile work environment for his law clerks. 
If confirmed by the U.S. Senate, Reardon would become one of three federal judges in Alaska serving lifetime appointments. 
Reardon was one of a dozen candidates that expressed interest in the judgeship when U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski solicited applications last year. 
Reardon was appointed as chief magistrate judge for Alaska by Judge Sharon Gleason in September 2025. He is based in Anchorage and has served as a magistrate judge in Alaska since 2021, according to his resume. Magistrate judges are appointed by district court judges to four-year terms, and oversee a variety of judicial proceedings supporting the federal courts. They have many of the same powers as federal judges to hear criminal and civil cases. 
Over the last two years, Alaska’s two U.S. senators have been split about the selection process and who to nominate for the federal judgeship. In 2023 U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan created the Alaska Federal Judiciary Council to vet candidates for vacant federal judge positions, a special committee designed to serve as an alternative to the Alaska Bar Association’s traditional review process.  
Under longstanding Senate tradition, judge picks normally advance only with the assent of both home state senators.
On Wednesday, both of Alaska’s Republican senators issued statements of support for Reardon. 
“Kyle brings extensive knowledge of both our state and our court system to the federal bench, having served the District of Alaska as a federal prosecutor and U.S. Magistrate Judge, a position he has held in Alaska for the past five years,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski wrote.
“His extensive experience, professionalism, and judicial temperament make him exceptionally well-qualified for this role,” she said. “I thank the President for nominating Kyle and helping bring Alaska’s District Court back to full capacity.”
A spokesperson for Murkowski’s office said Wednesday she has recommended and advocated for Reardon since the beginning of Trump’s second term in 2025, but declined to give more information about the delay in his appointment.
Murkowski shared a list of candidates who expressed interest in the role with members of the Alaska Bar Association who weighed in on each in a survey. For Reardon, 21% of the 407 total respondents said he was qualified, well qualified or extremely well qualified. One percent said he was not qualified, and 75% responded “don’t know.”
U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan also praised the nomination, but his office also did not respond to requests for comment on the delay on Wednesday.
“Kyle has a strong background of public service in the law and the military,” Sullivan wrote. “Kyle offers a wealth of legal experience, a deep understanding of the numerous federal laws that uniquely impact Alaska, and a commitment to the principle that a judge’s role is to interpret the law, not to write law. Lastly, I want to thank members of my Alaska Federal Judiciary Council for working to evaluate candidates, including Kyle, for this critically important role.”
Reardon’s resume details a long career in law before his magistrate appointment. Prior to serving as a magistrate judge, Reardon served as a federal prosecutor as Assistant U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska Anchorage from 2014 to 2021, and for the Eastern District of California from 2007 to 2014. He served as a judge advocate for the U.S. Army Judge Advocate General Corps from 1999 to 2005, including as a military prosecutor and an advisor on legal matters related to the Bush administration’s Global War on Terror. He attended the University of Virginia School of Law. 
In his letter of interest, Reardon noted the state’s judicial vacancies, and his knowledge and experience working in Alaska’s federal court system.  
“The law is essential for ensuring a just, civil, and prosperous society. At this time, when confidence in the judiciary is at historic lows, it is critical that a district court judge be someone who has a demonstrated record of service and leadership; is respected in their community; and brings a seriousness and commitment of purpose to the position,” he wrote.
“Moreover, in light of the current judicial vacancies that exist within the District of Alaska, it is essential that the person who is nominated to the position have experience and familiarity with the federal courts so they can serve effectively from the moment of their confirmation. I believe I am that person.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Prediction market firm sues to escape Wisconsin gambling law
description: The prediction market platform Novig is suing to stop the state Department of Justice from using the state’s gambling laws to prevent the firm from operating in Wisconsin.  Novig’s federal lawsuit follows DOJ’s lawsuits in April that charged three other prediction market platforms with violating Wisconsin’s recently adopted online sports gambling law.  In th[...]
text:
The prediction market platform Novig says in a lawsuit that Wisconsin's sports gambling law doesn't apply to its business. (Getty Images)The prediction market platform Novig is suing to stop the state Department of Justice from using the state’s gambling laws to prevent the firm from operating in Wisconsin. 
Novig’s federal lawsuit follows DOJ’s lawsuits in April that charged three other prediction market platforms with violating Wisconsin’s recently adopted online sports gambling law. 
In the new lawsuit, filed by Novig’s parent firm Ludlow Exchange LLC, the business asserts that it isn’t engaged in “gambling” but instead is “providing sports-based event contracts to customers across the United States.”
Event contracts pay out to customers who purchase a contract for a specific outcome, such as victory by a particular team in a particular game. In the lawsuit Ludlow Exchange asserts that an event contract is a “derivative” investment regulated exclusively by the federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
“The field here is not gambling,” the lawsuit states. “It is the regulation of trading on federally designated contract markets — the discrete activity over which Congress conferred exclusive jurisdiction” to the CFTC. 
DOJ communications director Riley Vetterkind referred a request for comment on the lawsuit to the department’s April 23 press release that announced its lawsuits against three other prediction market firms. 
“Thinly disguising unlawful conduct doesn’t make it lawful,” Attorney General Josh Kaul said then. “These companies’ alleged facilitation of sports betting in Wisconsin should be shut down.”
Novig entered the Wisconsin market the first week of August. Ludlow Exchange and Novig said in their lawsuit, which was first reported by WisPolitics, that they were filing the complaint because DOJ “could bring an enforcement action premised on the false notion that Novig is violating state gambling laws, exposing Novig to criminal liability for a Class I felony.”
The emergence of prediction markets including Kalshi and Polymarket has prompted states across the country to enact legislation and file lawsuits, Stateline reported in March.
The online platforms have been estimated to generate more than $13 billion every month, with the bulk of those revenues coming from sports betting, Stateline reported.
DOJ sued Kalshi, Coinbase, Polymarket and other prediction platforms in April, charging that their engagement in online sports betting violated the state’s online sports gambling law signed earlier that month. 
The new law legalized online sports betting in Wisconsin on the condition that the computer servers required are housed on tribal land. Until the law’s enactment, sports betting had been legal in Wisconsin since 2021, but only in person at tribal casinos.
The DOJ’s lawsuits said transactions on the prediction market platforms are “indistinguishable from an ordinary sports bet” as defined in Wisconsin law.
Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase and the other defendants in Wisconsin’s lawsuits have also asserted that they’re beyond the reach of state gambling bans. They contend they’re only subject to federal regulation by the CFTC, and that a federal appeals court has ruled states don’t have jurisdiction over prediction markets.
The defendants have moved Wisconsin’s cases into federal court, where lawyers are currently arguing over whether they should remain there or return to Dane County’s court.

name: Nevada Current
title: Hope for Prisoners board was advised to fire Ponder in 2020, letter confirms
description: When President Donald Trump issued a pardon to Jon Ponder, a three-time convicted bank robber, at the Republican National Convention in August 2020, Ponder, the founder and CEO of Hope for Prisoners, unbeknownst to Trump, was under investigation by the organization’s board of directors and in danger of losing his job.  An attorney hired by […]
text:
Jon Ponder and Gov. Joe Lombardo after Lombardo was given the "Champion of HOPE" Award at at luncheon July 7, 2025.  Lombardo, along with current Clark County Sheriff Kevin McMahill, have long refused to say whether Metro conducted its own investigation of HFP, which is a community partner of the police department. (Photo posted on social media by Hope for Prisoners)When President Donald Trump issued a pardon to Jon Ponder, a three-time convicted bank robber, at the Republican National Convention in August 2020, Ponder, the founder and CEO of Hope for Prisoners, unbeknownst to Trump, was under investigation by the organization’s board of directors and in danger of losing his job. 
An attorney hired by the board to investigate allegations of sexual impropriety against Ponder eventually recommended to the board that Ponder be fired. The board ignored the recommendation. 
The revelation comes from a Sept. 2020 resignation letter submitted to the board by then-Hope for Prisoners board member Kristina Wildeveld, a Las Vegas attorney who assisted Ponder with his state pardon and applied for his federal pardon following Trump’s visit to an HFP graduation in the spring of 2020. 
According to Wildeveld, the board, which included Clark County Sheriff Kevin McMahill, who was undersheriff at the time to then-sheriff and now Gov. Joe Lombardo, and Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson, declined to accept the recommendation to fire Ponder after Trump issued the pardon. 
“Legitimate concerns regarding Jon Ponder and his actions and their effect on the program were brought to the Board’s attention,” Wildeveld wrote. “The Board dismissed those concerns despite the significant evidence…”
The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Dept. arrested Ponder on Tuesday. He is charged with nine felony counts and 11 gross misdemeanors. The charges include sexual assault, sexual abuse of a prisoner by an employee, contractor, or volunteer, and coercion of a sexual nature. His initial court appearance is scheduled for Thursday morning. 
The Current was first to report in April that Ponder had been banned from Nevada prisons and was under investigation. 
Metro is asking others who may have been victimized by Ponder to contact police. 
Lombardo, McMahill, and Wolfson did not respond when asked Wednesday if they regret not taking action to protect Nevada inmates and other potential victims. . 
‘Undying faith’
Wildeveld, in her 2020 letter, asserted that “disregarding the Board’s counsel’s advice to fire Jon” indicated the organization had lost its way, and wrote that “fundraising and promotion has been placed ahead of the original mission” to serve the reentry population, which she said was “replaced or overshadowed” with the goal of making Ponder a celebrity. 
Ponder’s “attitude toward the inmate population who have the opportunity to successfully reintegrate has morphed into something almost unrecognizable and that should be of great concern to this Board,” Wildeveld wrote, noting his votes as a member of the state’s sentencing commission against releasing some inmates during the pandemic, and voting against allowing pregnant women to be released from custody.
Wildeveld added the board’s “undying faith in a leader who has failed to lead by example, and who at a minimum has put the entire mission at risk through his conscious actions, is the height of hypocrisy and spells a certain implosion…” 
Hope for Prisoners, she added, “may benefit from portraying Jon as a reformed bank robber, who did his time (five years), found Jesus and devoted his life to others, but someday someone will probe into the rest of his criminal history and recent actions and conclude that the organization is in troubled hands.”
In addition to complaints from women in the program about Ponder’s behavior, the board’s outside counsel, Lynne McChrystal, investigated allegations made by former employee Rodney Taylor, who said Ponder gave favorable treatment to female employees. 
“Eventually, the harassment and promises not kept, threats, and witnessing inappropriate behavior with female staff, mentors, Hope graduates, and donors surpassed my boundaries of acceptable behavior in the workplace,” Taylor wrote to the board in May 2020, in a letter that was made public during a 2024 lawsuit brought by another former employee against the nonprofit and Ponder. 
Since Wildeveld’s resignation in 2020, Lombardo, McMahill, and Wolfson have refused to respond to questions and denied the Current’s repeated requests under the Nevada Open Records Act to turn over Wildeveld’s letter, which was sent to McMahill and Wolfson at their government email addresses.  
Lombardo and McMahill have long refused to say whether Metro conducted its own investigation of HFP, which is a community partner of the police department. Metro Undersheriff Andrew Walsh and Assistant Sheriff Michael Gennaro serve on HFP’s board of directors. The organization’s monthly graduation ceremonies are held at Metro headquarters. 
As governor, Lombardo has doubled down on his support for Hope for Prisoners by expanding the program in state prisons.
Wolfson, who is no longer on the HFP board, has remained close to Ponder and has featured him in campaign ads. Wolfson also formed a partnership with Ponder called Hope for Second Chances, in which individuals convicted of nonviolent felonies can complete the program in lieu of serving time.  
Former Metro Assistant Sheriff Todd Fasulo, who is now vice president of security for Wynn Las Vegas, served as president of the board in 2020. He declined to comment. 
Hope for Prisoners did not respond to requests for comment.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Advocates of Nebraska’s ‘most vulnerable’ call on Pillen to pause funding cuts pending review
description: LINCOLN — Some came in wheelchairs, with caretakers. Others, with intellectual disabilities, were escorted by parents. Among them were four state lawmakers and a host of advocates for a population they described as Nebraska’s “most vulnerable.” One young woman held a sign: “My sister cannot explain what she needs. That is why I am standing here.” […]
text:
Jennifer Henning of Omaha speaks about the impact a relatively new interRAI assessment system has had on her two children. She and others discussed their exasperation with the system, calling on Gov. Jim Pillen to pause funding reductions. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraskas Examiner)LINCOLN — Some came in wheelchairs, with caretakers. Others, with intellectual disabilities, were escorted by parents. Among them were four state lawmakers and a host of advocates for a population they described as Nebraska’s “most vulnerable.”
Advocates for people with disabilities hold signs and speak during an event Wednesday in the State Capitol. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
One young woman held a sign: “My sister cannot explain what she needs. That is why I am standing here.”
The few hundred people who converged Wednesday in the State Capitol were there to highlight concerns with the state’s implementation of a new system launched in July 2025 to assess Nebraskans with intellectual and developmental disabilities seeking Medicaid assistance.
Essentially, the interRAI tool determines the level of publicly assisted care, services and funding for Nebraskans with developmental disabilities. Several people who gathered for the media event offered personal accounts of why they believe the new assessment didn’t reflect their loved ones’ capabilities and put them at risk.
They called on Gov. Jim Pillen to pause any reduction in funding as a result of the new tool until an outside evaluation is done. An ongoing petition campaign, which has nearly 4,000 supporters, seeks to “pause, rollback, and fix or replace” the current process.
One dad, Lehn Straub, told the audience that his son Doug, 45, uses a feeding tube and tracheostomy, can’t move on his own and is unable to speak. He said an interRAI assessment last fall changed Doug’s service and funding tier from “advanced” to “intermediate,” meaning his one-on-one care at a day program dropped to a small group situation.
Nebraskans at a State Capitol news event led by Disability Alliance of Nebraska. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
An example of how that plays out, the dad said, is that instead of a caretaker helping his son interact in a shopping mall or bowling alley, Doug can only watch others. He said he gets skirted from participation in events.
“Doug has not changed,” Straub said. “The only thing that changed was his assessment tool. He still requires one-on-one care every day and every night to keep him safe.”
A mom, Jennifer Henning of Omaha, came to Lincoln with her two children. She described son Connor as nonverbal, with cerebral palsy and profound intellectual disabilities. An interRAI assessment dropped his level associated with resources. Meanwhile, she said, her 11-year-old daughter’s needs aren’t as intense, yet she was deemed eligible for more support. 
“How is this happening?” she asked, adding that the concern is about “putting money where it’s needed.”
Independent third party
The news conference organized by Disability Alliance of Nebraska came one day after the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services released its own news statement that the state has hired an independent third party to evaluate interRAI implementation and effectiveness.
Tony Green, director of the disability and aging services for Nebraska at a news conference announcing March as Developmental Disabilities Awareness Month in 2023. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Wednesday’s gathering of families and advocates had already been scheduled when DHHS announced its $420,000 contract with Alvarez & Marsal Public Sector. DHHS said it will partner with A&M over the next four months during which the team will analyze performance and reliability and identify potential ways to improve.
DHHS said the A&M contract was exempt from a local bidding process, as it was awarded through OMNIA, a multistate cooperative purchasing organization that already conducted a competitive bid on behalf of government agencies. 
Some advocates of the disability community earlier raised concerns that a former DHHS manager who was instrumental in Nebraska’s pivot to the interRAI tool is now employed by A&M. 
DHHS spokesman Jeff Powell provided a statement from A&M managing director Christoper Baglio, who said the former state employee, Kristen Smith, will not be involved in the project.
State records show the A&M contract starting in July, though DHHS said last week the contract had not been finalized. The document was not available Wednesday on the government website.
State officials, in defense of interRAI, said the tool is not new and is used in more than 25 other states. “Its value is that it replaces subjective, fragmented assessments with a standardized process that uses validated information to help guide decisions about care and services,” DHHS said.
The agency said its previous assessment tool, Inventory for Client and Agency Planning, or ICAP, was no longer being updated. 
Since the interRAI launched for developmental disability waivers, DHHS said it has “significantly expanded” access to home and community-based services. The agency said about 80% of Nebraskans’ funding levels have stayed the same or increased.
Lawmakers join rally
Nebraska lawmakers attending the Disability Alliance’s Wednesday news conference included state Sen. John Fredrickson of Omaha, vice chair of the Legislature’s Health and Human Services Committee, which has oversight of DHHS. Also attending were state Sens. Victor Rountree of Bellevue, George Dungan of Lincoln and Merv Riepe of Ralston.
State Sen. John Fredrickson of Omaha speaks at a press conference highlighting flaws he and others see in the implementation of interRAI for developmental disability waivers. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Fredrickson echoed comments from alliance leaders who welcomed the A&M independent evaluation as an encouraging step, but noted criticism of the process so far.
“Hundreds of Nebraskans are being denied life-altering care, not because of any change in condition or level of need, but because of a change in algorithm,” Fredrickson said. 
He said that “obscure classifications and assessment processes” erode trust in the health care system and that state officials should listen to Nebraska families. “If they say a tool is not working, that tool is not working.”
Fredrickson directed a message at Pillen’s team: “Chipping away at resources for the most vulnerable in our state is in no way a badge of honor. It’s shameful.”
In response to the call for a pause, Powell said that would disrupt service to new applicants and those in need of an annual renewal. He said an assessment process or tool must be in place and verified by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to offer a waiver that leads to funding and services. 
Tony Green, DHHS Division of Disability and Aging director, called interRAI a nationally accredited tool to determine services based on a cost-to-serve model. It was the DHHS choice after the agency in 2024 started seeking a “more modern, standardized, person-centered and comprehensive tool.”
An independent evaluation like that to be provided by A&M was always intended, Green said. 
Another parent who spoke in the Capitol Rotunda, just outside the chamber where state laws are made, was Heather Vanourney of Lincoln. Her 21-year-old son Trenton was diagnosed with severe autism and developmental delay before age 2. 
She said she did not bring Trenton along because he runs away, is afraid of stairwells and would likely screech throughout the conference. 
“He will forever be a toddler in an adult’s body,” Vanourney said.
Lehn Straub of Lincoln speaks about impact the interRAI assessment program has had on son Doug. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Yet, she said, after an interRAI assessment reduced his funding level,  she cannot send him to day services. 
“The state has essentially taken away that option,” she said. “He’s now forced to just stay at home.”
Appeal failed
Straub said he filed an appeal after he learned of his son’s assessment. He said he got the feeling early that it would not succeed and was correct.
“It wasn’t going to make any difference,” Straub said. “It was locked in.”
Mike Browne is a parent of two sons in their 40s who have profound intellectual disabilities and who saw their funding levels reduced even though their conditions had not changed. He also is a member of the Disability Alliance and Pillen’s advisory committee on developmental disabilities.
Browne said he welcomed the independent review but opposed continuing the current system in the meanwhile.
“If DHHS believes the Nebraska model requires a $420,000 independent examination of its reliability, validity and implementation, then it should not continue reducing people’s funding based upon that same model while the examination is underway.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: ICE no longer intends to turn Salt Lake City warehouse into detention center, court filing says
description: Through their attorneys, Department of Homeland Security officials told Salt Lake City leaders that they “no longer intend to convert” a Salt Lake City warehouse purchased earlier this year for $145.4 million with now abandoned plans to turn it into a massive detention center.  That’s according to new court documents filed Wednesday, in which Salt […]
text:
A warehouse purchased by U.S. Immigration Customs and Enforcement at 6020 W. 300 South in Salt Lake City is pictured on Friday, March 13, 2026. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)Through their attorneys, Department of Homeland Security officials told Salt Lake City leaders that they “no longer intend to convert” a Salt Lake City warehouse purchased earlier this year for $145.4 million with now abandoned plans to turn it into a massive detention center. 
That’s according to new court documents filed Wednesday, in which Salt Lake City attorneys asked a judge to push pause on the lawsuit the city filed in June against DHS seeking to block the detention center. 
City attorneys filed Wednesday’s motion for a 60-day stay in light of DHS and the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s reversal, the filing says.
ICE plans to offload Salt Lake City warehouse, report says

“On July 17, 2026, Defendants, through counsel, informed Plaintiffs that they no longer intend to convert the Salt Lake Warehouse into an immigration detention facility and instead intend to designate the Salt Lake Facility as excess property for disposition by the General Services Administration,” Salt Lake City attorneys wrote in the motion. 
That filing confirms earlier reporting by The New York Times that the Department of Homeland Security planned to offload seven warehouses across the country, including the one in Salt Lake City. 
“In light of this development,” Salt Lake City attorneys wrote, city and federal officials “have conferred and agree this case should be stayed” for 60 days as stipulated in the city’s proposed motion, which requires the Department of Homeland Security to not “take any action to convert the Salt Lake (warehouse) into an immigration detention center during the stay.”
As of Wednesday evening, the proposed motion filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Utah had not yet been signed. 
Through a spokesperson, Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall’s office declined to comment on the filing, citing pending litigation. 
Salt Lake City, county, sue feds to stop ICE detention center from coming online 

The Salt Lake City warehouse, one of ICE’s most expensive purchases as part of a planned $45 billion expansion of immigration detention centers across the country, was purchased just days after DHS Secretary Kristi Noem was fired.
In the months after, uncertainty swirled around what would come of the Salt Lake warehouse as DHS officials said they were “reviewing agency policies and proposals” as it transitioned under newly sworn-in Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s leadership.
Democratic local leaders including Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall and Salt Lake County Mayor Jenny Wilson fought vehemently against any possibility of the warehouse being turned into a detention center large enough to hold up to 10,000 people. 
They raised concerns ranging from overtaxed city water and sewer systems, air pollution and a burden on already strained police resources. 
“This kind of facility has no place in Salt Lake City,” Mendenhall said in June, “not only due to its inhumane nature but also because of our limited water supply, the increased strain on public utilities systems, and the potentially drastic public health and safety impacts it would have on our residents.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Rounds announces bipartisan bill to encourage converting cropland back to pasture
description: MITCHELL – Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds unveiled a bipartisan bill Wednesday at Dakotafest that would pay farmers to convert less-productive cropland back to grass and allow the acres to be grazed by livestock all season. The Rebuilding America’s National Cow Herd Act, or RANCH Act, would create a voluntary federal program with an enrollment […]
text:
U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Sen. Mike Rounds, both Republicans from South Dakota, speak with an attendee of Dakotafest in Mitchell on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)MITCHELL – Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds unveiled a bipartisan bill Wednesday at Dakotafest that would pay farmers to convert less-productive cropland back to grass and allow the acres to be grazed by livestock all season.
The Rebuilding America’s National Cow Herd Act, or RANCH Act, would create a voluntary federal program with an enrollment cap of 20 million acres. Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota co-sponsors the legislation. 
Under the proposal, eligible land would need to have had crops planted on it in at least four of the previous six years or have history of being cropped, according to a bill summary from Rounds’ Office. Farmers would sign 10- to 15-year contracts and establish and maintain perennial grasses or non-woody vegetation like wildflowers, buckwheat or radishes.
The program has additional incentives for beginning farmers and ranchers, and would prioritize contracts for poorly performing and highly erodible cropland.
Tax laws favor cropland over grassland, ranchers and conservation groups tell lawmakers

A South Dakota State University study estimated the state lost about 1.8 million acres of grassland between 2006 and 2012, predominantly to cropland conversion. Across the Great Plains, 32 million acres of grassland were converted from 2012 through 2021, with row-crop expansion identified as the leading cause, according to a World Wildlife Fund analysis.
Under Rounds’ new bill, participants would receive annual payments equal to 75% of their county’s average cropland cash rental rate. The program would also pay 50% of the cost of establishing grass, increasing to 75% for beginning farmers and ranchers. Producers are still eligible for other federal cost-share programs that help establish things like fencing. 
The federal government has a program that permits livestock grazing while paying landowners to maintain it as grassland, called the Grassland Conservation Reserve Program. In April 2024, nearly 1.5 million South Dakota acres were enrolled in that program, totaling $23.67 million in payments; the average annual payment per acre was about $16.
The existing program, however, pays to preserve existing grass. Rounds’ bill would pay to convert cropland back to grass, and it does not include seasonal grazing restrictions like the current program. It would also pay landowners at a rate based on the land’s cropland value, rather than its pastureland value, which would amount to larger payments. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rounds said the legislation’s cost has not yet been calculated. Its supporters await a congressional budget estimate that accounts not only for the new payments, but also the savings that would come with removing up to 20 million marginal crop acres from federal subsidized crop insurance programs. 
“You might very well save money on the insurance side of it,” Rounds told reporters. 
Rounds said he hopes to add the proposal to this year’s farm bill, which has not yet advanced out of the Senate Agriculture Committee. 
Rounds shared the news of the proposal during a panel discussion held by South Dakota Farm Bureau that also included U.S. Congressman Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota.
All three agreed that getting the 60 votes in the Senate needed to pass the farm bill — which would require some Democrats to support it in an election year where they’re assumed to gain more control — was unlikely.
