name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Judge allows both new Nebraska political parties on fall ballot
description: With the emergency injunction delaying their certification being lifted, both parties will likely be certified.
text:
Lancaster County District Judge Darla Ideus addresses attorneys during a hearing at the Lancaster County Courthouse on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Kenneth Ferriera-Pool/Lincoln Journal Star)LINCOLN — A Lancaster District Court judge has dismissed objections to two new Nebraska political parties from the state’s two major parties.
Judge Darla Ideus said the Nebraska Democratic Party and National Working Families Party filed their objections too late for the Nebraska Working People Party. 
In a separate ruling, she ruled that state law doesn’t address the “confusion” that the Republican Party is claiming the America First Party would cause for voters. 
“The statute simply does not address this kind of ‘confusion.’ Also, the America First Party has not yet nominated any candidates,” Ideus wrote in her order on the Republican lawsuit. “The America First Party’s members and candidates might support the ‘America First’ agenda as the Nebraska Republican Party understands it. If so, then it is hard to see in what relevant sense the voters will be confused.”
GOP lawyers had asked Ideus to give Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen more authority to reject a party or candidate. In its lawsuit, the GOP has called John Cartier’s effort to establish the America First Party “political sabotage.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Attorneys for the Nebraska Democratic Party and the national Working Families Party had sought to compel Evnen to remove the Nebraska Working People Party because its name is too similar to the Working Families Party.
In her ruling on the Democratic lawsuit, Ideus pointed to the Nebraska Supreme Court’s ruling on the candidacy of former Democratic Senate candidate Cindy Burbank, which overruled Evnen’s decision to remove her from the primary ballot because Republicans had filed their objection too late. 
Evnen’s lawyer had argued during the hearing on the Working People Party that a seven-day window to object started after the last day to turn in signatures for a new party — July 15. The Democratic Party filed its objection Aug. 9. 
Robin Richards, sponsor of the Nebraska Working People Party, said the court decision “marks a significant victory for voter choice and the hardworking people of Nebraska.”
“For too long, Nebraska’s working families have upheld their end of the social contract. They work diligently, pay their taxes, raise their children, and sustain their communities. Yet, they have been met with a government and a political class that has failed to reciprocate that commitment,” Richards said.
With the emergency injunction delaying their certification being lifted, both parties will likely be certified.

name: VTDigger
title: Sanders rallies at St. Albans dairy processing plant, calling its closure ‘devastating’
description:
Sen. Bernie Sanders rallied support Wednesday for unionized Dairy Farmers of America workers and called for the co-op’s milk processing plant to remain open.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Sanders rallies at St. Albans dairy processing plant, calling its closure ‘devastating’.
text:
The St. Albans Creamery & Supply store on Federal Street in St. Albans on Wednesday, August 19, 2026. Photo by Bear Savage/VTDigger
ST. ALBANS — In light of the recent idling of a dairy processing plant in St. Albans, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., visited the site Wednesday to rally support for unionized workers, who have described the shutdown as an illegal act of retaliation.
Against the backdrop of the facility and speaking to the media, Sanders described Dairy Farmers of America’s decision to close the plant as having a devastating impact on workers, farmers and the Franklin County community.
The plant “has been an important part of Vermont’s dairy economy and a critical source of decent-paying jobs that workers are extremely proud of,” he said.
“While workers, farmers and community members are left searching for concrete answers and security, DFA is refusing to engage in a meaningful discussion with the union and the community and provide a transparent rationale for its decision to idle this plant,” he said. 
“Bottom line: This plant is vital to dairy farmers,” Sanders added. “It’s vital, vital to this entire community. It must not be closed, and I stand with the Teamsters to do everything that we can to make sure that it is not closed.”
Monday was the day DFA set for the plant’s idling. But after a complaint filed Friday by the Teamsters Local No. 597, claiming that the decision to close the plant was related to last year’s strike and therefore illegal, U.S. District Judge William K. Sessions III on Monday issued a temporary restraining order to halt the closure for five days.
The district court will hold a hearing Thursday afternoon, where the union will argue for a longer stay until its grievances have been resolved in keeping with the collective bargaining agreements made with DFA.
“The Teamsters will not allow DFA to punish our members for exercising their rights,” said Curtis Clough, president of the Teamsters Local 597, at the rally. “If DFA thinks they can get away with this, they are picking a fight with the wrong workers, the wrong community, the wrong union and the wrong state.” 
As soon as Sanders finished speaking to the media, he turned and spoke directly to the workers, who had been gathered behind him for the press conference. He offered his support and asked questions, listening as they described some of their experiences as the plant started to close down in recent weeks.
Multiple workers described a marked worsening in their treatment at the plant after the latest union contract was signed last fall and leading up to the plant’s idling.
“Hang in there,” Sanders said to the workers at the rally. “Thank you all for what you’re doing.”

 
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., rallied in support of unionized Dairy Farmers of America workers, calling for the plant to remain open. A federal judge this week ordered DFA to temporarily halt plans to idle the plant. Video by Bear Savage/VTDigger

The workers then went to try to clock in, but Clough said the doors to the plant were locked.
The Vermont Dairy Producers Alliance, in a July statement, said the closure of the plant in St. Albans and Franklin Foods in Enosburg Falls would mean the loss of about 150 jobs in Franklin County. The alliance also said costs will rise for farmers as more milk gets transported out of state to be processed. 
Sanders and U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., wrote a letter Tuesday to DFA President and CEO Dennis Rodenbaugh urging the co-op to keep the St. Albans plant open and reach a fair agreement with the union. DFA issued a statement in response Wednesday saying, “In June, the Cooperative informed both senatorial offices of the planned idling and have also reconfirmed the timeline in ongoing communications. It is disappointing and causes unnecessary confusion that a rally would be held asking to reverse this decision after the idling has already taken place.”
In a letter responding to Sanders and Welch on Wednesday, Rodenbaugh said, “Abiding by your request to maintain the plant’s operations and tremendous level of ongoing financial losses would inflict direct and irreparable financial harm to Vermont dairy farmers and all DFA farmer-owners and their families in the surrounding region.”
“The sole rationale for this plant closure is to protect these farm families from the financial damage of an unviable plant and provide them with an opportunity to participate in the best milk markets available in the region,” Rodenbaugh continued, saying the closure decision had been “grossly” mischaracterized. 
In closing, he wrote: “The U.S. farmer is already under tremendous pressure. We would ask and appreciate any support, including passage of a critical Farm Bill.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Judge: DOJ claims are ‘hard to take seriously’ in Iowa deportation case
description: A judge has ordered the federal government to immediately release an immigrant held in an Iowa jail, saying it’s “hard to take seriously” the U.S. Department of Justice’s arguments in the case. It’s one of an increasing number of cases in which federal judges have expressed skepticism or outright disbelief in some of the claims […]
text:
(Photo via Getty Images)A judge has ordered the federal government to immediately release an immigrant held in an Iowa jail, saying it’s “hard to take seriously” the U.S. Department of Justice’s arguments in the case.
It’s one of an increasing number of cases in which federal judges have expressed skepticism or outright disbelief in some of the claims made by U.S. Department of Justice lawyers, particularly in immigration cases.
Court records show Nyamuoch Thomas Duoth, a citizen of South Sudan, was detained by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement for the first six months of 2026. During that time, federal officials said they were trying, without success, to send her to a third country, Ethiopia.
According to federal records in the case, Duoth was born in a refugee camp in Ethiopia, and, in 1994, arrived in the United States as a refugee at the age of 4.
In August 1995, her status in the United States was adjusted to that of a lawful permanent resident. From 2008 to 2017, she was convicted of multiple criminal offenses, including resisting arrest and shoplifting, as well assault on an officer, for which she was sentenced to a term of imprisonment of two to four years.
In September 2020, an immigration judge ordered her removed to South Sudan or, in the alternative, Ethiopia. In May 2022, she was released from custody on an order of supervision after it was determined there was no “significant likelihood” the government could send her to either country.
In March 2025, ICE detained Duoth again, announcing it intended to send her back to South Sudan or Ethiopia, and asserting she would remain in custody due to the “significant likelihood of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future.”
An immigration judge’s order for removal in the case became final on Dec. 26, 2025.
After several months in custody, Duoth sought relief in the federal courts, suing ICE, Homeland Security and Pottawattamie County where she was being held. The lawsuit sought her immediate release since there appeared to be no chance of her being deported anytime soon.
U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher recently ruled in Duoth’s favor without taking the matter to a full hearing. Locher noted Duoth had been released from ICE custody in May 2022 due to there being no significant likelihood of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future. Despite that, Locher said, ICE detained her again in March 2025, and in July 2026 — more than six months since her most recent order of removal became final – she remained in ICE custody and still had not been deported.
While the federal government told the court it was “actively working with the Department of States and the Department of Homeland Security on removal to a third county,” Locher said the government provided no details on specific actions taken or explained what “actively working” meant in Duoth’s case.
“In short,” Locher wrote in his decision, the government offered “no meaningful evidence or information as to the likelihood of Ethiopia accepting (Duoth) and providing the required travel documents.” The government, he said, had failed to show any progress made toward removal since detention proceedings began.
While the government suggested Duoth’s criminal history warranted her ongoing detention, Locher said in his decision that “this argument is hard to take seriously” given that Duoth’s criminal history dated back to 2017 and earlier and she had been “on release in the community without incident for most of the years since then.” As a result, Locher concluded, Duoth had “already shown” she could safely be released.
On July 16, Locher ordered ICE to immediately release Duoth from custody, or, if she was not in Iowa, to return her to Iowa within 24 hours and then immediately release her from custody with all of her personal effects.
Duoth’s attorneys are now asking the court to order the federal government to reimburse Duoth’s attorneys for their fees and expenses.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Legislature will decide whether to apply Gov. Pillen’s 5% spending cuts during 2027 session
description: LINCOLN — When a new Nebraska Legislature convenes for its 2027 session, lawmakers will have the authority to accept or reject Gov. Jim Pillen’s plan to cut all state agencies’ budgets by a minimum of 5%. Pillen announced the spending cuts in a July memo. Though the memo announced the reductions would begin immediately, there […]
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen greets State Sen. Paul Strommen of Sidney on the final day of the 2026 legislative session. April 17, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — When a new Nebraska Legislature convenes for its 2027 session, lawmakers will have the authority to accept or reject Gov. Jim Pillen’s plan to cut all state agencies’ budgets by a minimum of 5%.
Pillen announced the spending cuts in a July memo. Though the memo announced the reductions would begin immediately, there have been some exceptions.
State officials confirmed the cuts will not apply to Nebraska’s funding formula for K-12 public schools, while the funding formula for community colleges will be impacted later in 2027. State Budget Director Neil Sullivan said Nebraska Public Employees Retirement Systems won’t be immediately impacted as the agency receives its state appropriations once per year.
Since the memo came out, there have been questions about whether Pillen has the authority to implement the cuts. Several lawmakers say it’s blatantly unconstitutional, as it oversteps the Legislature’s power to approve the state’s two-year budget, colloquially referred to as “the power of the purse.” Others say it’s not a breach because Pillen isn’t truly amending the budget.
Lee Will, director of the state Department of Administrative Services, said that when the Legislature considers budget adjustments next year to fix a projected deficit that currently stands at $208 million, lawmakers can decide to apply whatever dollars have been saved as a result of the memo and use it to help fill the gap. Or, he said, lawmakers could reject the cuts and restore the funding to the affected agencies.
A straight 5% cut across state agencies would generate about $276 million per year, according to Pillen spokesperson Laura Strimple.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
State Sen. Ashlei Spivey of Omaha, who sits on the Legislature’s Appropriations Committee, said she doesn’t want to use those dollars to fill the deficit because she is of the mindset that Pillen’s memo is unconstitutional. She said the framing of the memo was “misleading” to Nebraskans, and she doesn’t view the collected funds as savings.
“The cuts that would actually create a savings and that we need to be able to address, (Pillen is) not addressing,” Spivey said. “This is a self-imposed deficit, and so until he is willing to reconcile that and have serious conversations, then we in the Legislature need to continue to do our jobs.”
Spivey said she hopes agencies challenge Pillen’s memo through litigation. She added that the Legislature’s Executive Board, which manages the Legislative Council’s allotment in the state budget, will take up the matter of the Legislature’s own budget being reduced as part of the cuts.
Sen. Ben Hansen of Blair, the term-limited chair of the Executive Board, didn’t immediately know how much the Legislative Council would be cut, and said he hasn’t yet met with Sullivan to discuss it.
If he were returning to the Legislature in 2027, Hansen said he would encourage lawmakers to accept the cut funds. Balancing the budget is becoming more challenging with repeated sessions dealing with projected deficits, and he said lawmakers have a tough job ahead of them next year.
Hansen said he doesn’t view the governor’s spending memo as a separation of powers issue, because Pillen isn’t actually changing the budget, but instead is weighing how the appropriated funds should be spent.
Term-limited Sen. Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha, who sits on the Appropriations Committee, agreed with Spivey that Pillen’s memo is unconstitutional and misleading. She said if the governor wanted to reduce state spending, he could call a special session or request code agencies make spending cuts, which he has done before.
Sen. Paul Strommen of Sidney, who sits on the Appropriations Committee, declined to comment on whether he thought Pillen’s memo was within the governor’s authority, but noted that the process is similar to the normal process the Legislature follows to form the state budget. The governor presents a budget proposal at the start of the session, and the Legislature makes adjustments to that proposal before finalizing it.
Strommen said he was undecided on whether the Legislature should use the money saved through the cuts to reduce the deficit, noting that it was too early to determine the need for it. He acknowledged that the state is in a tough financial position, and said people need to come with ideas to solve it.
Strommen said the next meeting of Nebraska’s Economic Forecasting Advisory Board in October is the “biggest piece of the puzzle” in determining how lawmakers should form the budget next session. The board’s projections will solidify the size of the projected deficit in the state’s current budget and the next biennial budget that lawmakers are tasked with finalizing in 2027.
“If those numbers come up, and we’re only $100 million (in the red), it changes the way that we’re going to approach cuts and deficit spending,” Strommen said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Invasive beetle that has wiped out millions of ash trees confirmed in Washington
description: One of the most destructive invasive pests in the nation has arrived in southern Washington, posing a grave threat to ash trees.  State officials confirmed the presence of the emerald ash borer Wednesday after two people passing through Vancouver spotted the insect on their windshield in early August. They took photos, collected the specimen and […]
text:
(Photo by Stephen Ausmus/U.S. Department of Agriculture)One of the most destructive invasive pests in the nation has arrived in southern Washington, posing a grave threat to ash trees. 
State officials confirmed the presence of the emerald ash borer Wednesday after two people passing through Vancouver spotted the insect on their windshield in early August. They took photos, collected the specimen and turned it over to officials for identification.
“We anticipated it would only be a matter of time before emerald ash borer arrived in our state,” said Sven Spichiger, pest program manager at the Washington State Department of Agriculture. “This is yet another example of how alert, observant members of the public help us detect new, invasive pests.” 
There has never been a successful eradication of the emerald ash borer, a metallic green beetle that feeds on wood, according to the state’s Department of Agriculture. The insect has wiped out more than 100 million ash trees in the United States since its initial detection twenty years ago. 
All true ash species are vulnerable to an infestation. 
Without efforts to manage an outbreak, municipalities can expect to lose 90% to 100% of their ash trees within 10 to 12 years of an initial infestation, according to a Department of Natural Resources analysis. 
The only reliable method to contain an outbreak is by limiting firewood transportation and replacing infested trees with non-ash species, according to the Department of Agriculture. On Tuesday, the department started a firewood quarantine, which prohibits the transportation of untreated firewood in the state. 
State officials have been preparing for the pest’s arrival for years. Washington state agencies have developed an Emerald Ash Borer Resource and Management Guide and an Urban Forest Pest Readiness Playbook to help residents and local governments detect and respond to infestations. 
Forestry assistance for municipalities is available through the Department of Natural Resources as long as funding is available. 
State officials are urging the public to keep an eye out for the pest and report suspected sightings to the Washington Invasive Species Council or via the Washington Invasives app.
“This is deeply unfortunate, but we knew the emerald ash borer would arrive here and we’ve been preparing for it,” said Dave Upthegrove, Commissioner of Public Lands. “Please use our shared resources to educate yourselves and heed the recommendations to slow the spread of this destructive pest.” 
The beetle has been active on the West Coast since it was detected in Forest Grove, Oregon, west of Portland, in 2022. It was detected a year later in Vancouver, British Columbia.

title: Arkansas governor appoints temporary justice to state  Supreme Court
description: Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders appointed attorney Cory Cox to temporarily serve on the state Supreme Court for Justice Barbara Webb, who is recovering from a head injury sustained during a fall. Webb has been absent from the court since May, when she injured her head in a fall, and has been recuperating in Houston. Chief […]
text:
The Arkansas Justice Building on the state Capitol grounds in Little Rock on Jan. 14, 2025. The building houses the state Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals and the Administrative Office of the Courts. (Photo by Sonny Albarado/Arkansas Advocate)Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders appointed attorney Cory Cox to temporarily serve on the state Supreme Court for Justice Barbara Webb, who is recovering from a head injury sustained during a fall.
Supreme Court Justice Barbara Webb (Photo courtesy of the Arkansas Supreme Court)
Webb has been absent from the court since May, when she injured her head in a fall, and has been recuperating in Houston. Chief Justice Karen Baker last week requested Sanders appoint someone to fill in for Webb as she recovers.
“Cory is a highly accomplished attorney, has decades of government experience, and is a dedicated public servant,” the Republican governor said in a statement. “As we pray for Justice Webb’s recovery, I know Cory has the character and work ethic to serve on the Court and uphold our Constitution.”
When a justice is temporarily unable to serve, the Arkansas Constitution requires the governor to appoint a special justice to take their place.
Cox previously served as Republican Lt. Gov. Leslie Rutledge’s chief of staff when she was attorney general. He was also deputy legal counsel for Sanders’ father, former Republican Gov. Mike Huckabee, during his time in office.
Cox said he was “deeply honored” by the appointment. The court is nonpartisan, but Republican-supported justices hold a 5-2 majority, including Webb.
“I pray that Justice Webb makes a full and speedy recovery. Until that time, I look forward to working with the Court’s other justices to uphold Arkansas law and protect and defend the rights of Arkansas citizens,” he said in the press release.
Webb’s absence first became known on May 12, when Baker wrote to the governor that she was temporarily unable to serve on several appeals the high court was set to hear. Cox was subsequently appointed to hear those cases, both involving special elections, where lower courts had ruled Sanders violated the state constitution in the way she scheduled them. 
The Democratic Party of Arkansas, the plaintiffs in the case over House District 70’s special election, objected to his appointment and argued Sanders could not select a special justice to hear a case where she was the defendant. 
The cases were ultimately dismissed as moot since the special elections had occurred in March, and Cox was never sworn in.
Webb’s injury was not made public until last month. Her husband Doyle Webb, a former chairman of the state GOP and Arkansas Public Service Commission chairman, said in July that he expected his wife would return for the court’s fall term.
Cox’s appointment runs until Barbara Webb returns to the Supreme Court, or Dec. 31, whichever comes first.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell announces he’s running for attorney general
description: State Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell announces his candidacy for attorney general at the Republican Party headquarters in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026.
text:
Sean Tindell, commissioner of the Department of Public Safety, announced on Wednesday that he will run in the Republican primary next year for attorney general, Mississippi’s top legal official. 
Tindell launched his campaign Wednesday morning in Gulfport and began a statewide tour with stops in Jackson, Tupelo and Southaven. 
“Mississippi needs leaders who are focused less on petty disputes and more on working together and getting things done for the people we serve,” Tindell said. “That’s what I’m running for attorney general.” 
Tindell has led DPS since Gov. Tate Reeves appointed him to the post in 2020. Tindell previously served as a judge on the Mississippi Court of Appeals for three years and previously represented the Gulfport area in the state Senate for five years. 
Tindell said he is “uniquely qualified” to serve as attorney general because of his legislative, judicial and agency experience. He specifically pointed to his initiative to reduce the time the public waits at driver’s license bureaus and his efforts to reduce the autopsy backlog at the Mississippi Forensics Laboratory. 
“With me, there is no need for on-the-job training,” Tindell said. 
The state attorney general is the chief legal officer and advisor for the state, handles civil and criminal legal matters, represents state agencies and public officials in court and issues legal interpretations of state laws. 
Supporters gather as Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell announces his candidacy for attorney general at the Republican Party headquarters in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
If elected, Tindell said he plans to ask the Legislature to expand the scope of his office to handle more public corruption cases and work to provide public bodies with AGl opinions quicker. He also said he plans to eventually resign as commissioner to focus on campaigning for attorney general full time, though he doesn’t have a specific timeline for the resignation.
The attorney general slot will be an open seat because current Attorney General Lynn Fitch has announced she will run for governor next year. Tindell is the only candidate so far to announce he’s seeking the office. 
Henry Babour, a national GOP strategist, said on Mississippi Today’s “The Other Side” politics podcast that state Sen. Briggs Hopson, a Republican from Vicksburg who leads the Senate Appropriations Committee, will soon announce he’s running for attorney general.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: US ag exports ‘on the right track,’ trade rep says, but farmers still wary
description: GRAND FORKS, N.D. — North Dakota farm group representatives called for more certainty in U.S. ag trade policy, while U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak and a U.S. trade representative said tariffs and tough trade negotiations will pay off in the long run.  U.S. Chief Agricultural Negotiator Julie Callahan fielded questions about Trump administration trade policies on[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak, right, hosted trade negotiator Julie Callahan to discuss agriculture in Grand Forks, North Dakota, on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor) GRAND FORKS, N.D. — North Dakota farm group representatives called for more certainty in U.S. ag trade policy, while U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak and a U.S. trade representative said tariffs and tough trade negotiations will pay off in the long run. 
U.S. Chief Agricultural Negotiator Julie Callahan fielded questions about Trump administration trade policies on beef, soybeans, sugar and other commodities Wednesday at an ag roundtable in Grand Forks hosted by Fedorchak, R-N.D. 
The ag sector has been under pressure from lost exports and higher farm operating costs, prompting the Trump administration to offer assistance payments to help farmers stay in business.
“I think, as we move forward, really addressing some of the uncertainty that persists in our markets is really important, and making sure that we have stable trade relationships is key,” said Matt Perdue, president of the North Dakota Farmers Union.
Higher ethanol blends would benefit consumers, corn industry, panel says

Perdue, who farms with his family in northwest North Dakota, said Trump trade policies have affected North Dakota farmers beyond ag markets. He said farmers in his area have had more difficulty getting steel grain bins and parts to repair equipment that come from Canada. 
Callahan and Fedorchak pointed to 10 trade agreements reached under the Trump administration and others still to be finalized as signs that some of the market access lost in trade wars with China and other countries is coming back. 
“I’m not going to rest until we have an ag trade surplus with the world, and we’re really on the right track,” Callahan said. 
Callahan said the U.S. is “serious about enforcing” commitments from China to buy U.S. soybeans. 
Brent Kohls, a representative of the North Dakota Soybean Growers Association, said after the meeting that he has seen improvement from the early days of Trump’s second term 
“It was kind of shock and awe right away,” he said. But the soybean market has improved in recent weeks. 
Brent Kohls of the North Dakota Soybean Growers Association, left, speaks Aug. 19, 2026, in Grand Forks at ag roundtable event. At right is TJ Hall of the North Dakota Potato Growers Association. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
North Dakota relies on soybeans exports through the Pacific Northwest with China as the main market.
“The conversation today versus a year ago is a whole lot different with China, and for the better,” he said. 
But he said he is not certain the roller-coaster ride the ag industry has been on is over yet, with uncertainty on the costs of farm needs such as fertilizer and fuel and whether trade agreements will last.  
“We’re hanging on. We haven’t taken our seat belt off,” said Kohls, who farms south of Mayville. 
Beef producer Lacey Grann Wirth, representing the North Dakota Stockmen’s Association, asked why the U.S. was not putting tariffs on beef imports from Brazil. 
Callahan said that was a decision by President Donald Trump as a way to address affordability of beef for U.S. consumers. 
Grann Wirth, a beef producer near Sheyenne, has a problem with that. “It takes away the value of our own products,” she said. 
Fedorchak noted that beef is one of the bright spots in the U.S. ag industry, with consumer demand still high despite inflated prices. She said the U.S. should be trying to expand its beef industry, which has been affected by drought in key states over several years. 
“From the producer’s standpoint, anything we do as a country to incentivize others to come into the market to lower prices takes away the incentive for people to get into that industry here,” Fedorchak said. 
Callahan’s visit also included a trip to a honey farm and a tour of the state-owned North Dakota Mill and Elevator.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Vilsack endorses Sand and his farm policy proposals
description: ANKENY – Democratic candidate for governor Rob Sand spoke with farmers and former Iowa governor and former U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Tom Vilsack Wednesday about his plans to support Iowa’s rural and agricultural economies.  Vilsack said he was “excited” by Sand’s “innovative” approach that aims to make farms, rather than farmers, work harder.  “It’s very[...]
text:
Former Iowa governor and former U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Tom Vilsack, left, speaks at a roundtable Aug. 19, 2026 supporting Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, center, and lieutenant governor nominee Dave Muhlbauer, right. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) ANKENY – Democratic candidate for governor Rob Sand spoke with farmers and former Iowa governor and former U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Tom Vilsack Wednesday about his plans to support Iowa’s rural and agricultural economies. 
Vilsack said he was “excited” by Sand’s “innovative” approach that aims to make farms, rather than farmers, work harder. 
“It’s very direct, and I think it speaks significantly and centrally to the challenges that many Iowa farmers face today,” Vilsack said of the policy proposal. “And I think, frankly, it will have a profound impact on not just the farm community but on rural communities generally.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sand’s “Opportunities for All” policy includes a plan to invest in programs that will diversify the family farm with things like manure digesters that process manure into renewable natural gas and an easily transportable, rather than liquid, fertilizer. Vilsack has been a proponent of this technology, which can add an additional, on-farm revenue stream. 
Vilsack said farmers have been in a “farm crisis since 1973” when the focus of the farm shifted “solely on productivity and production.” 
“American farmers have done exactly what we asked them to do,” Vilsack said. “The problem is that it only benefits fairly large-scale operations, and as a result, over the course of the last 50, 60 years, we’ve lost nearly a million farms in America.” 
The loss of these farms, he said, was a “significant hit to rural communities.” 
“I think you two gentlemen have laid out a plan that addresses the fundamental weakness of our current farm policy,” Vilsack said, speaking to Sand and lieutenant governor nominee Dave Muhlbauer. “Your plan is predicated on a very simple proposition which is, it’s not the farmer that you have to work harder.” 
Vilsack, along with more than 50 other farmers and former Iowa agricultural leaders comprise the list of “Ag Leaders for Sand” who endorsed Sand and Muhlbauer Wednesday. 
The list included former Iowa Secretary of Agriculture and former lieutenant governor Patty Judge, along with two former presidents of the Iowa and National Corn Growers Associations, former officials who served in various U.S. Department of Agriculture offices and farmers from counties across the state. 
LaVon Griffieon, a Polk County century farmer who hosted the roundtable and also endorsed Sand, said the “Opportunities for All” policy was a “breath of fresh air.” 
The plan also includes Sand’s aim to raise the state minimum wage to $12 per hour, to end the state’s privatized system for Medicaid, build more houses in rural Iowa and to establish a “rural prosperity” office.  
When asked about funding these programs to help farmers diversify their operations, Sand said Iowa’s Natural Resources and Outdoor Recreation trust fund, often referred to as Iowa’s Water and Land Legacy or IWILL, could be a “massive source of funding.” 
The trust was approved by voters in 2010 to fund things like outdoor recreation and cleaner water, but the trust, which would receive three-eighths of one cent revenue from a sales tax increase, has never been funded. 
Sand said if it had been funded 16 years ago when 63% of Iowans voted for the measure, “we would be 16 years ahead of where we are right now.” 
“Farmers are part of the solution, Sand said. “They sign up for these conservation programs, they get put on a wait list. The problem is politicians.” 
It’s politicians’ responsibility to “fix this” and support programs that help farmers with things like conservation, at the level that farmers want to participate, Sand said. 
The Democratic nominee for secretary of agriculture Chris Jones has proposed policies to diversify Iowa’s crop land and work to improve the state’s water, though his approach involves a significant deviation from Iowa’s current model that prioritizes corn, soybeans and ethanol. When asked by reporters about Jones’ policy, Sand said he hasn’t read Jones’ proposals and that he has not been “weighing in” on other races and doesn’t plan to do so. 
Sand is running against Republican Zach Lahn, who has proposed anti-trust lawsuits against agricultural input companies and protecting Iowa land ownership, among other things, as ways to support family farms.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: To build healthcare affordability in Alaska, we need to look at care costs
description: Imagine tearing a ligament on a weekend hike and calling around for a price on the surgery, only to find that the same procedure costs twice as much at one hospital as it does at another less than a hundred miles away. No difference in the treatment, no difference in the outcome. Just a difference […]
text:
Trinitas Regional Medical Center in Elizabeth, Monday April 20, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Imagine tearing a ligament on a weekend hike and calling around for a price on the surgery, only to find that the same procedure costs twice as much at one hospital as it does at another less than a hundred miles away. No difference in the treatment, no difference in the outcome. Just a difference in the location.
That’s not a hypothetical. It’s what KFF Health News reported happened to Marcelle Crago, a nurse in Asheville, North Carolina, who tore her meniscus while cross-country skiing. Her local hospital quoted her more than $9,000 for the procedure. She postponed the surgery, shopped around, and found an outpatient center down the road, unaffiliated with the hospital, that charged less than a third of that price for the same operation.
It’s a North Carolina story, but Alaskans should recognize the shape of it immediately because we’ve been living a version of it for years.
Alaska has carried the highest or near-highest healthcare costs in the nation for 15 consecutive years, according to Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development data. Costs in Anchorage, Juneau and Fairbanks run about 50% above the U.S. urban average. Urban Alaskans spend roughly 12% of household income on medical care, compared with 8% nationally. Providers here charge commercial insurers more than twice what Medicare pays for the same professional services, the highest ratio of any state in the country.
These numbers matter because they eventually show up in the places that affect everyday life: family budgets, business expenses, employee paychecks and monthly premiums.
 Hospital care drives the bulk of it. Nationally, hospitals accounted for roughly 40% of the total growth in healthcare spending between 2022 and 2024, more than any other part of the system, and consolidation is a major reason why. As more physicians and clinics become part of larger hospital-owned systems, the same visit or procedure often costs more, simply because of where it happens to take place. Alaska is especially exposed. A small population spread across enormous distances means limited providers in any given region. When the next option for care is a plane ticket away rather than a drive across town, the competitive pressure that holds prices down elsewhere doesn’t exist.
To be fair, delivering care in Alaska is genuinely expensive. Recruiting clinicians in a high-cost state, maintaining services across roadless geography and absorbing federal reimbursement pressures are real burdens our providers carry. Healthcare affordability is a challenge we all must tackle together.
But after 15 years among the most expensive healthcare markets in America, we should be willing to ask hard questions about what is driving those costs and who ultimately bears them. Premera Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alaska has served this state since 1952, before statehood. We believe Alaska families and employers deserve a healthcare system that is both high quality and affordable. When healthcare costs rise faster than wages, inflation and economic growth, the consequences are felt by every household and every business that provides coverage. Increasing health insurance claims and premiums are a function of the underlying cost of care, with more than 90% of every premium dollar received going straight to the providers of care, largely driven by hospital costs.
The conversation about healthcare costs cannot stop at premiums. We need greater transparency into the prices charged throughout the healthcare system so Alaskans can better understand what drives the bills they receive. We also need policymakers, purchasers and healthcare organizations to work together to address the factors that make Alaska an outlier year after year.
Affordability is not an insurance issue. It is an Alaska issue.
The nurse in North Carolina only had a road to drive down for more affordable care. For too many Alaskans, that road doesn’t exist. There’s only a plane ticket and a much longer wait.
Until it does, making healthcare more affordable should be a priority for all of us.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming’s primary election drew a 55% turnout among registered voters
description:
Registered voter turnout was much less than in 2022 when Hageman challenged Cheney, but otherwise tracked primary elections going back to about 2016.
The post Wyoming’s primary election drew a 55% turnout among registered voters appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming voter turnout in the primary election — among registered voters — was on pace with primaries going back to about 2016.
Of 273,705 registered voters, 150,359 cast a ballot, putting the primary election turnout rate at about 54.9%, state data shows. That’s a fraction more than the 2024 primary at 54.3%, but significantly lower than the 63.5% turnout rate in 2022 — a standout primary that pundits chalked up to Harriet Hageman’s Trump-backed bid to oust U.S. Rep. Liz Cheney that year.
Turnout among all eligible voters, however, looks much different. 
Based on Wyoming’s voting-age population — last estimated by the state in 2024 at 454,508 — eligible voter turnout was closer to 33%. The state recorded a 27% turnout among voting-age residents in the 2024 primary, 40.8% in 2022 and 31.5% in 2020.


Total ballot tallies followed Wyoming demographics, with the most populated counties — Laramie and Natrona — counting 23,325 ballots and 17,744, respectively.
Registered voter turnout also followed the blend of political-and-population county characteristics.
Wyoming’s least-populated counties — Niobrara, ranked 23rd of 23 counties at about 2,400, 22nd-ranked Hot Springs (4,600) and 19th-ranked Crook (7,913) — also tend to have the highest percentage of registered Republicans. Those counties showed the highest percentages of ballots cast among registered voters: 69.6%, 69.4% and 68.7% respectively. Teton and Albany — with the highest percentages of registered Democrats — had the lowest percentages of total ballots cast, followed by Carbon County.
Of the 150,359 ballots cast, 88% were Republican and 9% were Democratic, which closely tracks Wyoming’s Republican-Democratic split among registered voters. 
Always an area of interest in any Wyoming primary is whether crossover voting — voters changing their party affiliation to participate in the crowded GOP nomination process — might have factored into the results. Not only is it a sore point among hard-line politicos and some candidates, but drawing definitive conclusions from raw registration figures is rife with nuance.
Albany County, for example, listed 10,702 registered Republicans in January, and 11,130 on Aug. 1, while the number of registered Democrats shrunk from 4,400 to 4,119 during the same period, state data shows. But the 428 registration gain for Republicans can’t be directly tied to the 281 loss in Democratic registrations, considering first time registrations and people dying or leaving the state.
Casper resident and Vietnam veteran Budd Pitt proudly shows off multiple forms of identification he took with him to the polls on Aug. 18, 2026. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Lawmakers in 2023 passed a law shortening early and absentee voting from 45 days to 28 days. In an effort aimed at discouraging so-called crossover voting, lawmakers also passed in 2023 another law requiring voters wanting to change their party to do so before candidates for partisan positions begin filing for office. 
This year, registered Republicans cast 132,705 ballots amid the high-profile battle between more moderate lawmakers and the hard-line Freedom Caucus-aligned faction of the party. 
Casper resident Rexine Collins had a clear preference in the Republican ideological battle. Her priority, she told WyoFile, was “making sure we have very conservative, unapologetic Republicans in office.”
The caucus, which took over the State House in 2025, lost 13 incumbents in the House and failed to make significant gains in the Senate. Freedom Caucus-aligned candidates also failed to win nominations in all four contested executive seat races, including the governor’s office.  
After casting her ballot at Restoration Church on Casper’s east side, a woman told WyoFile, “I’m voting against the people I don’t want in there.” Another voter in Evansville told WyoFile, “I just vote for the lesser of evils — the ones I think might do the least damage.”
