name: Florida Phoenix
title: The James Fishback campaign has ended. What about the movement behind it?
description: TAMPA — Investment firm CEO James Fishback’s time in the Florida political spotlight ended Tuesday night when he finished a distant third with 10% of the vote in the race for the Republican nomination for governor. “He didn’t do great, but as someone who was considered somewhat of a fringe candidate, and sort of dismissed […]
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback greets a supporter after his concession speech at the Hilton Tampa Airport Westshore on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)TAMPA — Investment firm CEO James Fishback’s time in the Florida political spotlight ended Tuesday night when he finished a distant third with 10% of the vote in the race for the Republican nomination for governor.
“He didn’t do great, but as someone who was considered somewhat of a fringe candidate, and sort of dismissed by the mainstream Republican Party, he got 10%. So, that’s the other way at looking at it,” said University of Central Florida political science professor Aubrey Jewett.
Fishback’s election night watch party at the Hilton Tampa Airport Westshore was dominated by young white men, the demographic that responded most enthusiastically to his unconventional, anti-establishment campaign.
Jake Hoffman, executive director of the Tampa Bay Young Republicans, attributed Fishback’s appeal to the fact that Americans, and not just Republicans, “are still searching for disruptive candidates that give a middle finger to the political establishment.
“He appealed to 18–30-year-old males because he spoke directly to their economic pains, such as being unable to own a home, find a job, and start a family,” he said. “The other candidates in the race have been in politics long enough that they represented more of the same broken promises by Washington, D.C.”
Several of those young males told the Phoenix Tuesday night that they appreciated Fishback’s “Florida First” agenda.
“I think that he has been very successful in marketing to our generation with a lot of social media,” said David Ramirez, 18, from Plant City. “And our generation, I think we’ve seen what the establishment Republicans have done for us, which is not very much. And James is very against that, and he’s been very vocal about trying to help us when we grow up be able to afford anything.”
Loving ‘this anti-establishment stance’
Corey Griffore, 20, said he dropped out of high school to start a boat detailing company that now employs 10 people in Pinellas County. In dealing with “this older generation,” he said, he doesn’t see a lot of evidence of critical thinking.
Corey Griffore, 20, from Land O’ Lakes, at the James Fishback campaign watch party in Tampa on August 18, 2026 (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix).
“I just see a lot of, ‘Hey, we’re going with the party kind of thing.’ So, I love this anti-establishment stance,” he said about Fishback.
Like several people the Phoenix spoke to Tuesday night, Griffore said he won’t vote for Byron Donalds and may in fact vote for David Jolly in November.
“The reason being, if we always just blanket vote for who our party puts up front, well then how are we going to get real change?” he said. “If we can always just have people funding our primaries, and then we’re just going to vote for them anyway because we’re a red state? How are we ever going to have real change?”
Hoffman believes many in Tuesday crowd had never voted in a Republican primary before, “so are we missing votes if they didn’t exist in the equation already?”
Fishback campaigned against data centers, Flock cameras, and H-1B visas. He frequently invoked his Christian faith and promised every abortion clinic would be shut down if he had the power to do so. He targeted Donalds by calling him a “slave” to corporate interests and a “DEI Republican.”  His strong criticisms of the Israeli government led to accusations of antisemitism.
Tuesday night, Nick Fuentes, a far-right activist known for his antisemitic views, effusively praised Fishback’s campaign.
“He is truly a model that everyone should look up towards,” Fuentes said. “That is what a proto-groyper president is gonna look, sound and act like.”
Controversies
How wild was Fishback’s campaign? Here’s a sampling of some of the non-policy issues that emerged since he entered the governor’s race late last year:

A federal judge rule that he owes his former hedge fund employer, Greenlight Capital, more than $1.3 million for breaching his employment agreement by misappropriating and disseminating Greenlight’s confidential information.
Was sued for allegedly stiffing a high school debate champion by not delivering $8,000 in scholarship money she won from a company he founded.
Avoided being thrown off the ballot after gubernatorial candidate Jay Collins went to court to challenge whether he had violated the state’s seven-year residency requirement. In a court hearing, Fishback acknowledged he had voted in Washington, D.C., in 2020 and held a homestead exemption there. However, a Leon County judge agreed Fishback hadn’t meant to establish residency in D.C. and said it wasn’t the court’s job to decide who would become Florida’s next governor.
Selected a running mate, Sean Lozano, who’d been fired from the Lauderhill Police Department and deemed “permanently unfit for duty” and is now being investigated for his conduct in a particular incident there by the Broward County State Attorney’s office.
Made various comments perceived as being racist and antisemitic and was banned from the Republican Party of Florida’s “Sunshine Showdown Summit” in June that he had originally been invited to.
Alleged Donalds was under federal investigation for sex trafficking. “They are investigating him because there is credible evidence that he committed a serious crime,” Fishback said in a press release. The Department of Justice announced the next day that it was not.

“Obviously, the accusations were some of the most ridiculous things I’ve ever heard in my life,” Donalds told the Phoenix two days later in Tampa. “And I’ve heard some doozies in my years in politics. … It’s unfortunate that people decide they just want to assassinate your character because they have not proven any ability to be competitive and win on their own, so they have to stoop to that level.”
 The movement
In his concession speech, Fishback said while his candidacy has ended, the movement behind it has not.
“Our opposition had over $100 million,” he said. “We had one percent of that. And yet, we secured 10 times as many votes as the dollars we raised because this campaign from the beginning has not been about AIPAC, it’s been about impact here in Florida. The truth is that it’s quite fitting that our movement has taken to new heights.
“Remember how they tried to sue us off the ballot. Not because they were afraid of me, but because they were afraid of you. Remember the attack ad during the World Cup? They knew this race would turn out the next generation, and the next generation is fed up. Now is the time to recommit ourselves to the founding values that set this great nation into motion.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Jefferson County clerk seeks court’s guidance on questions about voters’ residency
description: Jefferson County Clerk David Yates said his office will take legal action to get judicial guidance on how to handle the reassignment of dozens of voters on the Jefferson-Oldham County line.  Yates, a Democrat, plans to file a Petition for a Declaration of Rights, a Wednesday morning press release said. With that action, the Franklin […]
text:
Democratic Jefferson County Clerk David Yates announces that his office has filed a motion to intervene in the U.S. Department of Justice's lawsuit demanding sensitive Kentucky voter information. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)Jefferson County Clerk David Yates said his office will take legal action to get judicial guidance on how to handle the reassignment of dozens of voters on the Jefferson-Oldham County line. 
Yates, a Democrat, plans to file a Petition for a Declaration of Rights, a Wednesday morning press release said. With that action, the Franklin County Circuit Court can “provide guidance regarding the duties of election officials, the rights of affected voters, and the legal effect of election residency determinations when those determinations appear inconsistent with other governmental records.” 
“My office has a responsibility to maintain accurate voter registration records and to follow Kentucky election law,” Yates said in a statement. “At the same time, residents have raised legitimate questions that deserve clear answers and a fair process. Rather than have election officials resolve those questions independently, I believe the courts are the appropriate forum to provide clarity, consistency, and confidence for everyone involved.”
Questions about which county voters reside in were prompted by a review of voter information Yates’ office began earlier this year after eight voters were unable to vote in the 44th House District primary. Yates appeared before a legislative committee Tuesday morning with Franklin County Clerk Jeff Hancock to discuss how a 2022 law to centralize state mapping may not reflect what’s happening at the local level. Yates said in some cases where a person resides on a county line, they may pay taxes in one county but vote in another. 
The information from the state mapping system, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), is used for the election system across all of Kentucky’s 120 counties, the clerk’s office press release said. The court guidance could be used by county clerks statewide when questions come up about a voter’s county residence. 
During the legislative meeting, Rep. James Tipton, R-Taylorsville, said the mapping issue affected voters in Spencer and Shelby counties ahead of the 2024 primary election. That prompted not only voting-related questions, but also concerns about where school buses should go and which first responder departments served those residents, he added.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ strikes 5,100 from voter rolls in wake of registration gaffe
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Wednesday her administration is committed to conducting “strong and fair elections.” A state review found thousands of noncitizens may have been registered to vote.
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Wednesday her administration is committed to conducting “strong and fair elections.” A state review found thousands of noncitizens may have been registered to vote. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey officials have deleted 5,100 registered voters from state voter rolls and directed another 1,650 to county election officials for review, one month after Gov. Mikie Sherrill revealed that thousands of noncitizens may have registered to vote after interactions with the Motor Vehicle Commission.
Sherrill announced the moves Wednesday, saying only about 340 of 6,600 erroneously registered to vote in 2023 and 2024 actually voted. She has blamed the problem on a software error by Idemia, the vendor that has managed driver’s license printing in New Jersey since 2010, and blasted former Gov. Phil Murphy’s administration for transparency and accountability failures. Idemia has denied responsibility for the problem, and Murphy has said he was unaware of it.
NJ Republicans target two laws as they seek probe into non-citizen voting reveal

Sherrill on Wednesday said state officials have worked around the clock to fix the issue and review state records “to preserve the integrity of our voter rolls, and ensure that our elections remain free and fair.”
“I said we would conduct a thorough, complete, and fair investigation, and that is exactly what we are doing. Because that is what accountable government looks like,” she said in a statement. “My commitment to the people of New Jersey is to confront this issue with the urgency it deserves, so we have strong and fair elections.”
Republicans, including those in the Trump administration, have criticized Sherrill for the voter registration debacle, saying it proves their claims that noncitizens have committed widespread voter fraud. On Wednesday Sherrill said the GOP’s “only interest has been in trying to use this issue for political gain.”
Assemblyman Paul Kanitra (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Assemblyman Paul Kanitra (R-Ocean), one of the Republicans who have sharply criticized the Sherrill administration and Democrats on this issue, believes the number of noncitizens who have cast ballots could be far larger than state officials have admitted. Kanita told the New Jersey Monitor Wednesday that the governor has been less than fully transparent here by not specifying where and in what elections noncitizens have voted.
“Governor Sherrill has over and over again minimized the harsh reality created by her own party members: hundreds of noncitizens have voted in several elections in New Jersey,” he said, adding, “We need total and full cooperation of the Sherrill Administration right now. Anything less is a betrayal of the office of governor.”
State officials took New Jersey’s voter registration system offline briefly so state election officials could copy and preserve it and then update it to remove or modify the status of people impacted, she said.
That review drove the state to delete 5,100 of the improperly registered voters from voter rolls because officials could find no other proof of their eligibility to vote. State officials also changed the status of about 1,450 others to “rejected” pending further review, because they found separate voter registrations or other transactions in the system suggesting eligibility. County election officials have been tasked with verifying their eligibility and further amending their status after that review.
Sherrill, who has previously said fewer than 400 of the wrongly registered people had actually cast ballots, put that number at 340 on Wednesday. An additional 220 voted but had previously been registered to vote or otherwise had made attestations in state systems suggesting they are eligible, Sherrill said. County officials also are reviewing that second batch of people, too, to verify eligibility.
Sherrill said her administration has directed county officials to complete their reviews before voting begins in the upcoming general election. The state’s investigation remains ongoing, she added.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Direct cash assistance program for single moms to expand with $1.4M funding boost
description: A direct cash assistance program for low-income single mothers is expanding to include dozens more families after receiving an anonymous $1.47 million donation.  Project Home Trust, started in 2024 by Portland-based nonprofit Project Home, is currently helping its third cohort of families, with 50 mothers and their children in three counties receiving monthl[...]
text:
Portland's economic director Melissa Hue with future Project HOME Trust participant Zeinab Hijazi, former participant Allison Edwards and her daughter and the project's program director, Peace Mutesi, on stage at a Quality Housing Coalition Event. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/ Maine Morning Star)A direct cash assistance program for low-income single mothers is expanding to include dozens more families after receiving an anonymous $1.47 million donation. 
Project Home Trust, started in 2024 by Portland-based nonprofit Project Home, is currently helping its third cohort of families, with 50 mothers and their children in three counties receiving monthly direct cash assistance. 
So far, the program has helped people in Cumberland, York and Androscoggin counties, but the donation will help it expand to another county, which the organization hopes will help single moms in more rural areas of the state. It will also allow 100 mothers and their children to receive $500 in financial assistance each month for the next three years. To qualify, a single mom has to make no more than 60% of the area median income.
The expansion comes at a time when many vulnerable families, including the immigrants who are served through this program, are being cut off from social safety nets after eligibility changes to federal healthcare and food aid.
“There definitely is a need. We’re also seeing that just across the board with the cuts to SNAP and Medicaid. People are hungry who were not hungry before, and families are stretched so incredibly thin because costs continue to rise,” said Victoria Morales, executive director of Project Home.
“So that’s impacting children …and single moms too, obviously, in ways that we hadn’t seen two years ago.”
After strong start, organizers hope to expand Maine’s guaranteed income pilot program

Direct cash assistance provides financial support without restrictions on how it must be spent, allowing families to respond to their most urgent needs, including housing, food, childcare, transportation, healthcare and education. Surveys conducted by one of Project Home’s partner organizations found that this kind of assistance has reduced poverty, improved health and nutrition, supported children’s education and strengthened local economies.
The program also helps families navigate the “benefits cliff,” Morales said, which occurs when an increase in income reduces or eliminates a household’s eligibility for public programs that help cover necessities.
It “gives mothers room to navigate that transition while building toward greater stability,” said Peace Mutesi, the group’s director of economic opportunity.
Participants in the first cohort two years ago received $1000 per month to help with rent, household expenses and emergencies , which they described as life-changing. After that cohort, the amount was gradually reduced to $500, Morales said.
The organization has not yet looked at how reducing the assistance amount will impact the benefits previous cohorts reported. Morales told Maine Morning Star that the reduction was based on national studies on the 2021 child tax credit, which showed that $6000 annually was sufficient to pull families out of poverty. She added that Project Home Trust comes with peer support and housing assistance to offer holistic support throughout the duration of the program.
An evaluation of Project Home’s second cohort, completed in late 2025, found that by the program’s conclusion, all participants were caught up on rent, their average weekly work hours had increased and food insecurity had decreased. Some families also enrolled in educational programs or training opportunities. The first cohort reported many of the same outcomes.
“This model is showing that people stay in the same homes, they’re able to continue to pay their rent, and even we’ve had a few of our moms purchase homes who started out in this program,” Morales said. “And so, really seeing this as a driver of lasting financial and housing security.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine voters wanted limits on political spending. What they got was another Big Money race.
description: Maine voters didn’t just cap super PAC contributions in 2024, they did it by a landslide. Three out of four said yes to Question 1, a citizen’s initiative that limited campaign contributions to political action committees that make uncoordinated expenditures in support of a candidate to $5,000. But right now, in the middle of the […]
text:
A Question 1 campaign sign in Portland. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Maine voters didn’t just cap super PAC contributions in 2024, they did it by a landslide. Three out of four said yes to Question 1, a citizen’s initiative that limited campaign contributions to political action committees that make uncoordinated expenditures in support of a candidate to $5,000.
But right now, in the middle of the state’s consequential governor’s race, that cap does not exist. Two super PACs sued the state of Maine to stop the new contribution limit from taking effect, and a federal judge sided with them, calling it unconstitutional on its face, and the case is sitting before the First Circuit Court of Appeals waiting on a ruling. 
In the meantime, Maine’s governor’s race and other key elections are being run under the same rules the law was written to replace.
Hannah Pingree, a former speaker of the Maine House and now the Democratic nominee for governor, built her campaign on volume, not size. 
By January, her filings showed contributions from more than 1,800 individual donors with roughly 40% of her $1.4 million made up of gifts of $50 or less. 
Pingree will now face Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett in the November general election and her campaign has seemingly shifted away from courting small-dollar donations. The latest filing shows that between late May and mid-July, the candidate received just over $900,000 with only about $40,000 coming from donations of $50 or less.
What’s more, a Democratic Governors Association-aligned super PAC, Pine Tree State Prosperity, has committed $11 million in ad spending through Election Day, more than every other outside group in this race combined. Right now, a single donor can give an unlimited sum to that group and dominate the airwaves. 
That was the case in the Republican primary, when one outside group spent more than $2 million backing a single candidate, former Maine Senate Majority Leader Garrett Mason. The money came from just two people, Illinois shipping magnate Richard Uihlein and New York investor Thomas Klingenstein, funneled through a super PAC called Restoration of America. Mason was a paid consultant for Klingenstein in 2022. He lost the primary anyway, but two donors were able to outspend what took others thousands of donors and months of town halls to raise. 
As a state senator, Bennett, a former Republican now running for governor as an independent, was one of Question 1’s most vocal supporters when it went before voters in 2024, and now he’s an intervenor in Dinner Table Action v. Schneider, the pending case that will determine whether the cap he helped pass gets to take effect. But even his super PAC, Maine Wins Together, has taken in roughly $100,000 from just two individual households.
The legal theory that keeps this law blocked comes from a 2010 case called SpeechNow v. FEC, which found that since super PAC spending isn’t coordinated with a candidate’s campaign, the money donated to the super PACs can’t corrupt that candidate either. 
But in practice, that theory has allowed just a handful of wealthy individuals to spend more than thousands of others combined. 
The First Circuit will likely rule before the end of 2026. When it does, it will decide whether the next race, and the one after that, gets to run under the limit voters have asked for. Until then, Maine’s governor’s race is worth watching for a simple reason: it’s showing us the exact thing Maine voters chose to stop.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont education officials face sophisticated phishing scheme this summer
description:
“What we saw was that credential harvesting was only one part of the malware kill chain, but not the sole purpose of this exploit,” wrote Vermont Digital Services Secretary Denise Reilly-Hughes. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont education officials face sophisticated phishing scheme this summer.
text:
Signs on a bank of computers tell visitors that the machines are not working due to a cyber attack. File photo by Tony Gutierrez/AP Photo

A number of Vermont school districts were hit with an insidious phishing scheme this summer, following a pattern of cybercriminals attacking crucial institutions in rural communities. 
“This is a really common hacking methodology, unfortunately,” said Denise Reilly-Hughes, secretary of the Agency of Digital Services. “Even the most skilled individual can become a victim because they can be very sophisticated. They can look very real. In this particular case it was directing folks to click on a link, and they did.”
It appears no student or staff data was stolen this time. But the scheme spread through real, trusted accounts, and serves as a preview of a threat that could reach any Vermonter. 
Phishing is a form of digital fraud that aims to steal personal information such as usernames and passwords. State officials and technology experts warn that such credential theft is often just the first stage of a longer attack that can end in ransomware, fraud or a hijacked network, striking the rural school districts with thin cybersecurity defenses.
Brooke Olsen-Farrell, superintendent of Slate Valley Unified Union School District, said there has been a jump in these phishing schemes in the past month that exactly mimic a legitimate email.
Olsen-Farrell said that she and other Slate Valley staff clicked on an “excel secure portal” link in an email. That caused a script to run in the background of their accounts to read and delete emails and generate more phishing emails to their contact list, said Walter Ripley, technology coordinator for Slate Valley. There was no data compromised, as the district acted quickly, Ripley said.
Randy Rose, vice president of security operations and intelligence for the cyberthreat protection nonprofit Center for Internet Security, verified for VTDigger through cyberthreat intelligence analysis that the emails were credential-phishing attempts. Such emails are sent from real accounts to trusted contacts with an invented portal link, which serves to lure people into clicking and proliferating the scam further, Rose said.
Some educational leaders reported seeing phishing attempts from Vermont state emails that referenced state programs. However, there is no record of ingoing or outgoing phishing emails from state accounts, according to Reilly-Hughes.
The state identified the malicious software embedded in the header of the phishing emails and tracked the source to a Google Drive with an IP address based in Germany, Reilly-Hughes said in an interview last week. The cybercriminals may have just intended to cause disruption through collecting credentials — but also might have been seeking further sensitive information, said Reilly-Hughes. There has been no evidence of money exchange in this particular instance, she said. 
“What we saw was that credential harvesting was only one part of the malware kill chain, but not the sole purpose of this exploit,” Reilly-Hughes wrote in an email last week. “This type of attack can be used to propagate other malware including ransomware or for use in a botnet campaign. I can’t make assumptions on the intent of this bad actor.”
Early-stage attack
Vermont is no stranger to cybersecurity attacks. Last year, dozens of Vermont school districts were impacted by a national data breach of a student information system. Earlier this year, Chittenden County Solid Waste District recovered more than $2 million after a cyberfraud incident. 

READ MORE

Cybercriminals have increasingly targeted schools and other public sector infrastructure, especially in rural areas, because of their large budgets, limited cybersecurity resources and the critical nature of these community services, said Rose. 
Credential phishing is often an early-stage attack that leads to further invasions, Rose said. The aim could be to trick workers into responding to seemingly legitimate requests from a known source to send money or share sensitive information. The goal could also be a ransomware attack, which locks people or institutions out of accounts and encrypts files until people pay to release their systems.
Jacquelyn Ramsay-Tolman, superintendent of Orleans Central Supervisory Union in the Northeast Kingdom, said she and other staff members of the supervisory union also encountered the “excel secure portal” email phishing scam that has been circulating in Vermont school districts this summer. But Ramsay-Tolman said the incident was addressed quickly before the network was compromised. 
The supervisory union plans to change password policies for school accounts to ensure the district is protected from increasing cybersecurity threats, Ramsay-Tolman said. 
“We are continuously monitoring our security measures as new threats emerge, and we are currently maintaining two-factor (authentication) for general users, multifactor for administrative personnel, and considering additional measures like physical security keys for all staff,” Ramsay-Tolman said.
The Consumer Assistance Program with the Vermont attorney general’s office did not receive any reports of this particular scam. Attorney General Charity Clark said in an interview last week that phishing schemes are more effective if scammers know information about someone, so it is important to implement a personal “data minimization policy” and keep accounts private. 
“In today’s world, our data is something that’s at a premium, and also being used and collected by very legitimate companies, and it can make it difficult for the consumer to distinguish between what is legitimate and what is a scam,” Clark said. 
When using multifactor authentication, Clark recommended avoiding the use of biometric data such as a face scan or voice recognition, because artificial intelligence technology can create synthetic images or sounds that mimic real people, called deep fakes. The proliferation of “edtech,” hardware and software services used by the education system, contributes to an increase in scam opportunities, Clark said. 
Cybercriminals have many sophisticated tools these days, including QR codes, SMS messages and voice messages. Rose recommended that people use phishing-resistant multifactor authentication and verify the sender of messages before clicking any links or attachments. Phishing scams have kept evolving and continue to be effective because they take advantage of human trust, not just technology, he said. 
“Slowing down is a really effective way to make sure you’re making the right decision, and you’re forcing your body to think critically about things in every walk of life,” Rose said.
How to avoid “shared a file” scams
Before you click:

Didn’t expect a file? Don’t open it.
Check the “To” line — is it really to you?
Verify with the sender by phone or text.
Never enter your password to “view” a doc.
Hover to preview a link; when unsure, don’t click.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Vast scale of wildfire threats to Colorado watersheds far exceeds funding
description: High on a ridgeline near the headwaters of the Yampa River, a ditch dug more than a century ago snakes for miles through the rugged terrain of the Routt National Forest, shepherding water from the Yamcolo Reservoir across a 9,000-foot-high mesa to an area south of the town of Yampa, in southern Routt County. About […]
text:
The Yamcolo Reservoir, a water storage project owned by the Upper Yampa Water Conservancy District, is pictured on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)High on a ridgeline near the headwaters of the Yampa River, a ditch dug more than a century ago snakes for miles through the rugged terrain of the Routt National Forest, shepherding water from the Yamcolo Reservoir across a 9,000-foot-high mesa to an area south of the town of Yampa, in southern Routt County.
About a dozen cattle ranches rely on water from the Stillwater Ditch to irrigate their hay meadows longer into the growing season — at least in a good year. It’s been dry this summer as water users in the Upper Yampa Water Conservation District, which manages the ditch and the reservoir above it, faced severe cuts to their allotments amid unprecedented drought conditions that are gripping much of the state.
But even as farmers and ranchers dealt with the immediate impacts of a historically dry summer, a segment of the Stillwater Ditch last month became the site of another, longer-term battle that Colorado water managers are increasingly having to wage against a warmer, drier climate: protecting watersheds from severe wildfire impacts.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
For a month, a “hand crew” of 20 to 30 workers hiked up and down the slope above the ditch with chainsaws and other heavy equipment, putting in grueling 12-hour shifts trimming and thinning trees in the overgrown forest.
“We used to play a game when I first started working here, and we’d come up and work on the ditch on our lunch breaks: How far can you walk through the forest without touching the ground?” said Andy Rossi, the Upper Yampa water district’s general manager, during a tour of the project site this week for media and students. “Because there was so much deadfall and it was so thick.”
A federal environmental review shaped the water district’s plans for the project, which was funded by a state grant program but took place on national forest land. Buffer zones around eagle’s nests and other areas flagged as important for wildlife were off-limits, and the work couldn’t begin until July 1, after elk-calving season.
As with most “hand thinning” projects, trees in the treated area were delimbed or cut down according to certain predetermined criteria, with an eye toward reducing fuel for wildfires and increasing biodiversity — in this case, favoring aspen and Engelman spruce, compared to the overabundant, and less fire-resilient subalpine fir. The cut limbs and trunks are heaped into “slash piles” and left to dry out for at least a year before they’re safely burned in the winter.
Slash piles from a “hand thinning” wildfire mitigation project along Stillwater Ditch in southern Routt County, in a section of the Routt National Forest, are pictured on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
The main objective for the Upper Yampa district — and for a growing number of Colorado water managers undertaking the painstaking work of wildfire mitigation — isn’t to prevent fires altogether, but to reduce burn severity and the risk of post-fire impacts like floods, debris flows and water contamination. If post-fire debris flows were to damage the Stillwater Ditch, Rossi said, it could take years to fix.
“If thousands of acres of ranch land are out of business for one, two, three seasons, they’re done,” he added. “So taking water infrastructure … and elevating it to a very high level in the risk assessments, when you’re looking at landscapes for wildfire mitigation, all of a sudden becomes critically important, and this is happening all over the state of Colorado.”
Sheer scope of the problem
More than 13 million acres of mountain watersheds across western and central Colorado are now covered by a Wildfire Ready Action Plan, or WRAP, developed as part of a watershed protection program administered by the Colorado Water Conservation Board, the state’s lead water agency. The program was launched with an initial $30 million in funding appropriated by the state Legislature in 2021, in the aftermath of the previous year’s record-shattering outbreak of wildfires.
Five years on, the program has conducted a sweeping analysis of statewide post-fire risks and guided more than a dozen water managers through the WRAP planning process. But as climate change continues to intensify wildfire hazards in Colorado — the town of Beulah, in the burn scar of this summer’s Aspen Acres Fire, was the latest to be hit by deadly post-fire floods this week — all this new data also serves to illustrate the sheer scope of the problem.
Heat-related illnesses spike in Colorado as climate change fuels record temperatures

The forestry work above Stillwater Ditch — a heavy lift, involving years of local planning, a state grant and close coordination with the federal government — treated about 300 acres deemed the highest priority within the 33,308-acre Bear River watershed, itself only a small part of an Upper Yampa basin measured in hundreds of square miles.
About 10% of Colorado’s roughly 24 million acres of forest “need urgent attention to address forest health, wildﬁre risk and threats to water supplies,” the Colorado State Forest Service wrote in its most recent action plan. The Stillwater Ditch project’s hand crews were a relative bargain at $1,700 per acre; depending on factors like equipment and terrain, treatment costs routinely range from $3,000 to $5,000 per acre or more — making even the state’s highest-priority to-do list a multibillion-dollar proposition.
Two-thirds of those forested acres are owned by the federal government. Getting permits for projects on public land can be a headache, especially when staffing at agencies like the U.S. Forest Service has been “completely diminished,” Rossi said, by Trump administration cuts. But across landscapes spanning millions of acres, permitting bottlenecks pale in comparison to factors like cost, workforce capacity and other logistical limitations.
“The problem is so big, there is not enough time and energy to do it,” Rossi said. “The scale of it is so vast that you have to step back and say, ‘OK, what are we trying to do here?’”
Far more work than funding
Denver Water, the state’s largest water utility, has learned the hard way how costly and disruptive wildfires can be for a water system. The 1996 Buffalo Creek Fire and 2002 Hayman Fire both impacted the utility’s infrastructure in the South Platte River basin southwest of metro Denver.
“We are still, 20 years on, working on removing debris in our Strontia Springs Reservoir,” Alan Salazar, Denver Water’s CEO, told an audience at the annual summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs on Tuesday. “It’s a multimillion — not single-digit million, but tens of millions of dollars’ worth of engineering and removal.”
Denver Water’s board of commissioners voted earlier this month to endorse Proposed Initiative 308, a 2026 ballot measure that aims to raise up to $175 million in new revenue by exempting sporting goods sales tax collections from the caps set by the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights. About half the new funding would be directed toward the CWCB’s watershed protection grants and other wildfire mitigation programs.
“There is far more work than there is funding, so this initiative, should it come before voters and be approved, would be a key source of dollars to reduce wildfire risk,” Madelene McDonald, Denver Water’s manager of watershed planning, said in a statement. “Every project we can complete helps ensure a clean water supply and reduces property damage — saving enormous amounts of money and resources down the line.”
Post-fire floods hit the town of Beulah in Pueblo County earlier this week in the aftermath of the Aspen Acres Fire. (Photo courtesy of Pueblo County Sheriff’s Office)
“Money is a big limiting factor,” Aaron Citron, Colorado policy director at the Nature Conservancy and one of Initiative 308’s sponsors, said in an interview. “We know we can’t treat every acre. I think if we can get to something like 10% of the acres treated, we can make a real meaningful difference, and there’s a lot of good science identifying where those priority landscapes are.”
Even as the idea of more effective forest management catches on with the public, support for substantial new sources of dedicated funding for such efforts isn’t always assured. A proposal floated this summer in Routt County to raise local sales taxes for wildfire mitigation projects isn’t expected to move forward after a poll showed a lack of support. In a time of severe budget crunch at the state Capitol, measures backed by Western Slope lawmakers to invest in forestry projects are among the many bills that have failed to advance in recent legislative sessions.
Initiative 308, as a statutory measure, can’t “bind” future legislatures into mandatory spending, Citron said at the Water Congress, but sponsors hope its passage would send a clear message to lawmakers that wildfire mitigation should rank high on the state’s priority list. The initiative is pending certification for the ballot after submission of the required number of signatures.
“We see it as putting ourselves in line,” he said. “In some years, when there’s not enough, we will leave the final decision to our elected officials. In years like this, they might have to cut this back.”
Widespread misconceptions
As the West’s wildfire crisis has intensified in recent years, misconceptions about the scope of and strategy behind mitigation efforts have proliferated.
That’s due in large part to leading Republicans like President Donald Trump, a denier of human-caused climate change who has repeatedly invoked forest management — “raking and cleaning and doing things,” as he put it while touring the aftermath of California’s deadly Paradise Fire in 2018 — as a catch-all solution to catastrophic fire risk.
“(Electric vehicles) aren’t the answer. Sending your money to D.C. for wind and solar isn’t the answer,” U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert told the Colorado Water Congress on Wednesday. “It’s being good stewards of our land, managing our forests, so we aren’t battling these catastrophic wildfires year after year.”
“Policy, not climate, fueled fires” in the record-breaking 2020 wildfire season, argued one Colorado conservative commentator at the time. “They could just allow logging in the areas and the problem fixes itself,” wrote one social media user impacted by the Aspen Acres Fire last month.
A sign advises visitors to Grand Lake of a fire ban in effect in July 2026. Much of the area surrounding the Grand County resort town was scorched by the 2020 East Troublesome Fire. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
By the same token, there’s lingering hesitation among many environmentalists who fear that forest management could prove synonymous with clear-cutting timber projects across Colorado’s treasured national forests.
But large-scale logging as a forest management tool is a nonstarter in Colorado, which has virtually no timber industry to speak of — a reality that has far less to do with regulatory barriers than with the challenging economics of harvesting relatively low-value wood products from Colorado’s rugged alpine terrain.
“What we’re talking about is thinning, pile burning, prescribed fire, fuels mitigation — around communities, around reservoirs,” Citron said. “It’s projects that are identified by HOAs, local governments, fire districts. There has not been a particularly robust timber industry in Colorado for a number of years.”
“If this were lodgepole pine, it might be worth a logging operation, because it’s a viable timber resource,” said Sally Ross of Quandary Consulting, the contractor in charge of the Stillwater Ditch mitigation project. “But nobody’s really interested in a bunch of little subalpine fir.”
Even with a major funding boost for mitigation projects, large, destructive wildfires are likely here to stay. Protection of homes and other structures is often the highest-priority objective, while larger-scale fuel reduction treatments and prescribed burns aim primarily to decrease burn severity in the event of a fire, and to mimic the lower-intensity “fire regimes” that characterized the landscape in previous centuries.
“The science tells us there should be some fire in the landscape. … You have to learn to live with that fire,” Rossi said. “You’re not going to control it all, so it almost becomes more like, ‘What does the post-fire look like? It’s happening. What do we want it to look like after it burns?'”
The supercharging of wildfire activity by a warmer and drier climate, meanwhile, is unmistakable. One widely-cited 2016 study found that human-caused climate change alone doubled the area burned by fires in the western U.S. between 1984 and 2015. More recent research on the causes of California’s fivefold increase in forest acreage burned since 1971 concluded “that nearly all of the observed increase in (burned area) over the past half-century is attributable to anthropogenic climate change.”
“The severity of catastrophic wildfire in Colorado has intensified — I think, unfortunately, we have to expect that that will continue,” Salazar said. “It’s now a bigger and more emerging state economic risk, human risk, and all that goes with it.”

title: New Mexico AG Torrez says new ‘crime gun’ tracking effort leading to arrests across jurisdictions
description: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Wednesday announced that a statewide initiative to track guns used in shootings has identified more than 500 crimes since launching late last year.
text:
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez joins law enforcement leaders — from left to right: McKinley County Sheriff James Maiorano III, Gallup Police Chief Erin Toadlena-Pablo, Ohkay Owingeh Police Chief and Public Safety Director Jace Trujillo and Farmington Police Sgt. Eduardo Arreola — on Aug. 19, 2026, to announce early results from his departments Crime Gun Intelligence Center initiative. (Photo courtesy of the New Mexico Department of Justice) New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Wednesday announced that a statewide initiative to track guns used in shootings has identified more than 500 crimes since launching late last year.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The New Mexico Department of Justice in December announced its Crime Gun Intelligence Center, which lets investigators review and compare spent shell casings from crime scenes using a digital database in a manner similar to the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s national fingerprint database. At the time, Torrez said he hoped the new system would help police departments track guns used in multiple violent crimes across New Mexico cities, counties and towns.
On Wednesday, he said that roughly half of the leads generated under the new system identified such cases.
“We have long known, for those of us in law enforcement, that crime guns are passed, usually within groups,” he told reporters alongside law enforcement leaders from Gallup, Farmington and the Pueblo of Ohkay Owingeh. “Guns that are being used on the streets of Albuquerque may actually be coming from Ohkay Owingeh. Guns that are originating in Farmington may then end up in Gallup and then may end up back in Farmington.”
Torrez added that officers across the state have uploaded about 2,000 ballistics into the statewide network. More than 40% of leads generated this way lead to an arrest, he said.
Analysts in one case identified a gun that was used in 17 different crimes, Torrez said. Officials have taken more than half the guns identified through the database off the street, he said.
New Mexico Department of Justice Special Investigations Bureau Director Kyle Hartsock, pictured on Dec. 15, 2025, shows how the department’s new Crime Gun Intelligence Center will help law enforcement agencies find common links between firearm crimes in multiple jurisdictions. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)
Departments use specialized machines that are tied into the National Integrated Ballistic Information Network to compare spent ammunition to those in the database. When Torrez announced the initiative in December, he said his office was installing these machines in the Gallup and Roswell police departments and the San Juan and Doña Ana county sheriff’s offices to enable those agencies to serve as regional hubs.
Previously, the Albuquerque Police Department had the most advanced NIBIN machine in the state, meaning officers from rural departments had to drive several hours to use it.
McKinley County Sheriff James Maiorano III said the machine has already shown promising results for his office’s investigations.
He cited the case of a drive-by shooting in Phoenix, where someone fired more than 50 rounds from inside a vehicle. One of the spent casings clearly belonged to a 9mm firearm. Months later, officials with the New Mexico Department of Transportation called Maiorano’s office to say they had found a gun that had been left on the side of the interstate.
Once recovered, New Mexico officials were able to run the gun’s ammunition through the database and confirm that they appeared to match the 9mm shell found on the ground in Phoenix.
That technology gave investigators “the opportunity to look at the last person who owned that firearm and give the investigation a place to go,” Maiorano said. “It would have otherwise been dead and considered a closed case.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Judge dismisses lawsuit seeking to dissolve Minnesota nursing home labor standards board
description: A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit brought by nursing home industry leaders seeking to dissolve the state’s nursing home labor standards board, which the Legislature created in 2023 to set minimum wages and employment standards. The ruling is a victory for nursing home workers, many of whom will receive raises next month because of the […]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images) A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit brought by nursing home industry leaders seeking to dissolve the state’s nursing home labor standards board, which the Legislature created in 2023 to set minimum wages and employment standards.
The ruling is a victory for nursing home workers, many of whom will receive raises next month because of the board. It will also fuel the labor movement’s push to win higher wages and working conditions across entire industries rather than just negotiations at individual workplaces.
Nursing home associations — LeadingAge Minnesota and Care Providers of Minnesota — argued in their lawsuit that the Minnesota Nursing Home Workforce Standards Board is unconstitutional and violates federal labor and antitrust laws, calling it an unprecedented “experiment in workplace regulation.”
Labor standards boards have experienced a revival in the United States — versions of them date back to the New Deal and are common in Europe — and now exist in California for fast food workers and Nevada for home care workers, among other venues.
Their arguments did not convince U.S. District Judge Nancy Brasel, whose Monday ruling granting the Walz administration’s motion for dismissal dealt the second legal blow to the nursing home industry since the board’s creation. Last year, another federal judge dismissed the two associations’ legal challenge to the board’s rule requiring nursing homes pay workers time-and-a-half on 11 holidays. The associations have appealed that decision.
The associations said in a statement they disagree with the ruling, signaling another appeal is likely.
“Our challenge has never been about whether caregivers deserve to be paid family-sustaining wages. It is about whether the Nursing Home Workforce Standards Board is a lawful and a sustainable way to achieve that shared goal,” the statement said.
Dr. Rasha Ahmad Sharif, executive vice president of SEIU Healthcare Minnesota & Iowa, celebrated the decision in a statement, saying the union looks forward to working with the standards board for “years to come.”
The state Department of Labor and Industry, which was a defendant in the lawsuit, declined to comment.
The Minnesota Nursing Home Workforce Standards Board was created under a Democratic trifecta after a campaign by SEIU Healthcare Minnesota and Iowa, which represents nearly 50,000 healthcare and long-term care workers. The union’s president, Jamie Gulley, serves on the labor standards board.
The board in Minnesota comprises three worker representatives, three industry leaders and three state government officials. (Nursing homes receive most of their money through state and federal Medicaid funding.)
The wage and holiday rules passed without support from industry leaders, who abstained from voting. In 2024, the board voted to set minimum wages and mandate 11 paid holidays without the support of the three industry representatives, who all abstained.
The hourly minimum wages set to take effect Sept. 10 are $22.50 for certified nursing assistants, $23.50 for trained medication aides, $27 for licensed practical nurses, and $19 for all other nursing home workers. The hourly wages will increase another $1.50 per hour across all job categories on Jan. 1.
The rules set by the board were approved by the Minnesota Legislature with bipartisan support last year. The Minnesota Legislature appropriated an additional $37 million to fund the raises in its 2024 health and human services budget bill, and the federal government will contribute a comparable amount.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: As Meta faces trial for hooking kids on social media, NC’s attorney general offers parents advice
description: “This is the big one.” That’s how North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson described the landmark federal trial that got underway Tuesday, in which Meta is accused of designing its platforms to be addictive to  children. Jackson and a bipartisan group of 28 other attorneys general allege the tech giant deceived the public about the […]
text:
A bipartisan group of  29  attorneys general allege the tech giant Meta deceived the public about the addictive nature and the harms of their product.
(Photo: Getty Images) “This is the big one.”
That’s how North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson described the landmark federal trial that got underway Tuesday, in which Meta is accused of designing its platforms to be addictive to  children.
Jackson and a bipartisan group of 28 other attorneys general allege the tech giant deceived the public about the harms of their product.
“I know [parents] have seen headlines of Meta in the news and litigation before, but this is very different,” said Jackson. “This is about children, their mental health, and the deliberate ways that Meta engineered Facebook and Instagram to be addictive to children and then misled parents about it.”
North Carolina and other states filed suit against Meta in 2023. The social media behemoth has tried repeatedly to have the case thrown out but has failed.
Meta has rejected the states’ claims, pointing to efforts to improve safety and be more transparent. Meta says its “teen” accounts can filter out topics like dieting and body image that may be triggering for some youth, and daily time limits can be used to reduce screen time. More recently, Meta says it added a parental alert feature to notify a parent or guardian if the teen mentions suicide or self-harm to Meta AI. However, some parents and observers have said the safety features don’t work for them.
The technology giant says it doesn’t allow children under 13 to create accounts. But Meta attorney Paul Schmidt said during his opening statement that it’s an unfortunate reality that some children who are under 13 can and do lie about their age to get on the social media platform.
The trial, being heard in U.S. District Court in Oakland, California, is expected to last six weeks. The attorneys general are asking the court to force Meta to follow laws designed to protect children, pay penalties, and give up profits it gained from breaking the law.
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
Jackson said the money they are seeking isn’t meant to be a remedy, but rather a deterrent and punishment for bad behavior.
Regardless of the outcome, Jackson said, parents have a critical role in deciding how much time on social media is suitable and enforcing boundaries.
“One of the core questions here is, how much time can children really spend on these platforms in a healthy way?” said Jackson in an interview with NC Newsline.
“I’m a dad, and to be honest with you, we fight this fight on a daily basis,” said Jackson.
In his own home, North Carolina’s attorney general said he has limits on social media usage, allowing his kids to earn more screen time based on doing chores or other things around the house.
“There is no world in which we don’t need parents to be involved in how much screen time their kids are getting,” said Jackson.
From algorithms to AI chatbots, child advocates push for greater protection for NC youth

Social media safety at the statehouse
Mick Tobin is co-founder and advocacy director for the Young People’s Alliance, a youth-led nonprofit advocacy group. He said he’s hopeful that Meta is held accountable.
Mick Tobin (Photo: Young People’s Alliance)
“This case shows that manipulating young people has not only financial consequences, but social ramifications as well,” said Tobin, a recent Duke graduate.
Tobin said this and other cases brought against Meta underscore the urgency of passing stronger legislation to protect youth.
North Carolina legislators are considering a bill that would prohibit children under age 14 from signing up for social media accounts, with parental consent required for 14- and 15-year-old users. House Bill 301 would also impose a fine of $50,000 per violation against tech companies that fail to use age-verification for their account holders. A conference committee was appointed in late June to hammer out a final agreement between the state House and Senate’s versions of the measure.
Tobin wants to see legislators go farther than age limits.
“We hope lawmakers begin to pass legislation that limits social media’s dangerous designs, including addictive feeds, infinite scroll, and autoplay, as many states have already done,” said Tobin in a statement to NC Newsline. “We stand ready to work with lawmakers and mobilize our generation to pass that legislation.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s opiate policy is killing us
description:
Vermont has embraced harm reduction while opiate deaths climb far higher than in poorer, more punitive states. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s opiate policy is killing us.
text:
This commentary is by Matt Wormser, the chair of the Shelburne Selectboard.
I traveled to Fayetteville, Arkansas, earlier this year for work. Having not been to the state in decades, I didn’t know what to expect, but anticipated an environment similar to many Southern cities I’d been to in recent years: long on MAGA and sprawl and short on local color. Instead, I found a colorful small city that reminded me of Burlington. It’s home to the vibrant University of Arkansas campus. The tourism welcome center sold “Keep Fayetteville Funky” shirts. Pride flags abounded, as did a variety of great restaurants, coffee shops, small parks and well-maintained older homes. I spent a couple of days biking around town, and it seemed like a great place to live.
One striking difference in my meanderings was that there was no evidence — zero — of public drug use or addiction. 
I’ll contrast that with my recent bike ride into my downtown Burlington office this week, where, passing City Hall Park, I saw a nice new pickup doing a tidy business with a long line of customers obviously stuck in the abyss of addiction. Walking to lunch revealed plenty more of the same. While Vermont has made progress on opiate deaths, looking at 2024 data from the Kaiser Family Foundation, it still has the fifth-worst opiate-related death rate in the country at 29 per 100,000 people. By contrast, Arkansas, a state with a significantly higher poverty rate than Vermont, offering far fewer public health and housing assistance resources, saw the fourth-lowest rate nationally, at 6.2 per 100,000. In short, Vermonters die of opiates at nearly five times the rate of Arkansans. Nationally, seven of the 10 states with the highest rates of opiate-related deaths are so-called blue states, while nine of the 10 states with the lowest rates are “red” ones. It’s hard to avoid the conclusion that whatever we’re doing in blue states to combat drug abuse, it isn’t working.

READ MORE

What’s different? While multiple factors drive addiction, states like Vermont in recent years have embraced the strategy of harm reduction, with the goal of minimizing addiction-related deaths. Most days, to many Vermonters, this simply feels like an abandonment of drug law enforcement, with the hope that users will summon the agency to seek treatment and then stay sober. What is evident from the data is that this de facto policy is killing Vermonters at a far higher rate than necessary and impacting the quality of life for everyone else. From a visibility standpoint, Burlington is the poster child for public drug use and addiction, but this is by no means simply a “crazy Burlington progs” issue, as the per capita death rate from opiates is not notably higher in Chittenden County versus other Vermont counties.
The issue can also be attributed to the highly decentralized nature of our policing in Vermont, where small local departments with limited resources by necessity spend far more time responding to the byproducts of trafficking and addiction — shoplifting, car break-ins, disorderly conduct, no-trespass orders — than addressing the root cause itself.
Few families have been unaffected by the opiate crisis over the past decade; mine is certainly not on the exception list. Families supporting their loved ones struggling with addiction know that there is a fine line between support and enablement, and statewide we’ve dipped far too strongly into the latter category. Advocates of harm reduction say the policy is working and we only need time, ever more time. To me, the numbers tell the exact opposite story. While some leaders decry the whack-a-mole nature of scooping up low-level dealers, I think most Vermonters would enthusiastically welcome more incarceration of dealers of all stripes in preference to the current policy in Burlington and beyond.
We need Vermont’s leaders to work far more actively, and in a far more coordinated way, on enforcement of laws for our most life-destroying drugs: opiates and methamphetamines. This includes aggressive targeting of dealer networks from low to high, while holding out a hand for addicts seeking treatment. It also includes addressing some of the known issues enabling trafficking in Vermont, such as the drugs-for-guns trade resulting from our very laissez-faire gun laws.
Well over 1,000 Vermonters have died due to opiates since Covid-19. Our current enforcement policy is a choice, resulting in tremendous costs to affected individuals, families and communities. Many other blue states have successfully changed course in their tolerance and policies for drug distribution and public use, without losing their humanity in treating addiction. We need leaders from all our parties to do likewise.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa lawmaker urges universities to heed U.S. Secretary of Education call to action
description: The chair of the Iowa House Higher Education Committee is urging public and private universities in the state to release their responses to a national call to action from the U.S. Secretary of Education. Secretary Linda McMahon released “A National Call to Action to University Presidents and Governing Boards” Aug. 3. It asks university leadership […]
text:
Rep. Taylor Collins is encouraging Iowa colleges and universities to answer the call to action from U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The chair of the Iowa House Higher Education Committee is urging public and private universities in the state to release their responses to a national call to action from the U.S. Secretary of Education.
Secretary Linda McMahon released “A National Call to Action to University Presidents and Governing Boards” Aug. 3. It asks university leadership and those  who govern them to “reaffirm their commitment to serving the American people” through public declarations.
Rep. Taylor Collins, R-Mediapolis, chair of the Higher Education Committee, sent a letter Aug. 19 to the Iowa Board of Regents and Iowa Association of Independent Colleges and Universities to “strongly urge” the colleges and universities under their purview to heed this call and address questions of transparency in admissions, free speech, affordability, protection of research and more.
“Secretary McMahon’s letter offers Iowa’s public universities and private colleges an opportunity to demonstrate that the reforms we have enacted are not merely statutory compliance, but a genuine recommitment to the core mission of higher education,” Collins said in the letter.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In McMahon’s call to action, she asks higher education leaders to answer seven questions through “statements of principle” and have them posted on institutional websites before the end of the year. Trust in higher education is lower than ever, she said, and this work can help publicize or launch reforms to build that trust back up.
Universities must answer questions about ensuring transparent admissions policies and merit-based admissions, protecting free debate without allowing “unruly and violent protestors” to disrupt campus, encouraging academic pluralism, offering affordable degrees with a return on student investment, incentivizing “rigor” among artificial intelligence and other factors, prioritizing “excellence in teaching and learning,” and protecting programs and research from “foreign influence.”
Iowa universities can “lead by example” in answering these questions and showcasing how they’re working to restore trust in higher education, Collins said, as legislation passed in the Statehouse has already put them down the right path.
In the past two years, Iowa’s state government has passed laws to bar offices of diversity, equity and inclusion at public universities, establish the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa, make civic education a general education requirement in public higher education and require universities to post syllabi and financial materials online, all and more of which Collins said has helped grow trust and keep enrollment high.
In a 2026 free speech survey conducted by the Iowa Board of Regents, more than 80% of participating students reported agreeing that their university provides an environment for free speech. However, the faculty and staff response to the same question dropped nearly 10 percentage points from the previous survey to just over 67%.
The higher education committee has also focused on reduced-credit degrees and other ways of ensuring students can earn credentials faster to join the workforce in high-demand fields, Collins said in the letter. McMahon’s call to action provides an opportunity for Iowa institutions to show “the reforms we have enacted are not merely statutory compliance, but a genuine recommitment to the core mission of higher education,” he said.
“The House Committee on Higher Education Committee stands ready to support institutions to embrace this moment of renewal and to hold accountable those that do not,” Collins said.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Insect fans are all abuzz about this week’s pollinator count, which helps the ag industry bloom
description: This week, citizen scientists throughout the southeast region will take 15 minutes to help make a headcount of the buzzing, scuttling little critters that help our flowers bloom and gardens grow. The counting is part of the University of Georgia’s Great Southeast Pollinator Census. The event, which takes place this Friday and Saturday, started eight […]
text:
Students at West Fannin Elementary take part in the Great Southeastern Pollinator Count. Becky Griffin/University of Georgia ExtensionThis week, citizen scientists throughout the southeast region will take 15 minutes to help make a headcount of the buzzing, scuttling little critters that help our flowers bloom and gardens grow.
The counting is part of the University of Georgia’s Great Southeast Pollinator Census. The event, which takes place this Friday and Saturday, started eight years ago in Georgia and is now also open to residents of South Carolina, North Carolina, Florida, Alabama and Mississippi.
You can learn how to participate at the Great Southeastern Pollinator Census website. Last year, more than 27,000 participants logged more than 500,000 insects.
Becky Griffin, a pollinator health associate for the University of Georgia Extension and mastermind behind the count, said participants don’t need any special knowledge of bugs or plants.
“It has caught on, and it’s even caught on to people or groups that you would not think of as insect conservation people, like the Daughters of the American Revolution and the Georgia Aquarium,” she said.
Nearly 600 schools participated in last year’s count, including Blue Ridge Elementary School in Fannin County, where STEM teacher Tori Arp leads the count for pre-K to fifth grade students.
Arp said she took part for the first time in 2020 and the lessons are always a hit with the kids.
“It’s a great time when we come back to school because the kids want to be outside,” she said. “There are a ton of things blooming at the time still, and the pollinators are really active.”
Arp has the youngest students make little honeybees out of pipe cleaners and simulate pollinating flowers using colorful chalk as pollen. They also learn what she called a “little waggle dance” to simulate how bees communicate.
“And then as I get up to fourth and fifth grade, we do the parts of the flower dissection to understand about how the flowers are fertilized and the role of the pollinator in the ecosystem, things like that,“ she said.
Another early adopter for the bug count is master gardener Tim Mullen, who tends a garden attached to Slow Pour Brewing Company in Lawrenceville.
In addition to hosting events for the brewery, the garden there is formally certified by UGA as an educational demonstration garden and regularly hosts educational events, including the pollinator census.
Mullen, a retired teacher with a background in environmental protection, said people often join the count after inadvertently wandering over to the tent.
“People come to drink a beer, and we’re sitting there with our UGA master gardener tent, and they say, ‘What are you – what is this?’ They have no idea what we’re doing,” he said
“When was the last time you were in a class learning something you enjoyed, sitting down at a table and having a beer?” he added with a laugh. “You can’t drink beer at school, but we can here.”
Griffin said the count represents a fun time for participants, but it’s also important for the state’s economy. In 2023, Gov. Brian Kemp issued an official commendation praising the census’ contribution to the agriculture industry.
Griffin said pollinators contribute $600 million to the state’s agriculture industry, and that farmers, developers and local governments use the data to help them decide what plants they should grow.
“They’re looking at, if I’m a watermelon grower in Peach County, what kind of insects are people finding in Peach County, and do I need to add pollinator habitat to my farm to make sure that we have the kind of pollinators I need?” she said.
“So it’s not just a feel-good project,” she added. “We want to make sure our plants survive, but it’s also an economic issue as well.”
This year’s count is dedicated to Walter Reeves, an expert Georgia gardener who died this year after a decades-long career offering advice on TV, radio and print.
