name: WyoFile
title: Short, Harshman and Meier take state executive seats in GOP primary
description:
The Campbell County rancher and state senator defeated candidates endorsed by Trump and the Wyoming Republican Party. 
The post Short, Harshman and Meier take state executive seats in GOP primary appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Robert Short, Steve Harshman and Curt Meier are the apparent GOP primary winners for secretary of state, superintendent of public instruction and state treasurer, respectively, according to preliminary results from Tuesday’s primary election.
State Auditor Kristi Racines, a Republican, is running for reelection unopposed, and Eric Barlow is the apparent GOP primary winner for governor.
In November’s general election, Short will face Democratic challenger Bryan McCarty, and Harshman goes up against Democrat Ana Cordova — who edged out Sergio A. Maldonado, Sr.
All three of the contested state primary challenges indicate Wyoming voters bucked against Freedom Caucus-aligned candidates, particularly in the secretary of state race where caucus chair Rachel Williams vied to succeed Freedom Caucus-aligned Chuck Gray who made his bid for U.S. House.
Secretary of state
“The people of Wyoming absolutely care about who works for them in the secretary’s office,” Short told WyoFile Tuesday night, “and the importance of having rational, balanced and thoughtful consideration for all decisions associated with the secretary’s office is paramount to the people of Wyoming. 
“If I’m the chosen person for that position,” Short added, “the people can expect a voice of reason, a very willing listener and a tireless advocate for all things Wyoming.”
From left, Republican candidates for Wyoming Secretary of State Qwenton Eagle Oviatt, Robert Short and CJ Young chat Wednesday, July 15, 2026, during a candidate forum at the Albany County Public Library in Laramie. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
After the governor’s office, secretary of state is perhaps the most high-profile elected state office, overseeing elections, registering businesses and recording and maintaining many state records. In a pinch, Wyoming’s secretary of state is also the first in line for gubernatorial succession.
Whether it’s Republican Short or Democrat McCarty who prevails in the general election, they will take the helm of a state office where outgoing Gray — with cooperation from Freedom Caucus members in the House — enacted several controversial election reforms during his four-year-term.
Gray, while still a Wyoming legislator, paved the way for a more restrictive voter identification law. As secretary, he successfully rallied the Legislature to limit the time voters are allowed to “cross-over” to another party during an election cycle — an effort to limit the success of moderate Republicans. Gray also clashed with county clerks over whether to restrict the use of “drop boxes” in elections.
Cody Republican Rep. Rachel Williams was seen as the most politically aligned successor to Gray’s election reform agenda running for the secretary’s post.
During a secretary of state forum, much of the GOP primary field — Short, Qwenton Oviatt and CJ Young — expressed confidence in the security of Wyoming elections and that county clerks are doing a good job of overseeing elections without major reforms. 
Short, a Converse County commissioner, raised $429,521 for his campaign and outspent his competitors by about $360,000 ahead of Tuesday’s primary election, campaign finance reports showed.
Superintendent of public instruction 
Harshman was among three Republicans in the primary running to replace current Superintendent Megan Degenfelder, who chose to run for governor rather than seek reelection. Degenfelder lost her bid for governor to Barlow.
The state’s education chief oversees considerable record-keeping, enforces provisions of the Wyoming Education Code, maintains a list of accredited schools and gathers reports and statistics. But the position is also one of political power, particularly when it comes to education funding and social issues.
Chad Auer, Steve Harshman and Tom Kelly take questions on Thursday, July 16, 2026, during a forum for candidates for the Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction at the Albany County Public Library in Laramie. (Molly Walters for WyoFile)
The Legislature passed a recalibration bill in March that represents a new funding model for school districts; Wyoming’s universal school choice program is being challenged in court and the state just overhauled literacy standards and instruction — a change fought for by Degenfelder.
Though the three Republican candidates mostly aligned on conservative ideals, they diverged in their philosophies for helming the Department of Education, particularly on whether to pursue a “top-down” approach to practical things like literacy instruction, as well as hot-button education issues like public funding for homeschooling.
The Legislature this spring passed a law spearheaded by Degenfelder that establishes new guidelines for literacy instruction based on “the science of reading.”
Harshman, a high school coach, has served as House District 37 representative since 2003, including two terms as Speaker of the House, and along the way earned a reputation as politically moderate while carrying institutional knowledge of the inner workings of the Legislature.
State treasurer
Two-term Treasurer Curt Meier easily topped Lingle Rep. Scott Smith, who is listed as a member of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus and who earned the state GOP’s endorsement. 
Marilyn Kite, former chief justice of the Wyoming Supreme Court, interviews Wyoming Treasurer Curt Meier during a July 15, 2026 candidate forum. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
Meier, regarded as a moderate in today’s Wyoming GOP, served for 23 years in the Wyoming Senate before running for treasurer back in 2018. He’s generally won accolades among supporters for overseeing a more aggressive approach — backed by the Legislature — in investments, playing a key role in making those returns Wyoming’s top source of revenue.
“What I think the voters that voted for me understood is that, you know, I’m kind of a big tent guy,” Meier told WyoFile Tuesday evening. “We’re doing this for all of Wyoming, we’re just not doing it for people that think the way that we think.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The science that protects our children doesn’t take a summer vacation
description: Connecticut's own biopharmaceutical community has played an important role in advancing vaccine science.
text:
For families, the end of summer can often seem like a never-ending to do list: enjoying the last pool and beach days, shopping for school supplies, and signing up for fall sports and after school activities. But for those in Connecticut’s life sciences community, back to school is also a reminder that protecting the next generation never pauses, and neither should our commitment to the science that keeps them safe.
As Connecticut families finish their summer breaks, allow me to offer an important reminder: vaccines are safe, effective, and backed by decades of rigorous scientific evidence.
Yet recent measles outbreaks across the country demonstrate how quickly vaccine-preventable diseases can return when vaccination rates decline. Many communities are still working to recover from the disruptions to routine healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic, leaving some children behind on recommended vaccination schedules.
The consequences of falling behind are serious. Measles is not a minor childhood illness. It can cause pneumonia, brain swelling, permanent hearing loss, and in rare cases, death. With back-to-school season only a few days away, the window to act is now.
The good news is that the tools to protect our children are well-established and thoroughly tested. Vaccines undergo one of the most rigorous approval processes of any medical product. Before reaching patients, they are evaluated through years of research, clinical trials, and independent scientific review. Even after approval, they continue to be monitored through multiple safety systems designed to identify even the rarest potential concerns.
Connecticut’s own biopharmaceutical community has played an important role in advancing that science. Across our state, researchers, healthcare providers, manufacturers, and innovators work every day to develop treatments and technologies that improve and save lives. Their work is grounded in rigorous science, transparency, and an unwavering commitment to patient safety.
And yet, doubt persists, often fueled by misinformation that has been repeatedly disproven. Questions about vaccines are understandable, and science welcomes scrutiny. In fact, scientific progress depends on it. But after decades of research and millions of administered doses, the evidence remains clear that vaccines are one of the most successful public health interventions in history.
No issue better illustrates the importance of separating fact from fiction than the long-debunked claim linking vaccines to autism. The original study that sparked those concerns was retracted for serious ethical and scientific violations, and numerous large-scale studies conducted around the world have found no link between vaccines and autism. Yet the myth persists, highlighting how difficult it can be to rebuild trust once misinformation takes hold.
For parents navigating an increasingly complex information environment, there is a clear place to start. If you have questions about vaccines, ask your child’s pediatrician rather than social media. Use the start of the school year as an opportunity to schedule a wellness visit, review your child’s immunization record, and discuss any concerns with a trusted healthcare professional.
Connecticut’s life sciences community stands ready to help. They are your neighbors, your fellow parents, and your partners in building a healthier future. Connecticut families may be wrapping up their summer vacations, but the science that protects our children never takes a break.
Tony Sheridan is President of the Chamber of Commerce of Eastern Connecticut.

name: WyoFile
title: Republican Hageman will face Democrat Byrd after landslide victories in Wyoming’s US Senate primary
authors: Angus M. Thuermer Jr. and Maya Shimizu Harris
description:
Currently Wyoming’s lone representative in the US House, Hageman won by a landslide in Tuesday’s primary election for US Senate. 
The post Republican Hageman will face Democrat Byrd after landslide victories in Wyoming’s US Senate primary appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Republican Harriet Hageman, currently Wyoming’s lone U.S. House representative, will face Democrat James Byrd in the November general election after each won their party’s nomination in Tuesday’s primary, according to preliminary results.
The Associated Press called the Republican primary for Hageman at 8:52 p.m. with 26% of the votes counted and with Sam Mead as runner-up.  
In the Democratic tilt, the AP called the race for James Byrd with 27% of votes counted.
Hageman said in a statement that she is “grateful to the people of our great state for entrusting me with the responsibility of promoting and defending our ideals in Congress at this moment in history,” describing it as a “struggle for the existence of the United States of America as we know them, with patriots on one side and a rising tide of Marxists on the other.” 
She emphasized keeping taxes low, ensuring that “property rights mean something,” producing domestic energy “by responsibly accessing our natural resources” and enforcing immigration laws.  
“In short, we are a nation of laws and accountability, and we must make sure we continue to act like one,” Hageman concluded. “And we must aggressively defend freedom and capitalism, or we will descend into the dreary, soul-sapping, certain failure of communism.” 
Hageman thanked President Donald Trump for his endorsement, as well as Wyoming’s current U.S. Sens. John Barrasso and Cynthia Lummis. 
Voters elected Hageman to Congress in 2022 and again in 2024. Endorsed by Trump, she ran a $2 million MAGA campaign eight times larger than Mead’s.
Mead, the nephew and great-grandson of two former Wyoming governors, campaigned under the banner of protecting public lands. That struck a contrast with his opponent who signed onto a Utah lawsuit that claimed the U.S. government’s ownership of land in Wyoming amounted to a justification for war.
“I knew this was going to be a pretty big challenge,” Mead said Tuesday evening. “I wanted to make huge improvements to the state and country. 
To not have an opportunity to do that is disappointing.”
Mead said he is still seeking ways to help the state and will offer his services when needed. Meantime, he said, he will “get some tractor time in.”
In a July survey of likely GOP voters, taxes and government spending were listed by 14% of respondents as their top issue. Illegal immigration was the next most important subject, listed by 13%, jobs and the economy by 11% and public lands by 11%.
Hageman and Mead faced three other Republican opponents. 
Jimmy Skovgard, married, and the father of four, began his career as a data analyst and retired from his oil field business cleaning drilling sites and spills. 
Jill Edwards, a Laramie resident, is a self-described “Wyoming mom who works multiple jobs … busy putting food on my children’s tables.” 
John Allan Holtz, is a Laramie resident and former Douglas circuit court judge with a military, law and technical engineering background.
In the Democratic primary, Byrd, a former state representative who served from 2009-2019, also rode the public lands bandwagon, criticizing Hageman, now his opponent in the November election, for what he characterized as an anti-conservation position.
Billy Benavidez, a greenskeeper from Sheridan and the father of two, had to contend with the fact he is on probation. He was put on a year’s unsupervised probation on Aug. 20, 2025, for a breach-of-peace conviction, court records show.

name: WyoFile
title: Eric Barlow wins GOP nomination for Wyoming governor
description:
The Campbell County rancher and state senator defeated candidates endorsed by Trump and the Wyoming Republican Party. 
The post Eric Barlow wins GOP nomination for Wyoming governor appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Sen. Eric Barlow, a Gillette rancher and former speaker of the House, won the GOP nomination for Wyoming governor Tuesday, making him the overwhelming favorite to become the state’s next chief executive officer. 
The Associated Press called the race at 8:54 p.m. with 21% of the votes counted.
Barlow triumphed over a Trump-backed opponent in a state where the president remains deeply popular. He also succeeded despite the Wyoming GOP endorsing another candidate and steady criticism from the right wing of the party that he was too moderate.
His election puts Wyoming on track to welcome another traditional Republican governor with ranching roots. Current Gov. Mark Gordon and former Gov. Matt Mead also won office despite skepticism from their party’s flank. 
Barlow will still face two challengers in November, but given Republican domination of Wyoming politics, they face long odds.
Barlow sought the nomination against three other Republican candidates including Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder, who President Donald Trump endorsed, and Brent Bien, who was backed by the Wyoming Republican Party. The fourth candidate, Curt Blake of Centennial, ran a more informal, “word-of-mouth” campaign. 
Born in Gillette and raised on the family ranch southwest of town, Barlow served as a U.S. Marine and worked as a large-animal veterinarian and a rancher before getting elected to House District 3 in 2013. Voters elected him to Senate District 23 in 2022. 
As a lawmaker, Barlow led the House as speaker in 2021 and 2022 and now chairs the Senate Labor, Health and Social Services Committee as well as the Mental Health and Vulnerable Adult Task Force.  
“I am a leader who stands firmly on sound, conservative principles and who will fiercely defend your rights, including the Second Amendment and the sanctity of life,” Barlow said in his announcement. “I will protect your private property rights, safeguard our public lands, and keep Washington, D.C. out of Wyoming’s business.”
Barlow kicked off his gubernatorial bid more than a year ago, and focused his campaign on protecting public lands, funding education and solving Wyoming’s healthcare access and affordability issues. 
Gordon did not run for re-election and was technically prevented from seeking a third term, though he could have challenged that, as the Wyoming Supreme Court has ruled that term limits on the other top elected positions in the state are unconstitutional. 
The last two times the governor’s seat was open in Wyoming, the Republican nominee handily won the general election after succeeding in the primary election. 
In late July, Barlow released internal polling that showed him with a comfortable lead. At that time, the polling indicated support for Barlow at 42%, followed by Degenfelder at 19%, Brent Bien at 14%, with 22% of respondents undecided.
A few weeks after Barlow released the poll, Trump hosted a telerally with Degenfelder. About 20,600 people joined the call, according to Degenfelder’s campaign, which is about twice as many as attended Trump’s 2022 in-person rally in Casper when he backed Hageman against Liz Cheney. 
When it came to fundraising, Barlow also pulled ahead of his opponents, raising $1.67 million since he announced his bid in August 2025. That beat out Degenfelder, who announced in January of this year, by about $380,000. Barlow’s fundraising also eclipsed the previous statewide record for individual fundraising. 
In November’s election, Barlow will face two opponents: Democrat Kenneth Casner of Casper and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel of Jackson. 
Bextel, the Teton County conservative activist at the center of the Checkgate controversy that dominated the 2026 legislative session, announced in May that she would run for the state’s post as an “insurance policy against Eric Barlow.” 
The most support a third party candidate for governor in Wyoming has received was in 1894, when Populist Party candidate, Lewis C. Tidwell, won 11.28% of the vote. 
The general election is Nov. 3.
